questions.q: In Goleman's opening story of the Madison Avenue bus, what did the driver do that gradually lifted his sullen passengers' mood?
options: He handed out cold drinks to passengers on the steamy afternoon
He kept up a lively running commentary on the city's sales, exhibits and films
He told jokes about the gridlock and the summer heat in midtown
He asked each passenger in turn about their plans for the day
questions.explain: The driver gave a running monologue on the passing scene, and his delight in what the city offered proved infectious. It was this commentary, not jokes or questions, that let passengers shake off their sullen shells.

questions.q: In the Prologue, why does Goleman say the bus driver's effect on his passengers was hard to explain when he first witnessed it?
options: The psychology of the day knew little or nothing of the mechanics of emotion
He had not yet trained in psychology and lacked the vocabulary
The passengers' changed mood lasted too briefly to be studied
Brain scans of the time showed no change in mood after such encounters
questions.explain: Goleman had just finished his doctorate in psychology, but the field paid scant attention to how such a transformation happens; it knew little of the mechanics of emotion. He was already trained, so lack of training is not the reason.

questions.q: In the Prologue's news item about the Manhattan rap club, what set off the shooting that wounded eight youngsters?
options: A dispute over money owed between two rival groups
An argument about who would be let into the club first
A long-running feud between neighbourhood gangs
An accidental bump in the crowd that was taken as an insult
questions.explain: An inadvertent bump led to a shoving match and then gunfire. Goleman notes that such shootings over seemingly minor slights, perceived as disrespect, had become increasingly common.

questions.q: A supermarket cashier greets every grumpy customer warmly and chats about the day's bargains, and most customers leave smiling. Which example from the Prologue does this most closely mirror?
options: The nine-year-old who vandalized his school to impress classmates
The New York bus driver whose good cheer spread to his passengers
The German youth who said he was infinitely ashamed of his crime
The parents who claimed they were only disciplining their child
questions.explain: Like the bus driver, the cashier transmutes others' irritability through infectious good feeling. Goleman calls the driver an urban peacemaker whose mood rippled out to others; the other examples show emotions out of control.

questions.q: From his perch as a psychologist and New York Times journalist, what two opposing trends does Goleman say he has observed?
options: Rising IQ scores alongside falling school standards
Growing wealth alongside shrinking leisure time
A growing calamity in shared emotional life alongside hopeful remedies
Stronger family ties alongside weaker community ties
questions.explain: Goleman says one trend portrays a growing calamity in our shared emotional life while the other offers some hopeful remedies. The rest of the book draws on the second trend, the science of emotion, to address the first.

questions.q: In the section on why Goleman wrote about emotion when he did, what does he single out as the most dramatic new source of insight?
options: Large surveys of parents and teachers across many countries
Long-term follow-ups of children given IQ tests
Clinical case notes gathered by psychotherapists
Glimpses of the brain at work made possible by brain-imaging technologies
questions.explain: He says the most dramatic findings are glimpses of the brain at work through new brain-imaging methods, which made visible how the brain operates while we think and feel. Clinical opinion is what he says underpinned the earlier self-help books.

questions.q: According to Goleman, what rushed in to fill the void left by scientific psychology's long neglect of the emotions?
options: Self-help books based at best on clinical opinion, with little scientific basis
Philosophical treatises modeled on Aristotle's ethics
Government reports on crime and violence
Neurological textbooks written for medical students
questions.explain: Because feeling was slighted by research, emotions were a largely unexplored continent, and a welter of well-intentioned self-help books filled the gap. Goleman says these rested at best on clinical opinion and lacked much, if any, scientific basis.

questions.q: A company decides to hire only the applicants with the highest IQ scores, sure they will be the most successful. Which point from Goleman's Prologue most directly challenges this plan?
options: IQ scores rise steadily with good schooling, so the scores are unreliable
People of high IQ often flounder while those of modest IQ do well, often because of emotional intelligence
Success at work depends mainly on genetic aptitudes that tests cannot measure
Emotional skills matter only in family life, not on the job
questions.explain: Goleman asks why high-IQ people flounder and modest-IQ people do surprisingly well, and argues the difference often lies in emotional intelligence. He also previews that the workplace puts an unprecedented premium on it, so it is not confined to family life.

questions.q: In arguing that emotional intelligence has a moral dimension, which two moral stances does Goleman say our times especially call for?
options: Honesty and loyalty
Courage and justice
Self-restraint and compassion
Humility and gratitude
questions.explain: Goleman ties impulse control to will and character and empathy to altruism, and concludes that the two stances our times call for are precisely self-restraint and compassion.

questions.q: In previewing Part Three, what does Goleman claim about toxic emotions and physical health?
options: They matter for health only in people already seriously ill
They affect mood but have no measurable effect on the body
They harm health only when combined with smoking or drinking
They put our physical health at as much risk as chain-smoking does
questions.explain: He says toxic emotions put our physical health at as much risk as chain-smoking, while emotional balance can help protect health and well-being.

questions.q: Maya is furious that a colleague took credit for her work. Following Aristotle's challenge as Goleman presents it, what should matter most?
options: Whether her anger fits the right person, degree, time, purpose and way
Whether she can stop herself from feeling angry at all
Whether she can hide her anger until it fades by itself
Whether her anger is stronger or weaker than her colleague's
questions.explain: Goleman stresses that, as Aristotle saw, the problem is not with emotionality but with the appropriateness of emotion and its expression. Suppressing the feeling altogether misses Aristotle's point that well-exercised passions have wisdom.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says the memory of his ride on the Madison Avenue bus has stayed with him for close to twenty years.
questions.explain: He writes that the memory of the encounter has stayed with him for close to twenty years, from the time he had just finished his doctorate in psychology.

questions.q: True or false: According to a report Goleman cites, for murder victims under twelve, 57 percent of the murderers are strangers to the child.
questions.explain: The report says 57 percent of the murderers are the children's parents or stepparents, and in almost half the cases the parents said they were merely trying to discipline the child.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman suggests that readers who are not drawn to neurological detail may want to go straight to Part Two.
questions.explain: Part One covers the brain's emotional architecture, and Goleman notes that readers not drawn to neurological detail may proceed directly to Part Two, on the nature of emotional intelligence.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman argues that because our genetic heritage gives us emotional setpoints, the brain circuitry behind temperament is essentially fixed for life.
questions.explain: He accepts that genes give us emotional setpoints but says the circuitry is extraordinarily malleable: “temperament is not destiny.” Childhood lessons at home and school shape these circuits.

questions.q: Goleman describes the cheerful Madison Avenue bus driver as an urban ____ of sorts, able to soften the irritability of his passengers.
questions.explain: Goleman pictures the driver's good feeling rippling through the city and calls him an urban peacemaker of sorts, wizardlike in his power to transmute sullen irritability.

questions.q: Goleman argues that the ability to control impulse is the base of will and ____.
questions.explain: Those at the mercy of impulse suffer a moral deficiency, because “The ability to control impulse is the base of will and character.”

questions.q: According to Goleman, the root of altruism lies in ____, the ability to read emotions in others.
questions.explain: He writes that without a sense of another's need or despair there is no caring, so altruism is rooted in empathy, the capacity to read others' emotions.

questions.q: Goleman takes his title challenge from Aristotle's The Nicomachean ____, an enquiry into virtue, character and the good life.
questions.explain: In The Nicomachean Ethics Aristotle's challenge is to manage our emotional life with intelligence, which gives the Prologue its title.

questions.q: Goleman compares bringing cognizance to the realm of feeling with the effect of an ____ at the quantum level in physics, which alters what is being observed.
questions.explain: He says understanding emotions can itself help to some degree, because awareness of feeling changes the feeling, much as an observer at the quantum level alters what is observed.

questions.q: In previewing Part Four, Goleman says our brain circuitry is extraordinarily malleable, so temperament is not ____.
questions.explain: Genes set emotional setpoints, but the emotional lessons of childhood shape the circuits; hence “temperament is not destiny.”

questions.q: Which of these abilities does Goleman list in the Prologue as part of emotional intelligence?
options: Self-control
A high IQ score
Zeal and persistence
The ability to motivate oneself
A strong memory for facts
questions.explain: Goleman says emotional intelligence includes self-control, zeal and persistence, and the ability to motivate oneself. IQ and memory belong to the narrow view of intelligence he is challenging.

questions.q: Which of these terms does Goleman say entered the common lexicon over the last decade, as a sign of rising emotional turmoil?
options: Emotional abuse
Emotional intelligence
Drive-by shooting
Post-traumatic stress
Self-help
questions.explain: He names emotional abuse, drive-by shooting and post-traumatic stress as newly common terms, alongside the shift from the cheery Have a nice day to the testy Make my day.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say the massive survey of parents and teachers found about the present generation of children compared with the last?
options: They are more lonely and depressed
They are calmer but less motivated
They are more impulsive and aggressive
They are more nervous and prone to worry
They are less troubled but more isolated
questions.explain: The survey showed a worldwide trend toward children being more troubled emotionally: more lonely and depressed, more angry and unruly, more nervous and prone to worry, more impulsive and aggressive. It found no group that was calmer or less troubled.

questions.q: Which of these competencies does Goleman foresee education one day routinely teaching?
options: Self-awareness
Rote memorization
Empathy
Resolving conflicts
Competitive test-taking
Speed reading
questions.explain: He foresees schools inculcating self-awareness, self-control and empathy, and the arts of listening, resolving conflicts and cooperation. Memorization and test-taking are not on his list.

questions.q: Put these moments of Goleman's Madison Avenue bus ride in the order they happened.
items: The driver greets each passenger, and few greet him back
The driver gives a running commentary on the passing city
Passengers shake off the sullen mood they boarded with
Passengers smile back at the driver's farewell
questions.explain: The startled passengers first ignored the greeting; the driver's infectious commentary then slowly transformed them, so that by the time they got off each gave a smiling response.

questions.q: Goleman traces how emotion becomes action. Put these in the order he describes, from first to last.
items: A feeling
An impulse bursting to express it
An action
questions.explain: Goleman says impulse is the medium of emotion and “the seed of all impulse is a feeling bursting to express itself in action.” So feeling comes first, impulse carries it, and action follows.

questions.q: Put these topics in the order Goleman's road-map in the Prologue says the five Parts of the book take them up.
items: The brain's emotional architecture
The nature of emotional intelligence itself
Its effects on relationships, work and health
How childhood lessons shape emotional circuits
Hazards of emotional deficits and schools that teach the skills
questions.explain: The road-map runs from Part One on the emotional brain, through Part Two on emotional intelligence and Part Three on where it makes a difference, to Part Four on childhood and Part Five on risks and school programs.

questions.q: Put these chapters of Emotional Intelligence in the order they appear in the book.
items: What Are Emotions For?
Anatomy of an Emotional Hijacking
When Smart Is Dumb
Know Thyself
The Roots of Empathy
questions.explain: Chapters 1 and 2 make up Part One on the emotional brain; Part Two then opens with When Smart Is Dumb (3), followed by Know Thyself (4), with The Roots of Empathy coming later as chapter 7.

questions.q: Match each news item Goleman cites in the Prologue to what happened.
pairs: A nine-year-old at a local school
Vandalized desks, computers and a car after being called a baby
Teenagers outside a Manhattan rap club
An accidental bump ended in a shooting that wounded eight
A German youth in a neo-Nazi group
Set a fire that killed five Turkish women and girls
Parents of murder victims under twelve
Often said they were only trying to discipline the child
questions.explain: Goleman uses these items from a single week's paper as a stark contrast to the bus driver, showing mean-spirited impulse running amok.

questions.q: Match each term to the role Goleman gives it in his argument about emotion and character.
pairs: The base of will and character
Often explains why modest-IQ people outdo high-IQ ones
questions.explain: Goleman links impulse control to character and empathy to caring, and argues emotional intelligence often explains why people of modest IQ do surprisingly well.

questions.q: Match each Part of Emotional Intelligence to its title in the book's contents.
questions.explain: The titles follow the Prologue's road-map: the brain first, then what emotional intelligence is, where it matters, the childhood windows when it is shaped, and finally teaching emotional literacy in schools.

questions.q: Goleman sees two opposing trends. Sort each item into the trend it belongs to.

items.t: A jump in depression around the world
Teens with guns in schools
Latchkey kids left with a TV for a babysitter
A burst of scientific studies of emotion
Brain-imaging glimpses of the brain at work
Schools teaching children emotional skills

questions.explain: The first group shows the spreading emotional malaise Goleman reads in the news; the second reflects the new science and the school programs he presents as remedies.

questions.q: Sort each claim into the narrow view of intelligence Goleman challenges or Goleman's own view.

items.t: IQ is a genetic given
Life experience cannot change intelligence
Our destiny is largely fixed by our aptitudes
Emotional skills can be taught to children
Modest IQ can still lead to success
We should ask what we can change

questions.explain: The narrow view treats IQ as fixed and decisive; Goleman counters that emotional intelligence often makes the difference and can be taught, helping children use whatever intellectual potential they have.

questions.q: Sort each topic into the Part of the book where Goleman's road-map says it is covered.

items.t: How emotional skills preserve or corrode relationships
The rising premium on emotional skills at work
Toxic emotions as a risk to physical health
Emotional deficits raising the risk of depression or violence
Links to eating disorders and drug abuse
Pioneering schools teaching social and emotional skills

questions.explain: Part Three examines the differences emotional intelligence makes in relationships, work and health; Part Five covers the hazards of failing to master emotions and the schools that teach these skills.

questions.q: Why does Goleman open the Prologue with the story of the cheerful Madison Avenue bus driver?
questions.a: The driver shows how one person's emotions can spread to others and transform a sullen crowd, a kind of urban peacemaking that psychology of the time could not explain. Goleman then sets this against news stories of emotions out of control, so the story frames the book's question: how do emotions work, and how can they be handled well?

questions.q: Why does Goleman say he had to wait until now to write a book on emotion?
questions.a: Research had long slighted feeling, leaving emotions a largely unexplored continent filled mostly by self-help books with little scientific basis. Only recently, with a burst of studies and brain-imaging technologies, had the scientific harvest become full enough to map the workings of emotion with some precision and suggest remedies.

questions.q: How does Goleman connect emotional intelligence to character and morality?
questions.a: He argues that basic ethical stances stem from emotional capacities. Impulse is the medium of emotion, so people who lack self-control suffer a moral deficiency, while empathy is the root of altruism, since without sensing another's need there is no caring. These yield the two stances our times most need: self-restraint and compassion.

questions.q: A parent says: My son's IQ is only average, so there is nothing anyone can do to help him succeed. How would Goleman respond, based on the Prologue?
questions.a: Goleman would say this reflects the narrow view that IQ is a fixed genetic given that settles our destiny. He argues that people of modest IQ often do surprisingly well because of emotional intelligence, such as self-control, zeal and persistence, and self-motivation, and that these skills can be taught to children, helping them use whatever potential they have.

questions.q: What is Aristotle's challenge, as Goleman presents it, and why does it suit the book?
questions.a: In The Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle's challenge is to manage our emotional life with intelligence. Passions well exercised have wisdom, but they easily go awry; the problem is not emotionality itself but the appropriateness of emotion and its expression. This is exactly the book's question: how to bring intelligence to our emotions.

questions.q: What remedy does Goleman propose in the Prologue for the emotional troubles of today's children?
questions.a: He says the remedy must lie in how we prepare the young for life, since we now leave children's emotional education to chance with disastrous results. He envisions schools educating the whole student, bringing together mind and heart, and routinely teaching competencies such as self-awareness, self-control, empathy, listening, resolving conflicts and cooperation.

questions.q: How does the Prologue prepare the reader for the rest of Emotional Intelligence?
questions.a: It sets out the problem, a growing crisis of emotions out of control, and the hope offered by new science on emotion. It then gives a road-map of the five Parts, from the emotional brain through the nature of emotional intelligence, its effects on relationships, work and health, and childhood windows, to emotional literacy in schools, all framed by Aristotle's challenge to bring intelligence to emotion.

questions.q: In the Chauncey family's train crash in Louisiana, what did Gary and Mary Jane Chauncey do as their car sank?
options: They pushed their daughter Andrea through a window to rescuers
They swam out and brought rescuers back to their daughter
They held their daughter above the water until divers came
They climbed out first and pulled their daughter after them
questions.explain: The parents managed to push Andrea, who used a wheelchair, through a window to rescuers, and then perished as the car sank. Their last act secured her survival, not their own.

questions.q: According to Goleman, how do evolutionary biologists and a parent in crisis view parental self-sacrifice differently?
options: Biologists see it as irrational; the parent sees it as a moral duty
Biologists see it as learned culture; the parent sees it as instinct
Biologists see it as reproductive success; the parent sees only love
Biologists see it as altruism; the parent sees it as self-interest
questions.explain: For evolutionary biologists such sacrifice serves reproductive success in passing on genes; for the parent making the desperate decision it is about nothing other than love.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says that, seen from the intellect, the Chaunceys' self-sacrifice was arguably irrational, while seen from the heart it was the only choice to make.
questions.explain: Goleman contrasts the two views directly: the intellect might call the sacrifice irrational, but the heart saw no other choice.

questions.q: Sociobiologists say our emotions guide us in facing predicaments and tasks too important to leave to ____ alone.
questions.explain: This is the sociobiologists' explanation for why evolution gave emotion such a central role in the human psyche.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman list as predicaments too important to leave to intellect alone?
options: Danger
Painful loss
Calculating household finances
Building a family
Learning a new language
questions.explain: The list includes danger, painful loss, persisting toward a goal despite frustrations, bonding with a mate and building a family. Tasks like doing sums or learning a language are not on it.

questions.q: According to the sociobiologists Goleman cites, each emotion offers a distinctive ____ to act.
questions.explain: Each emotion points us in a direction that has worked well to handle the recurring challenges of human life.

questions.q: According to the sociobiologists Goleman cites, how did our emotional repertoire become built into us?
questions.a: The same predicaments, such as danger, loss and bonding, recurred again and again over our evolutionary history. Because the emotions that handled them had survival value, they became imprinted in our nerves as innate, automatic tendencies of the human heart.

questions.q: Why does Goleman call the very name Homo sapiens, the thinking species, misleading?
options: Because humans think less clearly than other primates
Because feeling counts as much as, and often more than, thought in our decisions
Because most human thought happens without any awareness at all
Because the name ignores the role of language in human life
questions.explain: Goleman argues that in shaping decisions and actions feeling counts every bit as much, and often more, than thought, so a name built only on thinking leaves out half of human nature.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says that in shaping our decisions and actions, feeling counts somewhat less than thought, though it still matters.
questions.explain: He says feeling counts every bit as much as thought, and often more. He also warns that we have gone too far in emphasizing the purely rational, what IQ measures.

questions.q: What does Goleman take the Chauncey parents' sacrifice to reveal about the purpose and power of emotions?
questions.a: It shows that our deepest feelings, passions and longings are essential guides, and that our species owes much of its existence to their power. Their power is extraordinary: only a potent love, the urgency of saving a cherished child, could lead a parent to override the impulse for personal survival.

questions.q: A father runs back into a burning house to carry out his child without stopping to weigh his own chances. How would the opening of Chapter 1 of Emotional Intelligence explain his act?
options: As a learned habit taught by his culture's rules of duty
As a careful calculation that the child's survival mattered more
As a failure of emotion that let reason take over
As emotion taking precedence over intellect at a crucial moment
questions.explain: Goleman uses the Chauncey parents to show the preeminence of heart over head at crucial moments: love urges action that the intellect might judge irrational. It is not a calculation or a cultural rule.

questions.q: Goleman closes the opening of Chapter 1 by warning that intelligence can come to nothing when the ____ hold sway.
questions.explain: This line concludes his argument that we have overvalued the purely rational, what IQ measures, and ignored the power of emotion.

questions.q: Why did Bobby Crabtree enter his daughter Matilda's bedroom carrying a pistol?
options: He had been warned that burglars were active in the neighborhood
He believed Matilda was away and took the noises for an intruder
He heard Matilda scream and feared she was being attacked
He was returning the pistol to a safe kept in her room
questions.explain: The Crabtrees thought Matilda was staying with friends, so when Bobby Crabtree heard noises on coming home he armed himself to search for an intruder.

questions.q: Put the events of the Crabtree tragedy in the order they happened.
items: The parents come home at one in the morning
Bobby Crabtree hears noises and takes his pistol
Matilda jumps out of the closet as a joke
Her father shoots her in the neck
Matilda dies twelve hours later
questions.explain: The parents returned believing Matilda was away, the noises led her father to arm himself, and her practical joke was met by a shot before he could recognize her.

questions.q: True or false: In the Crabtree case, Goleman says fear primed Bobby Crabtree to shoot before he could fully register what he was shooting at, even before he recognized his daughter's voice.
questions.explain: Goleman uses the case to show how an automatic fear reaction can act before recognition catches up.

questions.q: Why does Goleman call the Crabtree shooting a sad irony from the point of view of evolution?
questions.a: The fear that made Crabtree reach for his gun is an evolved legacy that mobilizes us to protect our family from danger. Such automatic reactions mattered for the main task of evolution, bearing progeny who carry on these genetic predispositions. In this case the very reaction meant to protect offspring killed his own child.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say can be read as early attempts to harness, subdue and domesticate emotional life?
options: The Code of Hammurabi
The Magna Carta
The Ten Commandments of the Hebrews
The Edicts of Emperor Ashoka
The Hippocratic Oath
questions.explain: Goleman names the first laws and proclamations of ethics: the Code of Hammurabi, the Ten Commandments and the Edicts of Ashoka. The other two are not mentioned.

questions.q: Which work does Goleman cite for the idea that society must enforce rules from without to subdue the emotional excess that surges within?
options: Darwin's account of facial expressions
Erasmus's satire on reason and passion
Freud's Civilization and Its Discontents
Aristotle's challenge on anger
questions.explain: Goleman refers to Freud's Civilization and Its Discontents for this point. Erasmus appears later in the chapter on the tension between reason and passion, and Darwin on the disgust expression.

questions.q: Goleman says our basic neural circuitry for emotion is what worked best for the last 50,000 human ____, not the last 500.
questions.explain: Evolution shaped our emotions over about a million years, so recent history has left little mark on them.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says the last 10,000 years of rapid civilization have substantially reshaped our biological templates for emotional life.
questions.explain: He says the opposite: despite the rise of civilization and the growth of the human population from five million to five billion, the last 10,000 years have left little imprint on those templates.

questions.q: Goleman says we too often confront postmodern dilemmas with an emotional repertoire tailored to the urgencies of the ____.
questions.explain: Our emotions were shaped in the distant ancestral past, so they can be poorly suited to modern situations. Goleman calls this predicament the heart of his subject.

questions.q: Why, according to Goleman, do passions overwhelm reason time and again despite the rules societies impose?
questions.a: It arises from the basic architecture of mental life. Our emotional circuitry was shaped by slow evolution over about a million years and fits what worked for the last 50,000 generations, while civilization has arisen so rapidly that evolution cannot keep up. So our reactions are shaped not only by rational judgment and personal history but also by our distant ancestral past.

questions.q: Put the stages of Goleman's experience in the Colorado snow flurry in order.
items: A snow flurry blots out the car ahead
Anxiety floods his body as he brakes
Anxiety builds to fear and he pulls over
He waits half an hour until the snow stops
He finds an ambulance crew at a collision blocking the road
questions.explain: Fear built until it made him stop, and only after the flurry passed did he find the rear-end collision he would probably have hit.

questions.q: To what does Goleman compare the state that overtook him when he stopped in the Colorado snow flurry?
options: A rabbit frozen in terror at the hint of a passing fox
A snake hissing to signal the threat of an attack
A driver calmly reasoning through a set of options
A soldier steeling himself to charge into danger
questions.explain: He likens himself to a rabbit frozen at a passing fox, or a protomammal hiding from a dinosaur: an internal state that compelled him to stop and pay attention. The hissing snake appears later as the image of the brainstem.

questions.q: Goleman notes that the root of the word emotion is motere, the Latin verb meaning to ____.
questions.explain: With the prefix e-, meaning move away, the word itself suggests that a tendency to act is implicit in every emotion.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says the link between emotion and action is least obvious when we watch animals or young children.
questions.explain: He says it is most obvious in animals and children; it is in civilized adults that emotions are so often divorced from obvious reaction.

questions.q: What does Goleman call the great anomaly in the animal kingdom, and why?
questions.a: He means civilized adults, in whom emotions, which are root impulses to act, are so often divorced from obvious reaction. Everywhere else, in animals and in children, emotions plainly lead to action, because all emotions are in essence impulses to act.

questions.q: Match each emotion to the bodily change Goleman describes for it.
pairs: Blood flows to the hands, ready to grasp a weapon or strike
Eyebrows lift, widening the visual sweep
questions.explain: Each emotion has a distinctive biological signature that prepares the body for a different kind of response, as the chapter's list of emotions sets out.

questions.q: Match each emotion to the purpose Goleman gives for it.
pairs: Signals that something is offensive in taste or smell
Gives the body rest and readiness for whatever task is at hand
A hormone rush gives energy for vigorous action
questions.explain: Disgust rejects the offensive, happiness quiets the body and brings enthusiasm for goals, and anger's adrenaline supplies a pulse of energy.

questions.q: Match each part of the fear response Goleman describes to what it helps the body do.
pairs: Blood goes to the large leg muscles
Blood is shunted away from the face
Makes the face blanch and feel cold
The body freezes for a moment
Gives time to judge whether hiding is better
Helps evaluate what response to make
questions.explain: Goleman describes fear as readying the body for flight, pausing it briefly, putting it on general alert and focusing attention on the danger.

questions.q: Goleman says the parasympathetic pattern that comes with love, tender feelings and sexual satisfaction has been dubbed the ____ response.
questions.explain: It is the physiological opposite of the fight-or-flight mobilization shared by fear and anger, bringing calm and contentment that facilitate cooperation.

questions.q: Sort these into the two bodily patterns Goleman contrasts.

items.t: Anger
Fear
Love
Sexual satisfaction
A pulse of adrenaline for vigorous action
A general state of calm and contentment

questions.explain: Fear and anger share the fight-or-flight mobilization; love, tender feelings and sexual satisfaction bring the opposite, parasympathetic relaxation response.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman describe as part of the biology of happiness?
options: More activity in a brain center that inhibits negative feelings
A quieting of brain centers that generate worrisome thought
Blood flowing to the hands
Quicker recovery from the arousal of upsetting emotions
A slowing of the body's metabolism
questions.explain: Happiness brings no particular physiological shift beyond a quiescence that lets the body recover faster. Blood to the hands belongs to anger, and slowed metabolism to deepening sadness.

questions.q: Goleman notes that the facial expression of disgust looks the same around the world. Whose observation does he cite about its origin?
options: Freud's
Erasmus's
Aristotle's
Darwin's
questions.explain: Goleman cites Darwin's observation that the curled lip and wrinkled nose suggest a primordial attempt to close the nostrils against a noxious odor or spit out a poisonous food.

questions.q: What is the main function of sadness according to Goleman, and how might its drop in energy have helped early humans?
questions.a: Sadness helps us adjust to a significant loss, such as a death or major disappointment. Its drop in energy and withdrawal create the chance to mourn, grasp the loss's consequences for one's life and, as energy returns, plan new beginnings. The loss of energy may also have kept saddened, vulnerable early humans close to home, where they were safer.

questions.q: Put the course of sadness, as Goleman describes it, in order.
items: A significant loss, such as a death
Energy and enthusiasm for pleasures drop
Introspective withdrawal allows mourning
The loss's consequences for one's life are grasped
As energy returns, new beginnings are planned
questions.explain: Goleman presents sadness as a process that turns inward after a loss so that one can mourn, understand what the loss means and then plan anew.

questions.q: Sort these into what Goleman treats as universal biology and what he says is shaped by culture.

items.t: Losing a loved one brings sadness and grief
The look of the disgust expression
How grieving is displayed or kept private
Which people count as loved ones to be mourned
Fear sending blood to the leg muscles

questions.explain: The propensities to act are biological and universal, but life experience and culture shape how emotions are shown and to whom they apply.

questions.q: A quick-tempered teenager with easy access to a gun turns a minor quarrel into a fatal shooting. Which idea from Chapter 1 of Emotional Intelligence best explains this?
options: Sadness slows the body so a person withdraws from danger
A reaction once useful for survival has lost its fit with modern life
The rational mind grows stronger as feelings become more intense
Culture alone decides which emotions a person will feel
questions.explain: Goleman argues that as ancient survival pressures waned, so did the goodness of fit of parts of our emotional repertoire: a hair-trigger anger that once gave a survival edge becomes disastrous with automatic weapons.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say marked the long period of evolution when our emotional responses were hammered into shape?
options: Few infants survived to childhood
Few adults lived to thirty
Agriculture made food supplies reliable
Predators could strike at any moment
Population grew quickly with little check
questions.explain: It was a harsher reality than recorded history, with high death rates, predators and the risks of drought and flood. Agriculture, and the easing of pressures on population, came only in the last ten thousand years.

questions.q: Put these steps in Goleman's account of why parts of our emotional repertoire no longer fit, in order.
items: Harsh prehistoric pressures shape our emotional responses
Agriculture and rudimentary societies arise
Pressures holding population in check ease
Parts of our emotional repertoire lose their fit
questions.explain: The pressures that made our emotions valuable eased with agriculture in the last ten thousand years, and as they waned, so did the goodness of fit of some emotional reactions.

questions.q: In Goleman's story of the divorced friend, what does he say about noticing her eyes well up as she claims she no longer cares about her ex-husband?
options: It is a guess too unreliable to count as real understanding
It shows that the rational mind sees through spoken words
It is an act of comprehending, as real as reading a printed page
It proves she was lying deliberately to hide her feelings
questions.explain: Goleman says the empathic grasp that her watering eyes mean sadness despite her words is an act of comprehending just as surely as distilling meaning from words on a page; it belongs to the emotional mind, not the rational one.

questions.q: What does the story of Goleman's divorced friend illustrate about the human mind?
questions.a: Although she said she no longer cared, her eyes welled with tears, and reading that sadness despite her words is an act of the emotional mind, just as understanding printed words is an act of the rational mind. It shows that we have two minds, one that thinks and one that feels, two fundamentally different ways of knowing that together construct our mental life.

questions.q: Sort these traits into the two minds Goleman describes.

items.t: More prominent in awareness
Able to ponder and reflect
Impulsive and powerful
Sometimes illogical
Matches the folk idea of the head
Matches the folk idea of the heart
Dominates as feeling grows more intense

questions.explain: The rational mind is the thoughtful mode we are usually conscious of; the emotional mind is impulsive, powerful and sometimes illogical, and takes over as feelings intensify.

questions.q: Sort these everyday moments by which of Goleman's two minds is chiefly at work.

items.t: Sensing that a friend is hurt from her face, though she says she is fine
Swerving at once when a child runs into the road
Weighing the pros and cons of a job offer over a week
Working step by step through a tax form

questions.explain: The emotional mind reads feelings beneath words and drives instant responses when life is in danger; the rational mind is the deliberate mode that ponders and reflects.

questions.q: Goleman says that in a very real sense we have two minds, one that thinks and one that ____.
questions.explain: The rational and emotional minds are two fundamentally different ways of knowing that interact to construct our mental life.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says that the more intense a feeling becomes, the more dominant the rational mind becomes.
questions.explain: He describes a steady gradient running the other way: the more intense the feeling, the more dominant the emotional mind and the more ineffectual the rational.

questions.q: Why, according to Goleman, does the emotional mind become more dominant as feelings intensify?
options: Because strong feelings use up the energy the rational mind needs
Because culture teaches us to trust feelings in a crisis
Because the rational mind develops later in childhood
Because instant emotional responses helped when pausing could be fatal
questions.explain: Goleman traces the arrangement to eons of evolutionary advantage in letting emotions and intuitions guide instant responses when life is in peril, where stopping to think could cost us our lives.

questions.q: How do the emotional and rational minds ordinarily work together, according to Goleman?
questions.a: For the most part they operate in tight harmony, intertwining their different ways of knowing. Emotion feeds into and informs the operations of the rational mind, while the rational mind refines and sometimes vetoes the inputs of the emotions. The balance tips only when passions surge and the emotional mind swamps the rational one.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say about the relationship between the emotional and rational minds?
options: They are semi-independent faculties
One of them controls the other at all times
They reflect distinct but interconnected brain circuitry
Feelings play no part in good thinking
They are housed in a single brain structure
questions.explain: Goleman calls them semi-independent faculties reflecting distinct but interconnected circuitry. He insists that feelings are essential to thought, and the balance between the minds shifts rather than one always ruling.

questions.q: In the passage Goleman quotes from Erasmus of Rotterdam, what ratio of passion to reason does Jupiter bestow?
options: Two to one
Ten to one
Twenty-four to one
A hundred to one
questions.explain: Erasmus satirically says Jupiter gave far more passion than reason, calculating the ratio as 24 to one.

questions.q: Which of these does Erasmus name as the two raging tyrants set up against Reason?
options: Fear
Anger
Envy
Lust
Pride
questions.explain: In the satire Goleman quotes, Jupiter sets anger and lust in opposition to Reason's solitary power.

questions.q: What happens to Reason in the Erasmus satire Goleman quotes, and what does the passage illustrate?
questions.a: Reason shouts herself hoarse repeating formulas of virtue, while anger and lust mock her and grow ever noisier, until their ruler is exhausted and surrenders. Goleman uses it to illustrate the perennial tension between reason and emotion, in which surging passion swamps the rational mind.

questions.q: When mildly annoyed, Priya can still think through whether to let another driver merge, but when she is furious she cannot think straight at all. Which idea from Goleman best fits this?
options: A steady gradient: stronger feeling means more emotional control
Culture decides which emotions may be shown in public
Sadness slows the body to allow reflection
The neocortex adds thoughts to every feeling equally
questions.explain: Goleman describes a steady gradient in the ratio of rational-to-emotional control: the more intense the feeling, the more dominant the emotional mind and the more ineffectual the rational.

questions.q: Sam says he knows in his heart that a decision is right, and feels surer of it than of anything he has reasoned out. How does Goleman describe this kind of knowing?
options: As a mistake that the rational mind should always veto
As a different order of conviction, a deeper kind of certainty
As a sign that the rational mind is fully in control
As a learned habit with no link to emotion
questions.explain: Goleman says knowing something is right in your heart is a different order of conviction, somehow a deeper kind of certainty, than thinking so with the rational mind.

questions.q: Goleman says that over millions of years the brain has grown from the ____ up, with higher centers developing as elaborations of lower, older parts.
questions.explain: He adds that the growth of the brain in the human embryo roughly retraces this evolutionary course.

questions.q: Put these brain structures in the order Goleman says they appeared in evolution.
items: Brainstem
Olfactory lobe
Limbic system
Neocortex
questions.explain: The emotional centers grew from the brainstem, starting from the smell-analyzing olfactory lobe; the limbic system came with the first mammals; the neocortex was added later, growing from the emotional areas.

questions.q: What does Goleman say the brainstem, the most primitive part of the brain, does?
options: It sorts smells into edible or toxic and friend or foe
It plans ahead and comprehends what the senses perceive
It generates feelings of pleasure and sexual desire
It regulates breathing and metabolism without thinking or learning
questions.explain: The brainstem is a set of preprogrammed regulators for basic life functions and stereotyped reactions; it cannot be said to think or learn. Sorting smells belongs to the olfactory lobe and planning to the neocortex.

questions.q: What does Goleman say the fact that the thinking brain grew from the emotional brain reveals?
questions.a: It reveals much about the relationship of thought to feeling: the emotional centers came first, and the neocortex evolved out of them millions of years later. In his words, “there was an emotional brain long before there was a rational one.”

questions.q: What does Goleman identify as the most ancient root of our emotional life?
options: The brainstem's control of breathing
The olfactory lobe, which analyzes smell
The two-layered cortex of early mammals
The bond between mother and child
questions.explain: The emotional centers began to evolve from the olfactory lobe, because every living thing has a distinctive molecular signature carried on the wind, making smell a paramount sense for survival.

questions.q: Put the steps by which Goleman says the rudimentary olfactory center worked in order.
items: A smell is taken in
One layer of cells sorts it, such as edible or toxic
A second layer sends reflexive messages through the nervous system
The body bites, spits, approaches, flees or chases
questions.explain: The early olfactory center had little more than two thin layers of neurons: one that took in and sorted smells into categories, and one that told the body what to do.

questions.q: The limbic system is named from limbus, the Latin word for ____, because it borders the brainstem.
questions.explain: The new layers that came with the first mammals ring and border the brainstem, looking roughly like a bagel with a bite taken out at the bottom.

questions.q: Which two powerful tools does Goleman say the limbic system refined as it evolved?
options: Learning
Language
Memory
Long-term planning
Abstract reasoning
questions.explain: Learning and memory let an animal fine-tune its responses instead of reacting in fixed ways, so a food that caused sickness could be avoided next time. Planning and abstract thought are talents of the later neocortex.

questions.q: Goleman says the rhinencephalon, part of the limbic wiring and the rudimentary basis of the neocortex, literally means the ____ brain.
questions.explain: It compared present smells with past ones to discriminate good from bad, showing how closely smell and the early emotional brain were linked.

questions.q: Match each brain structure to Goleman's description of it.
pairs: Preprogrammed regulators that keep the body running
The cells that take in and analyze smell
Added emotions proper to the brain's repertoire
The seat of thought and the source of art and culture
questions.explain: The brain grew from the bottom up: the regulating brainstem, the smell-based roots of emotion, the limbic system of the first mammals, and finally the thinking neocortex.

questions.q: Match each term to the meaning Goleman gives for it.
pairs: The brainstem around the top of the spinal cord
questions.explain: Goleman explains each name as he traces the brain's growth: the limbic ring, the nose brain of the limbic wiring, the thinking neocortex and the primitive brainstem.

questions.q: Match each period to what Goleman says happened then.
pairs: The arrival of the first mammals
New layers of the emotional brain formed
Mammal brains took a great growth spurt
Agriculture eased the pressures on survival
questions.explain: The brain's emotional layers came with the first mammals and the neocortex with the later growth spurt, while the recent spread of agriculture has left little imprint on our emotional circuits.

questions.q: What happened, according to Goleman, when the mammal brain took a great growth spurt about 100 million years ago?
options: The olfactory lobe first grew around the brainstem
The brainstem took over the control of breathing
Several new layers were piled on the thin cortex to form the neocortex
The limbic system replaced the older smell-based centers
questions.explain: Several new layers of cells were added on top of the thin two-layered cortex, forming the neocortex, which gave an extraordinary intellectual edge.

questions.q: What does the neocortex add to emotional life, according to Goleman?
questions.a: It adds to a feeling what we think about it, and lets us have feelings about ideas, art, symbols and imaginings, and even feelings about our feelings. Its many connections to the limbic system allow nuance and a far greater range of reactions to our emotions, such as the long-term bond between parent and child.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says species with no neocortex, such as reptiles, lack maternal affection, so their newly hatched young must hide to avoid being cannibalized.
questions.explain: He uses reptiles to show that the mother-child bond depends on the neocortex and its connections to the limbic system.

questions.q: Which part of love does Goleman credit to the neocortex and its connections to the limbic system?
options: The feelings of pleasure that feed sexual passion
The surge of sexual desire
The relaxation response of tender feelings
The mother-child bond and long-term commitment to childrearing
questions.explain: Limbic structures generate pleasure and sexual desire, but the neocortex and its limbic links allow the mother-child bond, the basis of the family unit, and the long childhood during which the brain keeps developing.

questions.q: Goleman says that as we go up the phylogenetic scale from reptile to rhesus to human, the neocortex grows and brings a ____ rise in the interconnections of brain circuitry.
questions.explain: The larger the number of connections, the greater the range of possible responses, which is why humans have a more nuanced emotional repertoire.

questions.q: Faced with a frightening situation, a rabbit can only freeze or bolt, while a person might instead phone for help. What does Goleman credit for this difference?
options: The larger human neocortex and its links to the limbic system
The stronger human brainstem
The human sense of smell
The size of the human limbic system alone
questions.explain: Goleman says a rabbit or rhesus has a restricted set of fear responses, while the larger human neocortex allows a far more nimble repertoire, including calling 999.

questions.q: Sort these functions between the two brain regions Goleman contrasts.

items.t: Regulating breathing
Regulating the metabolism of organs
Stereotyped reactions and movements
Strategizing and long-term planning
Feelings about ideas, art and symbols
Comprehending what the senses perceive

questions.explain: The brainstem is the primitive root that keeps the body running; the neocortex is the seat of thought, planning and the fruits of culture.

questions.q: Sort these aspects of emotional life by the brain region Goleman credits.

items.t: Feelings of pleasure and sexual desire
Being in the grip of craving or fury
Taking over in emotional emergencies
The mother-child bond behind the family unit
Having feelings about our feelings
A nimble range of responses to fear

questions.explain: The limbic system generates raw emotion and holds sway in emergencies; the neocortex adds nuance, reflection and the long-term bonds of family life.

questions.q: Why, according to Goleman, do the emotional centers have such power over the rest of the brain, including its centers for thought?
questions.a: Many of the brain's higher centers sprouted from or extended the limbic area, so the emotional brain is the root from which the newer brain grew. The emotional areas are intertwined via myriad connecting circuits with all parts of the neocortex. That is why in crucial matters of the heart, and especially in emotional emergencies, the higher centers can be said to defer to the limbic system.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman attribute to the neocortex?
options: Talent for strategizing and long-term planning
Regulating breathing
The triumphs of art, civilization and culture
Generating feelings of sexual desire
Feelings about ideas, symbols and imaginings
questions.explain: The neocortex is the seat of thought and the source of planning and culture. Breathing is regulated by the brainstem, and sexual desire is generated by limbic structures.

questions.q: In which Part of Emotional Intelligence does Chapter 1, What Are Emotions For?, appear?
options: Part Two, The Nature of Emotional Intelligence
Part One, The Emotional Brain
Part Three, Emotional Intelligence Applied
Part Four, Windows of Opportunity
questions.explain: Chapter 1 opens Part One, The Emotional Brain, together with Chapter 2. Part Two is where the book turns to emotional intelligence itself as a set of skills.

questions.q: Why does Goleman place a chapter on the evolutionary purpose of emotions and the growth of the brain at the very start of the book, before discussing emotional intelligence itself?
questions.a: In the Prologue's road-map, Part One begins with discoveries about the brain's emotional architecture that explain the moments when feeling overwhelms rationality. Chapter 1 lays that groundwork by showing that emotions are evolved impulses to act and that the thinking brain grew out of the emotional brain. Only with this neurological basis in place does Part Two show how these givens play out in the skills of emotional intelligence.

questions.q: Put the examples of Chapter 1, What Are Emotions For?, in the order the chapter presents them.
items: The Chauncey parents save their daughter from a sinking train
Bobby Crabtree shoots his daughter, mistaking her for an intruder
The author pulls over in a blinding Colorado snow flurry
A divorced friend's eyes well up as she says she no longer cares
Erasmus's satire of Reason shouting herself hoarse
questions.explain: The chapter moves from emotion as a noble evolved guide (the Chauncey sacrifice), to emotion misfiring in modern life (Crabtree), to emotions as impulses to act (the snowstorm), to the two minds (the friend's tears and Erasmus) before turning to how the brain grew.

questions.q: Chapter 1 ends by stressing that the emotional centers, as the root of the newer brain, have immense power over the thinking centers. What does this set up for Chapter 2, Anatomy of an Emotional Hijacking?
options: A survey of how schools can teach emotional skills to children
An argument that IQ matters more than emotional intelligence for success
A closer look at how the emotional brain can take over the thinking brain
A history of the ethical codes societies used to tame emotion
questions.explain: Having shown that the emotional brain is intertwined with and can override the neocortex, the book next examines a neural takeover by the emotional brain, which its title calls a hijacking. Schooling the emotions comes at the very end of the book, in Part Five.

questions.q: True or false: In the Prologue's road-map, Part One is where Goleman explains emotional intelligence skills such as reining in impulse, reading others' feelings and handling relationships.
questions.explain: Part One, which contains Chapter 1, deals with the brain's emotional architecture. The skills of reining in impulse, reading feelings and handling relationships are the subject of Part Two.

questions.q: Chapter 1, What Are Emotions For?, belongs to Part One of the book, titled The Emotional ____.
questions.explain: Part One is The Emotional Brain, covering Chapters 1 and 2, which explain how the brain's emotional architecture works before Part Two turns to emotional intelligence.

questions.q: What does the title question of Chapter 1, What Are Emotions For?, signal, and what answer does the chapter give?
questions.a: The title signals that the chapter asks about the purpose of emotions from an evolutionary point of view. Its answer is that each emotion is an impulse to act, an instant plan for handling recurring life challenges that evolution built into us. But it also shows that this ancient repertoire can misfire in modern life, because civilization has changed far faster than evolution can.

questions.q: In Chapter 1, What Are Emotions For?, match each example to the point Goleman uses it to make.
pairs: The Chauncey parents' rescue of Andrea
A potent love can override the impulse for personal survival
Fear can trigger action before we recognize what we face
Fear's enforced caution can save a life
The emotional mind reads feelings that words deny
Reason is overwhelmed by anger and lust
questions.explain: Each story carries one step of the argument: emotion as an evolved guide, its misfiring in modern settings, emotions as impulses to act, and the two minds with passion able to swamp reason.

questions.q: In the Career Girl Murders, what made the burglar Richard Robles panic and lose control?
options: Janice Wylie warned him she would remember his face and help the police track him down
Emily Hoffert came home unexpectedly and began screaming for help from the neighbours
A neighbour heard the struggle in the apartment and telephoned the police at once
He realised the apartment held nothing valuable enough to pay for his heroin habit
questions.explain: Robles panicked when Wylie said she would remember his face and help police find him; Hoffert's arrival only led him to begin tying her up too. He later said, “My head just exploded.”

questions.q: In Chapter 2 of Emotional Intelligence, where does Goleman say a neural hijacking originates?
options: In the prefrontal lobes, just behind the forehead
In the amygdala, a center in the limbic brain
In the hippocampus, the long-assumed key limbic structure
In the neocortex, the thinking brain
questions.explain: Goleman calls the hijacking a neural takeover that originates in the amygdala. The prefrontal lobes are later shown to be the brake on such surges, not their source.

questions.q: Maria snaps furiously at her child over a spilled drink, and an hour later feels the outburst was far out of proportion and cannot understand what came over her. In Goleman's terms, what was this?
options: A considered neocortical response, in which she mulled over the spill and then chose to get angry
A case of affective blindness, in which she could not gauge the emotional significance of the spill
A neural hijacking, in which the amygdala took over before her thinking brain could weigh the reaction
A lapse of working memory, in which she forgot the rule she had set for her child earlier that day
questions.explain: Goleman says blowing up at a spouse or child to a degree that later seems uncalled for is in all probability a hijacking, and its hallmark is not knowing afterwards what came over you.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says neural hijackings are rare, horrific incidents largely confined to brutal crimes like the Career Girl Murders.
questions.explain: He says the opposite: in less catastrophic but not necessarily less intense form, hijackings happen to us with fair frequency, as when we lose it with a spouse, child or another driver.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman counts laughter so explosive that a joke seems uproarious as a limbic response, like a hijacking.
questions.explain: Not all limbic hijackings are distressing: explosive laughter and moments of intense joy are limbic responses too.

questions.q: Goleman calls sudden emotional explosions, in which a limbic center proclaims an emergency and recruits the rest of the brain, neural ____.
questions.explain: He writes that “Such emotional explosions are neural hijackings”, taken over by a limbic center before the neocortex can weigh what is happening.

questions.q: Richard Robles's 1963 crime, for which he was still in prison some three decades later, became known as the ____ Murders.
questions.explain: The killings of Janice Wylie and Emily Hoffert became known as the Career Girl Murders, Goleman's opening example of a hijacking.

questions.q: Which of these mark a neural hijacking as Goleman describes it?
options: It occurs in an instant
It triggers action before the neocortex can glimpse fully what is happening
Afterwards the person has the sense of not knowing what came over them
The thinking brain first approves the reaction as a good idea
It always ends in violence of the kind seen in the Career Girl Murders
questions.explain: A hijack happens in an instant, crucial moments before the neocortex grasps the situation, and leaves people unsure what came over them. The thinking brain has no chance to approve it, and Goleman stresses most hijacks are not violent.

questions.q: Put the events of the Career Girl Murders in the order Goleman tells them.
items: Robles ties up Janice Wylie, who was unexpectedly home
Emily Hoffert comes home as Robles is leaving
Wylie warns Robles she will remember his face
Robles panics and attacks both women
Years later Robles says his head just exploded
questions.explain: Robles found Wylie home and tied her up; Hoffert arrived as he left; Wylie's warning triggered his panic and frenzy; some twenty-five years later he looked back on the moment.

questions.q: Match each person in the opening of Chapter 2 to their description.
pairs: A seasoned burglar just paroled after a three-year sentence
A twenty-one-year-old researcher at Newsweek magazine
A speed skater who won Olympic Gold in the 1,000-meter race
questions.explain: Robles killed Wylie and Hoffert in the Career Girl Murders; Jansen's victory overwhelmed his wife, Goleman's example of a joyful limbic hijacking.

questions.q: Sort these limbic hijackings from the opening of Chapter 2 by their emotional tone.

items.t: Robles clubbing and stabbing the two women
Blowing up at another driver beyond what was called for
Losing it with your spouse or child
Laughter so explosive at a joke it seems uproarious
Dan Jansen's wife overcome when he won Olympic Gold

questions.explain: Goleman stresses that not all limbic hijackings are distressing: explosive laughter and the intense happiness of Jansen's wife are limbic responses too.

questions.q: Why does Goleman open Chapter 2 with the Career Girl Murders, and what does he say that case has in common with everyday life?
questions.a: The murders are a vivid example of a neural hijacking: an emergency proclaimed by the amygdala drove Robles to act in an instant, before his thinking brain could judge it, leaving him later unable to explain what came over him. Goleman stresses such hijacks are not isolated horrors; in less catastrophic but not necessarily less intense form they happen often, as when we blow up at a spouse, child or another driver.

questions.q: According to Goleman, what happens in the brain during a neural hijacking?
questions.a: A center in the limbic brain, the amygdala, proclaims an emergency and recruits the rest of the brain to its urgent agenda. This happens in an instant, crucial moments before the neocortex has had a chance to glimpse fully what is happening, let alone decide whether the reaction is a good idea. Afterwards the person typically has the sense of not knowing what came over them.

questions.q: In Goleman's account, what does the name amygdala come from?
options: The Latin word for ring
The Greek word for seat
The Latin word for alarm
The Greek word for almond
questions.explain: The amygdala is named from the Greek for almond because of its almond-shaped cluster of structures; the Latin word for ring gave the limbic system its name.

questions.q: According to Goleman, which two structures were the key parts of the primitive nose brain that gave rise to the cortex and neocortex?
options: The hippocampus and the amygdala
The thalamus and the amygdala
The prefrontal lobes and the hippocampus
The brainstem and the cingulate gyrus
questions.explain: Goleman names the hippocampus and the amygdala as the two key parts of the primitive nose brain, and says these limbic structures still do much or most of the brain's learning and remembering.

questions.q: What did Joseph LeDoux's findings on the emotional brain's circuitry do to the long-standing notion about the limbic system?
options: They confirmed the hippocampus as the key structure of emotional reactions, as long assumed
They put the amygdala at the center of the action and gave other limbic structures very different roles
They showed the limbic system plays almost no part in emotion compared with the neocortex
They proved that all emotional reactions must first pass through the thinking brain
questions.explain: LeDoux's work overthrew the old notion by putting the amygdala at the center; the hippocampus, long thought the key limbic structure, turned out to deal more with perceptual patterns and context.

questions.q: If the amygdala is severed from the rest of the brain, the result is a striking inability to gauge the emotional significance of events, a condition sometimes called affective ____.
questions.explain: Goleman says this condition is sometimes called affective blindness: without the amygdala, encounters lose their emotional weight.

questions.q: Goleman says the limbic structures do much of the brain's learning and remembering, and the amygdala is the specialist for ____ matters.
questions.explain: Among the limbic structures that do much of the brain's learning and remembering, the amygdala specialises in emotional matters.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman notes that the human amygdala is relatively small compared with that of our closest evolutionary cousins, the primates.
questions.explain: He says the human amygdala is relatively large compared with that in any of our closest evolutionary cousins.

questions.q: True or false: According to Goleman, tears are triggered by the amygdala together with a nearby structure, the cingulate gyrus.
questions.explain: Tears, an emotional signal unique to humans, are triggered by the amygdala and the nearby cingulate gyrus, and comforting soothes these same regions.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says being held, stroked or otherwise comforted soothes the same brain regions that trigger tears, stopping the sobs.
questions.explain: Comfort soothes the amygdala and cingulate gyrus, the regions that trigger tears; without an amygdala there are no tears of sorrow to soothe.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman report in animals whose amygdala has been removed or severed?
options: They lose the urge to compete or cooperate
They no longer have any sense of their place in their kind's social order
They become more aggressive toward rivals
They show a heightened fear of predators
They lack fear and rage
questions.explain: Without the amygdala, emotion in these animals is blunted or absent: no fear or rage, no urge to compete or cooperate, no sense of social place. Heightened aggression or fear is the opposite of what he reports.

questions.q: Which of these were true of the young man whose amygdala was surgically removed to control severe seizures?
options: He no longer recognised close friends, relatives or even his mother
He became prone to sudden fits of rage
He was deeply distressed by his family's anguish
He was still perfectly capable of conversation
He became completely uninterested in people
questions.explain: He could still talk, but without an amygdala he lost recognition of feeling: he preferred isolation, did not recognise his mother and stayed impassive in the face of his family's anguish.

questions.q: Sort these pieces of evidence by the brain region whose loss they show to empty out emotional life.

items.t: A young man stops recognising his mother and is indifferent to her anguish
Animals lack fear and rage and lose any sense of social place
There are no tears of sorrow to soothe
Patients of the 1940s lobotomy lose most of their emotional lives
Lacking any understanding that something merits a feeling, none comes

questions.explain: The young man, the animals and the missing tears show what goes without the amygdala; lobotomy patients and the point that no emotion comes without understanding show the prefrontal lobes are needed too.

questions.q: Match each brain structure to what Chapter 2 says about it.
pairs: Almond-shaped cluster perched above the brainstem
Nearby structure that helps the amygdala trigger tears
First stop in the brain for signals from eye or ear
Provides a keen memory of context
questions.explain: Each pairing follows the chapter: the amygdala's location, its partner in tears, the thalamus as sensory relay, the hippocampus's memory for context and the prefrontal cortex's working memory.

questions.q: Why does Goleman say that life without the amygdala is a life stripped of personal meanings?
questions.a: The amygdala acts as a storehouse of emotional memory, and so of significance itself. Without it, encounters lose their emotional weight and their hold on us, as with the young man whose amygdala was removed: he no longer recognised close friends or even his mother and was indifferent to their anguish. Since all passion depends on the amygdala, losing it strips experience of what it means to us.

questions.q: Why does Goleman say the workings of the amygdala and its interplay with the neocortex are at the heart of emotional intelligence?
questions.a: LeDoux's research explains how the amygdala can take control over what we do even while the neocortex is still coming to a decision. How emotion overwhelms thought, and how thought in turn manages emotion, depends on the interplay between these two systems. Emotional intelligence is about handling exactly that relationship between the emotional and the thinking brain.

questions.q: Put the events of the Boston brunch story in Chapter 2 in order.
items: Her boyfriend gives her a hard-to-find art print from Spain
She suggests they see a matinee after brunch
He says he cannot spend the day because of softball practice
She leaves the cafe in tears and throws the print in a garbage can
Months later she regrets losing the print, not walking out
questions.explain: The gift came first; her delight dissolved when the matinee suggestion met the softball news; on impulse she threw away the print, which is what she later regrets.

questions.q: In the Boston brunch story, what does the young woman say she regrets months later?
options: Walking out on her boyfriend, not losing the art print
Driving two hours to Boston for the day
Losing the art print, not walking out on her boyfriend
Suggesting the matinee in the first place
questions.explain: Goleman notes that it is not walking out she regrets, but the loss of the print she threw away on impulse.

questions.q: According to Goleman, what single kind of question does the amygdala, acting as a psychological sentinel, put to every situation?
options: The most practical kind: will this help me reach my long-term goals?
The most social kind: is this behaviour appropriate for the people around me?
The most analytic kind: what exactly is this object and where have I seen it?
The most primitive kind: is this something I hate, that hurts me, something I fear?
questions.explain: Goleman says the amygdala challenges every perception with one primitive kind of question about hate, hurt and fear; identifying exactly what something is belongs to the slower neocortex.

questions.q: Sam is reading when a loud bang outside makes his heart race, locks his attention on the window and brings to mind a burglary he once heard about. How would Goleman explain this?
options: The amygdala sounded an alarm that sped his heart, riveted his attention and pulled up memories relevant to the emergency
His prefrontal lobes ran a risk/benefit ratio of reactions and chose to recall the burglary
His hippocampus judged the bang dangerous and then switched off his other thoughts
His working memory improved under stress, sharpening his recall of past events
questions.explain: In a fear alarm the amygdala speeds heart rate, rivets attention on the source and has cortical memory systems retrieve knowledge relevant to the emergency, ahead of other thoughts.

questions.q: When a moment draws a yes to its primitive question, Goleman says the amygdala reacts instantaneously, like a neural ____, telegraphing a crisis message to all parts of the brain.
questions.explain: The section's title image: the amygdala reacts like a neural tripwire, sending a message of crisis to all parts of the brain.

questions.q: Which of these does the amygdala do when it sounds an alarm of fear, according to Goleman?
options: Slows heart rate and lowers blood pressure to calm the body
Suppresses memory retrieval so that only present perception counts
Triggers the secretion of the body's fight-or-flight hormones
Signals the release of norepinephrine to heighten the reactivity of key brain areas
Tells the brainstem to fix the face in a fearful expression and speed heart rate
questions.explain: The alarm mobilises hormones, norepinephrine and the brainstem; it speeds the heart and raises blood pressure, and it shuffles memory systems to retrieve relevant knowledge rather than suppressing them.

questions.q: True or false: In Goleman's account of a fear alarm, the amygdala's signals to the brainstem speed up breathing.
questions.explain: He lists the brainstem signals as speeding heart rate and raising blood pressure but slowing breathing.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says the newly discovered role of the amygdala is pivotal in moments when impulsive feeling overrides the rational.
questions.explain: He introduces the amygdala's role as pivotal precisely for such moments, like the woman throwing away her art print.

questions.q: Match each part of the amygdala's fear alarm to its effect, as Chapter 2 describes it.
pairs: Makes the senses more alert, setting the brain on edge
Fix the face in a fearful expression and freeze unrelated movements
Retrieves knowledge relevant to the emergency
Rivet attention on the source of the fear
questions.explain: Each pairing follows Goleman's list of the coordinated changes the amygdala orchestrates as it commandeers the brain.

questions.q: How can the amygdala capture the rational mind during an emotional emergency?
questions.a: The amygdala has an extensive web of neural connections, so when it sounds an alarm it can commandeer areas throughout the brain: fight-or-flight hormones, movement centers, heart and muscles, alertness of the senses, facial expression and attention. It also has cortical memory systems retrieve knowledge relevant to the emergency, taking precedence over other strands of thought. In this way it can capture and drive much of the rest of the brain, including the rational mind.

questions.q: Put the events of the canal story from England in order.
items: Goleman's friend eats brunch at a canalside cafe
Strolling down the stone steps, he sees a girl with her face frozen in fear
He jumps into the water in his coat and tie
In the water he realises a toddler has fallen in, and rescues the child
questions.explain: He jumped before he knew why, and only once in the water understood what the girl was staring at; Goleman credits his amygdala with the leap.

questions.q: In the canal story from England, what did Goleman's friend see before he jumped into the water in his coat and tie?
options: A toddler falling from the stone steps into the canal
A girl gazing at the water, her face frozen in fear
A mother screaming that her child had fallen in
A small boat capsizing near the canalside cafe
questions.explain: He saw only the girl's frightened face and jumped before he knew why; only once in the water did he realise she was staring at a toddler who had fallen in.

questions.q: What did LeDoux's experiment with rats whose auditory cortex had been destroyed show, and why did it matter?
questions.a: LeDoux destroyed the rats' auditory cortex and then paired a tone with an electric shock. The rats quickly learned to fear the tone even though it could not register in their neocortex, because the sound took the direct route from ear to thalamus to amygdala. This showed the amygdala could perceive, remember and orchestrate fear on its own, overturning the view that emotion must pass through the neocortex.

questions.q: In the experiment Goleman cites on oddly shaped geometric figures flashed too quickly to be consciously seen, what happened?
options: People could not recall the figures and showed no response to them at all
People consciously recognised the figures once shown them again
People acquired a preference for the figures without any awareness of having seen them
People developed a fear of the figures that faded within minutes
questions.explain: LeDoux proposes that the amygdala's hidden role in memory explains how people came to prefer figures they had no conscious awareness of having seen.

questions.q: Lena feels uneasy around a new colleague before she can say why, and only later realises he wears the same cologne as someone who bullied her. How does Chapter 2 explain such a reaction?
options: The prefrontal lobes reappraised the colleague and decided a cautious response was best
The hippocampus recognised the colleague's face and supplied a detailed memory of the bully
Her working memory was overloaded by the new job and produced a false feeling
The amygdala can store emotional memories via a shortcut that bypasses the neocortex, so we react without knowing why
questions.explain: Because the thalamus-to-amygdala shortcut bypasses the neocortex, the amygdala can house emotional memories and responses we enact without quite realising why.

questions.q: Within a split second of seeing a new company logo, Dev finds he dislikes it, before he can say anything about its design. What does Chapter 2 call the system that gives him this instant verdict?
options: The cognitive unconscious, which presents awareness with an opinion as well as an identity
Working memory, which holds the facts needed to judge a design
Affective blindness, which strips the logo of emotional significance
The hippocampus, which judges the logo against remembered context
questions.explain: Research shows that in the first few milliseconds we not only comprehend what something is but decide whether we like it; Goleman calls this the cognitive unconscious.

questions.q: Goleman likens the smaller bundle of neurons leading directly from the thalamus to the amygdala to a neural back ____.
questions.explain: This shorter pathway, something like a neural back alley, lets the amygdala receive direct inputs from the senses before the neocortex registers them.

questions.q: In the first few milliseconds of perceiving something we decide whether we like it; Goleman says the cognitive ____ presents our awareness with an opinion about what we see.
