questions.explain: The cognitive unconscious offers not just the identity of what we see but an opinion about it, so our emotions have a mind of their own.

questions.q: True or false: LeDoux found that the direct thalamus-to-amygdala pathway carries the larger share of neurons, with only a smaller bundle going to the cortex.
questions.explain: It is the other way round: a smaller bundle leads directly to the amygdala, while the larger path of neurons goes to the cortex.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says LeDoux's research was the first to work out neural pathways for feelings that bypass the neocortex.
questions.explain: That is why he calls it revolutionary: feelings taking this direct route include our most primitive and potent.

questions.q: Which of these follow from LeDoux's discovery of the shortcut from the thalamus to the amygdala?
options: The neocortex no longer plays any role in emotional reactions
The amygdala can begin to respond before the neocortex fully perceives what is happening
Some emotional memories can be formed without conscious, cognitive participation
The amygdala can hold emotional impressions we have never known in full awareness
The amygdala must depend entirely on signals from the neocortex
questions.explain: The shortcut overthrows the idea that the amygdala depends entirely on the neocortex; yet the larger route through the neocortex still works much or most of the time, with a parallel circuit between the two.

questions.q: Put the stages of the direct emotional route that LeDoux discovered in order.
items: A sensory signal arrives from the eye or ear
The signal reaches the thalamus
The signal crosses a single synapse to the amygdala
The amygdala begins a response before the neocortex fully perceives
questions.explain: Signals travel first to the thalamus and then across a single synapse to the amygdala, which can start responding while the neocortex is still working through its several levels of circuits.

questions.q: Put the stages of the conventional neuroscience view of emotional signals, which LeDoux revised, in order.
items: Sense organs transmit signals to the thalamus
Sensory areas of the neocortex assemble signals into objects
The signals are sorted for meaning
Signals are sent on to the limbic brain
The response radiates out through the brain and body
questions.explain: In the old theory every signal went through the neocortex before reaching the limbic brain; LeDoux kept this as the usual route but added a direct thalamus-to-amygdala path.

questions.q: Put the steps of LeDoux's crucial rat experiment in order.
items: He destroyed the auditory cortex of rats
He exposed them to a tone paired with an electric shock
The rats quickly learned to fear the tone
He concluded the amygdala could perceive, remember and orchestrate fear on its own
questions.explain: Because the tone could not register in the neocortex yet the rats learned to fear it, the fear had to travel ear to thalamus to amygdala, skipping higher avenues.

questions.q: Sort these claims into the old neuroscience view and LeDoux's discovery.

items.t: The amygdala must depend entirely on signals from the neocortex
Signals reach the limbic brain only after the neocortex sorts their meaning
The neocortex assembles every signal into an object before any emotion
A small bundle of neurons runs straight from the thalamus to the amygdala
The amygdala can start a response before the neocortex registers the input
Some emotional memories form without any conscious participation

questions.explain: The old theory routed everything through the neocortex first; LeDoux's direct pathway lets the amygdala react, and even learn, independently of it.

questions.q: Match each term from Chapter 2 to its meaning.
pairs: Inability to gauge the emotional significance of events
A reaction to unsorted sensory bits, coming before thought
Gives awareness an opinion as well as an identity
Attention that holds in mind the facts needed for a task
A limbic emergency that recruits the rest of the brain
questions.explain: Each definition paraphrases how Goleman introduces the term in the chapter.

questions.q: How did the conventional view of emotional signals differ from what LeDoux discovered?
questions.a: The old view held that signals went from the senses to the thalamus, then to sensory areas of the neocortex where they were assembled into objects and sorted for meaning, and only then to the limbic brain. LeDoux agreed this is how it works much of the time, but found a smaller bundle of neurons running directly from the thalamus to the amygdala. This back route lets the amygdala receive direct inputs and start a response before the neocortex fully registers them, so it need not depend entirely on the neocortex.

questions.q: Why does Goleman call LeDoux's research revolutionary for understanding emotional life?
questions.a: It was the first to work out neural pathways for feelings that bypass the neocortex. The feelings that take this direct route through the amygdala include our most primitive and potent, so the circuit does much to explain the power of emotion to overwhelm rationality. As LeDoux put it, the emotional system can act independently of the neocortex.

questions.q: In Chapter 2, what does Goleman's example of a bear in the zoo versus one in your backyard illustrate?
options: The amygdala reacts to every bear with the same surge of fear
The hippocampus supplies the context that gives the same thing a different significance
The prefrontal lobes decide whether a bear is worth thinking about
The thalamus sorts animals into safe and dangerous categories
questions.explain: The hippocampus's main input is a keen memory of context, vital for emotional meaning; it recognises the differing significance of a caged and a loose bear.

questions.q: According to Goleman, which nerve carries signals triggered by epinephrine and norepinephrine back into the brain, to the amygdala?
options: The optic nerve
The auditory nerve
The vagus nerve
The spinal cord
questions.explain: These hormones activate receptors on the vagus nerve, which regulates the heart and also carries signals back to the brain, chiefly to the amygdala.

questions.q: Years after nearly being hit by a lorry while cycling, Tom cannot remember the date, yet feels a jolt of anxiety whenever he approaches a similar junction. Which division of labour in memory does this fit?
options: The hippocampus stores the anxiety while the amygdala stores the date and place
The prefrontal lobes store the anxiety and the thalamus keeps the facts
Working memory holds the anxiety until he leaves the junction
The amygdala keeps the emotional flavor of the event even when the hippocampus's dry facts fade
questions.explain: Goleman's near-collision example: the hippocampus keeps the specifics, but the amygdala ever after sends a surge of anxiety in similar circumstances.

questions.q: How, according to Goleman, does the brain make emotional memories register with special potency?
options: The same alerting chemicals that prime the body to fight or flee also stamp the moment in memory with vividness
It replays emotional moments repeatedly during sleep until they are fixed
It sends emotional memories through the hippocampus alone for careful storage
It keeps emotional moments in working memory until the danger has passed
questions.explain: Goleman calls this a simple but cunning method: the neurochemical systems for life-threatening emergencies also make the moment vivid in memory.

questions.q: Sort these memory jobs between the hippocampus and the amygdala, as Chapter 2 divides them.

items.t: Remembers which stretch of road you were on
Recognises a face as that of your cousin
Tells a bear in the zoo from one in your backyard
Sends a surge of anxiety the next time you pass a car
Adds that you don't really like your cousin
Retains the emotional flavor that goes with the facts

questions.explain: The hippocampus remembers dry facts and context; the amygdala keeps their emotional flavor, as LeDoux's cousin remark shows.

questions.q: LeDoux told Goleman that the hippocampus is crucial in recognising a face as your cousin's, but it is the ____ that adds you don't really like her.
questions.explain: The remark captures the split: dry recognition is the hippocampus's work, the emotional verdict the amygdala's.

questions.q: Goleman concludes that the brain in effect has two memory systems, one for ordinary facts and one for emotionally ____ ones.
questions.explain: Amygdala arousal imprints emotionally charged moments with added strength, giving us a second memory system alongside the one for ordinary facts.

questions.q: Put the steps by which stress stamps a moment in memory in order, as Goleman describes them.
items: A nerve from the brain to the adrenal glands is triggered
The adrenal glands secrete epinephrine and norepinephrine
The hormones activate receptors on the vagus nerve
The vagus nerve carries signals back to the amygdala
Amygdala neurons signal other regions to strengthen memory
questions.explain: Stress triggers the adrenal hormones, which act on the vagus nerve; its signals reach the amygdala, which tells other brain regions to strengthen memory for what is happening.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says the more intense the amygdala arousal, the weaker the memory imprint, because strong feeling disrupts recording.
questions.explain: He says the reverse: the more intense the arousal, the stronger the imprint, so what scares or thrills us most is among our most indelible memories.

questions.q: True or false: Research cited in Chapter 2 suggests the hippocampus, long considered the key structure of the limbic system, is more involved in registering perceptual patterns than in emotional reactions.
questions.explain: LeDoux and others suggest the hippocampus mainly makes sense of perceptual patterns and supplies context, while the amygdala stores emotional memories.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman give as examples of memories made especially strong by amygdala arousal?
options: Where we went on a first date
What we were doing when we heard the space shuttle Challenger had exploded
The experiences that scare or thrill us most
An ordinary shopping list made last week
Times tables learned by rote at school
questions.explain: Each true example involves emotional arousal, which imprints memory with added strength; routine facts carry no such charge.

questions.q: Why does a special system for emotional memories make evolutionary sense, and what drawback does Goleman see in it?
questions.a: A special system ensures that animals have particularly vivid memories of what threatens or pleases them, which helps them survive. The drawback is that emotional memories can be faulty guides to the present. The vivid imprint of a past danger can fire again in a situation that only resembles it.

questions.q: Explain Goleman's example of nearly having a head-on collision while passing a car on a two-lane highway.
questions.a: The hippocampus retains the specifics of the incident: which stretch of road, who was with us, what the other car looked like. But it is the amygdala that ever after sends a surge of anxiety through us whenever we try to pass a car in similar circumstances. The example shows that the hippocampus remembers the dry facts while the amygdala retains their emotional flavor.

questions.q: In Chapter 2, what triggers a former army nurse's battlefield mix of dread, loathing and panic years later?
options: The sight of blood after her toddler grazed a knee
The stench of a dirty diaper her toddler had stashed in a closet
The sound of a helicopter passing low over her home
The antiseptic smell of a hospital waiting room
questions.explain: The stench when she opened the closet was the single element similar enough to her wartime experience to set off the amygdala's emergency proclamation.

questions.q: Once bitten by a large black dog, Owen feels a jolt of fear when he glimpses a black rug from the corner of his eye. Which feature of the amygdala does this show?
options: Its careful comparison, which waits until the neocortex confirms the danger is real
Its storage of dry facts, which reminds him of where he was bitten
Its associative matching, which calls a match on one key element and acts before full confirmation
Its role in working memory, which keeps the dog in mind during the day
questions.explain: Goleman says the amygdala's comparison is associative: one key similar element can count as a match, which is why the circuit is sloppy and acts before confirmation.

questions.q: Which basic tenet of psychoanalytic thought does LeDoux support with the amygdala's role in childhood?
options: That adult emotions are fixed by genes and owe little to early experience
That emotional lessons are learned mostly in adolescence, once words are available
That forgotten childhood memories are stored in full narrative detail by the hippocampus
That life's earliest interactions lay down emotional lessons based on attunement and upsets between infant and caretakers
questions.explain: LeDoux uses the quickly maturing amygdala to back the psychoanalytic idea that the earliest years lay down emotional lessons from contacts with caretakers.

questions.q: In Goleman's account of how memory works in early life, what does the amygdala determine while the hippocampus retrieves information?
options: Whether that information has any emotional valence
Whether that information is accurate
Where and when the event took place
Which words best describe the event
questions.explain: The two work hand in hand: the hippocampus retrieves the information, and the amygdala decides if it carries emotional valence.

questions.q: Goleman says the amygdala's method of comparing the present with the past is ____: when one key element is similar, it can call it a match.
questions.explain: Because the comparison is associative, the amygdala can react before there is full confirmation, which is why the circuit is sloppy.

questions.q: LeDoux believes the earliest emotional lessons are stored in the amygdala as rough, wordless ____ for emotional life.
questions.explain: Formed before infants have words for experience, these blueprints return in adult life with no matching set of articulated thoughts.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says the amygdala matures slowly and is far from fully formed at birth.
questions.explain: He says the amygdala matures very quickly and is much closer to fully formed at birth, while the hippocampus and neocortex are not yet fully developed.

questions.q: True or false: According to Goleman, many potent emotional memories, especially of traumatic events such as beatings or outright neglect, date from the first few years of life.
questions.explain: He adds this to the emotional brain's imprecision: many potent emotional memories come from infancy, in the relationship with caretakers.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman give as reasons our emotional outbursts can baffle us as adults?
options: They are stored in the amygdala as rough, wordless blueprints
When triggered, there is no matching set of articulated thoughts about the response
The neocortex deliberately keeps such memories hidden from us
The hippocampus stored them in full narrative detail that we cannot bear to recall
The earliest emotional memories were formed before we had words for experience
questions.explain: Goleman's explanation is about wordlessness: we have the chaotic feelings but not the words for the memories that formed them. The hippocampus, crucial for narrative memory, was not yet developed.

questions.q: Put the steps by which the amygdala sets off an out-of-date alarm in order.
items: It scans what is happening now
It compares the present with what happened in the past
It finds one key element similar and calls it a match
It commands a reaction that was imprinted long ago
questions.explain: The amygdala scans and compares by association; a single similar element counts as a match, and it orders an old response before there is full confirmation.

questions.q: Match each example from Chapter 2 to what it illustrates.
pairs: The army nurse and the stinking diaper
An outdated alarm from a past trauma
The waitress who dropped six dinners
Springing at or away from the wrong person
The friend who jumped into the canal
Dan Jansen's wife at the rinkside
questions.explain: Each story is Goleman's illustration for one part of the argument, from outdated and sloppy alarms to the prefrontal manager and pleasant hijacks.

questions.q: Match each brain structure to its state in early life, as Chapter 2 describes it.
pairs: Matures very quickly and is close to fully formed at birth
Crucial for narrative memories, not yet fully developed
Seat of rational thought, not yet fully developed
questions.explain: Because the amygdala is nearly mature at birth while the narrative and rational structures are not, the earliest emotional memories are stored without words.

questions.q: Why can our own emotional outbursts baffle us as adults, according to Goleman and LeDoux?
questions.a: Many potent emotional lessons are laid down in infancy, in the attunement and upsets between infant and caretakers. The amygdala is close to fully formed at birth, but the hippocampus and neocortex are not, so these lessons are stored as rough, wordless blueprints. When they are triggered later there is no matching set of articulated thoughts: we have the chaotic feelings but not the words for the memories that formed them.

questions.q: What is the trouble with the army nurse's reaction, beyond its being a false alarm?
questions.a: A few spare elements, here the stench of a diaper, were enough for the amygdala to match the present to her wartime trauma and proclaim an emergency. The trouble is that along with such emotionally charged memories come equally outdated ways of responding. So she reacts to her toddler's mess with the dread and panic that belonged to the battlefield years before.

questions.section: When Emotions Are Fast and Sloppy
questions.q: Put the events of Goleman's night-time fright in his bedroom in order.
items: A huge object comes crashing down around three in the morning
He leaps out of bed and runs out of the room
Realising he is safe, he cautiously peers back in
He finds a tall pile of boxes his wife had stacked has fallen
questions.explain: He fled first, terrified the ceiling was caving in, and only afterwards discovered that the noise was his wife's stack of boxes; there was no attic at all.

questions.section: When Emotions Are Fast and Sloppy
questions.q: In a rat, how quickly can the amygdala begin a response to a perception, according to Chapter 2?
options: In about twenty-four milliseconds
In as little as twelve milliseconds
In about two milliseconds
In about one hundred and twenty milliseconds
questions.explain: LeDoux's measurements give twelve thousandths of a second for the direct route; the route through the neocortex takes about twice as long.

questions.section: When Emotions Are Fast and Sloppy
questions.q: On a hike, Jo leaps back from a coiled shape on the path and only then sees it is a bent stick. How does Chapter 2 explain the leap?
options: Her prefrontal lobes weighed the risks and calculated that leaping back was the best option
Her hippocampus matched the shape to a remembered snake in a zoo
The quick-and-dirty thalamus-amygdala route reacted to a rough signal before the neocortex identified the object
Her neocortex identified a snake and then passed the signal on to the amygdala
questions.explain: As LeDoux says, you don't need to know exactly what something is to know it may be dangerous; the direct route sends only a rough signal, just enough for a warning.

questions.section: When Emotions Are Fast and Sloppy
questions.q: In Chapter 2, what does the waitress who dropped a tray of six dinners glimpse?
options: Her ex-husband arriving at the restaurant with his new partner
A customer who had once complained about her to the manager
A mouse running across the floor near the kitchen door
A woman with a huge mane of curly red hair, like the woman her ex-husband left her for
questions.explain: Her reaction was to a mere resemblance, an example of how the amygdala's imprecision can make us spring at or away from the wrong person.

questions.section: When Emotions Are Fast and Sloppy
questions.q: Goleman says the route from thalamus to neocortex to amygdala takes about ____ as long as the direct route.
questions.explain: The direct route can respond in about twelve milliseconds in a rat; the route through the neocortex takes roughly twice that.

questions.section: When Emotions Are Fast and Sloppy
questions.q: LeDoux calls a reaction based on neural bits and pieces of sensory information not yet sorted into a recognisable object ____ emotion.
questions.explain: Precognitive emotion is feeling prior to thought, which is why the amygdala can jump to conclusions without confirming evidence.

questions.section: When Emotions Are Fast and Sloppy
questions.q: True or false: Goleman reports that timing measurements in the human brain have confirmed the ratio found in rats.
questions.explain: He says similar measurements have yet to be made in the human brain, though the rough ratio would likely hold.

questions.section: When Emotions Are Fast and Sloppy
questions.q: Which of these does Chapter 2 say about the direct route from thalamus to amygdala?
options: It is the main brain system in non-mammals such as birds, fish and reptiles
It gives a precise identification of the object before any reaction
It is found only in the human brain
It carries only a small portion of sensory messages
What registers through it is at best a rough signal, just enough for a warning
questions.explain: The express route is small, fast and rough; LeDoux calls this minor mammalian system the main one in non-mammals, and it exists in every mammalian brain.

questions.section: When Emotions Are Fast and Sloppy
questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say about the survival value of the direct emotional route?
options: It shaves a few critical milliseconds off reaction time to danger
It likely saved so many protomammalian ancestors that it is now in every mammalian brain
It allows humans to make precise emotional judgments in social life
It is absent in reptiles, which rely on the neocortex instead
questions.explain: The milliseconds saved were valuable enough for the arrangement to spread to all mammals; in human social life its imprecision can be costly, and reptiles depend on it heavily.

questions.section: When Emotions Are Fast and Sloppy
questions.q: Sort these features between the two routes sensory signals take to the amygdala.

items.t: Can respond in about twelve milliseconds in a rat
Carries only a small portion of sensory messages
Gives a rough signal, just enough for a warning
Takes about twice as long
Carries the majority of sensory messages
Slower but more fully informed and refined

questions.explain: The direct route trades precision for speed; the main route is slower but carries most of the information and allows a more refined reaction.

questions.section: When Emotions Are Fast and Sloppy
questions.q: Match each image Goleman uses in Chapter 2 to what it describes.
pairs: The amygdala sending emergency calls throughout the brain
The left frontal lobe regulating unpleasant emotions
The short pathway from the thalamus to the amygdala
Precognitive emotion grasping a whole from its first parts
The prefrontal cortex dampening limbic signals
questions.explain: Each image is Goleman's own for one piece of the brain's emotional machinery, from the amygdala's alarms to the prefrontal brakes.

questions.section: When Emotions Are Fast and Sloppy
questions.q: Match each animal example in Chapter 2 to the point it makes.
pairs: Its amygdala can begin a response in twelve milliseconds
Its imprecision is fine since it errs on the side of safety
Their mental life revolves around the direct circuit
Saved milliseconds kept so many alive the circuit spread
questions.explain: The animal cases show the speed, the harmless imprecision in simple creatures and the evolutionary spread of the direct circuit.

questions.section: When Emotions Are Fast and Sloppy
questions.q: Why is the imprecision of the amygdala's quick-and-dirty circuit acceptable in a squirrel but potentially disastrous for humans?
questions.a: In a squirrel, imprecision leads to erring on the side of safety: springing away at the first sign of a looming enemy or toward a hint of food. In human emotional life the same imprecision means we can, figuratively speaking, spring at or away from the wrong thing or person. That can have disastrous consequences for our relationships, as with the waitress who dropped six dinners at the sight of red hair.

questions.section: When Emotions Are Fast and Sloppy
questions.q: What does Goleman's leap from bed at the sound of the falling boxes illustrate?
questions.a: It shows the power of the amygdala to propel us to action in emergencies, vital moments before the neocortex registers what is actually going on. The emergency route from ear to thalamus to amygdala saves time when an instant response is needed, and would have saved him had the ceiling truly fallen. But it carries only a rough signal, enough for a warning, so it can react to what turns out to be harmless.

questions.section: When Emotions Are Fast and Sloppy
questions.q: A man in a heated argument says something cruel and cannot explain afterwards why he said it. Using Chapter 2, explain why we have so little insight into explosive emotions while they hold us.
questions.a: The amygdala can react in a delirium of rage or fear before the cortex knows what is going on, because such raw emotion is triggered independent of, and prior to, thought. It jumps to a conclusion on a few bits of sensory information, before there is full confirming evidence. So in the grip of the feeling there is no considered thought behind it for the man to inspect or explain.

questions.q: Put the events of the story of Jessica's mother in order.
items: Her tension peaks near midnight on Jessica's first sleepover
The phone rings and she drops her toothbrush to race to it
She blurts Jessica's name into the receiver
A woman's voice says it must be a wrong number
She regains composure and politely asks what number was called
questions.explain: Anxiety primed an impulsive reaction; once she reappraised the call as a wrong number, a more fitting, measured response took over.

questions.q: In the story of Jessica's mother, which moment shows the prefrontal cortex at work?
options: Her calm, polite question about what number the caller wanted, once she realised it was a wrong number
Her racing to the phone with her heart pounding
The images of Jessica in distress rushing through her mind
Her dropping the toothbrush the moment the phone rang
questions.explain: The prefrontal cortex brings a more fitting response when a reappraisal calls for it; the racing heart and frightening images belong to the amygdala's anxious priming.

questions.q: How does the neocortical route to an emotional response differ from the amygdala's hijack mechanism?
questions.a: The neocortical response is slower in brain time because it involves more circuitry, but it can be more judicious and considered, since more thought precedes feeling. Normally the prefrontal lobes register and analyse what is perceived, weigh possible reactions and dictate an emotional response together with the amygdala. The hijack skips this, letting the amygdala act before the neocortex has fully grasped what is happening.

questions.q: What does Goleman say was the cost of the prefrontal lobotomy of the 1940s?
options: The patients became far more anxious and fearful
Most of the patients' emotional lives seemed to vanish
The patients lost most of their memory for facts
The patients' IQ scores dropped sharply
questions.explain: Severing the prefrontal lobes from the lower brain relieved distress only by destroying key circuitry, so most of emotional life went too.

questions.q: To what does Goleman compare the way the prefrontal cortex dampens activation signals from the amygdala?
options: An alarm company that calls the police whenever the security system signals trouble
A thermostat that turns the heating up whenever a room gets cold
A parent who stops an impulsive child from grabbing and tells it to ask properly or wait
A switchboard operator who connects every incoming call immediately
questions.explain: The parent image fits the prefrontal role of weighing reactions before acting; the alarm company is Goleman's image for the amygdala itself.

questions.q: Raj feels a surge of anger when a colleague takes credit for his work in a meeting, but pauses, decides a public row will backfire, and raises it privately later. How does Chapter 2 explain his restraint?
options: His amygdala failed to notice anything threatening about the colleague's behaviour
His hippocampus stored the facts while his anger simply faded away by itself
His thalamus routed the signal past the amygdala straight to working memory
His prefrontal lobes weighed possible reactions and dampened the amygdala's signals for activation
questions.explain: The prefrontal cortex acts as an efficient manager of emotion, weighing reactions before acting and stifling a feeling to deal more effectively with the situation.

questions.q: Which of these findings in Chapter 2 support the view that the left prefrontal lobe is an off switch for distressing emotion?
options: Animals without an amygdala became more fearful and aggressive
Stroke patients with left prefrontal lesions were prone to catastrophic worries and fears
Stroke patients with right prefrontal lesions were unduly cheerful during exams
A man whose right prefrontal lobe was partly removed became less easily upset
Lobotomy patients became more anxious once the prefrontal lobes were cut off
questions.explain: Losing the left lobe frees negative feeling, while losing the right, a seat of fear and aggression, leaves the left's calming influence unopposed. Lobotomy patients lost emotion rather than gaining anxiety, and amygdala-less animals lack fear and rage.

questions.q: Goleman calls the prefrontal lobes, just behind the forehead, the brain's ____ switch for the amygdala's surges.
questions.explain: The clamper switch lies at the other end of a major circuit from the amygdala, in the prefrontal lobes.

questions.q: When an emotion triggers, Goleman says the prefrontal lobes perform what amounts to a risk/____ ratio of myriad possible reactions and bet that one is best.
questions.explain: This weighing of options is what lets the prefrontal lobes choose among reactions, from attacking or running to placating or persuading.

questions.q: The desperate surgical cure of the 1940s that cut connections between the prefrontal cortex and the lower brain was the prefrontal ____.
questions.explain: The lobotomy relieved distress only at the cost of most of patients' emotional lives, which showed the prefrontal lobes' role in emotion.

questions.q: Goleman sums up the division of labour in a phrase: the amygdala proposes, the prefrontal lobe ____.
questions.explain: The amygdala acts as an emergency trigger, while the left prefrontal lobe is part of the off switch that settles what happens to the impulse.

questions.q: Studying patients with frontal lobe injuries, neuropsychologists found that one task of the left frontal lobe is to act as a neural ____, regulating unpleasant emotions.
questions.explain: The left frontal lobe works like a thermostat, keeping the negative feelings seated in the right lobes in check.

questions.q: Which of these are true of what Goleman calls the standard arrangement for emotional response?
options: The largest projection of sensory information from the thalamus goes to the neocortex
The prefrontal lobes coordinate the response as the seat of planning toward goals
If an emotional response is called for, the prefrontal lobes dictate it together with the amygdala
The amygdala governs every emotional reaction from the start
The prefrontal lobes play no part in emotion unless there is an emergency
questions.explain: Ordinarily the prefrontal areas govern our emotional reactions from the start; the amygdala takes over only in emotional emergencies.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman list among the extra emotional options humans have beyond attacking and running?
options: Seek sympathy
Put on a facade of bravado
Hibernate until the threat has passed
Erase the memory of the threat
Placate
questions.explain: His list of human emotional wiles includes placating, persuading, seeking sympathy, stonewalling, provoking guilt, whining, bravado and contempt.

questions.q: Sort these reactions by which part of the brain mainly drives them, according to Chapter 2.

items.t: Throwing a treasured art print into a garbage can
Leaping out of bed at a crash in the night
Dropping a tray at the sight of a red-haired woman
Becoming sad after registering a loss
Feeling happy after a triumph
Getting hurt after mulling over what someone said

questions.explain: The fast reactions come before thought; Goleman says the neocortex is at work when we register a loss, feel happy after a triumph or mull over something before getting hurt.

questions.q: Sort these findings between the left and right prefrontal lobes, as Chapter 2 reports them.

items.t: Acts as a neural thermostat for unpleasant emotions
Keeps raw emotions in check, probably by inhibiting the other side
Lesions here leave patients prone to catastrophic worries
A seat of negative feelings like fear and aggression
Lesions here leave patients unduly cheerful
Partial removal made a husband more affectionate

questions.explain: The right lobes house negative feelings; the left keeps them in check, so losing the left frees worry, while losing the right brings cheerfulness.

questions.q: Sort these jobs between the amygdala and the prefrontal lobes, as Chapter 2 assigns them.

items.t: Scans every experience for trouble
Sounds the alarm like a neural tripwire
Stores emotional memory
Dampens signals for activation from limbic centers
Weighs a risk/benefit ratio of possible reactions
Holds facts in working memory

questions.explain: The amygdala is the sentinel and emotional storehouse; the prefrontal lobes are the manager that weighs, plans and holds working memory.

questions.q: Match each patient or case in Chapter 2 to what happened.
pairs: Stroke patients with left prefrontal lesions
Prone to catastrophic worries and fears
Stroke patients with right prefrontal lesions
Unduly cheerful and joking in exams
Husband with part of the right prefrontal lobe removed
Less easily upset and more affectionate
Young man whose amygdala was removed
Uninterested in people, not recognising his mother
Most of their emotional lives seemed to vanish
questions.explain: These cases each show what follows when one part of the emotional circuitry is damaged or removed.

questions.q: According to Goleman, what two dynamics are presumably involved in an emotional hijacking?
questions.a: First, the amygdala is triggered. Second, the neocortical processes that usually keep emotional response in balance fail to activate, or else the neocortical zones are recruited to the emotional urgency. At such moments the rational mind is swamped by the emotional.

questions.q: Explain what Goleman means by saying the amygdala proposes, the prefrontal lobe disposes.
questions.a: The amygdala often acts as an emergency trigger, firing off urges such as fear or rage. The left prefrontal lobe appears to be part of the brain's off switch for disturbing emotion, able to switch off or dampen all but the strongest negative surges. So the amygdala puts forward a reaction, but the prefrontal cortex, weighing reactions before acting, largely decides what becomes of it.

questions.q: Why does Goleman conclude that without the prefrontal lobes much of emotional life would fall away?
questions.a: The prefrontal lobes supply the understanding that something merits an emotional response; lacking that understanding, none comes. Evidence came from the 1940s prefrontal lobotomy, which cut the prefrontal lobes off from the lower brain. It relieved patients' distress, but most of their emotional lives seemed to vanish too because the key circuitry had been destroyed.

questions.q: According to Chapter 2, why do we say we just can't think straight when emotionally upset?
options: Signals of strong emotion from the limbic brain create neural static that sabotages prefrontal working memory
Strong emotion shuts down the hippocampus so we lose memory for context
The amygdala deletes the facts we were holding in long-term memory
Upset raises our IQ temporarily, overloading the rational mind
questions.explain: Circuits from the limbic brain to the prefrontal lobes let anxiety and anger create neural static, sabotaging the prefrontal lobe's ability to maintain working memory.

questions.q: In the study Goleman cites of primary school boys with above-average IQ who were doing poorly in school, what did neuropsychological tests find?
options: Below-average hidden IQ
Impaired frontal cortex functioning
A damaged hippocampus
An unusually small amygdala
questions.explain: The tests found impaired frontal cortex function, suggesting faulty prefrontal control over limbic urges; the boys' intellect was not deficient.

questions.q: What is Antonio Damasio's counter-intuitive position on feelings and decisions?
options: Feelings must be set aside for decisions to be rational
Feelings matter only for decisions about relationships
Feelings are typically indispensable for rational decisions
Feelings help decisions only after logic has narrowed the options
questions.explain: Damasio argues that feelings point us in the proper direction, where dry logic can then be of best use; emotion comes first, not after logic.

questions.q: What does Goleman mean when he says that in a sense we have two brains, two minds and two kinds of intelligence?
questions.a: We have a rational mind and an emotional mind, the neocortex and the limbic system, and two kinds of intelligence: rational and emotional. How we do in life depends on both, not just IQ, and intellect cannot work at its best without emotional intelligence. Ordinarily the limbic system and neocortex are full partners, and when they interact well emotional intelligence rises, as does intellectual ability.

questions.q: A student who knows the material well goes blank in an exam after a bitter row with her parents that morning. Which idea from Chapter 2 best explains this?
options: Her amygdala stored the material as an emotional memory she cannot reach
Her hippocampus lost the context of the exam room
Her IQ fell temporarily because of lack of sleep
Anxiety and anger create neural static that sabotages the prefrontal lobe's working memory
questions.explain: Strong emotion disrupts the working memory that holds the facts needed for a task, which is why upset people cannot think straight.

questions.q: After damage to the circuit linking his prefrontal lobes and amygdala, a man with an intact IQ spends a whole afternoon unable to choose between two dates for a dentist appointment. How would Damasio explain this?
options: He has lost access to his emotional learning, so the options no longer feel better or worse
His intelligence has declined in a way IQ tests cannot detect
His amygdala is overactive, flooding the choice with fear
His working memory cannot hold both dates in mind at once
questions.explain: Damasio's patients have intact intelligence but no access to the likes and dislikes stored in the amygdala, so everything takes on a gray neutrality and even simple choices stall.

questions.q: Which old ideal does Goleman say his new view of reason and feeling turns on its head?
options: Aristotle's ideal of being angry at the right time and in the right way
Erasmus's ideal of doing away with emotion and putting reason in its place
Damasio's ideal of letting feelings guide every decision without logic
LeDoux's ideal of an emotional system independent of the neocortex
questions.explain: Goleman rejects the old paradigm of reason freed of emotion, as Erasmus had it, in favour of finding an intelligent balance of the two.

questions.q: Goleman notes that the brain region responsible for working memory is the ____ cortex.
questions.explain: Working memory sits in the prefrontal cortex, which is why limbic signals reaching the prefrontal lobes can disrupt clear thinking.

questions.q: Cut off from emotional memory in the amygdala, Damasio's patients find that everything takes on a gray ____.
questions.explain: Without access to emotional memory, a favourite pet or a detested acquaintance no longer triggers attraction or aversion.

questions.q: Goleman concludes that we have two brains, two minds and two different kinds of intelligence: rational and ____.
questions.explain: How we do in life depends on both, he says: not just IQ but emotional intelligence matters.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say strong emotions such as anxiety and anger can do to thinking?
options: Over time, cripple a child's capacity to learn
Raise performance on IQ tests
Strengthen working memory for the task at hand
Create neural static in the prefrontal lobes
Sabotage the ability to maintain working memory
questions.explain: Limbic signals disrupt prefrontal working memory, and continual distress can create deficits in a child's intellectual abilities; they do not improve test performance.

questions.q: Which of these did Goleman report about the primary school boys who had above-average IQs but were doing poorly in school?
options: Their intellect turned out to be deficient after all
Their impairment showed up clearly on their IQ tests
They were impulsive and anxious, often disruptive and in trouble
They were at highest risk for academic failure, alcoholism and criminality
Neuropsychological tests found impaired frontal cortex functioning
questions.explain: Their risk came not from deficient intellect but from impaired control over emotional life, which IQ tests did not tap.

questions.q: Put the steps by which, in Damasio's account, emotional learning streamlines a decision in order.
items: Life confronts us with an unwieldy array of choices
Emotional learning, such as memory of a bad investment, sends signals
Those signals eliminate some options and highlight others
Dry logic is then put to its best use
questions.explain: Feelings point us in the proper direction at the outset, and only then can dry logic be of best use; so the emotional brain is as involved in reasoning as the thinking brain.

questions.q: Sort these claims between the old paradigm of reason and feeling and Goleman's new one.

items.t: The ideal is reason freed of the pull of emotion
Emotion should be done away with and reason put in its place
How we do in life depends on IQ alone
We must harmonize head and heart
We need an intelligent balance of reason and feeling
The emotional brain is as involved in reasoning as the thinking brain

questions.explain: Goleman turns the old understanding on its head: the goal is not to replace emotion with reason but to harmonize them, since emotion matters for rationality.

questions.q: Sort what Damasio's patients with damage to the prefrontal-amygdala circuit lost and what they kept.

items.t: Their IQ
Their cognitive abilities
Access to their emotional learning
Attraction to a favourite pet or aversion to a detested acquaintance
The ability to make sound choices in business and personal life

questions.explain: These patients showed no deterioration in IQ or cognition, yet without access to emotional memory their decisions were terribly flawed.

questions.q: Match each person to the idea or words Chapter 2 links to them.
pairs: Showed the emotional system can act independently of the neocortex
Argued feelings are indispensable for rational decisions
Held the ideal of putting reason in place of emotion
Said that in the moment his head just exploded
Life is a comedy for thinkers and a tragedy for feelers
questions.explain: LeDoux and Damasio supply the chapter's science, Erasmus the old paradigm, Robles the opening hijacking and Walpole the epigraph.

questions.q: Why, according to Damasio, do patients with damage to the prefrontal-amygdala circuit make such bad decisions despite intact intelligence?
questions.a: They have lost access to their emotional learning. The prefrontal-amygdala circuit is the meeting point of thought and emotion and a doorway to the likes and dislikes acquired over a lifetime, stored in the amygdala. Cut off from it, whatever the neocortex considers takes on a gray neutrality, so nothing points them toward or away from options and they make disastrous choices or obsess over something as simple as an appointment time.

questions.q: What new paradigm does Goleman propose at the end of Chapter 2, and how does it differ from the old one?
questions.a: The old paradigm held an ideal of reason freed of the pull of emotion, as Erasmus had it: do away with emotion and put reason in its place. The new paradigm urges us to harmonize head and heart, finding the intelligent balance of the two, since emotion matters for rationality and intellect cannot work at its best without emotional intelligence. To do that, we must first understand what it means to use emotion intelligently.

questions.q: Why does Goleman warn that we leave children's emotional experiences to chance at our peril?
questions.a: The emotional brain, separate from the cortical areas tapped by IQ tests, controls rage and compassion alike, and its circuits are sculpted by experience throughout childhood. Bright children with impaired prefrontal control over limbic urges, like the boys with above-average IQs doing poorly in school, are at highest risk for academic failure, alcoholism and criminality. Their problem is not deficient intellect but impaired control over their emotional life.

questions.q: Where does Chapter 2, Anatomy of an Emotional Hijacking, sit in the structure of Emotional Intelligence?
options: It opens Part One, before the chapter on what emotions are for
It opens Part Two, introducing the skills that make up emotional intelligence
It closes Part One, The Emotional Brain, just before Part Two on the nature of emotional intelligence
It closes Part Three, after the chapters on relationships, work and health
questions.explain: Part One contains Chapter 1, What Are Emotions For?, and Chapter 2; Part Two begins with Chapter 3, When Smart Is Dumb.

questions.q: What does the chapter title Anatomy of an Emotional Hijacking signal about its content?
options: A history of famous crimes committed in fits of passion
A set of techniques for calming down during an argument
A survey of how different cultures describe losing one's temper
A close look at the brain mechanics behind moments when emotion seizes control from reason
questions.explain: Opening with the Career Girl Murders, the chapter dissects the neural machinery, chiefly the amygdala and its links to the neocortex, behind such takeovers.

questions.q: Why does Chapter 2 move from the amygdala's alarms to the prefrontal manager and then to harmonizing emotion and thought?
options: To show first how emotion can override thought, then how thought regulates emotion, and finally that the two must work as partners
To show that the amygdala is outdated and the prefrontal cortex should replace it
To trace the order in which these brain regions evolved, from newest to oldest
To separate the chapter's crime stories from its laboratory experiments
questions.explain: The sections build an argument: hijacking and its circuitry, the prefrontal off switch, then the conclusion that head and heart must be harmonized.

questions.q: Put these sections of Chapter 2 in the order in which they appear.
items: The Seat of All Passion
The Neural Tripwire
The Emotional Sentinel
The Specialist in Emotional Memory
When Emotions Are Fast and Sloppy
Harmonizing Emotion and Thought
questions.explain: The chapter introduces the amygdala, its alarm and the direct pathway, then emotional memory, then the speed and sloppiness of the circuit, and ends by harmonizing emotion and thought.

questions.q: Match each Part of Emotional Intelligence to its subject, as the Prologue lays out the journey.
pairs: How neurological givens play out in emotional intelligence
Relationships, work life and physical health
Temperament and the emotional lessons of childhood
The hazards of emotional illiteracy and school programs
questions.explain: The Prologue's road-map runs from brain science in Part One, which this chapter closes, through the skills, their uses, their roots in childhood and the costs of lacking them.

questions.q: Match each section of Chapter 2 to its main idea.
pairs: The amygdala scans every experience for trouble and sounds the alarm
The amygdala keeps the emotional flavor; the hippocampus the facts
Associative matches trigger responses learned long ago
The prefrontal lobes dampen the amygdala's surges
Emotion is crucial to clear thinking and wise decisions
questions.explain: Each section title names one step in the chapter's anatomy of how emotion and thought interact in the brain.

questions.q: Which of these does the Prologue say Part One's discoveries about the emotional brain will offer?
options: Visits to schools that teach emotional and social skills
An explanation of baffling moments when feeling overwhelms all rationality
Insight into how we learn emotional habits that undermine our best intentions
An opportunity for shaping children's emotional habits
An account of how market forces are reshaping work life
questions.explain: Chapter 2's hijackings are the baffling moments the Prologue promises to explain; work life belongs to Part Three and the school visits to the end of the book.

questions.q: In the Prologue, Goleman tells readers not drawn to neurological detail that they may proceed directly to Part ____, skipping chapters like Anatomy of an Emotional Hijacking.
questions.explain: Part Two, on the nature of emotional intelligence, follows the neurological chapters of Part One that end with this chapter.

questions.q: How does Chapter 2 build on Chapter 1, What Are Emotions For?
questions.a: Chapter 1 traced how the emotional brain evolved, from the brainstem to the limbic ring to the neocortex, and argued that in emotional emergencies the higher centers defer to the limbic system, which has immense power over the rest of the brain. Chapter 2 zooms in on how that happens: the amygdala as sentinel and storehouse of emotional memory, LeDoux's shortcut from thalamus to amygdala, and the prefrontal lobes as the manager that normally keeps emotion in balance.

questions.q: How does the ending of Chapter 2 prepare for Part Two of the book?
questions.a: The chapter concludes that we have two minds and two kinds of intelligence, rational and emotional, and that how we do in life depends on both, not just IQ. It calls for harmonizing head and heart and says we must first understand what it means to use emotion intelligently. That is exactly the subject of Part Two, which turns from brain circuitry to the nature of emotional intelligence, beginning with When Smart Is Dumb.

questions.q: In the case of Jason H., what grade did his physics teacher David Pologruto give him that Jason believed endangered his dream of Harvard medical school?
options: A failing mark on a final exam
An 80 on a quiz, a mere B
A C on a laboratory report
An incomplete for a missed test
questions.explain: Jason was a straight-A student who saw an 80, a mere B, on a physics quiz as a threat to his hopes of Harvard. The point of the story is how small the trigger was compared with his violent response.

questions.q: True or false: A judge found Jason H. guilty of assault for stabbing his physics teacher and sent him to a juvenile facility.
questions.explain: The judge found Jason innocent, ruling him temporarily insane during the incident after a panel of four psychologists and psychiatrists swore he was psychotic during the fight.

questions.q: Put the events of the Jason H. case in the order they happened.
items: Jason receives an 80 on a physics quiz
Jason stabs his teacher in the physics lab
A judge finds Jason temporarily insane
Jason transfers to a private school
Jason graduates at the top of his class
questions.explain: The B grade triggered the stabbing; the court then found him temporarily insane; after transferring to a private school he graduated two years later at the top of his class.

questions.q: After transferring to a private school, Jason H. took enough advanced courses to graduate with a grade-point average of ____, way beyond A+.
questions.explain: Advanced courses pushed Jason's average to 4.614, above the 4.0 a perfect record in regular classes would give, showing his academic intelligence was never in doubt.

questions.q: As Jason H. graduated with highest honors, what did his former teacher David Pologruto complain about?
options: Jason had been given an unfairly high grade-point average
The court had refused to hear his own account of the fight
Jason had never apologized or taken responsibility for the attack
The private school had admitted Jason without asking about the attack
questions.explain: Pologruto's complaint was that Jason never apologized or even took responsibility, a contrast with his glittering academic record that underlines the chapter's theme.

questions.q: What answer does Goleman give to the puzzle of how a straight-A student like Jason H. could do something so irrational?
questions.a: Academic intelligence has little to do with emotional life. The brightest people can founder on unbridled passions and unruly impulses, so that “people with high IQs can be stunningly poor pilots of their private lives.” Jason's grades said nothing about how he would handle a disappointment.

questions.q: According to Goleman, how do the exceptions to the rule that IQ predicts success compare with the cases that fit the rule?
options: There are as many or more exceptions as cases that fit
Exceptions are rare and found only among the very poor
Exceptions appear only among people with IQs over 130
Exceptions vanish when large groups are studied
questions.explain: Goleman says there are widespread exceptions, as many or more than the cases that fit. He grants a general relationship for large groups, so the claim that exceptions vanish in large groups reverses his point.

questions.q: Goleman says that, at best, IQ contributes about ____ percent to the factors that determine life success.
questions.explain: IQ contributes at best about 20 percent, leaving 80 percent to other forces, which is the space Goleman wants emotional intelligence to help fill.

questions.q: Why does Goleman quote Richard Herrnstein and Charles Murray, authors of The Bell Curve?
options: They proved that IQ can be raised greatly by schooling
They were the first to define emotional intelligence
Even they admit test scores are dwarfed by a person's other characteristics
They showed that SAT scores fully predict business success
questions.explain: The Bell Curve gives IQ primary importance, so its authors' admission that the link between test scores and achievements is dwarfed by other characteristics is strong support for Goleman's point.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman grants that for large groups as a whole there is a relationship between IQ and life circumstances.
questions.explain: He accepts that many people with very low IQs end up in menial jobs and high-IQ people tend to be well-paid, but adds that this holds by no means always.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says emotional intelligence, like IQ, has nearly a hundred years of research with hundreds of thousands of people behind it.
questions.explain: That long history belongs to IQ. Goleman calls emotional intelligence a new concept and admits no one can yet say exactly how much of the person-to-person variation in life's course it explains.

questions.q: Which of these abilities does Goleman list in his first description of emotional intelligence?
options: Keeping distress from swamping the ability to think
Motivating oneself and persisting in the face of frustrations
Memorizing facts quickly under exam pressure
Solving abstract logic puzzles at speed
Controlling impulse and delaying gratification
questions.explain: Goleman's list covers self-motivation and persistence, impulse control and delay of gratification, regulating moods so distress does not swamp thinking, empathy and hope. Fast memorizing and logic puzzles are academic skills of the IQ kind.

questions.q: How does Goleman contrast IQ and emotional competencies on the question of whether they can be changed?
questions.a: Some argue that IQ cannot be changed much by experience or education. Goleman says he will show in Part Five that the crucial emotional competencies can be learned and improved upon by children, if we bother to teach them. This makes emotional intelligence a more hopeful target for schooling than IQ.

questions.q: Maya scored at the top of every test at her university, yet she keeps losing jobs after angry outbursts at colleagues. Which claim from the opening of When Smart Is Dumb best explains her case?
options: Her test scores were probably measured wrongly
IQ predicts success only for people from wealthy families
Her outbursts show that her IQ has declined since college
High academic intelligence does not make someone a good pilot of their private life
questions.explain: Goleman's answer to the Jason H. puzzle is that academic intelligence has little to do with emotional life; the brightest can founder on unruly impulses. Nothing in the chapter suggests IQ declines or that her scores were wrong.

questions.q: Match each person in the opening of When Smart Is Dumb to their role.
pairs: Straight-A student who stabbed his teacher over a grade
Physics teacher who was stabbed by a star student
Authors of The Bell Curve who stress IQ
Panel of four psychologists and psychiatrists
Swore that Jason was psychotic during the fight
questions.explain: These are the people in the opening case and argument: the student and teacher in the stabbing, the experts at the trial, and the IQ-focused authors whose own words Goleman turns to his side.

questions.q: What happened to Goleman's Amherst classmate who had five perfect 800 scores on the SAT and achievement tests?
options: He graduated first in his class in three years
He became a professor of mathematics at Amherst
He took almost ten years to finally get his degree
He left college to found a successful business
questions.explain: Despite his formidable intellect, he spent his time hanging out, staying up late and sleeping until noon, and took almost ten years to get his degree.

questions.q: Goleman's Amherst classmate had attained five perfect ____ scores on the SAT and other achievement tests before entering college.
questions.explain: Five perfect 800 scores mark him as academically outstanding, which makes his nearly ten-year struggle to graduate a vivid case of IQ failing to predict destiny.

questions.q: True or false: In the follow-up of ninety-five Harvard students from the 1940s, the men with the highest college test scores were the most successful in salary, productivity, and status.
questions.explain: The highest scorers were not particularly successful compared with lower-scoring peers on salary, productivity or status, and they were not the happiest in friendships, family or romance either.

questions.q: Which of these were measures on which the top-scoring men in the Harvard follow-up of the 1940s classes were not particularly ahead of their lower-scoring peers?
options: Salary
Grades earned during college
Happiness with friendships and family
Scores on the original admission tests
Status in their field
questions.explain: In middle age the top scorers did not stand out in salary, productivity or status, nor in life satisfaction or happiness with friends, family and romance. By definition they were ahead on the college tests themselves.

questions.q: In the Somerville study of 450 boys who grew up near Harvard, what made the greater difference to how they fared in later life?
options: Childhood abilities such as handling frustration and getting on with others
Whether their families had been on welfare
Whether they had IQs above or below 90
How close to Harvard their families had lived
questions.explain: IQ had little relationship to how well the men did; abilities such as handling frustrations, controlling emotions and getting on with other people made the greater difference.

questions.q: The Illinois study tracked eighty-one valedictorians and ____ from the 1981 class of Illinois high schools.
questions.explain: All of them had the highest grade-point averages in their schools, which makes their merely average success by their late twenties striking.

questions.q: Match each study in Emotional Intelligence and Destiny to the group it followed.
pairs: Ninety-five students from the classes of the 1940s
450 boys, most sons of immigrants, from a poor area
Eighty-one top students from the 1981 high-school class
An Amherst classmate with five perfect test scores
questions.explain: Goleman moves from one striking individual to three group studies, each following people of high or varied IQ into adulthood.

questions.q: Match each figure from Emotional Intelligence and Destiny to what it describes.
pairs: Men unemployed ten years or more, whether IQ was under 80 or over 100
Valedictorians at the top level of their profession ten years on
Age at which Somerville men's IQ and socioeconomic level were compared
questions.explain: Each number shows IQ predicting less than expected: identical unemployment rates across IQ bands, and only a quarter of valedictorians reaching the top of their fields.

questions.q: What did Karen Arnold conclude about what it means to know that someone was a valedictorian?
questions.a: Arnold said the study had found the dutiful, people who know how to achieve in the system. Knowing someone is a valedictorian tells you only that they are exceedingly good at achievement as measured by grades. “It tells you nothing about how they react to the vicissitudes of life.”

questions.q: Goleman calls emotional aptitude a ____, because it determines how well we can use whatever other skills we have, including raw intellect.
questions.explain: As a meta-ability, emotional aptitude governs how well we use all our other skills, which helps explain why one person thrives while another of equal intellect dead-ends.

questions.q: Two cousins have the same IQ, went to the same schools and had the same opportunities, yet one thrives and the other dead-ends. How would Goleman's idea of a meta-ability explain this?
questions.a: Goleman holds that emotional life is a domain that can be handled with greater or lesser skill, like math or reading. Because “emotional aptitude is a meta-ability,” it determines how well a person can use their other skills, raw intellect included. The cousin who thrives is likely the one more adept at handling emotions.

questions.q: What point does Goleman make right after the children's joke that the answer to what you call a nerd fifteen years from now is Boss?
options: Even among nerds, emotional intelligence gives an added edge at work
Technical skill is the only reliable path to success today
Nerds usually lack the IQ to become good managers
The joke shows that grades predict who will become the boss
questions.explain: Goleman accepts that technical skill is one path to success in a knowledge-based society, but adds that even among nerds emotional intelligence offers an added edge in the workplace, a theme for Part Three.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say our schools and culture do?
options: Treat a high IQ as no guarantee of anything
Rank emotional intelligence above IQ
Teach emotional skills as carefully as reading
Ignore emotional intelligence
Fixate on academic abilities
questions.explain: Goleman complains that schools and culture fixate on academic abilities and ignore emotional intelligence, even though a high IQ is no guarantee of prosperity, prestige or happiness.

questions.q: Why does Goleman say academic intelligence leaves people unprepared for life?
questions.a: Academic intelligence offers virtually no preparation for the turmoil, or the opportunity, that life's vicissitudes bring. Emotional life is a domain that, like math or reading, needs its own set of competencies. People who cannot control their emotional life fight inner battles that sabotage focused work and clear thought.

questions.q: Sort these findings from When Smart Is Dumb by whether they show IQ mattering or IQ falling short.

items.t: Top Harvard scorers were no more successful in middle age
A general link between IQ and socioeconomic level at forty-seven
Valedictorians reached only average success by their late twenties
Many people with very low IQs end up in menial jobs
High-IQ people tend to become well-paid
Equal unemployment for Somerville men above and below average IQ

questions.explain: Goleman concedes a general IQ link for large groups, but the follow-up studies of Harvard men, Somerville boys and Illinois valedictorians show IQ failing to predict who succeeds.

questions.q: Put the steps of Goleman's argument in Emotional Intelligence and Destiny in order.
items: An Amherst classmate with perfect scores struggles to graduate
Group studies show test scores fail to predict adult success
Academic intelligence is shown to give no preparation for life's vicissitudes
Emotional aptitude is named a meta-ability that governs other skills
questions.explain: The section moves from a single anecdote, to group evidence, to a diagnosis of what academic intelligence lacks, and finally to the claim that emotional aptitude is a meta-ability.

questions.q: How was four-year-old Judy's social perceptiveness revealed at her preschool?
options: Through the Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scale
Through a video of classmates' facial expressions
Through the Classroom Game, a dollhouse replica with photo-headed figures
Through a teacher's ranking of the most popular children
questions.explain: In the Classroom Game Judy placed each child in their favourite play area and with their best friends with complete accuracy. Reading feelings from video comes later in the chapter as a way to test empathy.

questions.q: Put the steps of Judy's Classroom Game in order.
items: The teacher gathers the four-year-olds around a dollhouse classroom
Judy places each child in the corner they like to play in most
Judy places each child with the children they like to play with most
Judy's results show a perfect social map of her class
questions.explain: The game first tests where each child likes to play, then whom they like to play with; Judy's accuracy on both revealed her exceptional social map.

questions.q: True or false: Four-year-old Judy stood out because she was always at the center of games at playtime.
questions.explain: Judy hung back on the margins and might seem a wallflower; her sophistication only showed up in the Classroom Game.

questions.q: Judy's accuracy in the Classroom Game reveals that she has a perfect social ____ of her class.
questions.explain: A perfect social map is a level of perceptiveness exceptional for a four-year-old, the kind of skill that could later make her a star in fields where people skills count.

questions.q: Project Spectrum recognizes that human abilities go far beyond the three ____, the narrow band of word-and-number skills schools traditionally focus on.
questions.explain: Spectrum widens schooling beyond the three R's so that talents like Judy's social perceptiveness are nurtured rather than ignored.

questions.q: What is Project Spectrum trying to do, and how does it change what school is for?
questions.a: Project Spectrum is a curriculum that deliberately cultivates many kinds of intelligence, not only word-and-number skills. It treats capacities such as social perceptiveness as talents education can nurture rather than ignore or frustrate. By developing the full range of abilities children will actually use, school becomes an education in life skills.

questions.q: Who was the guiding visionary behind Project Spectrum?
options: Peter Salovey
Howard Gardner
Robert Sternberg
Lewis Terman
questions.explain: Howard Gardner of the Harvard School of Education led Project Spectrum. Salovey and Sternberg appear later as theorists following his lead, and Terman developed the early mass IQ test.

questions.q: A parent asks Howard Gardner how schools should treat her child, who is weak at math but gifted at building things. Based on what Gardner told Goleman, what would he say?
questions.a: Gardner says the most important thing education can do is help a child toward a field where his talents best suit him, where he will be satisfied and competent. Schools should spend less time ranking children against the narrow college-professor standard and more time identifying and cultivating natural gifts. As he put it, “There are hundreds and hundreds of ways to succeed.”

questions.q: Who developed the first mass paper-and-pencil form of the IQ test, used to sort two million American men during World War I?
options: Lewis Terman of Stanford
E. L. Thorndike of Columbia
Jack Block of Berkeley
Howard Gardner of Harvard
questions.explain: Gardner traces the glory days of IQ testing to Terman's test in World War I, which led to decades of what he calls the IQ way of thinking.

questions.q: Sort these beliefs into the IQ way of thinking and Gardner's multiple-intelligence view.

items.t: A single kind of aptitude determines your future
There is a wide spectrum of intelligences
People are either smart or not
A test can tell you if you are one of the smart ones
You are born smart and nothing much can change it
Children should be helped toward fields that suit their gifts
There are many different abilities that lead to success

questions.explain: Gardner describes the IQ way of thinking as a belief in one inborn, unchangeable, testable smartness, which the SAT also embodies; his own view is that intelligence is multiple.

questions.q: Gardner's influential 1983 book ____ was a manifesto refuting the IQ view of a single intelligence.
questions.explain: Frames of Mind proposed a wide spectrum of intelligences, with seven key varieties, rather than one monolithic intelligence.

questions.q: Match each of Gardner's intelligences to the example Goleman gives of it.
pairs: Carl Rogers or Martin Luther King, Jr.
questions.explain: Beyond verbal and mathematical-logical skill, Gardner's list adds spatial, kinesthetic and musical gifts and the two personal intelligences, each illustrated by famous examples.

questions.q: Sort Gardner's seven intelligences into the two standard academic kinds and those his list adds.

items.t: Kinesthetic
Interpersonal
Verbal
Intrapsychic
Musical
Spatial
Mathematical-logical

questions.explain: Gardner's list includes the two standard academic kinds, verbal and mathematical-logical, then goes on to spatial, kinesthetic, musical and the two personal intelligences.

questions.q: Goleman says the operative word in Gardner's view of intelligences is ____.
questions.explain: Gardner's model pushes beyond IQ as a single, immutable factor; intelligence is multiple.

questions.q: True or false: Gardner holds that seven is the exact, fixed number of human intelligences.
questions.explain: Gardner calls seven an arbitrary figure; there is no magic number, and at one point his team stretched the list to twenty varieties.

questions.q: Which of these were among the four abilities that interpersonal intelligence broke down into when Gardner's team expanded his list to twenty varieties?
options: Skill at social analysis
Musical sensitivity
Kinesthetic grace
The ability to resolve conflicts
Leadership
Self-motivation
questions.explain: Interpersonal intelligence split into leadership, nurturing relationships and keeping friends, resolving conflicts, and the social analysis that Judy excels at.

questions.q: When Spectrum students were tested on both the Stanford-Binet scale and Gardner's Spectrum battery, what was found?
options: High Stanford-Binet scores predicted strength in every Spectrum area
Spectrum scores were simply a copy of IQ scores
Low-IQ children had no Spectrum strengths at all
No significant relationship between the two sets of scores
questions.explain: There was no significant relationship between the two tests; Gardner concluded the Stanford-Binet did not predict success across or on a consistent subset of Spectrum activities.

questions.q: Which of these were areas of strength among the five highest-IQ children in the Project Spectrum comparison?
options: Movement
Mechanics
Music
Visual arts
Numbers
Language
questions.explain: Their strengths were scattered across music (four of them), the visual arts, social understanding, logic and language. None was strong in movement, numbers or mechanics.

questions.q: What did Gardner conclude from comparing Stanford-Binet scores with Spectrum scores, and why does he value the Spectrum scores?
questions.a: He concluded that the Stanford-Binet did not predict successful performance across or on a consistent subset of Spectrum activities. Spectrum scores, by contrast, show parents and teachers the realms a child will take a spontaneous interest in and do well in. Those are the areas where passions can develop that may lead beyond proficiency to mastery.

questions.q: A parent wants to know which activities her six-year-old will take a spontaneous interest in and might one day master. According to Gardner, which assessment would guide her better?
options: A Stanford-Binet IQ score
A Spectrum assessment of the child's range of strengths
The child's SAT-style aptitude rank
A single grade-point average
questions.explain: Gardner says Spectrum scores give clear guidance about the realms a child will take a spontaneous interest in, while the Stanford-Binet did not predict Spectrum performance.

questions.q: Match each term from A Different Kind of Intelligence to its description.
pairs: Understanding other people and how to work cooperatively with them
Forming an accurate model of oneself and using it to live effectively
A dollhouse test of social perceptiveness
A curriculum that cultivates many kinds of intelligence
Once the gold standard of IQ tests
questions.explain: These are the key terms of the section: Gardner's two personal intelligences, the game that revealed Judy's gift, the curriculum built on Gardner's ideas, and the IQ test it was compared against.

questions.q: Gardner describes intrapersonal intelligence as a capacity to form an accurate, veridical ____ of oneself and use it to operate effectively in life.
questions.explain: Intrapersonal intelligence is the inward counterpart of interpersonal intelligence: an accurate model of oneself put to use in living.

questions.q: Leo, a car salesman, quickly senses what motivates each customer and how to work cooperatively with them. Which of Gardner's intelligences does he show most?
options: Intrapersonal intelligence
Interpersonal intelligence
Kinesthetic intelligence
Mathematical-logical intelligence
questions.explain: Interpersonal intelligence is understanding what motivates other people and how to work with them; Gardner names successful salespeople as typical examples. Intrapersonal intelligence is the same ability turned inward.

questions.q: Which of these does Gardner name as people likely to have high interpersonal intelligence?
options: Religious leaders
Politicians
Architects
Successful salespeople
Research mathematicians
questions.explain: Gardner lists salespeople, politicians, teachers, clinicians and religious leaders. Architects appear in the chapter as an example of spatial intelligence.

questions.q: Sort these descriptions into Gardner's two personal intelligences.

items.t: Discriminating among one's own feelings to guide behavior
Access to one's own feelings
Understanding what motivates other people
Working cooperatively with others
Forming an accurate model of oneself
Responding well to others' moods and desires

questions.explain: Interpersonal intelligence faces outward, toward others' motives, moods and desires; intrapersonal intelligence is the correlative ability turned inward, the key to self-knowledge.

questions.q: Put these milestones in the history of thinking about intelligence, as Gardner tells it, in order.
items: Two million American men take Terman's mass IQ test
Decades of the IQ way of thinking
Frames of Mind proposes seven intelligences
Gardner gives nutshell summaries of the personal intelligences
questions.explain: Mass IQ testing began in World War I and shaped decades of thinking; Gardner's 1983 book challenged it, and some ten years later he summarized the personal intelligences.

questions.section: Spock vs. Data When Cognition Is Not Enough
questions.q: What dimension of personal intelligence does Goleman say is broadly pointed to but little explored in Gardner's work?
options: The role of language
The role of emotions
The role of physical skill
The role of memory
questions.explain: Goleman's criticism is that Gardner focused on cognitions about feeling rather than the rich sea of emotions itself.

questions.section: Spock vs. Data When Cognition Is Not Enough
questions.q: Why, according to Goleman, did Gardner's account of the personal intelligences give so little attention to emotions?
questions.a: Gardner's work is strongly informed by a cognitive-science model of mind, so it stresses cognition: understanding oneself and others in motives and habits of working. His team focused more on thoughts about feeling than on feeling itself. That emphasis reflects the Zeitgeist of psychology that shaped him.

questions.section: Spock vs. Data When Cognition Is Not Enough
questions.q: True or false: Goleman compares the realm of the emotions to the kinesthetic realm because both extend beyond the reach of language and cognition.
questions.explain: Just as physical brilliance shows itself nonverbally, the emotions reach beyond language and cognition, which a purely cognitive account misses.

questions.section: Spock vs. Data When Cognition Is Not Enough
questions.q: Goleman says Gardner's emphasis on the cognitive elements of the personal intelligences reflects the ____ of psychology that shaped his views.
questions.explain: Gardner's cognitive emphasis is traced to the spirit of the times in psychology, which had long sidelined emotion.

questions.section: Spock vs. Data When Cognition Is Not Enough
questions.q: What did behaviorists in the mold of B. F. Skinner believe about studying the mind?
options: Emotions were the key to understanding intelligence
Only behavior seen objectively from outside could be studied scientifically
The mind works like a computer storing information
Intelligence is a cold, hard-nosed processing of fact
questions.explain: The behaviorists ruled all inner life, including emotions, out of bounds for science. The computer model and cold-processing view belong to the later cognitive revolution.

questions.section: Spock vs. Data When Cognition Is Not Enough
questions.q: When the cognitive revolution arrived in the late 1960s, what happened to the study of emotions?
