options: Emotions were still off-limits while the mind's information handling was studied
Emotions became the central topic of psychological science
Emotions were studied only through outward behavior
Emotions were explained as faulty computer programs
questions.explain: The cognitive revolution turned to how the mind registers and stores information and to the nature of intelligence, but emotions stayed off-limits.

questions.section: Spock vs. Data When Cognition Is Not Enough
questions.q: Put these stages in psychology's treatment of emotion in historical order.
items: Behaviorists rule all inner life out of bounds for science
The cognitive revolution studies how the mind stores information
Psychology begins to recognize the role of feeling in thinking
questions.explain: Behaviorism dominated the middle decades of the century; the cognitive revolution came in the late 1960s; only gradually has psychology started to recognize feeling's essential role in thinking.

questions.section: Spock vs. Data When Cognition Is Not Enough
questions.q: Goleman likens the cognitive scientists' hyperrational view of intelligence to Star Trek's Mr. ____, the archetype of dry information unmuddied by feeling.
questions.explain: Spock embodies the idea that emotions have no place in intelligence and only muddle our picture of mental life.

questions.section: Spock vs. Data When Cognition Is Not Enough
questions.q: What does Goleman say cognitive scientists were seduced by as the operative model of mind?
options: The behaviorist's stimulus and response
The dollhouse classroom
The IQ test
The computer
questions.explain: They took orderly silicon as the guiding metaphor, forgetting that the brain's wetware is a messy, pulsating puddle of neurochemicals.

questions.section: Spock vs. Data When Cognition Is Not Enough
questions.q: What is Goleman's main criticism of the cognitive model of mind?
questions.a: Modeled on the computer, it ignores that the brain is awash in neurochemicals rather than orderly silicon. Its models fail to acknowledge that rationality is guided by, and can be swamped by, feeling. It is therefore an impoverished view of the mind that cannot explain how feelings give flavor to the intellect.

questions.section: Spock vs. Data When Cognition Is Not Enough
questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say cognitive scientists had to ignore in order to keep their emotionally flat view of mind?
options: Their professional jealousies
How the mind stores information
Their marital squabbles
Their own hopes and fears
The computer as a model of mind
questions.explain: To persist in their view they had to ignore the wash of feeling in their own lives, which biases how well or poorly information is processed. Information storage and the computer metaphor were what they did attend to.

questions.section: Spock vs. Data When Cognition Is Not Enough
questions.q: Why does Goleman use the character Data from Star Trek: The Next Generation?
options: Data proves that pure logic always brings the right human solution
Data stands for the behaviorists who ignored inner life
Data shows that machines feel more deeply than people
Like psychology now, Data sees that cool logic misses something and seeks to feel
questions.explain: Data's cool logic fails to bring the right human solution, so he yearns to feel; psychology is likewise coming to appreciate the power and virtues of emotions. Spock, not Data, is the archetype of the emotion-free view.

questions.section: Spock vs. Data When Cognition Is Not Enough
questions.q: Sort these descriptions into Star Trek's Mr. Spock and Data as Goleman uses them.

items.t: Seeks to feel, knowing something essential is missing
Plays music with technical virtuosity but without passion
Wants friendship and loyalty
Embodies the idea that emotions only muddle mental life
Stands for the cognitive scientists' hyperrational view
The archetype of dry information unmuddied by feeling

questions.explain: Spock stands for the old cold-cognition view; Data stands for psychology's growing recognition that something essential is missing without feeling.

questions.section: Spock vs. Data When Cognition Is Not Enough
questions.q: Goleman says that, like the ____ in The Wizard of Oz, Data lacks a heart.
questions.explain: The comparison stresses that Data, for all his logic, lacks the feeling that makes us human, and knows it.

questions.section: Spock vs. Data When Cognition Is Not Enough
questions.q: Which of these higher values of the human heart does Goleman say are missing entirely from the coldly cognitive view?
options: Love
Precision
Devotion
Faith
Logic
Efficiency
questions.explain: Goleman names faith, hope, devotion and love; logic, precision and efficiency are just what the cold view keeps. “Emotions enrich; a model of mind that leaves them out is impoverished.”

questions.section: Spock vs. Data When Cognition Is Not Enough
questions.q: Match each figure from Spock vs. Data to what it stands for in Goleman's argument.
pairs: Intelligence as dry information unmuddied by feeling
Cool logic that yearns to feel
Behaviorism, which ruled inner life out of science
Cognitive science's guiding metaphor for mind
questions.explain: Goleman uses these figures to trace psychology's neglect of emotion and its gradual change of heart.

questions.section: Spock vs. Data When Cognition Is Not Enough
questions.q: When Goleman asked Gardner about his emphasis on thoughts about feelings, how did Gardner explain it?
questions.a: Gardner admitted he tended to view intelligence cognitively, but said that when he first wrote about the personal intelligences he was talking about emotion, especially emotionally tuning in to yourself. In practice, the theory evolved to focus more on meta-cognition, awareness of one's mental processes, rather than the full range of emotional abilities.

questions.section: Spock vs. Data When Cognition Is Not Enough
questions.q: Gardner says that in practice the theory of multiple intelligence evolved to focus more on ____, that is, awareness of one's mental processes.
questions.explain: Gardner's theory drifted toward meta-cognition, thoughts about feeling, rather than the full range of emotional abilities Goleman wants to explore.

questions.section: Spock vs. Data When Cognition Is Not Enough
questions.q: True or false: Gardner says that in the day-to-day world no intelligence is more important than the interpersonal.
questions.explain: Gardner adds that without it you will make poor choices about whom to marry and what job to take, and that children should be trained in the personal intelligences at school.

questions.q: What did E. L. Thorndike propose about social intelligence in a Harper's Magazine article?
options: It was a useless concept
It was itself an aspect of a person's IQ
It was a skill for manipulating people
It could not be separated from musical talent
questions.explain: Thorndike, who helped popularize IQ, saw social intelligence, the ability to understand others and act wisely in human relations, as part of IQ. The useless label came from a 1960 textbook, and manipulation was the cynical view of other psychologists.

questions.q: How did some other psychologists of Thorndike's time view social intelligence?
options: As the main ingredient of IQ
Cynically, as skills for getting people to do what you want
As the same thing as musical intelligence
As a talent only therapists possess
questions.explain: Those psychologists took a more cynical view, seeing social intelligence as manipulating others whether they want it or not.

questions.q: True or false: By 1960 an influential textbook on intelligence tests had pronounced social intelligence a useless concept.
questions.explain: Neither Thorndike's view nor the cynical one held much sway with IQ theorists, and the 1960 textbook dismissed social intelligence as useless.

questions.q: Put these stages in the history of the idea of social intelligence in order.
items: Thorndike proposes social intelligence as part of IQ
A textbook pronounces social intelligence useless
Sternberg's research returns to Thorndike's conclusion
Sternberg and Salovey reinvent intelligence around leading life successfully
questions.explain: Thorndike wrote in the 1920s and 1930s; the dismissal came by 1960; later Sternberg's systematic research revived the idea, and psychologists such as Sternberg and Salovey widened the concept of intelligence.

questions.q: Why, according to Goleman, would personal intelligence not be ignored even after it was dismissed?
questions.a: It makes both intuitive and common sense. When Sternberg asked people to describe an intelligent person, practical people skills were among the main traits they listed. His more systematic research led back to Thorndike's conclusion that social intelligence is distinct from academic abilities and a key part of doing well in life's practicalities.

questions.q: Robert Sternberg's systematic research led him back to ____'s conclusion that social intelligence is distinct from academic abilities.
questions.explain: Thorndike had already argued for social intelligence; Sternberg's research confirmed it was distinct from academic ability and key to practical success.

questions.q: What example does Goleman give of a practical intelligence highly valued in the workplace?
options: The sensitivity that lets effective managers pick up tacit messages
The ability to score well on aptitude tests
Speed at mathematical calculation
A wide range of intellectual interests
questions.explain: Among practical intelligences, Goleman singles out the sensitivity that allows effective managers to pick up tacit, unspoken messages.

questions.q: True or false: Psychologists such as Sternberg and Salovey argue that doing well on IQ tests predicts success better and better as a person's life path moves away from academe.
questions.explain: They argue the reverse: IQ tests most directly predict success in the classroom or as a professor, and less and less so as life's paths diverge from academe.

questions.q: How does Peter Salovey's definition of emotional intelligence relate to Gardner's personal intelligences?
questions.a: Salovey subsumes Gardner's personal intelligences in his basic definition of emotional intelligence. He expands them into five main domains: knowing one's emotions, managing emotions, motivating oneself, recognizing emotions in others, and handling relationships. In doing so he maps in detail how we can bring intelligence to our emotions.

questions.q: Put Salovey's five domains of emotional intelligence in the order Goleman lists them.
items: Knowing one's emotions
Managing emotions
Motivating oneself
Recognizing emotions in others
Handling relationships
questions.explain: The list starts with self-awareness, the keystone, moves through handling and harnessing one's own emotions, and ends with empathy and the art of relationships.

questions.q: In Salovey's scheme, self-awareness, recognizing a feeling as it happens, is the ____ of emotional intelligence.
questions.explain: Self-awareness is the keystone because the other abilities, such as managing emotions and empathy, build on it; an inability to notice true feelings leaves us at their mercy.

questions.q: Match each of Salovey's domains to the ability Goleman links it with.
pairs: Recognizing a feeling as it happens
Soothing oneself and shaking off anxiety or gloom
Delaying gratification and getting into flow
Skill in managing emotions in others
questions.explain: Each domain names an ability: self-awareness, self-soothing, self-motivation, empathy and managing others' emotions.

questions.q: Goleman says being able to get into the ____ state enables outstanding performance of all kinds.
questions.explain: Flow belongs to the domain of motivating oneself, along with marshaling emotions toward a goal and delaying gratification.

questions.q: Ana is trying to get better at the domain Salovey calls managing emotions. Which of these would count as progress in that domain?
options: Reading what a client wants from his face
Calming herself after a bad meeting
Bouncing back quickly from a setback
Shaking off a mood of gloom
Leading a team through a conflict
questions.explain: Managing emotions means handling one's own feelings so they are appropriate: soothing oneself and recovering from upsets. Reading a client is empathy, and leading a team belongs to handling relationships.

questions.q: Which of these callings does Goleman say empathic people are better at?
options: Sales
Long-distance driving
Teaching
Solitary laboratory research
The caring professions
questions.explain: Empathic people are more attuned to subtle signals of what others need, which suits the caring professions, teaching, sales and management.

questions.q: Sort these everyday actions by whether they draw mainly on handling one's own emotions or other people's.

items.t: Noticing you are irritable before a meeting
Settling a dispute between two coworkers
Skipping TV to finish a project on time
Sensing that a quiet colleague feels left out
Calming a friend's anger
Talking yourself out of a gloomy mood

questions.explain: The first three of Salovey's domains, knowing, managing and motivating oneself, concern one's own emotions; empathy and handling relationships concern the emotions of others.

questions.q: Raj is great at calming his own nerves before exams but clumsy at soothing his upset younger sister. What does Goleman say this kind of case shows?
options: People differ in their abilities across the separate domains
Raj must be low in emotional intelligence overall
Skill at self-soothing always brings skill with others
Raj's ability is fixed and cannot be improved
questions.explain: Goleman gives just this example: someone may be adept at handling their own anxiety but inept at soothing someone else's. He also says lapses can be remedied, so a fixed ability is wrong.

questions.q: Mei skips a party to keep studying for a goal she cares about, holding off the fun for later. Which of Salovey's domains is she using?
options: Knowing one's emotions
Recognizing emotions in others
Motivating oneself
Handling relationships
questions.explain: Motivating oneself means marshaling emotions in the service of a goal, including delaying gratification and stifling impulsiveness.

questions.q: Sam is popular, a natural leader and skilled at keeping interactions smooth because he manages how others feel. Which of Salovey's domains does he excel in?
options: Handling relationships
Managing emotions
Motivating oneself
Knowing one's emotions
questions.explain: “The art of relationships is, in large part, skill in managing emotions in others.” These abilities undergird popularity, leadership and interpersonal effectiveness.

questions.q: A man says he has always been hopeless at controlling his temper and that it is just how he is wired. How would Goleman answer him?
questions.a: Goleman grants that the basis of our level of ability is neural, but says “the brain is remarkably plastic, constantly learning.” Lapses in emotional skills can be remedied, because each domain is largely a body of habit and response that can be improved with the right effort.

questions.section: IQ and Emotions Intelligence: Pure Types
questions.q: True or false: Goleman says IQ and emotional intelligence are opposing competencies, so being strong in one means being weak in the other.
questions.explain: “IQ and emotional intelligence are not opposing competencies, but rather separate ones.” We all mix the two in varying degrees.

questions.section: IQ and Emotions Intelligence: Pure Types
questions.q: What relationship does Goleman report between IQ and some aspects of emotional intelligence?
options: A strong correlation, so one predicts the other
A strong negative correlation
No measurable relationship has ever been studied
A slight correlation, small enough that they are largely independent
questions.explain: There is a slight correlation, but small enough to show IQ and emotional intelligence are largely independent entities.

questions.section: IQ and Emotions Intelligence: Pure Types
questions.q: Why is there no single paper-and-pencil test of emotional intelligence, and how are some of its parts measured instead?
questions.a: Unlike IQ, emotional intelligence has no single test yielding a score, and there may never be one. Some components, such as empathy, are best tested by sampling a person's actual ability at the task. For example, people can be asked to read someone's feelings from a video of their facial expressions.

questions.section: IQ and Emotions Intelligence: Pure Types
questions.q: Jack Block's measure, which is quite similar to emotional intelligence and includes the main social and emotional competences, is called ego ____.
questions.explain: Block used ego resilience to compare two theoretical pure types: people high in IQ and people high in emotional aptitudes.

questions.section: IQ and Emotions Intelligence: Pure Types
questions.q: In Jack Block's comparison of pure types, which profile fits each male trait: the purely high-IQ man or the emotionally intelligent man?

items.t: Socially poised and cheerful
Emotionally bland and cold
Committed to people or causes
Fastidious and inhibited
Critical and condescending
Uneasy with sensual experience
Sympathetic and caring
Has an ethical outlook

questions.explain: The high-IQ male is adept in the realm of mind but inept in the personal world; the emotionally intelligent man is poised, committed, ethical and caring.

questions.section: IQ and Emotions Intelligence: Pure Types
questions.q: Sort these traits into Block's high-IQ woman and emotionally intelligent woman.

items.t: Adapts well to stress
Playful and spontaneous
Hesitates to express anger openly
Values intellectual matters
Prone to anxiety, rumination and guilt
Expresses her feelings directly

questions.explain: The purely high-IQ woman is intellectually confident but anxious and indirect with anger; the emotionally intelligent woman is assertive, adapts well to stress and is open to new people and experience.

questions.section: IQ and Emotions Intelligence: Pure Types
questions.q: Which of these traits does Block's comparison give to men high in emotional intelligence?
options: Comfort with themselves and others
Detached and unexpressive
Prone to worried rumination
Taking responsibility
A notable capacity for commitment
questions.explain: Emotionally intelligent men are poised, cheerful, committed, responsible, ethical and comfortable with themselves. Detachment belongs to the high-IQ man, and they are described as not prone to worried rumination.

questions.section: IQ and Emotions Intelligence: Pure Types
questions.q: Nadia voices her feelings directly, feels good about herself, adapts well to stress and easily reaches out to new people. Which of Block's pure types does she most resemble?
options: The high-IQ woman
The high-IQ man
The emotionally intelligent woman
None, since Block studied only men
questions.explain: Block's emotionally intelligent woman is assertive, expresses feelings directly, adapts to stress and reaches out easily. The high-IQ woman tends to be anxious and expresses anger only indirectly.

questions.section: IQ and Emotions Intelligence: Pure Types
questions.q: Match each item from IQ and Emotional Intelligence: Pure Types to its description.
pairs: Berkeley psychologist who compared two theoretical pure types
A measure quite similar to emotional intelligence
Ambitious and productive but emotionally bland
Intellectually confident but prone to guilt
questions.explain: Block used ego resilience to contrast pure types; the high-IQ profiles show strength in the realm of mind alongside weaknesses in the personal world.

questions.section: IQ and Emotions Intelligence: Pure Types
questions.q: Why does Goleman call the high-IQ pure type almost a caricature of the intellectual?
questions.a: Setting aside emotional intelligence, the high-IQ type is adept in the realm of mind but inept in the personal world. The high-IQ man, for example, has wide intellectual interests and is ambitious and productive, yet tends to be critical, condescending, inhibited, detached and emotionally bland and cold.

questions.section: IQ and Emotions Intelligence: Pure Types
questions.q: What conclusion does Goleman draw from Block's portraits of the pure types?
questions.a: The portraits are extremes, since all of us mix IQ and emotional intelligence, and in people with both the pictures merge. They show what each dimension adds separately. Of the two, “emotional intelligence adds far more of the qualities that make us more fully human.”

questions.section: IQ and Emotions Intelligence: Pure Types
questions.q: Put the steps of IQ and Emotional Intelligence: Pure Types in the order Goleman presents them.
items: IQ and emotional intelligence are called separate, not opposed
No single paper-and-pencil test of emotional intelligence exists
Block compares high-IQ and high-emotional pure types
The portraits are called extremes that all of us mix
Emotional intelligence is said to add more of what makes us human
questions.explain: The section first sets out the relation between the two, explains the measurement problem, presents Block's pure types, adds the caveat that they are extremes, and ends with the verdict.

questions.section: IQ and Emotions Intelligence: Pure Types
questions.q: How common does Goleman say people with a high IQ but low emotional intelligence are?
options: Very common, just as the stereotype suggests
Found mainly among valedictorians
Unknown, because the two cannot be measured apart
Relatively rare, despite the stereotypes
questions.explain: We all mix intellect and emotional acuity, so people high in one and low in the other are, despite the stereotypes, relatively rare.

questions.section: IQ and Emotions Intelligence: Pure Types
questions.q: Sort these statements by whether Goleman makes them about IQ or about emotional intelligence.

items.t: Some argue it cannot be changed much by education
Adds more of the qualities that make us fully human
Has nearly a century of research behind it
Has familiar paper-and-pencil tests
Contributes at best about 20 percent to life success
Its competencies can be learned by children
Is a new concept
Some parts are best tested by sampling actual ability

questions.explain: Goleman contrasts IQ's long testing history and limited predictive power with emotional intelligence, a newer, harder-to-test set of abilities that can be taught.

questions.q: Match each figure from the opening of When Smart Is Dumb to what it describes.
pairs: IQ's best contribution to life success
Share of life success left to other forces
Length of research history behind IQ
questions.explain: The numbers frame the opening: a modest grade sparked the attack on a teacher by a student whose record was outstanding, and IQ explains only a small part of success despite its long research history.

questions.q: A counselor tells a student with a modest SAT math score to give up on running his own business one day. How would the words Goleman quotes from Herrnstein and Murray answer the counselor?
questions.a: Even Herrnstein and Murray, who give IQ primary importance, say such a student should not give up dreams of running a business, becoming a senator or making a million dollars. A low score may argue against becoming a mathematician, but the link between test scores and those achievements is dwarfed by the totality of his other characteristics.

questions.q: What does the chapter title When Smart Is Dumb signal about Goleman's argument?
options: Intelligent people should distrust their own IQ scores
IQ tests are dumb and should be abolished
Academic intelligence does not keep people from acting foolishly in emotional life
Smart people are usually poor at school
questions.explain: The title captures the Jason H. case and the chapter's thesis: academic intelligence has little to do with emotional life, so the very bright can act very unwisely.

questions.q: How does When Smart Is Dumb follow on from Part One of the book, on the emotional brain?
questions.a: Part One explained, through the brain's emotional architecture, the baffling moments when feeling overwhelms rationality. When Smart Is Dumb opens Part Two, on the nature of emotional intelligence, by showing such a moment in a brilliant student. It then asks what kind of intelligence, other than IQ, governs how well we handle those emotions.

questions.q: Put the stages of When Smart Is Dumb in order.
items: A star student's attack over a B grade
Studies of high scorers' adult destinies
Gardner's multiple intelligences
Cognitive science's neglect of emotion
Salovey's five domains
Block's pure types
questions.explain: The chapter moves from a puzzling case, to evidence that IQ falls short, to Gardner's wider view, to its cognitive limits, to Salovey's emotional model, and ends by contrasting IQ and emotional intelligence.

questions.q: Salovey's five domains preview the chapters that follow When Smart Is Dumb. Match each domain to its chapter.
questions.explain: Goleman explicitly points each domain to a later chapter: self-awareness to Chapter 4, managing emotions to 5, motivation to 6, empathy to 7 and social competence to 8.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman presents Salovey's five domains of emotional intelligence as a preview of the chapters that follow, Chapters 4 through 8.
questions.explain: Each domain description names the chapter that will examine it, so the list serves as a road-map for the rest of Part Two.

questions.q: Which of these later Parts of the book does Goleman point to in When Smart Is Dumb as places where he will develop his points?
options: Part Three, on the workplace edge of emotional intelligence
Part Four, on IQ testing in schools
An appendix on IQ test design
Part One, on the emotional brain
Part Five, on teaching children emotional competencies
questions.explain: Goleman says Part Three will show emotional intelligence's edge in the workplace and Part Five will show emotional competencies can be learned by children. Part One comes before this chapter, and Part Four is not about IQ testing.

questions.q: Put the Parts of the book in order, starting with the Part before When Smart Is Dumb.
items: The Emotional Brain
The Nature of Emotional Intelligence
Emotional Intelligence Applied
Windows of Opportunity
Emotional Literacy
questions.explain: When Smart Is Dumb opens Part Two, The Nature of Emotional Intelligence, which follows Part One on the emotional brain and comes before the Parts on applications, childhood windows of opportunity and emotional literacy.

questions.q: Why does When Smart Is Dumb move from Gardner's multiple intelligences to Salovey's model?
questions.a: Gardner broke the single-IQ view and named personal intelligences, but his work focused on cognition about feelings rather than emotions themselves. Salovey, following Gardner's lead, maps in detail how we can bring intelligence to our emotions. His five domains give Goleman the framework for the chapters that follow.

questions.q: Why does Goleman present the studies of high scorers' destinies before introducing theories of intelligence in When Smart Is Dumb?
questions.a: The studies establish the problem: IQ and grades predict surprisingly little about who succeeds or is happy, leaving most of life success to other forces. Once IQ is shown to fall short, Goleman can introduce Gardner and Salovey as offering a different kind of intelligence that fills the gap.

questions.q: Why does When Smart Is Dumb end with Block's comparison of pure types?
options: To prove that emotional intelligence can be measured by one test
To show that high-IQ people are usually low in emotional intelligence
To introduce the brain circuits behind emotional hijackings
To show IQ and emotional intelligence are separate and what each adds
questions.explain: The pure types show what each dimension adds on its own and support Goleman's conclusion that emotional intelligence adds more of what makes us fully human. He stresses such pure types are rare and that no single test exists.

questions.q: In which Part of Emotional Intelligence does Chapter 4, “Know Thyself”, sit, and what does that Part do?
options: Part One, which maps the brain's emotional architecture and the amygdala's hijackings
Part Three, which applies emotional intelligence to marriage, work and health
Part Two, which sets out the nature of emotional intelligence one ability at a time
Part Four, which shows how childhood shapes the emotional circuits for life
questions.explain: Chapter 4 opens the run of Part Two chapters that each take up one domain of emotional intelligence, after Chapter 3 has listed the five domains. Part One is the neurological groundwork; Parts Three and Four come later and apply the abilities.

questions.q: What does the title of Chapter 4, “Know Thyself”, signal about the chapter's subject?
options: That emotional intelligence is mainly a matter of knowing other people's motives
That awareness of one's own feelings as they occur is the keystone of emotional intelligence
That self-knowledge comes chiefly from rational analysis of one's past decisions
That the Greek philosophers already held a full theory of emotional intelligence
questions.explain: Goleman borrows Socrates's injunction because it speaks to the keystone of emotional intelligence: “awareness of one's own feelings as they occur.” The chapter is about knowing one's own feelings, not reading others.

questions.q: In the tale of the samurai and the Zen master that opens Chapter 4, what does the samurai's sudden calm illustrate?
options: That anger is best handled by obeying the authority of a wiser teacher
That insults lose their power once a person decides not to take offense
The difference between being caught up in a feeling and becoming aware of being swept away by it
That strong emotions always fade on their own if a person simply waits
questions.explain: The samurai's awakening to his own fury, which the monk names as hell, shows the shift from being gripped by a feeling to noticing it. That shift, not obedience or waiting, is what calms him.

questions.q: Put these moments of the samurai and Zen master tale in the order they happen.
items: The samurai asks the monk to explain heaven and hell
The monk scornfully calls the samurai a lout
The samurai draws his sword in a rage
The monk says that this is hell
The samurai sheathes his sword and bows in thanks
The monk says that this is heaven
questions.explain: The insult provokes the rage, the monk names the rage as hell, and the samurai's grateful recognition of his own state is then named as heaven.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, Goleman notes that psychologists use the term ____ for awareness of one's own emotions, alongside metacognition for awareness of thought process.
questions.explain: Metacognition refers to awareness of thought process; metamood is the parallel term for awareness of one's own emotions.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, Goleman says that instead of the ponderous technical terms he prefers to call ongoing attention to one's internal states ____.
questions.explain: Goleman chooses self-awareness, meaning an ongoing attention to one's internal states in which the mind observes experience, emotions included.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, match each source with the image of self-awareness Goleman draws from it.
pairs: An evenly hovering attention commended to psychoanalysts
The observing ego that monitors one's own reactions
A second self, a wraithlike observer during his depression
questions.explain: Each source supplies a picture of the same faculty: a part of the mind that watches feelings without being swept away by them.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, how does Goleman characterize the quality of Freud's “evenly hovering attention”?
options: It takes in whatever passes through awareness impartially, as an interested yet unreactive witness
It focuses sharply on the most distressing feelings so they can be expelled
It judges each passing feeling as healthy or unhealthy before letting it go
It suppresses emotions so that pure reason can take over the analysis
questions.explain: The attention is impartial, “an interested yet unreactive witness.” It neither judges nor suppresses what passes through awareness.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, Goleman notes that some psychoanalysts call the capacity of self-awareness that lets an analyst monitor his own reactions the “observing ____”.
questions.explain: The observing ego is the analyst's self-awareness of his own reactions, a capacity that free association also nurtures in the patient.

questions.q: According to Chapter 4, which brain activity would self-awareness seem to require?
options: A quieted neocortex, so that the limbic system can speak freely
An aroused amygdala, so that feelings are vivid enough to notice
Heightened brainstem activity to register bodily sensations
An activated neocortex, particularly the language areas that identify and name emotions
questions.explain: Goleman ties self-awareness to an activated neocortex, especially its language areas, attuned to identify and name the emotions being aroused; an aroused amygdala is the feeling itself, not the awareness of it.

questions.q: Raj is furious with a colleague in a meeting, yet even as he seethes he notices to himself that he is getting really angry. In Chapter 4's terms, what is Raj showing?
options: Self-observation at a minimum: a slight stepping-back, a parallel stream of awareness above the feeling
Engulfment: he is lost in his mood and helpless to escape it
Somaticizing: he is mistaking an emotional ache for a physical one
Repression: he is pushing the anger below the threshold of awareness
questions.explain: Goleman's example is having the thought “This is anger I'm feeling” even while enraged; at a minimum, self-observation is this slight stepping-back from experience, aware of it rather than lost in it.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, why does Goleman treat awareness of one's own emotions as the starting point for the other emotional skills?
questions.a: Noticing a feeling as it happens means neocortical circuits are monitoring the emotion, which Goleman calls a first step in gaining some control. He calls this awareness “the fundamental emotional competence on which others, such as emotional self-control, build.” Without first knowing what we feel, we cannot manage it.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, John Mayer defines self-awareness as being aware of both our mood and our ____ about that mood.
questions.explain: Mayer, coformulator of the theory of emotional intelligence with Peter Salovey, puts it as being “aware of both our mood and our thoughts about that mood.”

questions.q: Which of these thoughts does John Mayer give, in Chapter 4, as typical of emotional self-awareness?
options: “I shouldn't feel this way”
“I'm thinking good things to cheer up”
“Nothing I do will ever change this”
“Don't think about it”
“Everyone else is to blame for this”
questions.explain: Mayer lists these three to show that self-awareness can be less than equanimous; the thought “Don't think about it” marks a more restricted self-awareness. Hopeless or blaming thoughts are not among his examples.

questions.q: True or false: In Chapter 4, Mayer finds that for practical purposes recognizing a foul mood and wanting to get out of it usually go hand in hand.
questions.explain: Although being aware of a feeling and acting to change it are logically distinct, Mayer finds the two usually come together: to recognize a foul mood is to want to escape it.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, what does the example of telling an angry child “Stop that!” show about the difference between curbing an impulse and becoming aware of a feeling?
questions.a: Saying “Stop that!” may stop the child hitting a playmate, but the anger still simmers because his thoughts stay fixed on the trigger, the stolen toy. Restraining the action is distinct from self-awareness. Realizing “This is anger I'm feeling” gives a greater freedom: not only the option not to act on the anger but also the option to try to let go of it.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, match each of John Mayer's styles for attending to emotions with its description.
pairs: Aware of moods as they happen and able to get out of bad ones sooner
Swamped by emotions and feeling helpless to escape them
Clear about their moods but making no attempt to change them
questions.explain: Mayer's three styles differ in both clarity and action: the self-aware see and manage, the engulfed are lost in their moods, and the accepting see clearly but leave their moods alone.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, sort these traits into Mayer's self-aware style or his engulfed style.

items.t: Autonomous and sure of their own boundaries
Tend to have a positive outlook on life
Don't ruminate about a bad mood
Mercurial and lost in their feelings
Do little to escape bad moods
Feel their moods have taken charge

questions.explain: Mayer's self-aware people have clarity that supports good psychological health and quick recovery from bad moods; the engulfed lack perspective and feel emotionally out of control.

questions.q: Which of these does Chapter 4 say characterize people of Mayer's self-aware style?
options: They are in good psychological health
They get out of a bad mood sooner
They feel overwhelmed and out of control
They accept bad moods with a laissez-faire attitude
They feel emotions far less intensely than others
questions.explain: Self-aware people are in good psychological health and, not ruminating, get out of bad moods sooner. Feeling overwhelmed belongs to the engulfed, and the laissez-faire attitude to one branch of the accepting.

questions.q: Maria knows clearly that she has been depressed for months, but she has given up trying to feel better and simply lives with it. Which of Mayer's styles in Chapter 4 does she fit?
options: Engulfed, because she is swamped by moods she cannot see clearly
Self-aware, because she can name her mood as she has it
Accepting, because she is clear about her mood yet does nothing to change it
Indifferent, because she barely experiences any feeling at all
questions.explain: Mayer's accepting type includes people clear about their bad moods who accept them and do nothing to change them, such as depressed people resigned to their despair. The engulfed, by contrast, are not clear about what they feel.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, what are the two branches of Mayer's accepting style?
questions.a: Both branches are clear about what they feel but do not try to change their moods. One branch is usually in good moods and so has little motivation to change them. The other is prone to bad moods yet accepts them with a laissez-faire attitude despite the distress, a pattern seen in depressed people resigned to their despair.

questions.q: True or false: In Chapter 4, Goleman says self-awareness is an attention that gets carried away by emotions, amplifying what is perceived.
questions.explain: Goleman says the opposite: self-awareness is not an attention carried away by emotions but a neutral mode that keeps its self-reflectiveness even amid turbulent feelings.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, what was Suzanne Miller's airplane-turbulence test item designed to assess?
options: How accurately people can estimate real risk during an emergency
Whether people tend to be vigilant under distress or to distract themselves
Whether people's fear is driven more by the amygdala or the neocortex
How much people trust authority figures like pilots and flight attendants
questions.explain: Miller's test asks what you do in rough turbulence to reveal your favored attentional stance under duress: attending carefully to every detail, or tuning out by distraction.

questions.q: In Suzanne Miller's airplane-turbulence item from Chapter 4, sort each response into tuning in or tuning out.

items.t: Reviewing the emergency card
Watching the flight attendants for signs of panic
Straining to hear the engines
Burying oneself in a book or magazine
Continuing to watch the movie

questions.explain: Checking for danger signs is the vigilant stance; absorbing oneself in reading or the movie is the distracting stance.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, what are the emotional consequences of tuning in versus tuning out under duress?
questions.a: Those who tune in can, by attending so carefully, unwittingly amplify the size of their own reactions, especially if their attention lacks the equanimity of self-awareness, so their emotions seem all the more intense. Those who tune out notice less about their reactions and so minimize the experience of their emotional response, though not necessarily the size of the response itself.

questions.q: Which of these does Chapter 4 say about people who tune in to every detail under duress?
options: They can unwittingly amplify the magnitude of their own reactions
Their emotions seem all the more intense
The amplifying is worse when their attention lacks the equanimity of self-awareness
They notice less about their own reactions
They shrink the actual size of their emotional response
questions.explain: Vigilant attention amplifies reactions and makes emotions feel stronger, especially without equanimity. Noticing less belongs to those who tune out.

questions.q: True or false: In Chapter 4, Goleman says that people who distract themselves under duress reduce the actual size of their emotional response.
questions.explain: Those who tune out minimize their experience of the response, “if not the size of the response itself.” What shrinks is what they notice, not necessarily the reaction.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, psychologist Edward Diener is described as studying the ____ with which people experience their emotions.
questions.explain: Diener's case studies range people along a spectrum of emotional intensity, from the student who felt no urgency at a fire to the woman distraught for days over a pen.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, sort these into the low-intensity or high-intensity end of Edward Diener's spectrum.

items.t: Walking, not running, to fetch a fire extinguisher
Feeling little or nothing even in an emergency
Being distraught for days after losing a favorite pen
Driving three hours on impulse to a shoe sale
The least provocation unleashing emotional storms

questions.explain: Diener's college student felt no urgency even at a fire, while the woman at the other extreme reacted strongly to small losses and pleasures.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, match each person with what Goleman reports about them.
pairs: Devised a test using an item about airplane turbulence
Studied how intensely people experience their emotions
Walked to put out a dorm fire, feeling no urgency
Drove three hours to a store on seeing a sale ad
questions.explain: Miller's work concerns attentional stance under distress; Diener's concerns emotional intensity, illustrated by his two extreme cases.

questions.q: Which of these findings does Chapter 4 attribute to Edward Diener?
options: Women in general feel both positive and negative emotions more strongly than men
Emotional life is richer for those who notice more
Men feel negative emotions more strongly than women do
People who feel little have the richest inner lives
Emotional intensity is fixed entirely by the amygdala's size
questions.explain: Diener finds women feel emotions of both kinds more strongly, and that emotional life is richer for those who notice more. The other claims are not in the book.

questions.q: Dan is crushed for a week when his umbrella is stolen and elated for days after finding a good parking space. Where does Chapter 4 place someone like Dan?
options: Among those who tune out under duress and so feel little
Among the alexithymics, who cannot say what they feel
Among Mayer's accepting type, who leave their moods unchanged
Near the high-intensity end of Diener's spectrum, where small provocations unleash storms
questions.explain: Like Diener's woman who was distraught over a lost pen, Dan's heightened emotional sensitivity means the least provocation sets off strong feelings, heavenly or hellish.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, what does Goleman conclude from Diener's spectrum about people who notice their emotions more?
questions.a: Emotional life is richer for those who notice more. But the same enhanced sensitivity means that for them the least provocation unleashes emotional storms, whether heavenly or hellish. At the other extreme, people barely feel anything even in the most dire circumstances, so for some emotional awareness is overwhelming while for others it barely exists.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, the emotional flatness of Gary the surgeon exemplifies what psychiatrists call ____.
questions.explain: Gary had no words for his feelings and did not know what he felt, the defining features of alexithymia.

questions.q: Put these moments in the account of Gary, the man without feelings in Chapter 4, in order.
items: Ellen is infuriated by Gary's emotional flatness
Gary sees a therapist at Ellen's insistence
Gary admits he has no strong feelings to talk about
His therapist remarks that such people bore everybody
questions.explain: Ellen's frustration drives Gary into therapy, where he confesses his emotional blankness and the therapist explains why wives send such men for treatment.

questions.q: According to Chapter 4, why could Gary not speak openly about his feelings with anyone in his life?
options: He was ashamed of how intense his feelings were
He had been taught as a child never to show emotion
He believed feelings had no place in a surgeon's life
He did not know what he felt in the first place
questions.explain: Gary confided to his therapist that he did not know what he felt; so far as he could tell he had no angers, sadnesses or joys. Shame or upbringing are not the reasons the book gives.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, match each Greek element of the word alexithymia with its meaning.
questions.explain: Put together, the roots mean a lack of words for emotion, which is exactly the alexithymic's difficulty.

questions.q: According to Chapter 4, who coined the term alexithymia, and when?
options: John Mayer, a psychologist at the University of New Hampshire, in 1990
Peter Sifneos, a Harvard psychiatrist, in 1972
Antonio Damasio, a neurologist, in 1972
Sigmund Freud, while treating untreatable patients
questions.explain: Dr. Peter Sifneos, a Harvard psychiatrist, coined the term in 1972. Psychoanalysts had first noticed such patients, but the name is Sifneos's.

questions.q: Which of these does Chapter 4 list among the clinical features of alexithymics?
options: Difficulty describing feelings, their own or anyone else's
A sharply limited emotional vocabulary
Trouble telling emotion apart from bodily sensation
A vivid and elaborate fantasy life
Crying often and knowing exactly why
questions.explain: Alexithymics struggle to describe feelings, have few words for them, and might report butterflies or palpitations without knowing they are anxious. They report no fantasies, and when they do cry they are bewildered about why.

questions.q: True or false: In Chapter 4, alexithymics were first noticed by psychoanalysts, who found them untreatable because they reported no feelings, no fantasies and colorless dreams.
questions.explain: Such patients had no inner emotional life to talk about, so the psychoanalytic method could not work with them.

questions.q: True or false: In Chapter 4, Goleman concludes that alexithymics never feel emotions at all.
questions.explain: Goleman says it is not that alexithymics never feel, but that they cannot know, and especially cannot put into words, precisely what they feel.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, what does the alexithymic woman who cried herself to sleep after a movie reveal about the condition?
questions.a: She was deeply upset by a film about a mother of eight dying of cancer, yet sat bewildered when her therapist linked it to her own mother's dying of cancer. Asked how she felt, she could only say “awful.” She shows that alexithymics do feel, but experience feelings as a baffling bundle of distress they cannot identify or name.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, mistaking an emotional ache for a physical one, as alexithymics often do, is called ____.
questions.explain: Somaticizing is the alexithymic's confusion of emotional distress with medical complaints; it differs from psychosomatic disease, where emotional problems cause genuine medical ones.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, match each term with its meaning.
pairs: Mistaking an emotional ache for a physical one
Emotional problems causing genuine medical ones
Knowing what we feel as emotions roil within us
questions.explain: Goleman separates somaticizing, a misreading of feelings as symptoms, from psychosomatic disease, where the medical problem is real, and sets both against self-awareness, which alexithymics lack.

questions.q: Since losing his job, Tom has seen several doctors about a churning stomach, palpitations and dizziness, but no medical cause is found and he insists he is not worried. What does Chapter 4 suggest is happening?
options: He has a psychosomatic disease in which stress has caused real organ damage
He is a vigilant type amplifying a real illness by attending to it
He is engulfed by a mood he knows well but cannot escape
He may be somaticizing, mistaking unrecognized anxiety for a physical illness
questions.explain: Goleman notes that alexithymics may report butterflies, palpitations, sweating and dizziness without knowing they feel anxious, and pursue fruitless medical diagnosis for what is an emotional problem.

questions.q: According to Chapter 4, why is much of the psychiatric interest in alexithymics focused on identifying them among people who visit doctors?
options: Because they are prone to lengthy, fruitless pursuit of medical treatment for an emotional problem
Because they are unusually likely to develop genuine heart disease
Because they tend to exaggerate their symptoms to obtain disability benefits
Because their limited vocabulary makes them unable to describe any symptoms
questions.explain: Alexithymics complain of vague medical problems when they are in emotional distress, so psychiatry wants to weed them out to spare them a long and futile search for a medical diagnosis.

questions.q: What cause for alexithymia does Dr. Peter Sifneos propose in Chapter 4?
options: An overactive amygdala that floods the neocortex with feeling
A childhood in which emotions were never discussed
A disconnection between the limbic system and the neocortex, especially its verbal centers
Damage to the language areas that leaves feelings intact but speech impaired
questions.explain: Sifneos proposes a limbic-neocortical disconnection, so that although the emotional brain reacts with feelings, the neocortex cannot sort them out and add the nuance of language.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, what evidence from seizure patients supports Sifneos's view of alexithymia?
questions.a: Patients with severe seizures who had the connection between the limbic system and the neocortex surgically severed became emotionally flat, like alexithymics. They could not put their feelings into words and suddenly lost their fantasy life. This fits the idea that the emotional brain may still react with feelings while the neocortex cannot sort them out and name them.

questions.q: In Chapter 4's account of the alexithymic's dilemma, put these steps in order.
items: The emotional brain reacts with feelings
The disconnected neocortex cannot sort the feelings out
No nuance of language is added to them
The person cannot make the feelings their own
questions.explain: Feelings arise in the limbic circuits, but without the neocortex's sorting and naming they stay wordless, and having no words for feelings means not owning them.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, Goleman quotes Henry Roth's novel ____ on the power of language: if you could put words to what you felt, it was yours.
questions.explain: Roth's line, from Call It Sleep, frames the alexithymic's dilemma: having no words for feelings means not making them your own.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, how does Henry Roth's observation about words and feelings capture the alexithymic's dilemma?
questions.a: Roth wrote, “If you could put words to what you felt, it was yours.” Goleman draws the corollary that having no words for feelings means not making the feelings your own. Alexithymics feel, but because their neocortex cannot name what the emotional brain produces, their feelings remain a baffling distress rather than something they know and own.

questions.q: Put these events in the story of Elliot from Chapter 4 in order.
items: A tumor behind his forehead is surgically removed
He undergoes a drastic personality change and cannot hold a job
His wife leaves and he squanders his savings
He consults a neurologist hoping for disability benefits
Damasio finds him oblivious to his own feelings
questions.explain: After the successful surgery Elliot's working and personal life collapsed; only when he sought a neurological diagnosis did Damasio notice what was missing.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, the neurologist who examined Elliot after his tumor surgery was Antonio ____.
questions.explain: Antonio Damasio saw that nothing was wrong with Elliot's logic, memory or attention, but he was virtually oblivious to his feelings.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, sort these into what remained intact in Elliot after surgery and what was impaired.

items.t: His logic
His memory
His attention
His sense of priority
Awareness of his own feelings
Ability to choose among options

questions.explain: Extensive intellectual tests found nothing wrong with Elliot; what he lost was feeling awareness, and with it priorities and the capacity to decide.

questions.q: True or false: In Chapter 4, Damasio felt more upset by Elliot's story than Elliot himself did.
questions.explain: Elliot narrated his losses with complete dispassion, without regret, sadness or anger, so his own tragedy brought him no pain.

questions.q: According to Damasio in Chapter 4, what did the removal of part of Elliot's prefrontal lobes do?
options: It severed ties between the amygdala and related circuits and the thinking neocortex
It destroyed the amygdala, so Elliot could no longer feel anything
It damaged his language areas, so he could feel but not name feelings
It weakened his memory, so he forgot what had happened to him
questions.explain: The surgery cut the links between the lower emotional centers, especially the amygdala, and the neocortex's thinking abilities; his memory and other cognitive abilities were intact.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, what does Goleman mean by saying that Elliot's thinking had become computerlike?
options: He could calculate faster than before but made careless errors
He could follow rules only when they were written down for him
He answered questions mechanically without understanding them
He could work through every step of a decision but could not assign values to the options
questions.explain: Elliot's reasoning could map the calculus of a decision but gave every possibility the same weight: “Every option was neutral.”

questions.q: In Chapter 4, match each part of Elliot's story with what it showed.
pairs: Lost in minor details, with no sense of priority
Recounted his losses with no regret or anger
Found reasons for and against every date but had no preference
Found nothing wrong with his mental faculties
questions.explain: Each episode points to the same deficit: intact reasoning with no awareness of feeling to give choices their value.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, what did Elliot's struggle to set a date for his next appointment with Damasio reveal?
questions.a: Elliot could find perfectly good arguments for and against every date and time Damasio proposed, but could not choose among them. Rationally every option was defensible; what he lacked was any sense of how he felt about the times. Without awareness of his feelings he had no preferences at all, showing that even mundane decisions depend on feeling.

questions.q: True or false: In Chapter 4, Goleman argues that strong feelings never disturb reasoning and that only a lack of feeling harms decisions.
questions.explain: Goleman grants that strong feelings can create havoc in reasoning; his point is that the lack of awareness of feeling can also be ruinous.

questions.q: Which of these decisions does Chapter 4 give as examples that cannot be made well through sheer rationality?
options: What career to pursue
Whom to date or marry
Which apartment to rent or house to buy
How to solve a problem in formal logic
Which arithmetic answer is correct
questions.explain: Goleman lists life's personal decisions, such as career, partner and home, as needing gut feeling; formal logic alone, he says, can never be the basis for such choices.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, why does Goleman say personal decisions such as whom to marry need gut feeling?
questions.a: Such decisions cannot be made well through sheer rationality; they require gut feeling and the emotional wisdom built from past experience. Formal logic alone can never decide whom to marry or trust or what job to take, since “these are realms where reason without feeling is blind.” Elliot shows that reasoning without awareness of feeling leaves every option neutral.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, Damasio calls the limbic-driven surges from the viscera that guide our choices “somatic ____”.
questions.explain: Somatic markers are, literally, gut feelings: automatic signals from the body that steer us toward or away from a course of action.

questions.q: According to Chapter 4, what does a somatic marker typically do?
options: It recalls in detail the past experience that taught us a lesson
It acts as an automatic alarm drawing attention to a potential danger in a course of action
It calms the amygdala so that the neocortex can reason clearly
It weighs every option equally so no choice is favored
questions.explain: The marker is an automatic alarm, usually warning of danger, though it can also flag a golden opportunity. We typically do not recall the specific experiences behind it; the signal alone is enough.

questions.q: In Chapter 4's account of how somatic markers aid a decision, put these steps in order.
items: Several possible courses of action are considered
A gut feeling rises up about one option
That avenue is dropped or pursued with greater confidence
The choices are pared down to a manageable decision matrix
questions.explain: The gut signal lets us quickly discard or embrace an option, shrinking the array of choices to something we can decide among.

questions.q: Priya has two job offers whose pro-and-con lists balance exactly, but she notices a sinking feeling each time she pictures the first office. How would Chapter 4 advise her to treat that feeling?
options: Ignore it, since only formal logic can be trusted with career choices
Wait until she can recall exactly which past experience produced it
Treat it as a signal worth heeding that can pare down her choices
Recognize it as somaticizing and seek a medical explanation
questions.explain: The sinking feeling is a somatic marker; Goleman says we need not recall its source, and that being attuned to such feelings is the key to sounder personal decision-making.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, how do somatic markers make decision-making more manageable?
questions.a: Somatic markers are limbic-driven gut feelings that act as an automatic alarm, usually warning that a course of action could be disastrous, though sometimes flagging an opportunity. We need not recall what experiences formed the feeling; the signal is enough. When one rises, we can drop or pursue that option with more confidence, paring our choices to a manageable set. So the key to sounder decisions is being attuned to our feelings.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, what conclusion does Goleman draw from Elliot's case using the logic of neuroscience?
options: That the relative strength of the same circuits in intact brains should yield differing levels of emotional self-awareness
That emotional self-awareness is either fully present or wholly absent in each person
That prefrontal damage is the only cause of poor emotional awareness
That emotional self-awareness can be measured reliably by intelligence tests
questions.explain: If losing a circuit causes a deficit, then variations in that circuit in intact brains should produce a spectrum of ability, so some people more easily detect the stirring of fear or joy than others.

questions.q: Which of these does Chapter 4 name as special symbolic modes of the emotional mind?
options: Metaphor and simile
Dreams
Formal logic
Myths
Statistical tables
questions.explain: Metaphor, simile, poetry, song and fable are “the language of the heart,” as are dreams and myths, whose narratives follow loose associations; formal logic is not.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, who does Goleman expect to be more adept at articulating the messages of the emotional mind, and why?
questions.a: People with a natural attunement to their own heart's voice, the language of emotion expressed in metaphor, poetry, song, fable, dreams and myth. Such inner attunement makes them better at giving voice to the felt meanings of dreams and fantasies, so they are likely to excel as novelists, songwriters or psychotherapists. This talent for introspection may hinge on the same prefrontal circuitry.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, Goleman notes that Howard Gardner's model for intrapsychic intelligence is Sigmund ____.
questions.explain: Freud, the great mapper of the psyche's secret dynamics, made clear that much of emotional life is unconscious, so self-awareness is fundamental to psychological insight.

questions.q: True or false: In Chapter 4, experiments on unconscious emotion found that people form definite likings for things they do not even realize they have seen before.
questions.explain: Goleman offers this finding as empirical support for Freud's axiom that much of emotional life is unconscious.

questions.q: In the Chapter 4 experiment with people who fear snakes, what did skin sensors show when snake pictures were flashed too quickly to be consciously seen?
options: No reaction, since an unseen picture cannot trigger emotion
Sweat signaling anxiety, even though the people said they felt no fear
A calming response, because the brief image reassured them
Anxiety only in those who could name the picture afterward
questions.explain: Sweat broke out even when people had no conscious idea what they had seen, showing that an emotion's physiological beginnings come before awareness of the feeling.

questions.q: According to Chapter 4, put these stages of an emotion's rise into awareness in order.
items: The physiological beginnings of the emotion occur
Preconscious emotional stirrings continue to build
The stirrings become strong enough to break into awareness
The emotion registers as such in the frontal cortex
questions.explain: The body reacts first, the unconscious stirring grows, and the moment it enters awareness is marked by its registering in the frontal cortex.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, Goleman concludes that there are two levels of emotion: conscious and ____.
questions.explain: Emotions start below awareness and only later break into consciousness, so they exist at both an unconscious and a conscious level.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, sort these into emotion working below awareness or emotion that has registered in awareness.

items.t: Sweat on a snake-fearer shown a flashed picture
Hours of peevish snapping after a rude encounter
Liking something one does not know one has seen
Deciding to shrug off the morning's annoyance
Thinking clearly that this is anger one is feeling

questions.explain: Unconscious emotions shape reactions without our knowledge; once they register in the cortex, we can name them and decide what to do about them.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, what does the example of the man made peevish by a rude encounter early in the day show?
questions.a: Emotions simmering below awareness can powerfully shape how we perceive and react: he takes affront where none is intended and snaps at people, oblivious to his irritability. Once the reaction is brought into awareness and registers in the cortex, he can evaluate things anew, shrug off the earlier feelings and change his mood. Self-awareness is thus the building block for shaking off a bad mood.

questions.q: Leo has snapped at his family all evening after a stressful commute, without noticing it, until his partner points it out. According to Chapter 4, what becomes possible once his irritation registers in awareness?
options: Nothing, since unconscious emotions cannot be influenced once formed
He will inevitably feel the irritation more intensely and for longer
He can evaluate things anew, decide to shrug off the feeling and change his mood
He will begin somaticizing the irritation as a physical complaint
questions.explain: Goleman's rude-encounter example shows that once a lingering reaction registers in the cortex, a person can reassess and shake it off, which is why self-awareness underlies mood management.

questions.q: In Chapter 4, Goleman says Socrates's injunction to know thyself speaks to the ____ of emotional intelligence: awareness of one's own feelings as they occur.
questions.explain: Goleman calls awareness of one's own feelings as they occur the keystone of emotional intelligence, the piece the other abilities rest on.

questions.q: Which of these does Chapter 4 say about unconscious emotions?
options: The physiological beginnings of an emotion typically come before conscious awareness of it
Emotions below the threshold of awareness can powerfully shape how we perceive and react
Only fear, among the emotions, can operate unconsciously
An emotion below awareness has no effect until it is noticed
questions.explain: Goleman says any emotion can be unconscious, and that emotions simmering beneath awareness shape our reactions even though we have no idea they are at work.

questions.q: Put these parts of Chapter 4 in the order Goleman presents them.
items: Mayer's styles of attending to emotions
The vigilant versus distracting stances and Diener's intensity spectrum
Gary and the condition of alexithymia
Elliot and Damasio's somatic markers
Unconscious emotion and its rise into awareness
questions.explain: The chapter defines self-awareness and its styles, surveys differences in emotional intensity, examines two cases of missing feeling awareness, and ends with emotions below awareness.

questions.q: Match each chapter of Part Two with the domain of emotional intelligence it takes up, as announced in Chapter 3.
questions.explain: Chapter 3 lists Salovey's five domains and promises a chapter for each; Chapter 4 takes the first, self-awareness, which the others build on.

questions.q: Which of these abilities does the book say build on the self-awareness examined in Chapter 4?
options: Managing emotions, such as shaking off a bad mood
Empathy, recognizing emotions in others
Raw academic intelligence as measured by IQ
The amygdala's instant alarm response
questions.explain: Chapter 3 describes managing emotions and empathy as abilities that build on self-awareness, and Chapter 4 ends by calling self-awareness the building block of shaking off a bad mood. IQ and the amygdala's alarm are not built on it.

questions.q: Chapter 4 surveys a spectrum of emotional awareness. Sort these cases into too little feeling awareness or overwhelming emotional intensity.

items.t: Gary, the surgeon with no words for his feelings
Elliot, who recounted his losses without regret
The student who walked calmly to a dorm fire
The woman distraught for days over a lost pen
The vigilant flyer who amplifies her own alarm

questions.explain: The chapter sets cases where feeling barely registers against cases where emotional awareness is overwhelming, to show that self-awareness lies between the extremes.

questions.q: How does the end of Chapter 4 prepare for the chapter that follows it?
questions.a: Chapter 4 closes by showing that once a lingering irritation is brought into awareness, a person can shake it off, so emotional self-awareness is the building block of the next fundamental, “being able to shake off a bad mood.” Chapter 5, Passion's Slaves, takes up that next domain, managing emotions, which Chapter 3 had said builds on self-awareness.

questions.q: In the epigraph to Goleman's chapter on managing emotions, what quality does Hamlet praise in his friend Horatio?
questions.explain: Hamlet wants the man who is not ruled by his passions and takes good and bad fortune evenly. That is self-mastery, the chapter's theme, not the absence of feeling.
options: Taking Fortune's blows and rewards with equal thanks, as one who is not passion's slave
Feeling every passion more deeply and openly than other men do
Showing no feeling at all, whether Fortune brings blows or rewards
Avenging every blow of Fortune swiftly and without hesitation

questions.q: What did the beeper studies of mood find about the link between grades or IQ and emotional well-being?
questions.explain: The studies found little or no relationship between grades or IQ and well-being, affirming that emotional intelligence is independent of academic intelligence.
options: High IQ strongly predicted greater well-being
There was little or no relationship between them
High grades predicted more frequent bad moods
Well-being rose steadily with years of schooling

questions.q: According to the theory Goleman attributes to psychoanalytic thinkers such as John Bowlby and D. W. Winnicott, how do emotionally sound infants learn to soothe themselves?
questions.explain: The theory holds that infants who have been soothed by caretakers learn to treat themselves the same way, which leaves them less vulnerable to upheavals of the emotional brain.
options: By being left alone to cry until they settle on their own
By copying the moods of their brothers and sisters
By treating themselves as their caretakers have treated them
By an inborn reflex that needs no learning at all

questions.q: What problem with manic-depression does Goleman point out regarding getting help?
questions.explain: Two thirds of sufferers have never been treated, and during mania people feel so overly confident that they see no need for help despite disastrous decisions.
options: Lithium and newer medications have no effect on the cycle of moods
Most people with the disorder are treated but stop their medication
The depressive phase makes people too ashamed to describe symptoms
In the throes of mania, people feel so confident that they see no need for help

questions.q: A bill collector deliberately works himself into a rage before phoning people who will not pay. In Diane Tice's findings, what does this illustrate?
questions.explain: Tice found some people seek unpleasant moods for pragmatic reasons; Goleman calls the bill collectors who work up a rage to be firmer with deadbeats positively Machiavellian.
options: A purposive cultivation of an unpleasant mood for a practical end
A mood purist who refuses to change any feeling
An emotional hijacking that the collector cannot control
A failed attempt to escape a foul mood by distraction

questions.q: After a draining day, Priya settles in to read a novel and then phones a cheerful friend. In Goleman's terms, what is she mostly doing?
questions.explain: Goleman notes that much of what we do, especially in free time, from reading a novel to choosing companions, is an attempt to manage mood and make ourselves feel better.
options: Suppressing her emotions so that she feels nothing
Managing her mood, which much of our free time is spent doing
Cultivating a bad mood for a practical purpose
Showing the dullness of emotions that are too muted

questions.q: True or false: Goleman reports that for most people extremely intense feelings are relatively rare, with most of us in a gray middle range of mild bumps.
questions.explain: Averaged over weeks or months, moods reflect overall well-being, and for most people intense feelings are rare; most fall into the gray middle range.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman reports that about two thirds of those who suffer from manic-depression have been treated successfully with lithium.
questions.explain: The figure is the reverse of success: two thirds of those with manic-depression have never been treated, even though lithium or newer drugs can thwart the cycle.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman holds up being happy all the time as the ideal of emotional well-being.
questions.explain: He says constant happiness suggests the blandness of 1970s smiley-face badges; downs as well as ups spice life, and suffering can even temper the soul.

questions.q: True or false: In the beeper studies, people who had strong episodes of anger or depression could still feel a sense of well-being if they had a countervailing set of equally happy times.
questions.explain: The point of the studies is balance: stormy feelings need not be avoided, only kept from going unchecked and displacing all pleasant moods.

questions.q: The Romans and the early Christian church called self-mastery ____, the restraining of emotional excess.
questions.explain: Goleman notes the Greek word sophrosyne and its Roman and church equivalent temperantia, or temperance, the restraining of emotional excess.

questions.q: In Diane Tice's survey, about 5 percent of people were ____ purists, who said they never try to change how they feel.
questions.explain: Tice called them mood purists: they hold that all emotions are natural and should be experienced just as they present themselves.

questions.q: Goleman calls the art of ____ ourselves a fundamental life skill, one that Bowlby and Winnicott saw as among the most essential psychic tools.
questions.explain: He writes that “The art of soothing ourselves is a fundamental life skill,” learned in infancy from how caretakers treat us.

questions.q: The ancient Greek word for self-mastery, the virtue of not being passion's slave, was ____.
questions.explain: Sophrosyne was the Greek word; Page DuBois translates it as care and intelligence in conducting one's life, a tempered balance and wisdom.

questions.q: Which of these did Diane Tice find among people who regularly sought out unpleasant moods for pragmatic reasons?
options: Physicians making themselves somber to give patients bad news
Comedians making themselves sad to sharpen their timing
Surgeons working up fear to keep their hands steady
Bill collectors working up a rage to be firmer with deadbeats
Social activists nurturing their outrage at injustice
questions.explain: Tice's examples were physicians, activists, bill collectors and a young man who worked up anger to help his brother with bullies. Comedians and surgeons are not in her findings.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman name as what emotions become when they are out of control, too extreme and persistent?
options: Immobilizing depression
Bland, constant cheerfulness
Overwhelming anxiety
Dullness and distance
Raging anger
questions.explain: Emotions out of control become pathological, as in immobilizing depression, overwhelming anxiety, raging anger and manic agitation. Dullness and distance come instead from emotions that are too muted.

questions.q: Match each source to what Goleman draws from it about self-mastery.
pairs: Praise for the man who is not passion's slave
Translation of sophrosyne as a tempered balance and wisdom
The Romans and early Christian church
Temperantia, the restraining of emotional excess
Emotion that is appropriate, proportionate to circumstance
questions.explain: Each source adds to the same ideal: Hamlet's epigraph, DuBois's translation of the Greek, the Latin temperantia, and Aristotle's call for appropriate emotion.

questions.q: Sort these into what Goleman says happens when emotions are too muted versus too extreme and persistent.

items.t: Dullness
Distance from others
A dull wasteland of neutrality
Immobilizing depression
Raging anger
Manic agitation
Overwhelming anxiety

questions.explain: Muted emotions create dullness and distance, and a life without passion is a wasteland of neutrality; emotions out of control become pathological states like depression, rage, mania and anxiety.

questions.q: Put in order the steps in the theory, attributed to Bowlby and Winnicott, of how emotionally sound infants come to soothe themselves.
items: Caretakers soothe the infant when it is upset
The infant learns to treat itself as its caretakers treated it
The child is left less vulnerable to upheavals of the emotional brain
questions.explain: The theory runs from the caretakers' soothing, to the infant internalizing that treatment, to lower vulnerability to the emotional brain's upheavals.

questions.q: Why does Goleman say the goal of emotional self-mastery is balance rather than suppression of feeling?
questions.a: Every feeling has its value and significance, and a life without passion would be a dull wasteland of neutrality. What Aristotle asked for is appropriate emotion, proportionate to circumstance. Muted emotions bring dullness and distance, while emotions too extreme and persistent become pathological, so the aim is keeping distressing emotions in check, not eliminating them.

questions.q: What did the beeper studies of mood show about the role of unpleasant feelings in a person's overall well-being?
questions.a: People carried beepers and recorded their moods at random times. Well-being depended on the ratio of positive to negative emotions, not on avoiding unpleasant feelings. Even people with strong bouts of anger or depression felt well if equally happy times balanced them; the danger is stormy feelings going unchecked and displacing all pleasant moods.

questions.q: Why does Goleman treat recognizing the need for medication as a possible sign of emotional self-regulation?
questions.a: When emotions are of great intensity and linger, they shade into extremes such as chronic anxiety, uncontrollable rage or depression, which may be too strong to overcome without drugs. Recognizing when chronic agitation of the emotional brain needs pharmacologic help is itself good self-management. Manic-depression shows the danger of not seeing this: in mania people feel too confident to seek any help.

questions.q: What did Diane Tice's survey of more than four hundred people conclude overall about how well we manage ordinary bad moods?
questions.a: For the usual range of bad moods we are left to our own devices, and those devices are not always effective. Apart from a few mood purists and people who cultivated unpleasant moods for practical ends, most people complained of being at the mercy of their moods, and their track records at shaking bad moods were decidedly mixed.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman name as everyday ways people try to manage their mood?
options: Refusing to feel any emotion at all
Watching television
Choosing the activities and companions we spend time with
Deliberately recalling past humiliations
Reading a novel
questions.explain: Much of what we do, especially in free time, is an attempt to manage mood, from novels and TV to the activities and companions we choose.

questions.q: Sort these aspects of an emotion by how much say Goleman says we have over them.

items.t: When we are swept by an emotion
Which emotion sweeps over us
How long the emotion lasts
Whether we keep stoking it with brooding thoughts
