Whether we seek help when it becomes chronic

questions.explain: The design of the brain gives us little control over when or which emotion strikes, but we can influence how long it lasts, including by how we think and whether we get help.

questions.q: In Goleman's freeway example, after another car cuts dangerously close, what matters most for the trajectory of rage?
questions.explain: Goleman says it matters immensely whether the reflexive thought is followed by more thoughts of outrage and revenge; that chain builds rage, while a charitable thought cuts it short.
options: Whether the other driver can be seen and identified clearly
How fast both cars were travelling at the moment of the near miss
Whether the first angry thought is followed by more thoughts of outrage and revenge
Whether the angry driver has had a hard day at work beforehand

questions.q: According to Goleman, which part of the brain most likely foments calculated angers such as cool-headed revenge or outrage at injustice?
questions.explain: The amygdala may be the main source of the sudden spark of rage, but the neocortex most likely foments more calculated angers, which are the ones most likely to seem to have good reasons.
options: The amygdala
The hippocampus
The brainstem
The neocortex

questions.q: In Diane Tice's survey, which mood were people worst at controlling?
questions.explain: Tice found anger is the mood people are worst at controlling; Goleman calls rage the most intransigent of the moods people want to escape.
options: Anger
Sadness
Anxiety
Boredom

questions.q: Why does Goleman call anger the most seductive of the negative emotions?
questions.explain: The self-righteous monologue fills the mind with convincing arguments for venting rage, and unlike sadness anger is energizing, even exhilarating.
options: It is the emotion most often praised by others as a sign of strength
Its self-righteous inner monologue supplies convincing arguments for venting, and it is energizing
It passes quickly, so people feel there is no cost in indulging it
It lowers arousal and so feels calming, unlike sadness or fear

questions.q: According to Zillmann, how is endangerment that triggers anger most often signaled?
questions.explain: Endangerment can be physical, but more often it is symbolic: being treated unjustly or rudely, insulted or demeaned, or frustrated in pursuing an important goal.
options: By an outright physical threat such as an attack or a near miss
By sudden loud noises or other startling sensory events
By a symbolic threat to self-esteem or dignity, such as being insulted or treated unjustly
By the loss of a close relationship or a loved one

questions.q: Why are people so much more prone to anger if they have already been provoked or irritated by something else, according to Zillmann?
questions.explain: Adrenocortical arousal can last hours or even days, creating a hair-trigger condition; stress of all sorts lowers the threshold for what provokes anger.
options: The catecholamine rush from the first provocation lasts for days
Earlier irritation uses up the energy needed to stay calm
The neocortex shuts down after any provocation until the next morning
Adrenocortical arousal from the earlier stress lingers and lowers the threshold for anger

questions.q: In Goleman's supermarket scene, why does the young mother explode when the baby drops the jelly jar?
questions.explain: Zillmann finds that when the body is already in a state of edginess, a new trigger produces an emotion of especially great intensity; the jar landed on anger already building.
options: She was already edgy from the struggle with her son, so the new trigger produced especially intense anger
The broken jar was a direct physical threat to her children's safety
She was a mood purist who never tried to change her feelings
Her anger was a calculated neocortical response to public embarrassment

questions.q: According to Zillmann, what does the high level of excitation at the peak of rage foster?
questions.explain: Zillmann says peak excitation fosters an illusion of power and invulnerability; failing cognitive guidance, the enraged person falls back on primitive responses.
options: A sudden insight into the other person's point of view
An illusion of power and invulnerability that may facilitate aggression
Exhaustion that makes violence very unlikely
A heightened ability to weigh consequences

questions.q: Why does Zillmann call distraction a highly powerful mood-altering device for anger?
questions.explain: Zillmann's simple reason is that “It's hard to stay angry when we're having a pleasant time,” though anger first has to cool enough for that to be possible.
options: Because it releases the anger through a safe outlet
Because it lets the person rehearse what to say later
Because it is hard to stay angry while having a pleasant time
Because it raises arousal enough to burn the anger off

questions.q: In Diane Tice's findings on cooling down alone, what did a large proportion of men do?
questions.explain: Many men translated going off alone into going for a drive, which gave Tice pause and inspired her to drive more defensively; a long walk may be safer.
options: Go for a long walk
Go to the gym
Go to a bar
Go for a drive

questions.q: Redford Williams worked to help hostile people control their irritability. Why were these people a particular concern?
questions.explain: Williams, a Duke psychiatrist, sought to help hostile people, who are at higher risk for heart disease, to control their irritability.
options: Hostile people are at higher risk for heart disease
Hostile people are more likely to become depressed
Hostile people are more often in car accidents
Hostile people are more prone to insomnia

questions.q: What did psychologists find when they began testing catharsis experimentally in the 1950s?
questions.explain: Time after time, experiments found that venting “did little or nothing to dispel it,” though because anger is seductive it may feel satisfying.
options: Venting anger reliably reduced it, as the popular theory held
Giving vent to anger did little or nothing to dispel it, though it may feel satisfying
Venting anger helped only when done in writing
Venting anger reduced it in men but not in women

questions.q: Dev is furious that a colleague ignored his email, but he is only moderately annoyed when a coworker mentions the colleague has just learned of a family emergency. What does Zillmann's research predict?
questions.explain: Zillmann finds mitigating information works well at moderate levels of anger; only at high rage does cognitive incapacitation make it useless.
options: The information will make no difference, since all anger is cognitively incapacitating
The information will make Dev angrier, since it seems like an excuse
The information will likely ease Dev's anger, since he is only moderately angry
The information will help only after Dev has vented his anger

questions.q: Two partners are in a heated argument that keeps escalating. Following Zillmann's second way of de-escalating anger, what should one of them do?
questions.explain: Cooling off means waiting out the adrenal surge away from further triggers, such as getting away from the other person; rehearsing angry arguments would only re-trigger the cycle.
options: Stay and say everything on their mind so the anger is vented
Keep arguing calmly until the other person admits fault
Go off alone and rehearse the arguments for being right
Leave for a while to a setting without further triggers and wait out the adrenal surge

questions.q: Leah is outraged by a rude customer and decides to cool off by going to the mall, where she replays the insult while browsing. What does Tice's research suggest?
questions.explain: A cooling-down period fails if used to pursue anger-inducing thoughts; Tice found shopping and eating do little because the indignant thoughts carry on.
options: Her anger will likely persist, because shopping lets her angry train of thought continue
Her anger will quickly fade, because treats are the best cure for anger
Her anger will turn into sadness, because she is alone
Her anger will vanish, because any time away from the trigger works

questions.q: True or false: Goleman reports that research supports the common view that venting anger in catharsis is all to the good.
questions.explain: He says a careful reading of research suggests the common attitudes toward anger, including that catharsis is good, are misguided if not outright myths.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says that, unlike sadness, anger is energizing, even exhilarating.
questions.explain: This energizing quality is part of why anger is the most seductive of the negative emotions and why people find it hard to control.

questions.q: True or false: According to Zillmann, the adrenocortical arousal of anger fades within a few minutes, much faster than the catecholamine rush.
questions.explain: It is the other way round: the catecholamine rush lasts minutes, while adrenocortical arousal can last hours and even days.

questions.q: True or false: According to Zillmann, mitigating information can completely short-circuit anger if it comes before the anger is acted on.
questions.explain: Timing matters, and the earlier in the cycle the better; anger can be completely short-circuited if the mitigating information comes before it is acted on.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman notes there may be specific conditions under which lashing out in anger works, such as when it is expressed directly to its target and rights an injustice.
questions.explain: He lists conditions such as expressing it directly to the target, restoring control or righting an injustice, but warns this may be easier said than done.

questions.q: Benjamin Franklin is quoted as saying that anger is never without a ____, but seldom a good one.
questions.explain: Franklin's line, “Anger is never without a reason, but seldom a good one,” captures how often anger surges past what is appropriate.

questions.q: Goleman writes that the longer we ruminate about what made us angry, the more reasons we invent: '____ fuels anger's flames.'
questions.explain: He writes “Brooding fuels anger's flames,” while seeing things differently douses them.

questions.q: In the first part of the limbic surge of anger, the release of ____ generates a quick, episodic rush of energy lasting minutes.
questions.explain: Catecholamines give the brief burst of energy for fight or flight, separate from the longer adrenocortical background arousal.

questions.q: The longer-lasting background readiness for anger, which can last hours or days, comes from the ____ branch of the nervous system.
questions.explain: An amygdala-driven ripple through the adrenocortical branch creates a tonic background of action readiness that outlasts the catecholamine surge.

questions.q: Zillmann's term for the state in which highly enraged people can no longer think straight is cognitive ____.
questions.explain: Cognitive incapacitation explains why mitigating information helps at moderate anger but makes no difference at high rage.

questions.q: Giving vent to rage, sometimes extolled as a way of handling anger, is called ____.
questions.explain: Goleman calls the belief that venting rage helps the ventilation fallacy; experiments since the 1950s found catharsis did little or nothing to dispel anger.

questions.q: Asked how best to handle anger, the Tibetan teacher Chogyam Trungpa replied: 'Don't suppress it. But don't ____ on it.'
questions.explain: Trungpa's advice, “Don't suppress it. But don't act on it,” sums up the middle path between suppression and venting.

questions.q: Redford Williams recommends using self-awareness to catch cynical or hostile thoughts as they arise and ____ them down.
questions.explain: Once captured in writing, angry thoughts can be challenged and reappraised, though this works better before anger escalates to rage.

questions.q: Which of these common views about anger does Goleman say research shows to be misguided, if not outright myths?
options: That reframing a situation can defuse anger
That venting anger in catharsis is all to the good
That anger can be prevented entirely
That anger is uncontrollable
That cooling off physiologically can ease anger
questions.explain: The myths are that anger is uncontrollable or should not be controlled, that catharsis is good, and that anger can be prevented entirely. Reframing and cooling off are the remedies the research supports.

questions.q: Which of these are the two main ways Zillmann sees of intervening in anger?
options: Cooling off physiologically by waiting out the adrenal surge
Venting the anger directly at the person who caused it
Challenging the thoughts that trigger the surges of anger
Suppressing all signs of anger until it disappears
questions.explain: Zillmann's two ways are to seize on and challenge the triggering thoughts, and to cool down physiologically away from further triggers. Venting and suppression are not his remedies.

questions.q: Which of these are conditions Goleman lists under which lashing out in anger may actually work?
options: When it is expressed while anger is at its peak
When the angry person feels exhilarated afterwards
When it restores a sense of control or rights an injustice
When it is directed at a bystander rather than the provoker
When it is expressed directly to the person who is its target
questions.explain: The listed conditions include expressing it directly to the target, restoring control or righting an injustice, and inflicting appropriate harm that changes the other's behavior without retaliation.

questions.q: Which of these are examples Zillmann gives of symbolic threats that can signal endangerment and trigger anger?
options: Losing a loved one in an accident
Being frustrated in pursuing an important goal
Hearing a sudden loud noise
Being treated unjustly or rudely
Being insulted or demeaned
questions.explain: Symbolic threats to self-esteem or dignity include injustice, rudeness, insults, being demeaned and frustration of an important goal. Loss is the classic trigger for sadness, not anger.

questions.q: Put the steps of Zillmann's snide-remarks study in the order they happened.
items: A confederate provokes volunteers with snide remarks
Volunteers watch either a pleasant or an upsetting film
Volunteers get the chance to rate the confederate for a job
Those who saw the upsetting film give the worst ratings
questions.explain: Provocation came first, then the film that varied arousal, then the chance to retaliate, with retaliation proportional to arousal from the film.

questions.q: Put the events of Zillmann's exercise-bike experiment, in the version with mitigating information, in order.
items: A rude assistant insults volunteers riding an exercise bike
A second confederate tells him he has a phone call
He makes a snide remark to her as he leaves
She explains he is under pressure about his graduate orals
Volunteers decline to retaliate and express compassion
questions.explain: The mitigating explanation came after the provocation but before the chance to retaliate, which is why it could defuse the volunteers' anger.

questions.q: Put the events of Goleman's supermarket scene in order.
items: The mother tells her son in measured tones to put the box back
The boy whines that he wants it and clings to the cereal box
The baby drops a jar of jelly that shatters on the floor
The mother slaps the baby and rushes off with both children
questions.explain: Anger built step by step: the struggle over the cereal box raised the mother's arousal, so the jelly jar landed on top of it and set off an explosion.

questions.q: Put the stages of escalating rage, as Zillmann describes them, in order.
items: An anger-provoking thought triggers a surge of catecholamines
A second trigger comes before the first surge has subsided
Each wave rides on the last, quickly escalating arousal
Rage, unhampered by reason, erupts in violence
questions.explain: Zillmann sees escalating anger as a sequence of provocations whose slowly dissipating reactions pile up until reason fails and rage erupts.

questions.q: Put the events of the New York cab scene in Goleman's ventilation fallacy section in order.
items: The driver honks at a young man standing in front of the cab
The young man answers with a scowl and an obscene gesture
The driver makes threatening lunges with the cab
The driver shouts a litany of expletives as the cab moves off
The driver says yelling back at least makes you feel better
questions.explain: The scene escalates through honking, insult and threat to a stream of curses, after which the still agitated driver voices the popular theory of catharsis.

questions.q: Match each part of the limbic surge in anger to its feature, as Zillmann describes it.
pairs: A quick rush of energy that lasts minutes
A tonic background of readiness lasting hours or days
Lowers the threshold for what provokes anger
Each builds on the hormonal momentum of those before
questions.explain: The catecholamine surge is brief and repeated surges stack up, while adrenocortical excitation lingers and leaves a hair-trigger readiness for further anger.

questions.q: Match each person to what Goleman quotes or reports from them about anger.
pairs: Anger is never without a reason, but seldom a good one
Do not suppress anger, but do not act on it
Yelling back at least makes you feel better
Escalating anger is a sequence of slowly dissipating provocations
questions.explain: Franklin and Trungpa offer wisdom about anger, the cab driver voices the popular catharsis theory, and Zillmann gives the scientific account of escalation.

questions.q: Match each anger strategy to what Diane Tice found about it.
pairs: Venting at the person who provoked you
Prolongs the angry mood rather than ending it
By and large help calm anger
One of the most potent ways to end anger
questions.explain: Tice found that distraction and reframing work, treats do little because angry thoughts continue, and venting makes anger last longer.

questions.q: Sort these strategies by whether Goleman and Tice found they help to cool anger or not.
groups: Do little or make it worse

items.t: Going for a long walk
Deep breathing and muscle relaxation
Watching TV or a movie
Going off alone to cool down
Shouting at the person who provoked you
Eating a piece of chocolate cake
Shopping for oneself
Brooding over the insult during a break

questions.explain: Walks, relaxation, distraction and time alone cool the body and stop angry thoughts; venting pumps up arousal, and treats or brooding let the angry train of thought run on.

questions.q: Sort these features of anger's physiology into the catecholamine surge or the adrenocortical arousal, as Zillmann describes them.

items.t: A quick, episodic rush of energy
Lasts for minutes
Enough for one course of vigorous action
Lasts for hours and even days
A general tonic background of action readiness
Explains why a hard day at work leads to rage at home

questions.explain: The catecholamine surge is short and readies the body for fight or flight; adrenocortical arousal lingers and lowers the threshold for later anger.

questions.q: Sort these kinds of anger by the brain region Goleman says most likely drives them.

items.t: The sudden spark of rage at a careless driver
An instant flare when shoved in a crowd
Cool-headed revenge
Outrage at unfairness or injustice
A slow, planned grudge against a rival

questions.explain: Goleman links sudden sparks of rage to the amygdala and calculated, thoughtful angers such as revenge or outrage at injustice to the neocortex.

questions.q: In each scenario, someone hears a mitigating explanation for another person's rudeness. Sort them by whether Zillmann's research predicts the explanation will help.

items.t: Mildly irritated, she hears the clerk's child is in hospital
Moderately annoyed, he learns the driver was rushing to an emergency
Before acting, she hears her friend misread her message
Shaking with rage, he is told the neighbor had a bad day
After a long chain of insults, she hears the caller is stressed

questions.explain: Mitigating information works at moderate levels of anger and best early in the cycle; at high rage cognitive incapacitation means it is brushed aside.

questions.q: Why does Goleman describe anger as the most seductive of the negative emotions, and what common views does this help explain?
questions.a: Anger's self-righteous inner monologue fills the mind with the most convincing arguments for venting it, and unlike sadness it is energizing, even exhilarating. This persuasive power may explain why people commonly believe anger is uncontrollable, should not be controlled, or is good to vent in catharsis. Research suggests these views, and the opposite one that anger can be prevented entirely, are myths.

questions.q: Explain Zillmann's account of the two-part limbic surge in anger and how it makes us more prone to anger after an earlier stress.
questions.a: A perceived threat triggers a release of catecholamines, a quick rush of energy lasting minutes, enough for fight or flight. Meanwhile, adrenocortical arousal creates a background of action readiness that can last hours or days. This lingering arousal lowers the threshold for anger, so someone who had a hard day at work may be enraged at home by noisy children who would not normally trigger an emotional hijacking.

questions.q: What does Goleman mean by 'anger builds on anger', and why is a thought late in the buildup so dangerous?
questions.a: Zillmann sees escalating anger as a sequence of provocations, each triggering an excitatory reaction that dissipates slowly. Each angry thought becomes a minitrigger for a new catecholamine surge that rides on the momentum of those before. So a later thought triggers far more anger than the same thought would at the start, until rage, unhampered by reason, can erupt in violence.

questions.q: Why does mitigating information defuse anger at moderate levels but not at the height of rage?
questions.a: Mitigating information allows the angry person to reappraise what happened, as when volunteers learned the rude experimenter was worried about his graduate orals and chose compassion over revenge. But at high levels of rage Zillmann finds cognitive incapacitation: people can no longer think straight and dismiss the information. So timing matters, and the earlier in the anger cycle the better.

questions.q: How does challenging angry thoughts work against anger, according to Zillmann's first way of intervening?
questions.a: The original appraisal of an interaction confirms and encourages the first burst of anger, and later reappraisals fan the flames. By seizing on and challenging those thoughts, a person undercuts the convictions fueling the anger. This works best early in the cycle, and anger can be completely short-circuited if mitigating information comes before it is acted on.

questions.q: Explain what cooling off physiologically involves, and why a cooling-down period can fail.
questions.a: Cooling off means waiting out the adrenal surge in a setting with no further triggers, such as getting away from the other person in an argument, and using distractions to halt the cycle of hostile thought. Walks, exercise and relaxation help shift the body to low arousal. But if the time is spent pursuing the train of angry thought, each thought becomes a fresh trigger and the anger continues.

questions.q: What is the ventilation fallacy, and what did Tice find works better?
questions.a: The fallacy is the popular belief that venting rage, or catharsis, makes you feel better. Since the 1950s experiments have found that venting does little or nothing to dispel anger, and Tice found outbursts pump up arousal and prolong the mood. Far more effective is to cool down first and then confront the person constructively or assertively to settle the dispute.

questions.q: Describe Redford Williams's recommendation for hostile people and its limit.
questions.a: Williams, a Duke psychiatrist, worked with hostile people, who are at higher risk for heart disease. He recommends using self-awareness to catch cynical or hostile thoughts as they arise and writing them down, so they can be challenged and reappraised. As Zillmann found, this works better before anger has escalated to rage.

questions.q: Match each scene or study in Goleman's discussion of anger to the point it illustrates.
pairs: A boy calmed by a long summer walk in 1899
Cooling off by waiting out the adrenal surge
A mother slapping her baby in a supermarket
Anger building on anger already present
A cab driver cursing a pedestrian
The popular but mistaken belief in venting
Volunteers told the rude experimenter faced his orals
questions.explain: Each story carries one lesson: the 1899 walk models cooling off, the supermarket shows escalation, the cab driver voices the ventilation fallacy, and the bike study shows the power of mitigating information.

questions.q: How does Goleman say worries are almost always expressed?
questions.explain: Worries are almost always expressed in words, not images, a fact that matters for controlling worry, because images are stronger triggers of physiological anxiety.
options: In vivid pictures, in the mind's eye
In words, in the mind's ear rather than its eye
In bodily sensations rather than thoughts
In dreams rather than waking thought

questions.q: What did Borkovec find was the main trouble keeping insomniacs awake?
questions.explain: The main trouble was not somatic arousal but intrusive thoughts; they were chronic worriers who could not stop worrying however sleepy they were.
options: Racing hearts and muscle tension rather than thoughts
Vivid catastrophic images rather than words
Intrusive worrying thoughts rather than somatic arousal
Too much caffeine and irregular routines

questions.q: Why does immersion in worried thoughts partially relieve anxiety, according to Borkovec?
questions.explain: Worried thoughts carry attention away from the catastrophic image that triggered the anxiety; since images are stronger triggers than thoughts, the worry is a halfway antidote.
options: Thoughts are more powerful triggers than images, so worry uses up the anxiety
Worry releases calming chemicals once it has run long enough
Worry convinces the person that the danger has been solved
Images are more powerful triggers of physiological anxiety than thoughts, and worry keeps the mind on thoughts

questions.q: What does Goleman mean by the cortical rigidity found in chronic worriers?
questions.explain: Chronic worry repeats the same ideas, and at a neurological level there seems to be a cortical rigidity, a deficit in responding flexibly to change.
options: A deficit in the emotional brain's ability to respond flexibly to changing circumstance
A physical stiffening of the muscles during an anxiety attack
A refusal to take medication for anxiety disorders
An inability to form vivid mental images

questions.q: Why can chronic worriers not follow the common advice to 'just stop worrying'?
questions.explain: Since chronic worries seem to be low-grade amygdala episodes, they come unbidden and by their nature persist once they arise.
options: Chronic worriers do not believe their worries are a problem
Chronic worries are low-grade amygdala episodes that come unbidden and persist
Stopping worry would trigger a full panic attack
Chronic worriers lack the words to describe their worries

questions.q: Why does Borkovec say relaxation is not enough on its own to control worry?
questions.explain: Worriers also need to take a critical stance toward their assumptions; without that, the worry spiral will keep returning.
options: Relaxation raises arousal and so makes worry worse
Relaxation works only for anger, not for worry
Worriers must also actively challenge the worrisome thoughts, or the worry spiral keeps coming back
Relaxation must be combined with venting the anxiety to others

questions.q: For people whose worries have flowered into phobia, obsessive-compulsive disorder or panic disorder, what does Goleman say about medication?
questions.explain: Turning to medication may be prudent and even a sign of self-awareness, but retraining the emotional circuitry through therapy lessens recurrence after medication stops.
options: It is never needed if the person practices relaxation
It is a complete cure that makes therapy unnecessary
It works for panic disorder but not for phobias
It may be prudent, but therapy is still needed to lessen the chance of recurrence

questions.q: Ana lies awake each night replaying money worries, although she is not physically tense. Based on Borkovec's insomnia work, what is most likely to help her sleep?
questions.explain: For Borkovec's insomniacs, the one thing that worked was getting their minds off their worries by focusing on the sensations of a relaxation method.
options: Shifting her attention onto the sensations produced by a relaxation method
Thinking her worries through to the end so they feel finished
Picturing the worst outcome vividly to get it over with
Drinking alcohol to slow her racing heart

questions.q: Tom worries before every flight, and every flight lands safely, so he feels his worrying is somehow keeping him safe. What does Borkovec's analysis say about this?
questions.explain: Since most worries are about events that rarely happen, the worry psychologically gets the credit for preventing the danger, which keeps the habit going.
options: It shows that worry is a constructive rehearsal that really solves problems
It shows how worry is reinforced like a superstition, getting credit for preventing unlikely dangers
It shows that Tom is a repressor who denies his anxiety
It shows that worry works because images calm the body

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says chronic worry has all the attributes of a low-grade emotional hijacking.
questions.explain: Chronic worries come from nowhere, are uncontrollable, generate a steady hum of anxiety, are impervious to reason and lock the worrier into one inflexible view.

questions.q: True or false: Borkovec found that chronic worry typically produces new solutions and fresh ways of seeing a problem.
questions.explain: New solutions do not typically come from worrying, especially chronic worry; worriers instead ruminate on the danger itself, staying in the same rut of thought.

questions.q: True or false: In Borkovec's account, chronic worriers mostly worry about things that have almost no chance of happening.
questions.explain: Chronic worriers worry about a wide range of things, most of which have almost no chance of happening, reading dangers into life that others never notice.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says the challenging strategies in Borkovec's method have never helped anyone whose worry was serious enough for a psychiatric diagnosis.
questions.explain: Even some people whose worrying qualified for a psychiatric diagnosis have been relieved of the worrying habit this way.

questions.q: Imagining some terrible tragedy, as worriers often do in their narratives, is called ____.
questions.explain: Worries typically jump from concern to concern and often include catastrophizing, as in the woman who escalated a one-minute task to never being happy.

questions.q: Anxiety comes in two forms: cognitive, or worrisome thoughts, and ____, the physical symptoms such as sweating and a racing heart.
questions.explain: Researchers distinguish cognitive anxiety from somatic anxiety; Borkovec found insomniacs' main trouble was the cognitive kind.

questions.q: According to Goleman, in all the anxiety disorders the common denominator is worry run ____.
questions.explain: He writes “In all these conditions the common denominator is worry run amok,” with each disorder fixing worry in its own way.

questions.q: Borkovec says chronic worry is reinforcing in the same way that ____ are, with the worry acting like an amulet.
questions.explain: To the primitive limbic brain, worry about unlikely events seems magical, getting credit for preventing the danger it obsesses about.

questions.q: Borkovec found that worry can be a halfway ____ to the very anxiety it evokes, which reinforces the habit.
questions.explain: Immersion in thoughts takes the mind off the catastrophic image, partially relieving anxiety and so reinforcing worry as “a halfway antidote to the very anxiety it evoked.”

questions.q: Goleman calls the combination of catching worries early and questioning them a mix of mindfulness and healthy ____.
questions.explain: This combination of mindfulness and healthy skepticism presumably acts as a brake on the neural activation underlying low-grade anxiety.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman list as attributes that make chronic worry like a low-grade emotional hijacking?
options: They reliably lead to a positive solution
They lock the worrier into a single, inflexible view
They are impervious to reason
They are expressed mainly as vivid images
The worries seem to come from nowhere
questions.explain: Chronic worries are unbidden, uncontrollable, a steady hum of anxiety, impervious to reason and rigid. They are expressed in words, not images, and they rarely reach a solution.

questions.q: Which of these are critical questions Borkovec teaches worriers to ask about their assumptions?
options: How can I stop feeling anything at all?
Is it very probable that the dreaded event will occur?
Who is to blame for this situation?
Are there constructive steps to be taken?
Does it really help to run through these same anxious thoughts?
questions.explain: Borkovec's questions test probability, alternatives, constructive steps and whether repetition helps. Blame and numbing feeling are not part of his method.

questions.q: Which of these did the Los Angeles freelance writer in Goleman's example experience?
options: Rituals of washing her hands twenty times a day
Finding her worries almost addictive
Picturing herself in an accident whenever she had to drive
Catastrophizing that every headache signaled a brain tumor
A sudden fear of dying during panic attacks
questions.explain: Without health insurance, she catastrophized about her health and driving and found her worries almost addictive. The washing rituals belong to the woman with obsessive-compulsive disorder.

questions.q: Which of these are ways Borkovec's strategies are thought to work against worry?
options: They establish mental activity that is incompatible with worry
They let worries repeat until they lose their force
Relaxation counters the anxiety signals the emotional brain sends through the body
They replace worried thoughts with vivid catastrophic images
questions.explain: Actively challenging thoughts and inducing relaxation create activity incompatible with worry. A worry left to repeat unchallenged actually gains persuasive power.

questions.q: Put the worried thoughts in Roemer and Borkovec's muffler example in the order they occur.
items: The muffler sounds bad
I can't afford the expense of the shop
I'd have to take money from Jamie's college fund
What if I can't afford his tuition?
What if his grades go down and he can't get into college?
questions.explain: The chain shows the worrying mind spinning on from concern to concern, from a car noise to a child's future, in an endless loop of low-grade melodrama.

questions.q: Put in order the thoughts of the woman with generalized anxiety disorder who was asked to worry aloud for one minute.
items: I might not do this right
This may be too artificial to show the real thing
If we don't get at the real thing, I won't get well
If I don't get well I'll never be happy
questions.explain: Within seconds her worry about the task escalated to a lifelong catastrophe, a virtuoso display of worrying about worrying.

questions.q: Put in order the sequence by which worry partly relieves anxiety, as Borkovec describes it.
items: Something triggers an image of a potential threat
The imagined catastrophe triggers a mild attack of anxiety
The worrier plunges into a long series of distressed thoughts
Attention to these thoughts takes the mind off the original image
Anxiety is partly eased, which reinforces the worry
questions.explain: Because images trigger anxiety more strongly than thoughts, immersion in worried thoughts distracts from the image, easing anxiety and reinforcing the habit.

questions.q: Put the steps of Borkovec's method for controlling chronic worry in order.
items: Learn to monitor cues for anxiety and spot worry early
Apply a practiced relaxation method as the worry begins
Take a critical stance toward the worrisome assumptions
questions.explain: Self-awareness comes first, then relaxation at the moment worry starts, then active challenge of the thoughts, without which the spiral returns.

questions.q: Match each anxiety disorder to where worry fixates, as Goleman describes it.
pairs: A fear of dying or of having the attack itself
questions.explain: Each disorder is worry run amok, but it fixes in a distinct way: on a situation, a calamity to prevent, the attack itself, or worry in general.

questions.q: Match each finding to what Borkovec learned about worry.
pairs: Kept awake by intrusive thoughts, not somatic arousal
Images are stronger triggers of physical anxiety
Worry gets credit for preventing unlikely dangers
Deficit in responding flexibly to change
questions.explain: Borkovec's findings explain why worry persists: it relieves some anxiety, seems to ward off danger, and runs in rigid grooves.

questions.q: Sort these into the two forms of anxiety Goleman describes.

items.t: Worrisome thoughts
Intrusive thoughts at bedtime
A narrative jumping from concern to concern
Sweating
A racing heart
Muscle tension

questions.explain: Cognitive anxiety is worrisome thought; somatic anxiety is its physiological symptoms. Borkovec found insomniacs were troubled by the cognitive kind.

questions.q: Sort these by whether Goleman says chronic worry does or does not achieve them.

items.t: Eases some anxiety
Takes the mind off catastrophic images
Repeats the same ideas over and over
Solves the underlying problem
Produces creative breakthroughs
Finds fresh ways of seeing a problem

questions.explain: Goleman sums up that chronic worry “eases some anxiety, but never solves the problem”; its rigid ideas do not move toward solutions.

questions.q: Sort these by whether they are part of Borkovec's method for controlling worry or are approaches that fail.

items.t: Catching the worry as soon as the catastrophic image appears
Practicing a relaxation method daily
Asking whether the dreaded event is really probable
Being told to just stop worrying
Being told not to worry and be happy
Relaxing without ever challenging the worry

questions.explain: Borkovec's method joins early awareness, relaxation and active challenge; worriers cannot simply stop, and relaxation alone lets the spiral return.

questions.q: Why does Goleman say worry can be useful, and where does it go wrong?
questions.a: Worry rests on vigilance for danger that was essential for survival; it is a rehearsal of what might go wrong and how to deal with it, and when it leads to constructive solutions it works. The trouble is chronic, repetitive worry that recycles without getting nearer a solution, ruminating on the danger itself in the same rut of thought.

questions.q: Explain how chronic worry relates to emotional hijacking and to the anxiety disorders.
questions.a: Chronic worry has the attributes of a low-grade emotional hijacking: it comes from nowhere, is uncontrollable, hums steadily, is impervious to reason and locks the worrier into one inflexible view. When this cycle intensifies and persists it becomes full-blown neural hijackings, the anxiety disorders such as phobias, obsessions and compulsions, and panic attacks, in which worry fixates in distinct ways.

questions.q: Why, according to Borkovec, does chronic worry persist even though it rarely solves anything?
questions.a: Worry gives a partial payoff that reinforces the habit. It works like a superstition: since most feared events never happen, the worry gets credit for preventing them. It also partly relieves anxiety, because absorption in worried thoughts takes the mind off the catastrophic images that trigger stronger physical anxiety.

questions.q: Describe Borkovec's method for helping chronic worriers and why each part is needed.
questions.a: First comes self-awareness: monitoring cues to catch worry as soon as the catastrophic image triggers it. Then a relaxation method, practiced daily, is applied the moment worry begins. Relaxation alone is not enough, so worriers also challenge their assumptions, asking whether the event is probable and whether constructive steps exist. This mindfulness and healthy skepticism create mental activity incompatible with worry.

questions.q: Why does challenging a worried thought with other points of view weaken it, according to Borkovec?
questions.a: A worry that repeats over and over unchallenged gains persuasive power. Contemplating a range of equally plausible points of view keeps the one worried thought from being naively taken as true. Actively generating such thoughts may also prime circuitry that inhibits the limbic driving of worry.

questions.q: When does Goleman say medication is appropriate for anxiety, and why is therapy still needed?
questions.a: For worries severe enough to have become phobia, obsessive-compulsive disorder or panic disorder, turning to medication to interrupt the cycle may be prudent, even a sign of self-awareness. But retraining the emotional circuitry through therapy is still needed to lessen the chance that the anxiety disorder will recur when medication is stopped.

questions.q: Which of these did Borkovec find about why the worry habit persists?
options: Worry gets the credit for preventing dangers that rarely happen
Worry typically produces fresh solutions to problems
Worry is mostly made of vivid images that calm the body
Worry seems to suppress some anxiety, at least as reflected in heart rate
questions.explain: Worry is reinforced because it partly relieves anxiety and, like a superstition, seems to ward off unlikely dangers. It rarely yields fresh solutions, and it is made of words rather than images.

questions.q: Match each person in Goleman's section on worry to their story.
pairs: Long showers and swabbing seats, driven by fear of germs
Turned a one-minute worry task into never being happy
Without health insurance, sure every headache was a tumor
Kept awake by intrusive worries, not bodily arousal
questions.explain: Each case shows worry in a different form: compulsions to prevent a feared calamity, catastrophizing, near-addictive health worry, and intrusive thoughts at night.

questions.q: What useful function does Goleman say the sadness of a loss serves?
questions.explain: Sadness closes down interest in pleasures and fixes attention on the loss, enforcing a reflective retreat that leads to psychological adjustment and new plans.
options: It energizes us to fight whatever caused the loss
It warns others to keep away while we recover
It enforces a reflective retreat in which we mourn, find meaning and make new plans
It blocks memory of the loss so that we can move on

questions.q: According to Tice, what is the most popular tactic for battling depression, and when does it work?
questions.explain: Going out with friends or family works if it gets the mind off the sadness, but it prolongs the mood if used to mull over what caused it.
options: Socializing, which works best when the person talks through the sadness
Exercise, which works best for people who already exercise daily
Sleeping, which works if the person sleeps longer than usual
Socializing, which works if it takes the person's mind off the sadness

questions.q: In Nolen-Hoeksma's example of the saleswoman, what would happen if she reacted to her depression by distracting herself?
questions.explain: Distraction could send her into the sales calls; sales would be less likely to fall and making a sale might lessen the depression somewhat.
options: She might plunge into her sales calls, keep sales up and bolster her confidence
She would lose more sales because she was not facing her feelings
She would fall into deeper depression from ignoring its causes
She would need medication to recover her motivation

questions.q: Tice found aerobic exercise lifts mild depression. For whom do its mood benefits work best?
questions.explain: The benefits work best for the lazy; for habitual exercisers the effect was strongest when they first took up exercise, and they feel bad on days they skip.
options: People with a daily exercise routine
People who usually do not work out very much
People with major clinical depression
People who exercise only when anxious

questions.q: After a breakup, Maya keeps telling herself she will always be alone. Which antidote does Goleman single out as potent for this kind of sadness?
questions.explain: Cognitive reframing, seeing the loss in a more positive light, is an antidote to sadness; staying alone, tearjerkers and alcohol tend to deepen it.
options: Spending a quiet weekend alone thinking about what went wrong
Watching a tearjerker film to have a good cry
Thinking about the ways the relationship was not so great and how they were mismatched
Having a few drinks with friends to dull the pain

questions.q: Sam, feeling low, finally clears out the garage he has been putting off for months and feels better. Which of Tice's mood-lifters is this?
questions.explain: Tice found tackling a long-delayed chore, an easy success, a constructive way to lift mood, as are small lifts to self-image like dressing up.
options: Cognitive reframing of a loss
A downward comparison with others
A sensual treat or pleasure
Engineering a small triumph or easy success

questions.q: Jo, mildly depressed, wants to watch a tragic film to take her mind off her sadness. What would Wenzlaff advise?
questions.explain: Wenzlaff says depressed people must take care not to choose something like a tearjerker or tragic novel; the best distractions shift mood, like a funny movie.
options: Choose something completely upbeat, such as a funny movie, instead
Watch the tragic film, since any distraction works equally well
Avoid all distractions and think the sadness through
Watch several hours of television to fully absorb her attention

questions.q: True or false: Goleman writes that bereavement is useful but full-blown depression is not.
questions.explain: The sadness of loss enforces a useful reflective retreat, but in major depression life is paralyzed and no new beginnings emerge.

questions.q: True or false: Tice found that buying oneself a gift or treat to escape a bad mood was particularly popular among men.
questions.explain: Buying oneself a gift or treat, and shopping in general, was particularly popular among women.

questions.q: True or false: According to Goleman, the idea of a good cry is misleading when the crying reinforces rumination.
questions.explain: Crying can sometimes break a spell of sadness, but crying that reinforces rumination only prolongs the misery.

questions.q: One of the main determinants Goleman names of whether depression persists is ____, worrying over and over about what is depressing us.
questions.explain: Worrying about what depresses us makes depression more intense and prolonged; Nolen-Hoeksma studied this rumination in depressed people.

questions.q: Goleman calls ordinary melancholy, at its upper limits, a ____ depression, which people can handle on their own.
questions.explain: Subclinical depression is the range of despondency people can manage with their own resources, unlike major depression.

questions.q: Comparing oneself to someone worse off, as cancer patients did, is what Goleman calls a ____ comparison.
questions.explain: He writes “Such downward comparisons are surprisingly cheering,” since the dispiriting suddenly looks less bad.

questions.q: According to Goleman, depression is a low-arousal state, which is why ____ exercise, which pitches the body into high arousal, can lift it.
questions.explain: Aerobics breaks the cycle by pitching the body into a state incompatible with depression's low arousal.

questions.q: A constructive mood-lifter Tice reports is engineering a small ____ or easy success, such as finishing a long-delayed chore.
questions.explain: Tice found that tackling a long-delayed chore or duty, a small triumph, was cheering, as were small lifts to self-image.

questions.q: Seeing things differently, such as viewing a lost relationship as a mismatch, is called cognitive ____.
questions.explain: Cognitive reframing is one of the most potent antidotes to depression, though it is little used outside therapy.

questions.q: Wenzlaff told Goleman that thoughts are associated in the mind not just by content, but by ____.
questions.explain: People have a set of bad-mood thoughts that come readily when they feel down, and depression-prone people build strong networks among them.

questions.q: Tice reports that praying, if you are very ____, works for all moods, especially depression.
questions.explain: Tice told Goleman that “Praying, if you're very religious, works for all moods, especially depression.”

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman name as invariable effects of the sadness that a loss brings?
options: It energizes us to seek revenge for the loss
It closes down our interest in diversions and pleasures
It fixes attention on what has been lost
It saps our energy for starting new endeavors
It makes us more eager to socialize
questions.explain: These effects enforce a reflective retreat for mourning and adjustment. Energy for revenge belongs to anger, and sadness reduces rather than raises interest in socializing.

questions.q: Which of these are the two strategies Goleman says cognitive therapy finds particularly effective against depression?
options: Challenging the thoughts at the center of rumination
Purposely scheduling pleasant, distracting events
Having a good cry whenever sadness arises
Reflecting at length, alone, on why one feels sad
questions.explain: The two strategies are questioning the validity of ruminative thoughts and scheduling pleasant distractions. Solitary brooding and crying that feeds rumination prolong misery.

questions.q: Which of these strategies for lifting sadness can backfire, according to Goleman?
options: Helping others in need
Making a downward comparison
Drinking alcohol
Heavy TV watching
Overeating
questions.explain: Overeating brings regret, alcohol is a depressant, and heavy TV watchers end up more depressed. Helping others and downward comparisons are effective lifters.

questions.q: Which of these does Wenzlaff say make the most effective distractions from sadness?
options: A tearjerker movie
A funny movie
An exciting sporting event
A tragic novel
questions.explain: Wenzlaff says the best distractions shift mood, like a sporting event, a funny movie or an uplifting book. Tearjerkers and tragic novels drag mood down.

questions.q: Which of these forms of rumination in depression does Goleman or Nolen-Hoeksma mention?
options: Replaying an insult and planning revenge on the person
Dwelling on how tired you feel and how little energy you have
Worrying that your spouse might reject you because you are depressed
Picturing a car accident whenever you have to drive
Wondering whether you will have another sleepless night
questions.explain: Depressive rumination centers on the depression itself and its effects. Revenge fantasies belong to anger, and picturing accidents to the anxious freelance writer.

questions.q: Put in order the stages of the reflective retreat that Goleman says the sadness of a loss enforces.
items: Interest in diversions and pleasures closes down
We mourn the loss
We mull over its meaning
We make the psychological adjustments and new plans to continue
questions.explain: Sadness first withdraws us from pursuits, then leaves us suspended to mourn, find meaning and finally adjust and plan, which is why bereavement is useful.

questions.q: Put in order the spiral of Nolen-Hoeksma's saleswoman.
items: She gets depressed
She spends hours worrying about her depression
She doesn't get around to important sales calls
Her sales decline and she feels like a failure
Her depression deepens
questions.explain: Rumination creates conditions that are more depressing: worry crowds out action, the results fall, and the sense of failure feeds the depression.

questions.q: Put in the order Goleman presents them the kinds of symptoms William Styron describes in his depression.
items: Self-hatred, worthlessness and dread
Confusion, failure of focus and lapses of memory
Sleeplessness, listlessness and restlessness
Food and all sensation utterly without savor
Vanishing hope, with suicide seeming a solution
questions.explain: Goleman moves from Styron's emotional manifestations to intellectual marks, physical effects, loss of pleasure and finally the vanishing of hope.

questions.q: Match each researcher to their contribution in Goleman's discussion of melancholy.
pairs: Studied how depressed people choose and use distractions
Surveyed the strategies people use to escape the blues
Wrote an eloquent description of his own major depression
questions.explain: Nolen-Hoeksma studied rumination, Wenzlaff distraction, Tice everyday strategies, and Styron supplied a first-hand account of major depression.

questions.q: Match each mood-lifter to the reason or caveat Goleman gives for it.
pairs: Works best for people who rarely work out
Lifts us out of preoccupation with the self
Makes what seemed dispiriting look less bad
A nervous system depressant that adds to depression
questions.explain: Exercise helps most the unfit, helping others breaks self-preoccupation, downward comparisons cheer, and alcohol backfires because it is a depressant.

questions.q: Match each group to what Goleman reports about how they handle sadness.
pairs: Three times as likely as men to eat to soothe sadness
Five times as likely to turn to drinking or drugs
Feel bad on days they skip their workout
More depressed after watching than before
questions.explain: These findings show how strategies can backfire or depend on who uses them: eating, drinking, habitual exercise and heavy TV each have their own drawbacks.

questions.q: Match each remedy to the state Goleman says it suits because it counters that state's level of arousal.
questions.explain: Each remedy pitches the brain into a level of activity incompatible with the mood: high arousal for depression, low arousal for anxiety and anger.

questions.q: Sort these by whether Goleman presents them as effective ways to lift ordinary sadness or as ones that tend to backfire.

items.t: Volunteering to coach Little League
Tackling a long-delayed chore
Comparing oneself to someone worse off
Going to a funny movie
Staying alone to think things over
Watching a tearjerker
Eating to excess
Drinking alcohol

questions.explain: Helping others, small triumphs, downward comparisons and upbeat distractions lift mood; isolation, sad films, overeating and alcohol deepen it.

questions.q: Sort these descriptions into ordinary sadness after a loss or full-blown depression, as Goleman contrasts them.

items.t: A reflective retreat to mourn
Making new plans so life can continue
Temporary loss of interest in pleasures
Life paralyzed with no new beginnings
Hope vanishing so that suicide seems a solution
Thought engulfed by a toxic tide

questions.explain: Bereavement is useful because it leads to adjustment and new plans; full-blown depression puts life on hold and can make suicide seem a solution.

questions.q: Sort these by whether Goleman reports them as more typical of women or of men.

items.t: Ruminating more when depressed
Being diagnosed with depression twice as often
Buying a treat or going shopping to lift mood
A rate of alcoholism about twice as high
Turning to drinking or drugs when down
Going for a drive to cool off when angry

questions.explain: Nolen-Hoeksma and Tice report these gender differences; Goleman notes other factors, such as women's openness about distress, may also play a part.

questions.q: Why does Goleman say not all sadness should be escaped?
questions.a: Melancholy, like every mood, has benefits. The sadness of loss closes down interest in diversions, fixes attention on what was lost and saps energy for new endeavors, enforcing a reflective retreat. In that suspended state we mourn, mull over the loss's meaning and finally make the adjustments and new plans that let life continue, which is why bereavement is useful while full-blown depression is not.

questions.q: How does rumination make depression worse, according to Goleman and Nolen-Hoeksma?
questions.a: Worrying about what depresses us, such as how tired we feel or how little we get done, makes depression more intense and prolonged, usually without any concrete action to fix the problem. It primes sadness, and it can create more depressing conditions, as with the saleswoman whose worry kept her from sales calls, so that falling sales made her feel a failure.

questions.q: Why does socializing sometimes lift sadness and sometimes prolong it?
questions.a: Socializing, Tice's most popular tactic, works if the net effect is to get the person's mind off the sadness, and it avoids the loneliness that staying alone adds. But if the person uses the occasion just to mull over what put them in the funk, it simply prolongs the mood. The difference is whether it distracts or feeds rumination.

questions.q: Why is distraction harder for depressed people, according to Wenzlaff's research?
questions.a: Depressing thoughts are automatic and have a magnetic effect on association; thoughts are linked by mood as well as content. Depression-prone people build strong networks of bad-mood thoughts, so they pick melancholy distractions, have more intrusions of upsetting scenes over time, and even use one depressing topic to distract from another. They must make a special effort to choose something completely upbeat.

questions.q: Explain why aerobic exercise helps depression while relaxation helps anxiety.
questions.a: Each remedy pitches the brain into a level of activity incompatible with the mood that has it in its grip. Depression is a low-arousal state and aerobics pitches the body into high arousal, while anxiety is high-arousal and relaxation brings the body to low arousal. So relaxation works well for anxiety but not so well for depression.

questions.q: What does Goleman say about crying as a way to end sadness?
questions.a: One theory holds that crying may be nature's way of lowering brain chemicals that prime distress, and it can sometimes break a spell of sadness. But it can also leave a person obsessing about the reasons for despair. So the idea of a good cry is misleading: crying that reinforces rumination only prolongs the misery.

questions.q: How does cognitive reframing work against sadness? Give one of Goleman's examples.
questions.a: Reframing means seeing the loss differently, in a more positive light. After a breakup, instead of wallowing in thoughts like always being alone, one can think about how the relationship was not so great and how the partners were mismatched. Similarly, cancer patients who compared themselves to someone worse off were in better moods; such downward comparisons are surprisingly cheering.

questions.q: Why is helping others in need an effective lift for depression, and what did Tice find about how often people use it?
questions.a: Depression feeds on ruminations and preoccupations with the self, and empathizing with others in pain lifts us out of those preoccupations. Volunteer work such as coaching Little League or feeding the homeless was one of the most powerful mood-changers in Tice's study, but also one of the rarest.

questions.q: Match each study in Goleman's discussion of melancholy to its finding.
pairs: Depressed people solved the depressing messages better
Keeping a car-crash scene out of mind
Depressed volunteers had more intrusions as time passed
Comparing to someone worse off brought better moods
They were more depressed after watching than before
questions.explain: The first two studies show depression's pull on thought, the cancer study shows the power of downward comparison, and the TV studies show that some distractions perpetuate depression.

questions.q: Which of these did people in Tice's study report turning to as distractions to shake garden-variety sadness?
options: Reading, TV and movies
Replaying the reasons for their despair
Daydreams such as planning a fantasy vacation
Video games and puzzles
Venting at the person who upset them
questions.explain: Tice's respondents named reading, TV and movies, games and puzzles, sleeping and daydreams. Replaying reasons for despair is rumination, and venting belongs to anger.

questions.q: Sort these by whether Goleman describes them as high-arousal or low-arousal.

items.t: Anxiety
Anger
Aerobic exercise
Depression
Relaxation techniques
The body at rest after exercise

questions.explain: Anxiety and anger are high-arousal states and depression a low-arousal one; aerobics raises arousal while relaxation, and the rebound after exercise, lowers it.

questions.q: In the sentence-completion test, a student completed 'He kicked his roommate in the stomach...' with '...but he meant to turn on the light.' What does Goleman say this shows?
questions.explain: Turning an act of aggression into a slightly implausible innocent mistake is repression in action, part of a larger pattern of tuning out emotional upset.
options: Alexithymia, an inability to name any feeling
Repression captured in vivo, turning aggression into an innocent mistake
Cognitive incapacitation caused by rising anger
Catastrophizing, imagining a terrible outcome

questions.q: What term does Goleman suggest might be more apt than repressors?
questions.explain: Because they regulate emotion so well, Goleman writes that “a more apt term might be unflappables.”
options: Alexithymics
Mood purists
Unflappables
Optimists

questions.q: According to Daniel Weinberger, about how common is the pattern of continually tuning out emotions such as anger and anxiety?
questions.explain: Weinberger estimates that about one person in six shows this pattern of tuning out emotion.
options: About one person in fifty
About one person in two
About one person in a hundred
About one person in six

questions.q: In Davidson's free-association study, how did unflappables tend to respond to an upsetting word such as 'hate'?
questions.explain: Their associations almost always tried to sanitize upsetting words by linking them to innocent ones, though their bodies showed distress.
options: With an innocent word, such as 'love', that sanitized it
With a more hostile word, intensifying the upset
With silence, refusing to respond at all
With a word about their own anxiety

questions.q: What is Davidson's theory for why unflappables show increased physiological arousal despite their upbeat mood?
questions.explain: Davidson suggests that “it is energy-demanding work to experience distressing realities in a positive light,” so the sustained effort to maintain positive feelings raises arousal.
options: They are secretly anxious and know it but deny it to others
Experiencing distressing realities in a positive light is energy-demanding neural work
Their right hemisphere is overactive while the left is idle
They have a heart condition unrelated to emotion

questions.q: Kofi's manager harshly criticizes his work. His heart races and he sweats, but he sincerely says, 'Honestly, it doesn't bother me at all.' Which pattern does Goleman's chapter describe that fits Kofi?
questions.explain: Repressors show the physical signs of distress yet genuinely report feeling calm, because their brain keeps the upsetting information from awareness.
options: The mood purist who will not change any mood
The chronic worrier caught in a hijacking
The unflappable or repressor pattern of upbeat denial
The ruminator whose sadness deepens

questions.q: True or false: Goleman writes that unflappableness may offer a clue to neural mechanisms in the more severe dissociative states of post-traumatic stress disorder.
questions.explain: He calls unflappableness upbeat denial, a positive dissociation, and possibly a clue to mechanisms in more severe dissociative states such as in PTSD.

questions.q: True or false: Davidson concluded that unflappability is a failed strategy for emotional self-regulation with a known high cost to health.
questions.explain: Davidson says that when it simply serves equanimity it seems a successful strategy for emotional self-regulation, though with an unknown cost to self-awareness.

questions.q: In Davidson's study, upsetting information recognized by the right hemisphere must cross the ____ to reach the speech center on the left.
questions.explain: The corpus callosum is the great divide between the brain's halves, across which the right hemisphere sends news that a word is upsetting.

questions.q: Goleman sums up unflappableness as a kind of upbeat ____, a positive dissociation.
questions.explain: He writes that “unflappableness is a kind of upbeat denial, a positive dissociation,” which also gives the section its title.

questions.q: Daniel Weinberger's repressors were studied with a sentence-____ test, in which they finished fragments such as one about kicking a roommate.
questions.explain: The sentence-completion test, combined with physiological monitoring, revealed both their innocent completions and their hidden bodily agitation.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman offer as possible ways children might learn to become unflappable?
options: Being praised for venting anger openly
Following the example of parents who are themselves repressors
Inheriting the trait as temperament
Surviving a family where a parent's alcoholism is denied
Growing up with constant exposure to frightening films
questions.explain: Goleman suggests a survival strategy in a family that denies a problem, the example of repressor parents, or inherited temperament; no one yet knows exactly how it begins.

questions.q: Which of these signs of anxiety did repressors show while saying they felt perfectly calm?
options: Sweating
Climbing blood pressure
A racing heart
Visible trembling and crying
Reporting strong discomfort
questions.explain: Monitoring showed a racing heart, sweating and rising blood pressure, yet repressors reported calm; they did not show or report distress outwardly.

questions.q: Match each brain feature to its role in Davidson's study of unflappables.
pairs: Key center for processing negative emotion
Carries information between the brain's halves
Center for good feeling, more active in unflappables
questions.explain: Upsetting words are recognized on the right and must cross the corpus callosum to the left speech center; extra left prefrontal activity may supply the mellow layer.

questions.q: Sort these findings about repressors into what their bodies or brains showed versus what they said or did.

items.t: A racing heart and sweating
Climbing blood pressure
More left prefrontal activity
Said they felt perfectly calm
Answered hate with love
Turned a kick into an accident

questions.explain: The gap between bodily distress and calm reports and sanitized answers is the signature of upbeat denial.

questions.q: Put the pathway of an upsetting word in Davidson's study, when shown in the left visual field, in order.
items: The word appears in the left half of the visual field
The right hemisphere recognizes it as upsetting
The information crosses the corpus callosum
It reaches the speech center in the left hemisphere
A word is spoken in response
questions.explain: This route let Davidson test whether upsetting information was slowed in transfer; unflappables lagged only on this route and only for upsetting words.

questions.q: What are repressors, and why does Goleman suggest calling them unflappables?
questions.a: Repressors are people who habitually and automatically seem to blot emotional disturbance from their awareness, as when a student turned a kick in the stomach into an attempt to turn on the light. Researchers first saw them as unable to feel, like alexithymics, but now see them as very proficient at regulating emotion, so good at buffering negative feelings that they are not aware of them. Hence unflappables.

questions.q: Explain how Davidson's study showed that unflappables are not simply faking their calm.
questions.a: Davidson used lenses to show words to one half of the visual field. Unflappables lagged in responding only to upsetting words shown to the right hemisphere, which processes negative emotion and must pass it across the corpus callosum to the left speech center. This suggests a neural mechanism slows the transfer of upsetting information, so their brain keeps the information from them rather than them pretending.

questions.q: How does Davidson explain the combination of upbeat mood and high physiological arousal in unflappables?
questions.a: Unflappables show more left prefrontal activity, linked to good feeling, which may lay mellow feeling over disturbing perceptions. Davidson's theory is that seeing distressing realities in a positive light is energy-demanding work, so the increased arousal may come from the brain's sustained effort to keep positive feelings up and suppress negative ones.

questions.q: What is Goleman's overall verdict on unflappableness as a way of handling emotion?
questions.a: He calls it upbeat denial, a positive dissociation, possibly a clue to the mechanisms behind more severe dissociation in post-traumatic stress disorder. When it simply supports equanimity, Davidson says it seems a successful strategy for emotional self-regulation, but it comes with an unknown cost to self-awareness.

questions.q: Match each method used to study repressors to what it revealed.
pairs: Aggressive fragments turned into innocent mistakes
A racing heart and sweating despite reported calm
Upsetting words linked to innocent ones
Words shown to one half of the visual field
A lag only for upsetting words reaching the right hemisphere
questions.explain: Together these methods showed that repressors' bodies register distress while their words sanitize it, and that a neural mechanism slows upsetting information.

questions.q: What does the chapter title 'Passion's Slaves', taken from Hamlet, signal about the chapter's subject?
questions.explain: The title invokes the opposite of the man Hamlet praises; the chapter is about not being ruled by distressing emotions, which is the skill of managing them.
options: Its subject is romantic love and the troubles it brings
Its subject is how emotions evolved to help us survive
Its subject is reading other people's hidden feelings
Its subject is self-mastery: managing emotions rather than being ruled by them

questions.q: Salovey's five domains of emotional intelligence are laid out earlier in the book. Which domain does this chapter on anger, worry and melancholy examine?
questions.explain: Goleman's list says the chapter on managing emotions will examine the capacity to soothe oneself and shake off rampant anxiety, gloom or irritability.
options: Managing emotions
Knowing one's emotions
Motivating oneself
Recognizing emotions in others

questions.q: In which Part of the book does this chapter on managing emotions sit?
questions.explain: Part Two covers the basic abilities of emotional intelligence, such as reining in emotional impulse, after Part One's account of the emotional brain.
options: Part One, The Emotional Brain
Part Two, The Nature of Emotional Intelligence
Part Three, Emotional Intelligence Applied
Part Four, Windows of Opportunity

questions.q: How does the preceding chapter, Know Thyself, prepare the way for this chapter?
questions.explain: Know Thyself closes by saying “emotional self-awareness is the building block of the next fundamental of emotional intelligence: being able to shake off a bad mood.”
options: It ends by showing that IQ predicts how well people manage their moods
It ends by describing how children learn empathy from their parents
It ends by calling emotional self-awareness the building block of being able to shake off a bad mood
It ends by arguing that emotions cannot be changed once they arise

questions.q: Which topic does Goleman's list of domains assign to the chapter that follows this one, The Master Aptitude?
questions.explain: The next domain is motivating oneself: marshaling emotions toward a goal, emotional self-control such as delaying gratification, and the flow state.
options: Handling relationships with social skill
Recognizing a feeling as it happens
Soothing anxiety and lifting gloom
Motivating oneself, including delaying gratification and getting into flow

questions.q: In the chapter's opening, Goleman notes that 'as we have seen' the brain's design gives us little control over when emotion sweeps us. Which earlier part of the book does this refer back to?
questions.explain: Part One explained the brain's emotional architecture and the moments when feeling overwhelms rationality; this chapter builds on it to ask what control remains.
options: Part One's account of the emotional brain and emotional hijackings
Part Three's account of emotions at work
Part Four's account of childhood temperament
Part Five's account of emotional literacy programs

questions.q: True or false: The chapter treats anger, anxiety and sadness in turn, the same big three emotions that the later chapter on Mind and Medicine examines for their effects on health.
questions.explain: Mind and Medicine looks in detail at the big three, anger, anxiety and depression, the same moods this chapter teaches us to manage.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter's closing section on repressors describes people who, like the alexithymics of the previous chapter, are simply unable to feel emotion.
questions.explain: Goleman says researchers first saw repressors as cousins of alexithymics, but current thinking sees them as very proficient at regulating emotion.

questions.q: Goleman's description of chronic worry as a low-grade emotional ____ ties this chapter back to the account of the amygdala in Part One.
questions.explain: Chapter 2, Anatomy of an Emotional Hijacking, explained how the amygdala can sweep us away; chronic worry is a low-grade version of that.

questions.q: Put the chapter's four main sections in the order they appear.
items: The Anatomy of Rage?
Soothing Anxiety: What, Me Worry?
Managing Melancholy
Repressors: Upbeat Denial
questions.explain: The chapter takes anger, anxiety and sadness in turn, then ends with repressors, who regulate distress so well they do not notice it.

questions.q: Put these chapters of Part Two in the book's order.
items: Know Thyself
Passion's Slaves
The Master Aptitude
The Roots of Empathy
The Social Arts
questions.explain: Part Two follows Salovey's domains: self-awareness, managing emotions, motivating oneself, empathy and handling relationships.

questions.q: Match each idea in this chapter to the later part of the book it foreshadows.
pairs: Hostile people's higher risk of heart disease
Mind and Medicine, on emotions and health
Infants learning to soothe themselves from caretakers
The Family Crucible, on emotional lessons at home
Self-soothing as a learnable life skill
Schooling the Emotions, on teaching emotional skills
questions.explain: The chapter plants seeds for Part Three's health chapter, Part Four's chapters on family and trauma, and Part Five's case for teaching emotional skills.

questions.q: How does this chapter answer Aristotle's challenge, introduced in the Prologue, to be angry with the right person, to the right degree, at the right time?
questions.a: The Prologue promises that Part Two will show the ability to rein in emotional impulse, quoting Aristotle's rare skill of appropriate anger. This chapter makes that concrete: it explains why anger escalates, why venting fails, and how reappraisal and cooling down keep anger proportionate. Its opening restates Aristotle's ideal of “appropriate emotion, feeling proportionate to circumstance.”

questions.q: Why does it make sense that this chapter comes right after Know Thyself in Goleman's sequence?
questions.a: Managing emotions builds on self-awareness: you must recognize a feeling before you can soothe or reshape it. Know Thyself ends by calling self-awareness the building block for shaking off a bad mood, and this chapter repeatedly makes awareness the first step, from catching hostile thoughts early to Borkovec's monitoring of worry cues.

questions.q: Why might Goleman end the chapter with repressors rather than with another distressing mood?
questions.a: After anger, anxiety and sadness, which show the costs of failing to manage distress, repressors show the opposite extreme: people who keep distress out of awareness so well that they report calm while their bodies are agitated. This rounds out the picture of self-regulation, showing it can succeed for equanimity yet at an unknown cost to self-awareness, which links back to the previous chapter.

questions.q: What overall argument about emotion does this chapter contribute to the book?
questions.a: It argues that while we cannot control when emotion strikes, we can influence how long it lasts, and that managing distressing moods is a learnable skill central to emotional intelligence. Through anger, worry and melancholy it shows that common strategies such as venting, brooding or isolating backfire, while reappraisal, distraction and changing arousal work, and that the goal is balance, not suppression.

questions.q: What does Goleman say his frozen calculus-exam hour was most likely a testament to?
options: The power of the emotional brain to overpower, even paralyze, the thinking brain
The harm done by too little sleep before an important test
The way a lack of study time lowers a student's IQ
The usefulness of fear in focusing a student's attention
questions.explain: He read the episode as emotional distress overpowering the thinking brain. His mind did not focus; it became constricted and fixated on terror.

questions.q: In the discussion of emotional upset and learning, what does working memory refer to?
options: The store of early emotional experiences that shape later reactions
The ability to hold in mind all the information relevant to the task at hand
The skill of recalling facts learned long ago under exam pressure
The habit of rehearsing worries so as to prepare for threats
questions.explain: Cognitive scientists use the term for holding task-relevant information, from a phone number to a novel's plot lines. Emotional distress swamps it.

questions.q: According to Goleman, which brain region executes working memory and is also where feelings and emotions meet?
options: The amygdala
The motor cortex
The prefrontal cortex
The hippocampus
questions.explain: Working memory is carried out by the prefrontal cortex, which is why limbic distress converging there costs thinking power.

questions.q: Studies of Olympic athletes, world-class musicians and chess grand masters find which unifying trait?
options: An unusually high score on standard intelligence tests
Rare natural talent that shows itself before age four
Parents who were themselves experts in the same field
The ability to motivate themselves to pursue relentless training routines
