questions.explain: The shared trait was self-motivation for years of arduous practice, not raw IQ or early talent as such.

questions.q: Why does Goleman say Asian-American students behave professionally as though their IQ were far higher than it measures?
options: From the earliest school years they work harder, a cultural work ethic that builds motivation and persistence
Their schools use teaching methods that raise measured intelligence
They score much higher than other groups on standard IQ tests
Their families steer them toward easier professions such as law
questions.explain: The measured IQ edge is only two or three points. The gap in outcomes is explained by an emotional edge: harder work, zeal and persistence.

questions.q: Why does Goleman call resisting impulse the root of all emotional self-control?
options: Impulses are always harmful, so every emotion must be suppressed
All emotions by their nature lead to an impulse to act, so self-control means resisting that impulse
Young children cannot feel emotions until they learn to delay
Resisting impulse is the first skill that schools set out to teach
questions.explain: He points to the root meaning of emotion, 'to move': every emotion pushes toward action, and the capacity to squelch that movement underlies regulation.

questions.q: In the marshmallow study, how did delay of gratification at age four compare with IQ as a predictor of later SAT scores?
options: It was about half as powerful a predictor as IQ at age four
It predicted equally well, since both reflect intelligence
It was about twice as powerful a predictor as IQ at age four
It predicted nothing once the children had learned to read
questions.explain: At four, delay beat IQ by a factor of two. IQ becomes the stronger predictor only after children learn to read.

questions.q: As adolescents, the roughly one third of children who had grabbed the marshmallow tended to be
options: self-reliant and confident, and quick to take initiative
trustworthy and dependable, though socially shy
academically strong, but unable to cope with failure
stubborn and indecisive, and easily upset by frustrations
questions.explain: The grabbers' portrait was more troubled: shying from contact, stubborn, indecisive, easily upset. Self-reliance and initiative described the waiters.

questions.q: Why does Goleman point ahead to Part Five when he compares impulse control with IQ?
options: Because there is ample evidence that emotional skills like impulse control can be learned, while IQ is argued to be fixed
Because Part Five proves that impulse control is mostly inherited
Because Part Five shows that IQ matters little for later success
Because Part Five reports a repeat of the marshmallow study
questions.explain: The point is hopeful: unlike a supposedly unbendable IQ, emotional skills can be taught, which Part Five takes up.

questions.q: Nine-year-old Maya passes the sweet shop every week with her hands over her eyes so she can save her allowance for a bike. Which of Goleman's ideas does she show?
options: A high IQ, which Mischel found predicts self-control best
Denying impulse in the service of a goal, as the waiting four-year-olds did when they covered their eyes
Test anxiety working as a motivator in a young child
Flow, in which the task itself is the reward
questions.explain: Mischel's waiting children used the same trick of looking away from temptation. It is goal-directed delay, the essence of emotional self-regulation.

questions.q: In the study of 1,790 trainee air traffic controllers, what did chronic anxiety predict?
options: Slightly slower progress, offset by better judgment under pressure
Higher scores, since the job rewards constant vigilance
Eventual failure in training or in the field, even given superior intelligence-test scores
No difference in outcome once intelligence was taken into account
questions.explain: Anxiety undermines the intellect: the anxious were more likely to fail despite excellent scores on intelligence tests.

questions.q: Nonworriers were asked to worry on purpose for fifteen minutes before a sorting task. What happened to their performance?
options: It improved, because worry sharpened their focus
It stayed the same, since they were not natural worriers
It sped up, but with many more careless errors
It deteriorated sharply
questions.explain: Inducing worry in nonworriers hurt the task, and relaxing worriers removed the problem, so the worry itself was the disruptor.

questions.q: In the inverted U relating anxiety to performance, what does too little anxiety produce?
options: Apathy, or too little motivation to try hard enough
Panic that disrupts clear thinking
A creative, fluid state of mind
Effortless absorption in the task
questions.explain: The low side of the U is apathy; the high side sabotages performance. The peak holds a modicum of nerves.

questions.q: In the candle, matches and tacks puzzle, what did people who had just watched television bloopers do better than other groups?
options: They worked out how to melt the wax so it stuck to the wall
They more often saw the tack box as a candle holder and escaped functional fixedness
They solved it faster by using the matches in an unusual way
They gave up sooner and so avoided wasting effort
questions.explain: The comedy group, compared with those who watched a math film or exercised, found the unconventional use of the box.

questions.q: Why do people in a good mood tend to make slightly more adventurous or risky choices?
options: A good mood switches off the memory of past mistakes entirely
Pleasant people care less about what others will think
Memory is state-specific, so a pleasant mood recalls more positive events and tilts the weighing of pros and cons
Good moods raise anxiety to its optimal level for choosing
questions.explain: While in a good mood we remember more positive events, and this biases evidence toward the positive. A foul mood does the opposite.

questions.q: Before a driving test, Jo feels moderately nervous and so practises extra hours, while Ben is so tense he cannot sleep or recall the rules. Which idea from Goleman best explains Jo's edge?
options: Worry always helps performance, so Ben simply worried too little
Good mood biases memory so that Jo recalls only positive events
Jo is in flow, in which self-consciousness drops away
Anticipatory anxiety near the peak of the inverted U can motivate good preparation
questions.explain: Skilled handling of emotion turns anticipatory anxiety into motivation to prepare. Too much anxiety, as in Ben, sits on the sabotaging side of the U.

questions.q: A team is stuck on a hard problem. Based on Goleman, which action could help them think it through?
options: Tell them a joke, since laughter helps people think more broadly and associate more freely
Warn them of the consequences, since fear sharpens focus
Ask each person to worry out loud about what might go wrong
Cut the break short so that nobody loses momentum
questions.explain: Goleman says one way to help someone think through a problem is to tell them a joke; elation and laughter widen thinking.

questions.section: Pandora's Box and Pollyanna: The Power of Positive Thinking
questions.q: When Snyder compared the actual achievement of freshmen high and low on hope, what did he find?
options: SAT scores were the better predictor, as designed
Hope was a better predictor of first-semester grades than SAT scores were
Hope and SAT scores predicted grades equally well
Hope predicted grades only for the students with low SATs
questions.explain: Given roughly the same range of abilities, emotional aptitude made the critical difference, outpredicting the SAT.

questions.section: Pandora's Box and Pollyanna: The Power of Positive Thinking
questions.q: In the hypothetical about getting a D on a first exam, how did students with moderate levels of hope respond?
options: They worked harder but could think of no ways to improve
They gave up on both ideas and effort, feeling demoralized
They thought of several ways to raise their grade but had far less determination to pursue them
They set a higher goal and pursued it with full determination
questions.explain: High hope brought both effort and ideas, moderate hope ideas without determination, and low hope neither.

questions.section: Pandora's Box and Pollyanna: The Power of Positive Thinking
questions.q: After a poor first test grade, Lena lists several new study methods and commits to trying them. Which of Snyder's ideas does she show?
options: Optimism as an inborn temperament she cannot change
Hypomania, a mildly elated and fluid state of mind
Impulse control, resisting a tempting reward
Hope, having both the will and the way to reach a goal
questions.explain: Snyder defines hope as will plus way: Lena has determination and several routes to the goal.

questions.q: After Matt Biondi was told a false, worse swim time, what happened when he tried again?
options: His performance, already very good, was even better
He did worse, as the pessimistic teammates did
He matched his first time exactly
He refused to try again until given the true time
questions.explain: Biondi, tested as an optimist, rebounded. The pessimistic teammates given the same false feedback did even worse.

questions.q: How does Seligman define optimism?
options: As an inborn temperament that cannot be changed
In terms of how people explain their successes and failures to themselves
As the belief that everything will turn out well regardless of effort
As a high score on tests of talent and intelligence
questions.explain: Optimists see failure as changeable; pessimists see it as a lasting personal flaw. It is an explanatory style, and it can be learned.

questions.q: New MetLife salesmen who were natural optimists sold how much more insurance than pessimists in their first two years?
options: 12 percent more
21 percent more
37 percent more
57 percent more
questions.explain: The natural optimists sold 37 percent more in two years; pessimists also quit at twice the rate in the first year.

questions.q: According to Seligman, what is missing in tests of ability?
options: Memory: whether a person can retain the relevant facts
Talent: whether a person has enough raw ability
Anxiety: whether a person can stay calm under pressure
Motivation: whether a person will keep going when things get frustrating
questions.explain: He says entrance exams measure talent while explanatory style tells who gives up; success needs reasonable talent plus persistence after defeat.

questions.q: What does Goleman, following Bandura, mean by self-efficacy?
options: The belief that one has mastery over life's events and can meet challenges as they come
The habit of explaining failures as someone else's fault
The ability to delay gratification for a distant goal
The feeling of effortless absorption in an activity
questions.explain: Self-efficacy underlies hope and optimism; each competency developed and challenge surmounted strengthens it.

questions.q: After being turned down for a job, Dev thinks, My résumé needs work; I'll ask a friend to look at it. Which pattern does Goleman describe?
options: The pessimist's pattern: blaming a lasting personal deficit
The optimist's pattern: seeing a setback as remediable and making a plan or seeking help
Flow: complete absorption in the task
Hypomania: a mildly elated, fluid state of mind
questions.explain: Optimists respond actively, formulating a plan or seeking advice, because they see the cause as something that can be changed.

questions.q: After many rejections, a saleswoman tells herself, I'm a failure at this; I'll never make a sale. What does Goleman say this interpretation is sure to trigger?
options: A change of approach on the next call
Anxiety at an optimal level for performance
Apathy and defeatism, if not depression
A stronger sense of self-efficacy
questions.explain: The pessimist reads each no as a personal, lasting flaw, so morale collapses. The optimist blames the approach or the situation instead.

questions.q: Priya fails her driving test and says, I'm just not a driver and never will be. Which explanatory style is this?
options: Optimistic: seeing the failure as changeable next time
Hopeful: believing she has both will and way
Self-efficacious: believing she can meet the challenge
Pessimistic: ascribing the failure to a lasting characteristic she is helpless to change
questions.explain: Seligman's pessimists take the blame and attribute failure to a lasting trait. Optimists point to something that can be changed.

questions.q: Who gave the name flow to the state of peak performance described in the chapter?
options: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi
Martin Seligman
Howard Gardner
Walter Mischel
questions.explain: Csikszentmihalyi, the University of Chicago psychologist, collected such accounts over two decades.

questions.q: Where does flow occur, in Csikszentmihalyi's words?
options: In the zone between rest and exhaustion
In the delicate zone between boredom and anxiety
In the zone between optimism and pessimism
In the zone between anger and calm
questions.explain: Too little demand bores people and too much makes them anxious, so flow sits between them: “Flow occurs in that delicate zone between boredom and anxiety.”

questions.q: What happens in the brain during flow?
options: A surge of limbic activity that captures the rest of the brain
Heightened cortical arousal to meet the difficult challenge
A cool state with lessened cortical arousal, in which active areas match the task's demands
A complete shutdown of attention-related circuits
questions.explain: Surprisingly, the most challenging tasks are done with a minimum of mental energy; strained, worried focus raises cortical activation instead.

questions.q: A surgeon in flow did not notice that part of the ceiling had caved in. What does this illustrate?
options: A lapse of emotional control brought on by stress
The brain's heightened arousal during difficult operations
Surgeons' special training in ignoring distractions
Attention so focused that awareness narrows to the immediate task, losing track of surroundings
questions.explain: In flow people are aware only of the narrow range of perception related to the task.

questions.q: Rahul bores himself with scales he mastered long ago and gets anxious on a piece far beyond his skill. By Csikszentmihalyi's account, what would most likely put him in flow?
options: A piece that is skilled enough to manage yet slightly taxes his ability
A much harder piece, so that anxiety sharpens his attention
Playing the easy scales faster until they are effortless
Thinking about how well he is playing while he practises
questions.explain: Flow arises when a person engages a task at a level that slightly taxes his skill. Reflecting on how well one is doing breaks flow.

questions.q: A programmer works through a tough bug so absorbed that she skips lunch and loses track of time. Which description from Goleman fits her?
options: Emotional hijacking: a limbic surge capturing the brain
Flow: undivided attention merged with the action, with no sense of time or self
Functional fixedness: seeing only the usual use of things
Hypomania: elation that is too fluid to finish anything
questions.explain: Flow involves paying undivided attention, losing track of time and space, and self-forgetfulness; a hijacking is incompatible with it.

questions.section: Learning and Flow: a New Model for Education
questions.q: In the Chicago high-school study, what did studying more often yield for the low achievers?
options: Flow, as it did in socializing
Boredom, as it did in watching television
Anxiety, with the demands outreaching their abilities
Rapture, as a reward for long hours
questions.explain: Studying gave low achievers flow only 16 percent of the time, against 40 percent for high achievers; they found flow in socializing.

questions.section: Learning and Flow: a New Model for Education
questions.q: According to Gardner, what does flow signify about a child?
options: That the child has outgrown the need for teachers
That the child is ready to be rewarded for progress
That the child is working below their ability
That the child is engaged in a task that is right for them
questions.explain: Gardner calls flow an internal state signalling engagement in a task that's right, a better motivator than threat or promise of reward.

questions.section: Learning and Flow: a New Model for Education
questions.q: A teacher learns that a boy loves drawing but is anxious in maths. Following Gardner's flow model, what is her best approach?
options: Use his natural strengths and offer maths at a level that gives an optimal challenge
Drop maths until he is older so it cannot cause anxiety
Offer rewards for good maths marks to motivate him from outside
Give him harder maths so he learns to handle pressure
questions.explain: Knowing a child's profile lets a teacher fine-tune lessons from remedial to advanced, so learning is neither fearsome nor a bore.

questions.q: How does Chapter 6 build on Chapter 5, which showed that out-of-control emotions can be brought back into line?
options: It argues that out-of-control emotions are best left alone
It argues that this emotional competence is a master aptitude that facilitates all other kinds of intelligence
It shifts to reading the emotions of other people
It reports the biology of the amygdala in greater detail
questions.explain: The chapter's opening and middle both look back to Chapter 5, and the point is that managing emotions governs how well other abilities can be used.

questions.q: What does the chapter title The Master Aptitude signal?
options: Emotional intelligence is the only ability worth having
A single master skill replaces the need for IQ
Emotional intelligence is a capacity that profoundly affects all other abilities, helping or hindering them
Emotional intelligence is inborn and cannot be learned
questions.explain: Goleman says emotional intelligence is a master aptitude “that profoundly affects all other abilities, either facilitating or interfering with them.”

questions.q: The Prologue's road-map lists reining in emotional impulse among the marks of emotional intelligence. Which section of Chapter 6 takes this up first?
options: Foul Moods, Fouled Thinking
Optimism: the Great Motivator
Flow: the Neurobiology of Excellence?
Impulse Control: The Marshmallow Test
questions.explain: After the opening, the first section is the marshmallow study, where Goleman calls resisting impulse the most fundamental psychological skill.

questions.q: How can emotional distress interfere with thinking, according to Goleman's opening, and what role does working memory play?
questions.a: Anxious, angry or depressed people cannot take in or handle information well because intrusive feelings capture attention. What is swamped is working memory, the ability to hold in mind all information relevant to the task at hand. It is executed by the prefrontal cortex, where feelings and emotions meet, so limbic distress costs us the ability to think straight, as in Goleman's calculus exam.

questions.q: What does Goleman say distinguishes those at the very top of competitive pursuits, and what evidence does he give?
questions.a: It is the ability, beginning early in life, to pursue an arduous practice routine for years, which rests on emotional traits such as enthusiasm and persistence in the face of setbacks. Evidence: Chinese divers began at age four and had logged as many dives at twelve as American team members in their early twenties; top Berlin violin students had about ten thousand lifetime hours against around seventy-five hundred for the second tier.

questions.q: Why does Goleman say Asian-American students show the payoff of motivation apart from IQ?
questions.a: Their measured average IQ edge is only two or three points, yet their professional outcomes are as if their IQ were much higher. The reason seems to be that from early school years they work harder, for instance spending 40 percent more time on homework, because of a cultural belief that effort can make anyone do well. That work ethic translates into motivation, zeal and persistence, an emotional edge.

questions.q: Describe the marshmallow test and what Mischel's follow-up found about the children as adolescents.
questions.a: Four-year-olds were offered one marshmallow right away or two if they waited for the experimenter to return from an errand. Those who waited were later more socially competent, self-reliant, trustworthy, able to cope with frustration and eager to take on challenges. The grabbers tended to be shy, stubborn, indecisive, easily upset and still unable to delay gratification.

questions.q: Why does Goleman treat the ability to resist impulse as so fundamental, and how might it work in the brain?
questions.a: All emotions by their nature lead to an impulse to act, and the word emotion itself means to move. Resisting that impulse underlies all emotional self-control. Goleman speculates that it corresponds to inhibition of limbic signals to the motor cortex, though he stresses this interpretation remains speculative.

questions.q: What did the marshmallow study reveal about school performance and about IQ, and why does Goleman call emotional intelligence a meta-ability?
questions.a: By the end of high school the children who waited were far better students and scored much higher on the SAT (610 verbal and 652 math against 524 and 528 for the grabbers). At four, delay of gratification predicted SAT scores twice as well as IQ. Because the ability to deny impulse for a goal governs how well other mental capacities are used, Goleman calls emotional intelligence a meta-ability.

questions.q: A parent wants to help a four-year-old wait for a bigger treat. Using the marshmallow study, what strategies and skills could the child draw on?
questions.a: The waiting children covered their eyes, rested their heads on their arms, talked to themselves, sang, played games with hands and feet or tried to sleep. Goleman says they had mastered reading the situation as one where delay pays, prying attention from the temptation, and distracting themselves while keeping up perseverance toward the goal. These are emotional skills that can be learned.

questions.q: How does worry undermine mental performance, and what evidence does Goleman cite?
questions.a: Worry is a useful preparation for threat gone awry, an intrusive mental rehearsal that captures attention needed elsewhere. Trainee air traffic controllers who were chronically anxious were likelier to fail despite superior intelligence scores, and 126 studies of over 36,000 people linked worry to poorer academic performance. The number of worries reported during a test directly predicts how poorly one does.

questions.q: Describe the inverted U relationship between anxiety and performance, with the example of creative work.
questions.a: Too little anxiety brings apathy and too little motivation; too much anxiety sabotages performance; a modicum of nerves at the peak propels outstanding achievement. For writers and others in creative callings, mild elation (hypomania) sits near the peak. Outright mania loses the cohesion needed to finish anything, since ideas flow too freely.

questions.q: What effects do good moods and laughter have on thinking, according to Goleman?
questions.a: Good moods, while they last, enhance flexible and more complex thinking and make solutions easier to find. Laughter, like elation, helps people think more broadly and associate more freely. People who had just watched television bloopers did better on the candle puzzle, seeing that the tack box could serve as a candle holder.

questions.q: Explain how moods bias decisions through memory.
questions.a: Memory is state-specific. In a good mood we remember more positive events, so as we weigh pros and cons our memory biases the evidence positively, making us more likely to do something slightly adventurous or risky. A foul mood biases memory in a negative direction and pushes us toward fearful, overly cautious decisions.

questions.q: Two friends feel the same nerves before an exam: one studies hard and does well, the other freezes. How does Goleman explain the difference?
questions.a: Goleman describes Richard Alpert, whose nerves ruined his test performance, and Ralph Haber, who found that exam pressure helped him. For some students the apprehension motivates study; for those who are too anxious it interferes with clear thinking and memory during both study and the test. Worries consume mental resources and become self-fulfilling prophecies.

questions.section: Pandora's Box and Pollyanna: The Power of Positive Thinking
questions.q: How does Snyder define hope, and what traits do highly hopeful people share?
questions.a: Snyder defines hope as believing you have both the will and the way to accomplish your goals. Highly hopeful people motivate themselves, feel resourceful, reassure themselves that things will get better, stay flexible about routes or even switch goals, and break a formidable task into smaller pieces. Hope in this sense is more than a sunny view that everything will turn out fine.

questions.section: Pandora's Box and Pollyanna: The Power of Positive Thinking
questions.q: Describe Snyder's study of students who got a D on a first exam and what it implied about hope.
questions.a: Students were asked what they would do after getting a D on an exam when they had hoped for a B. High-hope students worked harder and thought of many options, moderate-hope students had ideas but little determination, and low-hope students gave up on both counts. Hope also predicted first-semester grades better than SAT scores, showing emotional aptitudes matter for students of similar ability.

questions.q: What did Seligman's test with Matt Biondi show about optimism?
questions.a: Seligman had tested Biondi for optimism, and a coach then told him falsely that he had swum a worse time. Biondi did even better when he tried again, while pessimistic teammates given the same false time did worse. At the Olympics Biondi bounced back from two losses to win gold in his next five events.

questions.q: A woman is turned down for a job. How would an optimist and a pessimist, in Seligman's terms, explain and respond?
questions.a: The optimist sees the failure as due to something that can be changed so as to succeed next time, and responds actively and hopefully, with a plan of action or by seeking help and advice. The pessimist blames a lasting personal deficit she is helpless to change, assumes nothing can improve things and so does nothing. This is the difference in explanatory style.

questions.q: Describe Seligman's MetLife study and why optimism mattered for selling insurance.
questions.a: Natural optimists sold 37 percent more in two years than pessimists, and pessimists quit at twice the rate in the first year. A special group who scored high on optimism but failed the normal screening outsold pessimists by 21 percent in year one and 57 percent in year two. Each no is a small defeat; the pessimist hears I am a failure at this, while the optimist blames approach or circumstance and tries again.

questions.q: What is self-efficacy, and how can optimism and hope be developed?
questions.a: Self-efficacy is the belief that one has mastery over life's events and can meet challenges as they come. Developing any competency strengthens it, making people willing to take risks and seek harder challenges, and surmounting those challenges raises it further. Temperament may incline people toward optimism or pessimism, but Goleman says optimism and hope can be learned.

questions.q: What is flow, and what are its main characteristics?
questions.a: Flow, named by Csikszentmihalyi, is the state of peak performance in which people are utterly absorbed in a task with undivided attention and a merging of awareness and action. It brings spontaneous joy and is intrinsically rewarding. Time and self-consciousness drop away, so it is egoless and the opposite of rumination and worry, yet performers feel masterly control.

questions.q: How can a person enter flow, according to Goleman?
questions.a: One route is to focus a sharp attention on the task, which may take discipline at first but then takes on a force of its own, calming emotional turbulence. The other is to find a task one is skilled at and engage it at a level that slightly taxes one's ability, in the zone between boredom and anxiety. Emotional hijackings are incompatible with flow.

questions.q: Why is it paradoxical that the brain is relatively quiet during flow?
questions.a: In flow the brain is in a cool state with lessened cortical arousal, even though the person tackles the most challenging tasks, where one would expect more activity. This is possible because flow occurs only near the summit of ability, where skills are well rehearsed and neural circuits efficient. Strained, worried concentration, fatigue and boredom instead raise or blur activation, with superfluous areas active.

questions.section: Learning and Flow: a New Model for Education
questions.q: What did the Chicago high-school science students study show about flow and achievement?
questions.a: All the students had scored in the top 5 percent in math, and beepers prompted them to note what they were doing and feeling. High achievers did 27 hours of homework a week against about 15 for low achievers, and studying put the high achievers in flow 40 percent of the time against 16 percent for low achievers, who more often felt anxiety. The low achievers found flow in socializing instead.

questions.section: Learning and Flow: a New Model for Education
questions.q: What did Csikszentmihalyi's study of two hundred art-school graduates show, and what is his conclusion?
questions.a: Eighteen years on, those who as students had savored the sheer joy of painting had become serious painters, while those driven by dreams of fame and wealth mostly drifted away from art. He concludes that painters must want to paint above all else, because wondering about sales or critics blocks original avenues; creative achievement depends on single-minded immersion.

questions.section: Learning and Flow: a New Model for Education
questions.q: How does Gardner's approach use flow in education, and why does Goleman think it is a better model?
questions.a: Gardner wants to use children's positive states to draw them into learning, motivating from inside rather than by threat or reward. Schools identify a child's profile of competencies, play to strengths and shore up weaknesses, and offer lessons at an optimal challenge level. Goleman says drawing children to what they love, and sustaining flow by pushing their limits, is a more humane and likely more effective way to use emotion in education.

questions.section: Learning and Flow: a New Model for Education
questions.q: A student feels bored in some lessons and overwhelmed in others. How would the flow model, with Gardner's remarks, interpret this and what would it suggest?
questions.a: Boredom signals too little challenge and anxiety signals too much, so neither is flow. Gardner notes that bored kids fight and act up, and overwhelmed kids get anxious about schoolwork. The remedy is to match the level of the lesson to the child's skills and strengths so learning is neither fearsome nor a bore.

questions.q: How does Chapter 6 follow on from Chapter 5, and what does its title claim?
questions.a: Chapter 5 showed that out-of-control emotions can be brought back into line. Chapter 6 argues that this competence is the master aptitude, a capacity that profoundly affects all other abilities, either facilitating or interfering with them. It shows this through impulse control, moods, hope and optimism, and flow.

questions.q: The Prologue says Part Two will show how neurological givens play out in emotional intelligence. How does Chapter 6 deliver on that for reining in impulse?
questions.a: The Prologue lists reining in emotional impulse among the abilities that make up emotional intelligence, along with reading others' feelings and handling relationships. Chapter 6 takes up the first of these, through the marshmallow test and the wider case that self-control, mood regulation and motivation decide how we use our abilities. Reading others' feelings is left for the next chapter, on empathy.

questions.q: What links the four things the chapter's closing names: controlling impulse, regulating moods, persisting, and entering flow?
questions.a: Goleman says all four show that channeling emotions toward a productive end is a master aptitude. Each bespeaks the power of emotion to guide effective effort. Together they back the chapter's claim that emotional competence shapes how well every other ability is used.

questions.q: Cognitive scientists call the ability to hold in mind all information relevant to the task at hand ____ memory.
questions.explain: Emotions overwhelming concentration swamp working memory, an executive function that makes other intellectual efforts possible.

questions.q: Working memory is executed by the ____ cortex, where feelings and emotions meet.
questions.explain: Limbic circuitry converging on the prefrontal cortex can cost working memory its effectiveness when distress takes hold.

questions.q: International chess champions started on the game at an average age of ____.
questions.explain: Those who rose only to national prominence started at ten, showing the edge of starting early.

questions.q: The second-tier students at the best music academy in Berlin averaged around ____ hours of lifetime practice, against ten thousand for the top students.
questions.explain: The earlier and longer practice of the top students gave a lifetime edge.

questions.q: Walter Mischel's marshmallow study began at a preschool on the ____ University campus.
questions.explain: It involved mainly children of faculty, graduate students and other employees, and it tracked them up to high-school graduation.

questions.q: At age four, delay of gratification predicted SAT scores twice as well as ____ did.
questions.explain: IQ becomes the stronger predictor only after children learn to read.

questions.q: Mischel's own phrase for the essence of emotional self-regulation is goal-directed self-imposed ____ of gratification.
questions.explain: The ability to deny impulse in the service of a goal is what Goleman calls the essence of emotional self-regulation.

questions.q: The relationship between anxiety and performance is described by an upside-down ____.
questions.explain: At the peak is the optimal relationship, with a modicum of nerves propelling outstanding achievement.

questions.q: A mildly elated state, seen as optimal for writers, is technically called ____.
questions.explain: If euphoria gets out of control it becomes outright mania, and ideas flow too freely to finish anything.

questions.q: In the candle puzzle, most people fall into ____ fixedness, thinking of the objects only in conventional ways.
questions.explain: Those who had just watched something funny more often found the tack box could be a candle holder.

questions.q: Because memory is ____-specific, a good mood leads us to remember more positive events when weighing choices.
questions.explain: A foul mood, by the same token, biases memory negatively.

questions.q: The researcher who first studied test anxiety scientifically in the 1960s, whose own nerves hurt his exam results, was Richard ____.
questions.explain: His colleague Ralph Haber found that pre-exam pressure helped him do better.

questions.section: Pandora's Box and Pollyanna: The Power of Positive Thinking
questions.q: Snyder, the psychologist who studied hope, worked at the University of ____.
questions.explain: He found hope a better predictor of first-semester grades than SAT scores.

questions.section: Pandora's Box and Pollyanna: The Power of Positive Thinking
questions.q: Snyder defines hope as believing you have both the ____ and the way to accomplish your goals.
questions.explain: Hope in this technical sense is more than a sunny view that everything will turn out fine.

questions.q: Martin Seligman, who tested Matt Biondi for optimism, is at the University of ____.
questions.explain: He also studied the incoming freshman class of 1984 there and found optimism outpredicted SAT scores and high-school grades.

questions.q: Seligman says optimism is shown in a person's explanatory ____, the way failures are explained.
questions.explain: The explanatory style tells you who gives up, and it can be learned.

questions.q: The belief that one has mastery over the events of one's life is called ____.
questions.explain: Developing any competency strengthens it, and surmounting challenges raises it further.

questions.q: A cashier whose customer is rude thinks, He must be having a bad day, instead of I'm hopeless at this. Seligman would call this thinking ____, rather than pessimistic.
questions.explain: The optimist blames something in the situation, which can change, not a lasting personal flaw.

questions.q: The University of Chicago psychologist who named and studied flow is Mihaly ____.
questions.explain: He collected accounts of peak performance for two decades.

questions.q: Athletes know the state of flow as the ____.
questions.explain: It is a state of grace where excellence becomes effortless.

questions.q: A beginner chess player finds games against a grandmaster far too hard and ends up anxious. Csikszentmihalyi says flow occurs between ____ and anxiety.
questions.explain: Too little demand bores people; too much makes them anxious.

questions.section: Learning and Flow: a New Model for Education
questions.q: Howard Gardner developed the theory of multiple ____.
questions.explain: He sees flow as the healthiest way to motivate children from inside.

questions.section: Learning and Flow: a New Model for Education
questions.q: High achievers in the Chicago study found flow in ____ percent of their study hours.
questions.explain: Low achievers found it only 16 percent of the time.

questions.q: The chapter is titled The Master ____.
questions.explain: Goleman says emotional intelligence is a capacity that profoundly affects all other abilities.

questions.q: True or false: Emotional distress costs us effectiveness in working memory when the limbic circuitry that converges on the prefrontal cortex is in its grip.
questions.explain: This is how Goleman explains why we cannot think straight when upset.

questions.q: True or false: At the 1992 Olympics, twelve-year-old Chinese divers had put in as many lifetime practice dives as American team members of the same age.
questions.explain: The Chinese twelve-year-olds matched the total dives of Americans in their early twenties, because they began training at age four.

questions.q: True or false: Asian-American children have an average IQ advantage over whites of about twenty points, which explains their professional success.
questions.explain: The measured advantage is only two or three points. Harder work and motivation explain the rest.

questions.q: True or false: As adolescents, the children who had waited at four were more likely to embrace challenges and pursue them rather than give up.
questions.explain: The waiters were more socially competent, self-reliant and quick to take initiative.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman reports that poor impulse control in childhood predicts later delinquency less well than IQ does.
questions.explain: He says it is a powerful predictor of later delinquency, again more so than IQ.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman cites a study in which people prone to worry did better on a cognitive task once they had had fifteen minutes of relaxation.
questions.explain: Reducing their worrying removed the problem, so the worry itself was what disrupted them.

questions.q: True or false: Analysis of 126 studies found that the more prone to worry a person is, the better their academic performance.
questions.explain: The finding was the reverse: more worry went with poorer performance, however measured.

questions.q: True or false: A team stuck on a problem that watches a funny clip together is, on Goleman's account, more likely to think broadly about it afterwards.
questions.explain: Laughter helps people associate more freely and find creative solutions, as with the candle puzzle.

questions.section: Pandora's Box and Pollyanna: The Power of Positive Thinking
questions.q: True or false: Snyder found that SAT scores predicted first-semester grades better than hope did.
questions.explain: Hope was the better predictor, even though the SAT is highly correlated with IQ.

questions.q: True or false: A salesman who tells himself that the last customer was just in a bad mood is showing the optimist's way of explaining failure.
questions.explain: Optimists see the reason in the situation, not in themselves, so they can change their approach.

questions.q: True or false: In the MetLife study, the optimists quit in the first year at about twice the rate of the pessimists.
questions.explain: It was the pessimists who quit at twice the rate of the optimists.

questions.q: True or false: A pianist in flow who keeps telling herself, I'm playing wonderfully, deepens the state.
questions.explain: Reflecting too much on how well one is doing can break the feeling of flow.

questions.q: True or false: During flow the brain shows greater cortical arousal than usual, to meet the challenge of a hard task.
questions.explain: The brain is in a cool state in flow, with lessened cortical arousal; strained worried concentration raises it.

questions.section: Learning and Flow: a New Model for Education
questions.q: True or false: In Csikszentmihalyi's study of art-school graduates, those motivated by dreams of fame and wealth were the ones who became serious painters.
questions.explain: It was those who had savored the joy of painting itself who became serious painters.

questions.q: True or false: Chapter 6 opens with Goleman's own experience of freezing in a college exam to show how distress impairs thinking.
questions.explain: The story of the calculus exam is the chapter's opening evidence of emotional distress on mental clarity.

questions.q: True or false: Chapter 6 argues that emotional intelligence matters mainly for friendships and has little effect on intellectual abilities.
questions.explain: It argues the opposite: emotional intelligence is a master aptitude that facilitates or interferes with all other abilities.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman give as examples of what working memory can hold?
options: The digits of a telephone number
The plot lines a novelist is weaving together
The earliest memories of childhood
The names of everyone met that day
questions.explain: He names a phone number and a novelist's intricate plot lines as mundane and complicated examples.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman cite to show that an early start gives a lifetime edge?
options: Chinese divers who began serious training at age four
Violin virtuosos who began studying at around age five
International chess champions who started at an average age of seven
Concert pianists who began after age fifteen
questions.explain: The three early-start examples are the divers, the violinists and the chess champions.

questions.q: Which of these did four-year-olds in Mischel's study do to sustain their wait?
options: Covered their eyes
Talked to themselves or sang
Tried to go to sleep
Asked to see the second marshmallow
questions.explain: The waiting children used distraction and avoiding the sight of the treat.

questions.q: Which of these described the adolescents who had resisted the marshmallow at age four?
options: Better able to cope with life's frustrations
Self-reliant and confident
Mistrustful and resentful about not getting enough
Prone to jealousy and envy
questions.explain: The last two traits describe the grabbers.

questions.q: Which of these were later features of the roughly one third who grabbed the marshmallow?
options: They thought of themselves as bad or unworthy
They overreacted to irritations with a sharp temper
They plunged into projects on their own initiative
They were far superior as students
questions.explain: The grabbers' troubled portrait included low self-regard and a sharp temper; initiative and academic strength belonged to the waiters.

questions.q: Which of these did the worry studies show?
options: Negative thoughts directly disrupted worriers' decision-making
Nonworriers made to worry for fifteen minutes did worse
Relaxation made worriers' task performance worse
Worriers outperformed nonworriers on the sorting task
questions.explain: Negative thoughts disrupt decisions and worrying on purpose impairs nonworriers; relaxation helped worriers.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say good moods do?
options: Make flexible and complex thinking easier
Help people find solutions to intellectual or interpersonal problems
Narrow attention to the task at hand
Bias memory toward negative events
questions.explain: Good moods broaden thinking; narrowed attention and negative bias belong to other states.

questions.section: Pandora's Box and Pollyanna: The Power of Positive Thinking
questions.q: Which of these are traits of people with high hope, according to Snyder?
options: Flexibility in finding other routes or switching goals
Breaking a formidable task into smaller pieces
Sticking to one route whatever happens
Avoiding goals that might fail
questions.explain: Highly hopeful people are flexible and break tasks down; they do not cling to one route.

questions.q: In reaction to being turned down for a job, which of these do optimists tend to do?
options: Formulate a plan of action
Seek out help and advice
Conclude nothing can be done
See the setback as a personal deficit that will always plague them
questions.explain: Optimists think the setback can be remedied; the last two describe pessimists.

questions.q: Which of these predicted freshman grades better than SAT scores did, in studies Goleman describes?
options: Level of hope
Score on a test of optimism
Typical hours of sleep
Number of extracurricular clubs joined
questions.explain: Hope (Snyder) and optimism (Seligman) each outpredicted the SAT.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say about self-efficacy?
options: Developing a competency of any kind strengthens it
It makes people more willing to take risks
It is fixed at birth by temperament
It makes people avoid demanding challenges
questions.explain: Self-efficacy grows with competency and challenges; temperament can be tempered by experience.

questions.q: Which of these characterize a state of flow?
options: Self-forgetfulness
Intrinsic reward
Undivided attention
Close attention to one's own success
questions.explain: Flow is egoless; people in flow are unconcerned with thoughts of success or failure.

questions.q: A beginner wants to enter flow. Which of these could help, according to Goleman?
options: Focus a sharp attention on the task at hand
Find a task skilled enough to manage but slightly taxing
Pick a task far beyond current ability
Pick an easy task to avoid any anxiety
questions.explain: Flow arises from concentrated focus or from a task that slightly taxes one's skill. Too easy bores; too hard makes anxiety.

questions.section: Learning and Flow: a New Model for Education
questions.q: Which of these are true of the Chicago high-school science study?
options: Every student had scored in the top 5 percent on a math test
Students carried beepers that prompted them at random times
High achievers studied about fifteen hours a week at home
Low achievers found flow mainly in studying
questions.explain: The study used beepers and top-5-percent students; high achievers did about 27 hours; low achievers found flow in socializing.

questions.section: Learning and Flow: a New Model for Education
questions.q: Which of these are strategies in schools that apply Gardner's multiple intelligences?
options: Identifying a child's profile of natural competencies
Playing to strengths while shoring up weaknesses
Motivating children mainly with threats
Teaching every child at the same level
questions.explain: Teachers fit the topic and level to each child's profile, aiming at optimal challenge.

questions.q: Which of these does the chapter's closing name as ways that channeling emotions is a master aptitude?
options: Putting off gratification and controlling impulse
Regulating moods so they facilitate rather than impede thinking
Finding ways to enter flow
Reading the innermost feelings of other people
questions.explain: Reading others' feelings, empathy, is a later topic.

questions.q: Put these stages of Mischel's marshmallow study in the order they happened.
items: Four-year-olds are offered one marshmallow now or two if they wait
Some wait fifteen to twenty minutes; others grab one within seconds
Twelve to fourteen years later, adolescents are assessed socially and emotionally
At high-school graduation, academic performance and SAT scores are compared
questions.explain: The study followed the same children from the preschool test to adolescence and then graduation.

questions.q: Order the skills Goleman says some four-year-olds had mastered, as he lists them.
items: Read the situation as one where delay was beneficial
Pry attention away from the temptation
Distract themselves while keeping up perseverance toward the goal
questions.explain: Reading the social situation comes first, then redirecting attention, then sustained distraction toward the goal.

questions.q: Order the self-fulfilling cycle of test worry described in the chapter.
items: The student worries about flunking the test
Mental resources are spent on the worrying
Less attention is left for figuring out the answers
The student does poorly, fulfilling the prediction
questions.explain: Worries detract from resources available for the task and so propel us toward the disaster they predict.

questions.q: Order the chain by which a good mood makes people more adventurous in decisions.
items: The person is in a good mood
Memory brings up more positive events
The weighing of pros and cons tilts positive
The person may do something slightly adventurous or risky
questions.explain: State-specific memory biases the weighing of evidence, which affects the choice.

questions.q: Order the anxiety-performance relationship, from too little to too much anxiety.
items: Apathy or too little motivation
A modicum of nerves propelling achievement
Anxiety that sabotages any attempt to do well
questions.explain: The inverted U climbs from apathy to a peak, then falls into sabotage.

questions.q: Order what happened to Matt Biondi at the 1988 Olympics.
items: Sportswriters tout him as a likely seven-gold winner
He finishes third in the 200-meter freestyle
He is inched out for gold in the 100-meter butterfly
He wins gold in his next five events
questions.explain: He bounced back after two defeats, as Seligman's optimism test had suggested.

questions.q: Order the self-efficacy loop Goleman describes.
items: Developing a competency
A stronger sense of self-efficacy
Greater willingness to take risks and seek demanding challenges
Surmounting the challenges, which raises self-efficacy further
questions.explain: Competency and challenge feed self-efficacy in a rising loop.

questions.q: Order how a pessimistic salesperson's morale deteriorates.
items: Each rejection is a small defeat
The noes mount up and morale deteriorates
The salesperson reads it as I'm a failure at this
Apathy and defeatism set in, if not depression
questions.explain: The pessimist's interpretation of each no leads toward despair, where the optimist's leads toward hope.

questions.q: Order the process of entering flow by focused attention.
items: It takes discipline to get calm and focused
Focus starts to lock in
Focus takes on a force of its own
Emotional turbulence eases and the task becomes effortless
questions.explain: There is a feedback loop at the gateway to flow.

questions.q: Order the levels of demand compared with skill from least to greatest.
items: Too little demand, so people are bored
Demand slightly above usual, so flow occurs
Too much to handle, so people get anxious
questions.explain: Flow lies in the delicate zone between boredom and anxiety.

questions.section: Learning and Flow: a New Model for Education
questions.q: Order the way a child's passion can become high attainment, as the flow model describes.
items: The child is drawn to an area she spontaneously loves
The initial passion is the seed for attainment
She realizes pursuing the field is a source of the joy of flow
Pushing her limits to sustain flow motivates her to get better
questions.explain: Mastery should ideally happen naturally, drawn by what spontaneously engages the child.

questions.section: Learning and Flow: a New Model for Education
questions.q: Order the steps of the Chicago high-school science study.
items: Students in the top 5 percent in math were chosen
Their math teachers rated them high or low achievers
They carried beepers prompting them at random times to record activity and mood
Hours and moods of the two groups were compared
questions.explain: Reports from the beepers revealed that flow in studying separated high from low achievers.

questions.q: Put the chapter's sections in the order Goleman presents them, after the opening.
items: Impulse Control: The Marshmallow Test
Foul Moods, Fouled Thinking
Pandora's Box and Pollyanna: The Power of Positive Thinking
Optimism: the Great Motivator
Flow: the Neurobiology of Excellence?
Learning and Flow: a New Model for Education
questions.explain: The chapter moves from impulse control through mood and motivation to flow and its use in education.

questions.q: Match each group to when its members began serious training, as Goleman reports.
pairs: Best violin virtuosos of the twentieth century
Started at an average age of seven
Chess players of national prominence only
questions.explain: Earlier starts go with higher levels of excellence.

questions.q: Match each term from the chapter's opening to its description.
pairs: Holding in mind all information relevant to the task at hand
Executes working memory and is where feelings and emotions meet
questions.explain: These define the route by which distress impairs thinking.

questions.q: Match each group in the marshmallow study to its average SAT result.
questions.explain: The waiting children also did far better in high school.

questions.q: Match each study or researcher to what it showed about anxiety.
pairs: Chronic anxiety predicted failure despite high intelligence scores
More worry went with poorer academic performance
His nerves made him do poorly on tests
Pre-exam pressure actually helped him do better
questions.explain: Anxiety harms most, but for some it motivates.

questions.q: Match each level of mood or anxiety to its effect on thinking.
pairs: Sabotages any attempt to do well
Ideas flow too freely to finish anything
questions.explain: Each fits somewhere along the inverted U.

questions.q: Match each psychologist in the chapter to the idea he is linked with.
pairs: The marshmallow test of delayed gratification
questions.explain: Each is the main researcher cited for the idea.

questions.section: Pandora's Box and Pollyanna: The Power of Positive Thinking
questions.q: Match each level of hope to how students responded to getting a D on a first exam.
pairs: Worked harder and thought of a range of things to try
Thought of several ways but had far less determination
Gave up on both counts, demoralized
questions.explain: Hope combines will (determination) and way (ideas).

questions.q: Match each person's habit of explanation to what it means in Seligman's terms.
pairs: Due to something that can be changed
A lasting trait they are helpless to change
Makes a plan or seeks help and advice
Does nothing, assuming nothing will help
questions.explain: Explanatory style determines how people respond to setbacks.

questions.q: Match each MetLife figure to what it measures.
pairs: More insurance sold by natural optimists in two years
Pessimists' quitting compared with optimists in year one
Special group's first-year sales edge over pessimists
Special group's second-year sales edge over pessimists
Salesmen who quit in their first three years
questions.explain: The numbers show how optimism sustains sales effort.

questions.q: Match each aspect of flow to its description.
pairs: Undivided, aware of a narrow range tied to the task
A cool state with lessened cortical arousal
In the delicate zone between boredom and anxiety
questions.explain: Each pairs a feature with Goleman's description.

questions.q: Match each mental state to what happens in the brain.
pairs: Minimum mental energy, active areas matched to the task
questions.explain: Efficiency, not effort, marks flow.

questions.section: Learning and Flow: a New Model for Education
questions.q: Match each finding to the group it describes in the studies of flow and achievement.
pairs: High achievers in the Chicago study
In flow 40 percent of study hours
Low achievers in the Chicago study
In flow 16 percent of study hours
Art students who loved painting itself
Art students who dreamed of fame
questions.explain: Flow separated those who achieved from those who did not.

questions.q: Match each chapter number to its title from the book's table of contents.
questions.explain: Chapter 6 sits between emotional management in Chapter 5 and empathy in Chapter 7.

questions.q: Sort these traits by which group of children they described as adolescents.

items.t: Personally effective and self-assertive
Embraced challenges instead of giving up
Trustworthy and dependable
Took initiative and plunged into projects
Stubborn and indecisive
Easily upset by frustrations
Prone to jealousy and envy
Sharp temper that provoked arguments and fights

questions.explain: The waiters showed competence; the grabbers a more troubled portrait.

questions.q: Sort these effects by the mood that produces them.

items.t: Thinking becomes more flexible and complex
Memory favors positive events
More adventurous, slightly risky choices
Easier to find solutions to problems
Memory biased in a negative direction
Fearful, overly cautious decisions

questions.explain: Mood-linked memory biases how we weigh a course of action.

questions.q: Sort these features by whether they belong to hypomania or to outright mania.

items.t: Fluid, imaginative diversity of thought
Optimal for writers and creative callings
Sits near the peak of the inverted U
Agitation undermines cohesive thinking
Ideas flow too freely to produce a finished product
Seen in the mood swings of manic-depressives

questions.explain: Mild elation helps creative work; unchecked euphoria prevents finishing anything.

questions.section: Pandora's Box and Pollyanna: The Power of Positive Thinking
questions.q: Sort these descriptions by which group of students they fit in the hope study.

items.t: Worked harder after the D grade
Thought of a range of things to bolster the final grade
Set themselves higher goals
Gave up on both ideas and determination
Were demoralized
Did not see themselves as having the energy or means to reach goals

questions.explain: High hope pairs will with way; low hope has neither.

questions.q: Sort these thoughts after a sales rejection by who would think them.

items.t: I'm using the wrong approach
That last person was just in a bad mood
I can change what I do on the next call
I'm a failure at this
I'll never make a sale
Nothing I do will make things better next time

questions.explain: Optimists blame the situation or approach, which can change; pessimists blame themselves, permanently.

questions.q: Sort these items by the researcher and idea they belong to.

items.t: Defined as the will and the way to reach goals
Students' reactions to a D on a first exam
Predicted first-semester grades better than SAT
MetLife insurance salesmen
Matt Biondi's false swim time
Explanatory style

questions.explain: Hope is Snyder's focus; optimism is Seligman's.

questions.q: Sort these features by whether they describe flow or strained, worried concentration.

items.t: Relaxed yet highly focused attention
Minimum of mental energy spent
Even hard work seems refreshing
Increased cortical activation
Superfluous brain areas activated
Experienced as being highly distracted

questions.explain: Flow is efficient; worry-fueled strain is not.

questions.q: Sort these by whether they help a person enter flow or bar the way to it.

items.t: Sharp attention intentionally focused on the task
A task one is skilled at
Demands slightly beyond one's usual level
The ennui of depression
The agitation of anxiety
An emotional hijacking

questions.explain: Flow requires calm focus and a fitting challenge; depression, anxiety and hijackings block it.

questions.section: Learning and Flow: a New Model for Education
questions.q: Sort these facts by which group of Chicago students they describe.

items.t: About twenty-seven hours a week of homework
In flow about 40 percent of study hours
Drawn to study because it puts them in flow
About fifteen hours a week studying at home
In flow only 16 percent of study time
Found pleasure and flow in socializing

questions.explain: Studying gave the high achievers flow and the low achievers more often anxiety.

questions.q: Sort these by whether they hurt thinking or drive achievement, as in the chapter's opening.

items.t: Intrusive worry over an upsetting divorce
Hopelessness and helplessness that override all other thoughts
Anger that twists attention toward its own preoccupations
Enthusiasm and zeal
Persistence in the face of setbacks
An optimal degree of anxiety

questions.explain: Emotions can swamp working memory or propel us toward accomplishment.

questions.q: Sort these titles by whether they are sections of Chapter 6 or titles of later chapters.

items.t: The Marshmallow Test
Optimism: the Great Motivator
Flow: the Neurobiology of Excellence?
The Roots of Empathy
The Social Arts
Managing with Heart

questions.explain: Empathy, social skills and workplace use come after this chapter.

questions.q: Why, according to Goleman, are alexithymics like the surgeon Gary at a complete loss in knowing what other people feel?
questions.explain: Goleman writes that empathy builds on self-awareness: the more open we are to our own emotions, the better we read others. Gary's problem is not deliberate coldness but having no idea what he himself feels.
options: Because empathy builds on self-awareness, and they cannot tell what they feel themselves
Because they deliberately ignore other people's feelings in order to stay in control
Because their high IQ crowds out the slower work of reading other people
Because they were never taught the words that name the various emotions

questions.q: Goleman says alexithymics are emotionally ____: the tone of voice, shift in posture or telltale tremble in other people go by unnoted.
questions.explain: He calls them emotionally tone-deaf, because the emotional notes and chords that run through people's words and actions simply do not register with them.

questions.q: Which of these benefits did people who were good at reading feelings from nonverbal cues show on Rosenthal's PONS test?
options: Scoring higher on IQ tests
Being more popular
Scoring much higher on the SAT
Being more outgoing
Being better adjusted emotionally
questions.explain: The benefits included being better adjusted emotionally, more popular, more outgoing and more sensitive. Scores had only an incidental relationship to SAT, IQ or school achievement tests.

questions.q: True or false: In Rosenthal's PONS research, men were in general better than women at reading emotion from nonverbal cues.
questions.explain: It was the other way round: Goleman reports that in general women are better than men at this kind of empathy.

questions.q: What did Rosenthal's research find about the relationship between empathic acuity on the PONS and SAT or IQ scores?
questions.explain: As with other elements of emotional intelligence, scores on this measure had only an incidental relationship to SAT, IQ or school achievement tests: empathy is independent of academic intelligence.
options: High IQ was a strong predictor of high empathic acuity
There was only an incidental relationship between them
High empathic acuity went with markedly lower SAT scores
The two rose together until about age eighteen, then diverged

questions.q: A rule of thumb in communications research, cited by Goleman, is that ____ percent or more of an emotional message is nonverbal.
questions.explain: Goleman cites the rule of thumb that 90 percent or more of an emotional message is carried nonverbally, by tone, gesture and the like.

questions.q: Jon tells a friend he is fine, but his voice is tight and his words come out clipped and fast. On Goleman's account, where does the emotional truth of Jon's message lie?
questions.explain: Goleman writes that when words disagree with tone of voice or gesture, the emotional truth is in how a person says something rather than in what he says.
options: In the words he chooses, since words are the most precise channel
Nowhere clear, since mixed messages carry no emotional truth
In how he says it, since the mode of the emotions is nonverbal
In whatever he says next, once he has had time to reflect

questions.q: Sort these into where Goleman says empathy comes into play and where its absence is seen.
groups: Arenas where empathy comes into play
Where a lack of empathy is seen

items.t: Sales and management
Romance and parenting
Compassion and political action
Criminal psychopaths
Rapists
Child molesters

questions.explain: The ability to know how another feels matters in a vast array of arenas, from sales and management to romance, parenting and political action. Its absence is telling in criminal psychopaths, rapists and child molesters.

questions.q: Why does Goleman call the failure to register another's feelings not only a deficit in emotional intelligence but a tragic failing in what it means to be human?
questions.a: Because all rapport, the root of caring, stems from emotional attunement, from the capacity for empathy. Someone who cannot register another's feelings cannot connect with or care for others in the full human sense, as Gary's failure with Ellen shows. Empathy runs through love, parenting, work and compassion, and its absence is seen in the cruellest criminals.

questions.q: Robert Rosenthal's test of empathy, the PONS, stands for Profile of ____ Sensitivity.
questions.explain: The PONS uses videotapes in which some nonverbal channels are blanked out, so viewers must read emotion from one specific nonverbal cue.

questions.q: Why does Goleman say the key to intuiting another person's feelings lies in reading nonverbal channels?
questions.a: People's emotions are rarely put into words and far more often come through tone of voice, gesture and facial expression. When words disagree with a nonverbal channel, the emotional truth is in how something is said, and a rule of thumb is that 90 percent or more of an emotional message is nonverbal. Such messages are mostly taken in unconsciously.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say about how people take in and learn to read nonverbal emotional messages?
options: They are almost always taken in without paying specific attention to the message
The skills for reading them are for the most part learned tacitly
They are usually received only when the speaker names the feeling aloud
They are best learned through explicit classroom lessons
questions.explain: Anxiety in a tone of voice or irritation in a gesture is simply received and responded to, and the skill of doing so well or poorly is also learned tacitly. Goleman does not say these messages depend on being named or taught explicitly.

questions.q: Which of these did Gary, the alexithymic surgeon, do when his fiancée Ellen spoke of her feelings?
options: He failed to sympathize when she said she felt down
He changed the subject when she spoke of love
He asked detailed questions about why she felt that way
He urged her to see a therapist about her moods
questions.explain: Gary lacked empathy as well as insight, so he missed Ellen's down moods and deflected her talk of love. Nothing suggests he probed her feelings or sent her to a therapist.

questions.q: Match each finding about the PONS with what Goleman reports.
pairs: Good readers of nonverbal cues, in adults
More popular, more outgoing and better adjusted emotionally
Scores compared with SAT or IQ
Better relationships with the opposite sex
Women are in general better at this kind of empathy
Children skilled at the child version, 1,011 tested
Among the most popular and stable, and did better in school
questions.explain: Nonverbal empathy goes with social and emotional benefits and is independent of academic intelligence, as other elements of emotional intelligence are.

questions.q: Match each idea about emotional communication with Goleman's statement of it.
pairs: The mode of the rational mind
Rule of thumb in communications research
90 percent or more of an emotional message is nonverbal
When words disagree with tone of voice
The emotional truth is in how something is said
How such messages are usually received
Unconsciously, without attention to the message
questions.explain: Goleman contrasts words as the mode of reasoning with nonverbal cues as the mode of feeling, and says we usually absorb those cues tacitly.

questions.q: Sort these by whether Rosenthal's PONS research linked them to nonverbal empathy skill or found only an incidental relationship.

items.t: Popularity
Emotional adjustment
Being outgoing
Relationships with the opposite sex
SAT scores
IQ scores
School achievement test scores

questions.explain: Empathic acuity went with social and emotional strengths, but, like other elements of emotional intelligence, it bore only an incidental relation to SAT, IQ or school achievement scores.

questions.q: Sort these by whether they belong to the rational mind's mode of communication or to the emotions' mode.

items.t: The words a person speaks
The literal content of what is said
Tone of voice
Facial expression
Gesture
A shift in posture

questions.explain: Goleman says the mode of the rational mind is words, while the mode of the emotions is nonverbal: tone of voice, gesture, facial expression and the like.

questions.q: Match each young child in Goleman's account of how empathy unfolds with what the child did.
pairs: Teared up at another baby's fall and crawled to her own mother for comfort
Brought his own teddy bear, then his friend's security blanket, to a crying friend
Brought his own mother to comfort a crying friend whose mother was present
Offered cookies and toys to a neighbor's crying baby and patted his head
questions.explain: Each shows a stage: Hope reacts as though the hurt were her own, the one-year-old and Michael know the distress is another's but are confused about what helps, and Jenny tries actively to comfort.

questions.q: Virtually from the day they are born, infants are upset when they hear another infant ____, a response some see as the earliest precursor of empathy.
questions.explain: Newborns are upset by the sound of another infant crying, which some researchers take as the earliest precursor of empathy.

questions.q: True or false: Developmental psychologists have found that infants feel sympathetic distress even before they fully realize that they exist apart from other people.
questions.explain: Even a few months after birth, infants react to a disturbance in others as if it were their own, crying at another child's tears, before they grasp that they are separate beings.

questions.q: Why might a one-year-old put her own fingers in her mouth when another baby hurts her fingers, as Goleman describes?
questions.a: At about one year, children realize the misery is someone else's but are still confused about it. They imitate the other's distress, possibly to better comprehend what the other is feeling, checking whether they hurt too. This motor mimicry is the original technical sense of empathy.

questions.q: When a baby wipes his own tearless eyes on seeing his mother cry, he is showing what psychologists call motor ____.
questions.explain: Imitating another's distress physically is called motor mimicry, the original technical sense of empathy as used in the 1920s.

questions.q: What does the Greek word empatheia, from which English took empathy, mean?
questions.explain: Empatheia means feeling into; aesthetic theorists first used it for the ability to perceive the subjective experience of another person.
options: Loving beyond
Suffering with
Seeing through
Feeling into

questions.q: How did Titchener distinguish empathy from sympathy?
questions.explain: Titchener thought empathy came from physically imitating another's distress, which evokes the same feelings in oneself. He wanted a word distinct from sympathy, which involves no sharing of the other's feelings.
options: Sympathy can be felt for another's general plight without sharing at all what the other person feels
Sympathy involves physically imitating another's distress, while empathy does not
Sympathy is felt only for strangers, while empathy is felt only for loved ones
Sympathy is learned in adulthood, while empathy is present only in infancy

questions.q: True or false: Motor mimicry fades from toddlers' repertoire at around one year of age.
questions.explain: It fades at around two and a half years, when toddlers realize that someone else's pain is different from their own and become better able to comfort them.

questions.q: Put these steps in the early growth of empathy, as Goleman describes it, in order from earliest to latest.
items: Crying at another child's tears as though the hurt were one's own
Realizing the misery is someone else's, but unsure what to do about it
Motor mimicry fades and the child can comfort others better
questions.explain: A few months after birth infants react as if another's distress were their own; by about one year they know it is someone else's but are confused; at around two and a half mimicry fades and comforting improves.

questions.q: In the studies by Marian Radke-Yarrow and Carolyn Zahn-Waxler at the National Institute of Mental Health, what accounted for a large part of toddlers' differences in empathic concern?
questions.explain: A large part of the difference had to do with discipline: children were more empathic when discipline called strong attention to the distress their misbehavior caused someone else.
options: How many brothers and sisters they had
How their parents disciplined them
How early they had learned to speak
How much time they spent in day care

questions.q: Four-year-old Max knocks over his sister's block tower and she starts to cry. Which response from a parent fits what the NIMH studies found makes children more empathic?
questions.explain: Children were more empathic when discipline drew strong attention to the distress the misbehavior caused someone else, rather than simply labeling the act as naughty or punishing it.
options: That was naughty, so no dessert tonight
Go to your room until you can behave
Look how sad you've made your sister feel
Never mind, she can build another one

questions.q: Which of these did the NIMH research by Radke-Yarrow and Zahn-Waxler find shape a toddler's empathy?
options: Being praised for good behavior with small rewards
Seeing how others react when someone else is distressed
Being kept away from other children who are upset
The number of toys the child is made to share
Discipline that calls attention to the distress the child caused someone
questions.explain: Discipline that highlights the harm done fostered empathy, and so did watching how others respond to someone's distress, since children imitate it and build a repertoire of helping responses.

questions.q: Sort these toddler behaviors from Goleman's account by whether they show motor mimicry or an attempt to comfort.

items.t: Putting her own fingers in her mouth when another baby hurts her fingers
Wiping his own tearless eyes on seeing his mother cry
Fetching his own teddy bear for a crying friend
Stroking a crying neighbor's baby on the hair
Bringing his own mother over to a crying friend

questions.explain: Mimicry means copying another's distress, possibly to understand it, while the comforting acts are efforts to help, even when still confused about what helps.

questions.q: Why does Goleman say the roots of empathy can be traced to infancy?
questions.a: Mothers trained to record empathy saw babies such as nine-month-old Hope tear up at another baby's fall, and fifteen-month-old Michael fetch things for a crying friend. Infants are upset by another infant's crying virtually from birth, and they feel sympathetic distress even before they fully realize they exist apart from other people.

questions.q: True or false: In Stern's twin study, Mark broke off eye contact with people by turning his face down and away.
questions.explain: That was Fred's fearful way of breaking contact. Mark turned his head slightly upward and to the side, with a winning smile.

questions.q: Daniel Stern calls the process of letting a child know her emotions are met with empathy, accepted and reciprocated ____.
questions.explain: Stern calls this attunement, and he regards these moments as the most critical of the small exchanges between parent and child.

questions.q: According to Daniel Stern, what most shapes the emotional expectations adults bring to their close relationships?
questions.explain: Stern contends that repeated moments of attunement or misattunement shape these expectations, perhaps far more than the more dramatic events of childhood.
options: A few dramatic events of childhood, such as a loss or a move
The temperament each child inherits at birth
The friendships a child forms in adolescence
Countless repeated small moments of attunement or misattunement with a parent

questions.q: Stern finds that mothers send infants the reassuring message of attunement about once a ____ when they interact with them.
questions.explain: From hours of videotape, Stern finds the attuning message comes about once a minute in mother-infant interaction.

questions.q: Why, according to Stern, is attunement different from simply imitating a baby?
questions.explain: Stern told Goleman that imitation shows you know what he did, not how he felt; to show you sense his feelings you must play them back in another way.
options: Imitation shows only that you know what the baby did, not how he felt
Imitation takes much longer than attunement for the baby to notice
Imitation teaches the baby words, while attunement teaches gestures
Imitation is done by strangers, attunement only by the mother

questions.q: Baby Leo bangs his spoon on the tray and laughs. Which response from his father best fits Stern's idea of attunement?
questions.explain: Attunement plays back the baby's inner feeling in another way, roughly matching his level of excitement. Exact copying shows only what he did, and dampening the moment fails to share it.
options: Taking a spoon and banging it in exactly the same rhythm
Bouncing in his seat and giving an excited whoop that matches Leo's energy
Gently taking the spoon away so Leo calms down
Waiting quietly until Leo is finished before responding
