questions.q: True or false: Stern sees lovemaking as perhaps the closest approximation in adult life to the intimate attunement between infant and mother.
questions.explain: Goleman notes that lovemaking, at its best, involves sensing the other's subjective state in a synchrony that gives a tacit sense of deep rapport: an act of mutual empathy.

questions.q: How does the story of Sarah and her twins Fred and Mark illustrate Stern's idea of attunement?
questions.a: Sarah let Mark break off eye contact whenever he wished, but kept pursuing Fred's gaze when he turned away, a cycle that often left him in tears. She was attuned with Mark but out of emotional synch with Fred. A year later Fred was more fearful and dependent and broke off contact by looking down and away, while Mark met people's eyes. A small, repeated pattern of exchange had shaped each child's emotional style.

questions.q: Why does Daniel Stern believe the small, repeated exchanges between parent and child matter so much?
questions.a: Stern believes the most basic lessons of emotional life are laid down in these intimate moments, especially those that tell a child her emotions are met with empathy, accepted and reciprocated. Because they happen countless times, these moments of attunement or misattunement shape the emotional expectations adults bring to close relationships, perhaps far more than dramatic childhood events.

questions.q: Put the story of the twin Fred and his mother Sarah, as Daniel Stern observed it, in order.
items: At three months Sarah tries to catch Fred's gaze and he averts his face
Sarah tries again and Fred turns away more emphatically
Once she looks away Fred looks back, restarting the cycle and often ending in tears
A year later Fred is fearful and dependent, breaking eye contact by turning down and away
questions.explain: The cycle of pursuit and aversion at three months foreshadowed Fred's fearful way of breaking contact a year later, while Mark, never pursued, looked people straight in the eye.

questions.q: Which of these does Daniel Stern say about attunement between parent and infant?
options: It happens tacitly, as part of the rhythm of the relationship
It means playing back the baby's inner feelings in another way
It means copying exactly what the baby did
It is shaped mainly by the dramatic events of childhood
questions.explain: Attunement is unspoken and works by matching the feeling behind the behavior, unlike simple imitation. Stern stresses countless small moments, perhaps far more than dramatic events.

questions.q: What happens, according to Goleman, when a parent consistently fails to show any empathy with a particular range of a child's emotion, such as joys or the need to cuddle?
questions.explain: The child starts to avoid expressing and perhaps even feeling those emotions, so whole ranges of emotion may be obliterated from the repertoire for intimate relations.
options: The child finds the missing empathy among playmates instead, with no lasting effect
The child expresses those emotions all the more loudly to be noticed
The child begins to avoid expressing, and perhaps even feeling, those emotions
The child becomes highly skilled at reading those emotions in others

questions.q: True or false: Three-month-old babies of depressed mothers mirrored their mothers' moods in play, showing more anger and sadness and less spontaneous curiosity than other infants.
questions.explain: Even infants catch moods: these babies showed more anger and sadness and much less curiosity and interest than infants of mothers who were not depressed.

questions.q: Stern holds out hope in ____ relationships, with friends, relatives or a therapist, that can correct an early imbalance in attunement.
questions.explain: He says relationships throughout life continually reshape our working model of relationships, so an imbalance at one point can be corrected later.

questions.q: Daniela's parents rarely responded to her sadness when she was small. Now in her twenties, she has a close friend who reliably notices and shares her feelings. What does Stern's view suggest about this?
questions.explain: Stern calls this an ongoing, lifelong process: relationships with friends, relatives or in therapy keep reshaping one's working model, so an early imbalance can be corrected later.
options: Nothing can change, since emotional patterns are fixed by age eight months
The friendship will fail, because she cannot feel what she was not taught
Only a parent's apology can repair a childhood lack of attunement
Such a reparative relationship can reshape her working model of relationships

questions.q: Some psychoanalytic thinkers call the therapist's reflecting back to the client an understanding of his inner state, as an attuned mother does with her infant, ____.
questions.explain: Mirroring provides a reparative experience of attunement; the synchrony is unstated and outside awareness, though the patient may feel deeply acknowledged and understood.

questions.q: What paradoxical result does Goleman describe in children who endure intense, sustained emotional abuse, such as cruel threats and humiliations?
questions.explain: Unlike neglect, which seems to dull empathy, such abuse can produce a post-traumatic vigilance to the cues that have signaled threat, an obsessive preoccupation with others' feelings.
options: They can become hyperalert to the emotions of those around them
They lose all ability to sense what others are feeling
They become unusually calm and unbothered by others' moods
They come to prefer solitude and avoid all close relationships

questions.q: Psychologically abused children who in adulthood suffer mercurial, intense emotional ups and downs are sometimes diagnosed with ____ personality disorder.
questions.explain: Goleman notes that many people with borderline personality disorder are gifted at sensing what others feel and commonly report emotional abuse in childhood.

questions.q: Sort these outcomes by the kind of childhood mistreatment Goleman links them to.

items.t: Empathy seems dulled
A life history of foster homes or orphanages
Little opportunity for attunement
Post-traumatic vigilance to signs of threat
Obsessive preoccupation with others' feelings
Gifted at sensing what others feel

questions.explain: Neglect, as in being shuttled between foster homes, seems to dull empathy. Sustained abuse paradoxically makes children hyperalert to others' emotions, a vigilance seen in many adults diagnosed with borderline personality disorder.

questions.q: How, according to Goleman, can a parent's prolonged lack of attunement shape which emotions a child expresses?
questions.a: When a parent consistently fails to show empathy with a range of the child's emotions, the child begins to avoid expressing, and perhaps even feeling, them, so whole ranges of emotion can be obliterated from intimate relations. Conversely, children can come to favor an unfortunate range of emotion depending on which moods are reciprocated, as when babies of depressed mothers mirror their anger and sadness.

questions.q: Children who endure intense, sustained emotional abuse can develop a post-traumatic ____ to cues that have signaled threat.
questions.explain: Such children become hyperalert to the emotions of those around them, a paradoxical contrast with the dulled empathy that follows emotional neglect.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say can happen when a parent consistently fails to show empathy with a range of a child's emotion, such as joys or tears?
options: The child begins to avoid expressing those emotions
The child may even come to avoid feeling those emotions
The child expresses those emotions more loudly to be noticed
The child becomes unusually skilled at reading others' moods
questions.explain: Entire ranges of emotion can be obliterated from the repertoire for intimate relations. Hypervigilance to others' feelings comes instead from sustained abuse, not from unattuned parenting.

questions.q: Match each case from the discussion of misattunement with what Goleman reports.
pairs: A mother who consistently underreacted to her baby
The baby eventually learned to be passive
Mirrored the mood, with more anger and sadness and less curiosity
Friends, relatives or therapy can correct an early imbalance
The therapist reflects back the client's inner state, like an attuned mother
Had been shuttled between foster homes or raised in orphanages
questions.explain: Each case shows what a lack of attunement can do and how later relationships may repair it.

questions.q: A 1975 report described patients with lesions in the right area of the frontal lobes. What curious deficit did they have?
questions.explain: These patients understood words perfectly but missed the feeling carried by the voice; failing to express one's own feelings was the different deficit in the 1979 report.
options: They could not understand words, though they grasped the emotional tone
They could not grasp the emotional message in a tone of voice, though they understood the words
They could not express their own feelings through tone or gesture
They could not recognize the faces of people they knew well

questions.q: True or false: For patients with certain right frontal lesions, a sarcastic thanks, a grateful thanks and an angry thanks all had the same neutral meaning.
questions.explain: Because they could not read the emotion in tone of voice, the three versions of thanks all sounded neutral to them.

questions.q: Match each piece of brain evidence in Goleman's account of the neurology of empathy with what it showed.
pairs: Could not read the emotion in others' tone of voice
Knew what they felt but could not convey it by voice or gesture
Visual cortex cells fire only to specific facial expressions
Amygdala-cortex links cut in wild monkeys
Lost all sense of how to respond emotionally to their troop
questions.explain: Each finding points to a piece of the empathy circuitry: reading feeling, expressing it, recognizing particular expressions, and responding socially through the amygdala-cortical pathway.

questions.q: Leslie Brothers prefers to describe what nonhuman primates display as emotional ____ rather than empathy.
questions.explain: Brothers speaks of emotional communication among primates, shown not only in anecdotes but in studies like the rhesus monkey experiment.

questions.q: Put the steps of the rhesus monkey experiment on emotional communication in order.
items: Monkeys learn to fear a tone paired with an electric shock
Monkeys learn to push a lever on hearing the tone to avoid the shock
Pairs are caged apart, seeing only each other's face on closed-circuit TV
Only the first monkey hears the tone and looks afraid
The second monkey sees the fear and pushes the lever
questions.explain: The second monkey never heard the tone; it acted on the fear it saw in the first monkey's face, which Goleman calls an act of empathy, if not of altruism.

questions.q: What was surprising about the single-neuron studies of monkeys reading one another's faces, and what did Goleman conclude from it?
questions.explain: Neurons distinct from those that recognize familiar faces fire only to particular expressions, such as a fearful grimace, implying the brain is designed from the beginning to respond to emotional expressions.
options: The same neurons recognized every face and every expression, so emotion is not special
The amygdala did not respond to faces at all, suggesting empathy is wholly learned
Some visual cortex neurons fire only to specific expressions, suggesting empathy is a given of biology
Only monkeys raised by their mothers had any face-reading neurons

questions.q: Which of these did the monkey studies find specific visual cortex neurons responding to?
options: A fearful grimace
The sound of a warning cry
A docile crouch
A threatening opening of the mouth
The familiar face of a troop member
questions.explain: These emotion-specific neurons fired to expressions such as a threatening open mouth, a fearful grimace or a docile crouch; recognizing familiar faces is handled by other neurons in the same region.

questions.q: What happened to wild monkeys whose connections to and from the amygdala and cortex were severed before they were returned to their troops?
questions.explain: They managed ordinary tasks, but fled even friendly approaches and ended up living as isolates, shunning their own troop.
options: They could no longer feed themselves and had to be cared for by the troop
They behaved normally once they had recovered from the operation
They became unusually aggressive leaders who dominated the troop
They could still feed and climb but lost all sense of how to respond emotionally to other monkeys

questions.q: Halfway through a heated argument, furious and red-faced, Sam completely misses that his wife is hurt rather than angry. What does Levenson's research suggest explains this?
questions.explain: Goleman concludes that empathy needs enough calm and receptivity for another's subtle signals to be received and mimicked by one's own emotional brain; strong anger leaves little or none.
options: When the emotional brain drives the body with a strong reaction, there is little room for empathy
Sam lacks the visual cortex neurons that respond to facial expressions
Sam's wife is hiding her feelings too skillfully for anyone to read
Empathy works only between strangers, not between spouses

questions.q: Goleman concludes from Levenson's work that empathy requires enough calm and ____ for another person's subtle signals of feeling to be received and mimicked.
questions.explain: Empathy needs calm and receptivity, so that the subtle signals of another's feelings can be mimicked by one's own emotional brain.

questions.q: What evidence in Goleman's discussion of the neurology of empathy suggests that empathy is a given of biology?
questions.a: Single-neuron recordings in monkeys found cells in the visual cortex that fire only to specific facial expressions, such as a fearful grimace, distinct from cells that recognize familiar faces, with the signal passing to the amygdala. Monkeys whose amygdala-cortex connections were cut lost all sense of how to respond to their troop. Together these suggest the brain is built from the start to read and respond to emotional expressions.

questions.q: What does Robert Levenson's study of married couples suggest about the physiological basis and conditions of empathy?
questions.a: Spouses were most accurate at reading their partner's feelings when their own body's reactions, such as sweat response and heart rate, tracked the partner's moment by moment; those who replayed their own reactions read poorly. Empathy thus involves the body mimicking another's subtle physical reactions. It follows that when we are gripped by a strong emotion like anger, there can be little or no empathy, since it needs calm and receptivity.

questions.q: Put the steps of Robert Levenson's study of married couples in order.
items: The couple is videotaped, with physiology measured, discussing a troubling issue
Each partner reviews the tape and narrates their own feelings moment to moment
Each partner reviews the tape again, trying to read the other's feelings
Accuracy is compared with how closely the viewer's body tracked the spouse's
questions.explain: Levenson found the most accurate guessers were those whose own sweat response and heart rate followed their spouse's as they watched.

questions.q: Which of these deficits did Goleman describe in patients with injuries to the right frontal lobes or elsewhere in the right hemisphere?
options: Being unable to understand the emotional message in a tone of voice
Being unable to express their own emotions through voice or gesture
Being unable to understand the words people spoke
Being unable to know what they themselves felt
questions.explain: The 1975 patients missed emotion in tone though they understood the words; the 1979 patients knew what they felt but could not convey it.

questions.q: Which of these did Robert Levenson find in the husbands and wives with the greatest empathic accuracy?
options: Their sweat response rose when their partner's rose
Their heart slowed when their partner's heart rate dropped
Their physiology repeated their own reactions from the original discussion
Their bodies stayed calm whatever their partner felt
questions.explain: Their bodies mimicked their spouse's moment-to-moment reactions. Those who merely repeated their own earlier physiology were very poor at guessing their partner's feelings.

questions.q: Match each researcher or experiment from the neurology of empathy with what it showed.
pairs: The amygdala and its links to the visual cortex are key to empathy
Spouses whose bodies tracked their partner's were most empathically accurate
Rhesus monkeys watching a partner on TV
Seeing fear on the face led the second monkey to push the lever
questions.explain: Brothers' paper, the monkey experiment and Levenson's couples all point to a physiological basis for empathy.

questions.q: What did the study of wild monkeys with severed amygdala-cortex connections show, according to Leslie Brothers?
questions.a: The monkeys could still feed themselves and climb trees, but lost all sense of how to respond emotionally to others in their band. They ran away even from friendly approaches and ended up as isolates. Brothers takes this as evidence for the key role of the amygdala-cortical pathway in reading and responding to emotions.

questions.q: In the single-neuron studies, information from another monkey's face led to a neuron firing first in the visual cortex and then in the ____.
questions.explain: This is a standard route for emotionally arousing information, but the surprise was visual cortex neurons responding only to specific expressions.

questions.section: Empathy and Ethics: the Roots of Altruism
questions.q: In Goleman's account, since to feel with another is to care, the opposite of empathy is ____.
questions.explain: Because empathy is feeling with another, which leads to caring, Goleman calls its opposite antipathy.

questions.section: Empathy and Ethics: the Roots of Altruism
questions.q: Why does the empathy researcher Martin Hoffman argue that the roots of morality are to be found in empathy?
questions.explain: Hoffman holds that sharing the distress of someone in pain, danger or deprivation moves people to act, and that the same capacity leads people to follow moral principles.
options: Children learn moral rules first and only later come to feel empathy
Empathizing with potential victims, and sharing their distress, is what moves people to help them
Morality depends on reasoning, which empathy alone can switch on
Empathy makes people obey authority, which is the basis of all morality

questions.section: Empathy and Ethics: the Roots of Altruism
questions.q: Which of these moral dilemmas does Martin Hoffman pose to show that moral judgments engage empathy?
options: Whether to spend savings on a holiday or a new car
Whether to visit a sick friend as promised or accept a last-minute dinner invitation
Whether to lie to keep from hurting a friend's feelings
Whether to report a coworker who arrives late
When a life-support system should be kept going
questions.explain: Each of Hoffman's dilemmas involves a potential victim, which is why the empathic attitude is engaged again and again in moral judgment.

questions.section: Empathy and Ethics: the Roots of Altruism
questions.q: Put Martin Hoffman's progression of empathy in order, from earliest to most advanced.
items: Feeling another's distress as if one were hurt oneself
Actively soothing a crying child, for example with a teddy bear
Realizing another's feelings differ from one's own and reading their cues
Feeling for the chronic plight of a whole group, such as the poor
questions.explain: At one year the child is distressed as if hurt herself; after that she tries to soothe; from about two she grasps others' different feelings; by late childhood she can feel for whole groups in chronic distress.

questions.section: Empathy and Ethics: the Roots of Altruism
questions.q: Nina, aged three, sees an older friend crying after a fall. Knowing he is proud, she quietly hands him his toy rather than calling the teacher over. Which level of empathy in Hoffman's progression does this show?
questions.explain: From about age two, children grasp that others' feelings differ from their own and can see, for instance, that a proud child is best helped by not drawing undue attention to his tears.
options: Feeling for the chronic plight of an entire group
Feeling the other's distress as if she herself were hurt
Realizing another's feelings differ from one's own and sensing what will actually help
Simple motor mimicry of the other child's distress

questions.section: Empathy and Ethics: the Roots of Altruism
questions.q: John Stuart Mill called empathic anger, the natural feeling of retaliation extended to hurts done to others, the guardian of ____.
questions.explain: Mill dubbed empathic anger the guardian of justice: our natural retaliation, extended by intellect and sympathy to hurts that wound us through wounding others.

questions.section: Empathy and Ethics: the Roots of Altruism
questions.q: What does research on bystanders show about empathy and intervening on behalf of a victim?
questions.explain: Goleman cites this as another instance in which empathy leads to moral action.
options: Empathy makes bystanders freeze and so lowers the chance of intervening
Whether bystanders intervene depends only on how many others are present
Bystanders intervene most when they feel no personal connection to the victim
The more empathy a bystander feels for the victim, the more likely she is to intervene

questions.section: Empathy and Ethics: the Roots of Altruism
questions.q: True or false: Studies in Germany and the United States found that the more empathic people are, the more they favor allocating resources according to merit.
questions.explain: The principle more empathic people favored was allocation according to people's need, showing that empathy shades moral judgments.

questions.section: Empathy and Ethics: the Roots of Altruism
questions.q: How does Martin Hoffman connect empathy with morality, both in personal encounters and beyond them?
questions.a: Hoffman argues that the roots of morality lie in empathy: sharing the distress of potential victims, someone in pain, danger or deprivation, is what moves people to help them. Beyond these encounters, the same capacity for putting oneself in another's place leads people to follow moral principles. As empathy matures to feeling for whole groups, it can underpin adolescent convictions about alleviating misfortune and injustice.

questions.section: Empathy and Ethics: the Roots of Altruism
questions.q: How does Goleman link empathy to caring, and what does he call its opposite?
questions.a: Drawing on John Donne's line about the bell tolling for thee, he says another's pain is one's own, and to feel with another is to care. So the opposite of empathy is antipathy. Moral dilemmas involve potential victims, so the empathic attitude is engaged again and again in moral judgments.

questions.section: Empathy and Ethics: the Roots of Altruism
questions.q: Which of these does Goleman present as ways empathy underlies moral judgment and action?
options: Empathic anger, which Mill called the guardian of justice
Bystanders who feel more empathy for a victim being more likely to intervene
More empathic people favoring allocating resources by need
More empathic people favoring allocating resources only to those who earned them
questions.explain: Empathy fuels anger on behalf of others, intervention for victims and a preference for distribution by need. The studies found the opposite of an earned-only principle.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: Why does Goleman tell the story of Eric Eckardt, who arranged the attack on the skater Nancy Kerrigan?
questions.explain: Eckardt's remorse on seeing Kerrigan's tears led him to bare the secret to a friend, starting the chain that led to arrests: such is the power of empathy, Goleman writes.
options: Seeing Kerrigan sobbing on television gave him a rush of remorse that led him to confess, showing the power of empathy
He felt no remorse at all, showing how a psychopath's mind works
He was moved by Tonya Harding's distress, showing empathy's partiality
He confessed to avoid punishment, showing that fear outweighs empathy

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: What psychological fault line does Goleman say is common to rapists, child molesters and many perpetrators of family violence?
questions.explain: Their shared failing is an incapacity for empathy, which lets them tell themselves lies that encourage their crimes.
options: They are unusually anxious and fearful
They are incapable of empathy
They have below-average intelligence
They were all victims of emotional abuse

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: According to Goleman, what does the inability to feel a victim's pain allow offenders to do?
questions.explain: Without feeling the victim's pain, offenders can tell themselves self-justifying lies, such as an abusive parent's claim that it is just good discipline.
options: Plan crimes more intelligently than other people
Forget their crimes entirely once they are over
Tell themselves lies that encourage their crimes
Feel fear more strongly, which drives them to act

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: Match each type of offender with the kind of self-justifying lie Goleman reports.
pairs: A woman who resists is just playing hard to get
I'm not hurting the child, just showing love
questions.explain: These self-justifications were collected from what people being treated for these problems said they told themselves while brutalizing their victims or preparing to.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: Put the emotional cycle that typically leads to child molestation, as Goleman describes it, in order.
items: Feeling upset: angry, depressed or lonely
Seeking solace in a fantasy of warm friendship with a child
The fantasy turns sexual and brings brief relief
Depression and loneliness return even more strongly
Thinking about acting out the fantasy, with self-justifications
Planning and carrying it out as though the child had no feelings
questions.explain: The cycle starts in distress, seeks relief in fantasy, deepens when relief fades, and ends in action pursued with total emotional detachment from what a real child would feel.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: Put the steps of the perspective-taking treatment for sex offenders, described by Goleman, in order.
items: Read accounts of crimes like theirs told from the victim's view
Watch videotapes of victims describing what it was like
Write about their own offense from the victim's point of view
Read that account to a therapy group and answer as the victim
Go through a simulated reenactment, playing the victim
questions.explain: The program builds step by step from others' accounts to the offender's own crime, ending with a reenactment in which he plays the role of the victim.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: William Pithers's treatment, in which sex offenders imagine their crime from the victim's point of view, is called ____ therapy.
questions.explain: Goleman calls it perspective-taking therapy, because it has offenders take the victim's perspective at every step.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: How did sex offenders who went through Pithers's program in prison compare with those who had no such treatment?
questions.explain: Offenders who completed the program reoffended at half the rate of those who received no such treatment.
options: They had the same rate of reoffending, but committed lesser crimes
They had a slightly higher rate, because the program stirred up fantasies
None of them reoffended at all after release
They had only half the rate of subsequent offenses after release

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: True or false: William Pithers holds that without the initial motivation inspired by empathy with the victim, none of the rest of a sex offender's treatment will work.
questions.explain: Empathy with the victim makes denying the victim's pain difficult, even in fantasy, which strengthens the motivation to fight the urges; the rest of treatment depends on it.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: Why does empathy with the victim help sex offenders resist reoffending, according to William Pithers?
questions.a: Pithers says empathy with the victim shifts perception, so that denying the victim's pain, even in one's fantasies, becomes difficult. Offenders can no longer see victims through the lens of fantasy as having no feelings. This strengthens their motivation to fight their urges, and without that empathy-inspired motivation the rest of treatment will not work.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: Goleman notes that the psychopath has more recently been called the ____ as a psychiatric diagnosis.
questions.explain: The psychopath is more recently called the sociopath, a criminal type for whom there is much less hope of instilling empathy than for child molesters.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: A colleague is charming with clients, lies smoothly whenever it gets him what he wants, plays on people's feelings to manipulate them, and shows no remorse after getting a coworker fired. Which of Goleman's descriptions does this pattern most resemble?
questions.explain: Goleman describes psychopaths as charming, remorseless, glib liars who manipulate their victims' emotions with cynicism. The alexithymic, by contrast, is bewildered rather than calculating.
options: The psychopath: charming, a glib liar, manipulative and without remorse
The abused child grown up: hyperalert to every shift in others' moods
The alexithymic: confused about his own feelings and baffled by others'
The impulsive batterer: violent out of jealousy or fear of abandonment

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: Which of these roles does Goleman offer as ones where an opportunistic lack of empathy may be a kind of virtue?
options: A bad cop police interrogator
A corporate raider
A primary school teacher
A torturer for a terrorist state
A nurse in a children's ward
questions.explain: Goleman lists the bad cop interrogator and the corporate raider, and describes torturers who learned to dissociate from victims' feelings to do their job. The caring professions rely on empathy instead.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: What physiological anomaly did researchers find in many of the most violent wife batterers?
questions.explain: As their anger mounted, their heart rate dropped, so they grew physiologically calmer even as they became more belligerent: a cold, calculating state rather than the heat of fury.
options: Their heart rate climbed far higher than in other angry men
Their heart rate dropped as their anger mounted, rather than climbing
Their sweat response stopped entirely whenever they argued
Their brain waves showed no response to their wives' voices

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: Sort these traits between the coolly calculating wife batterers and most other men who batter their wives.

items.t: Heart rate drops as their anger mounts
Also violent outside the marriage, as in bar fights
Strike out seemingly for no reason at all
Not restrained by anything she does, even trying to leave
Strike out in rage after feeling rejected or jealous
Driven by fear of abandonment
Act impulsively, carried away by fury

questions.explain: The calculating batterers are a breed apart: physiologically calm, violent elsewhere too, and unprovoked. Most batterers act impulsively from rage, jealousy or fear of abandonment.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: What does the scrambled-words finding suggest about the brains of psychopaths?
questions.explain: Hare reads this as a shallow understanding of emotional words, reflecting psychopaths' general shallowness in the affective realm.
options: An overactive amygdala that floods every word with feeling
Damage to the visual cortex, which prevents them from reading words quickly
A disruption in circuits between the verbal cortex, which recognizes a word, and the limbic brain, which attaches feeling to it
A gap in memory that stops them recalling what words mean

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: True or false: In Robert Hare's earlier research, psychopaths about to receive an electric shock showed the normal fear response, but felt no remorse afterward.
questions.explain: Hare found that psychopaths about to receive a shock show no sign of the fear response normal in people about to experience pain.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: How does Robert Hare explain the callousness of psychopaths, drawing on his finding about the prospect of an electric shock?
questions.a: Psychopaths about to receive a shock show none of the normal fear response, suggesting an irregularity in the amygdala and related circuits. Because the prospect of pain does not trigger anxiety, they lack concern about future punishment for what they do. And because they do not feel fear themselves, they have no empathy or compassion for the fear and pain of their victims.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: True or false: Goleman reports that the best consensus is that there is a biological marker for crime, though no single criminal gene.
questions.explain: The best consensus, he notes, is that there is no biological marker for crime, and certainly no criminal gene.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: In his note of caution about biology and crime, what does Goleman say about people who have a biologically based lack of empathy?
questions.explain: Even where empathy's lack has a biological basis, most people with it will not turn to crime; it is one factor among many forces creating a vector toward criminality.
options: Most will eventually commit crimes unless they are treated early
Their lack of empathy is the sole cause of whatever crimes they commit
They should be identified by screening and kept under watch
Most will not drift to crime; the lack should be weighed with psychological, economic and social forces

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: Why does Goleman see some small hope for instilling empathy in child molesters but much less for psychopaths?
questions.a: Child molesters' lack of empathy is part of an emotional cycle in which they blot out the victim's feelings through fantasy, and perspective-taking therapy can make that denial difficult, halving reoffending in Pithers's program. Psychopaths, by contrast, seem incapable of empathy, compassion or conscience at all, forming only the shallowest connections, and Hare's research suggests a physiological basis in disrupted limbic circuits and an absent fear response.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: Why does Goleman call the discovery about the most violent wife batterers one of the more ominous ways an absence of empathy may show itself?
questions.a: These men beat or threaten their wives in a cold, calculating state: as their anger mounts, their heart rate drops, so they grow calmer while becoming more abusive. Their violence seems a calculated act of terrorism to control their wives by fear, not an impulsive loss of control. They are also violent outside the marriage and strike seemingly without reason, and nothing their wives do restrains them.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: Robert Hare contends that because psychopaths feel no fear themselves, they have no ____ for the fear and pain of their victims.
questions.explain: The prospect of pain does not trigger anxiety in psychopaths, so Hare says they lack concern about future punishment and about what their victims feel.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: William Pithers says that without the initial ____ inspired by empathy with the victim, none of the rest of a sex offender's treatment will work.
questions.explain: Empathy with the victim makes denial of pain difficult and strengthens the men's motivation to fight their perverse urges.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: Why do rapists, child molesters and abusive parents tell themselves self-justifying lies, according to Goleman?
questions.a: They are incapable of empathy, and this inability to feel their victims' pain lets them tell themselves lies that encourage their crimes, such as that a resisting woman is playing hard to get or that abuse is just discipline. Goleman collected these from people in treatment who said they had told themselves such things while brutalizing victims or preparing to.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: How does a child molester see the child as the emotional cycle carries him toward the crime?
questions.a: He sees the child through the lens of his perverted fantasy, not with empathy for what a real child would feel. Everything from the plan to the execution is pursued as if the child had no feelings, and he projects on her the cooperative attitude of the child in his fantasy. Her revulsion, fear and disgust do not register, since they would ruin things for him.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: What did Robert Hare's scrambled-words test show about psychopaths, and how does he interpret it?
questions.a: Most people decide faster about emotional words such as kill and show a distinctive brain-wave pattern, but psychopaths showed neither response. This suggests a disruption in circuits between the verbal cortex and the limbic brain. Hare reads it as a shallow understanding of emotional words, reflecting their general shallowness in the affective realm.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: What non-biological explanations for a lack of empathy does Goleman offer, and what caution does he add about biology and crime?
questions.a: Intimidating others may be a perverse emotional skill with survival value in violent neighborhoods, and an opportunistic lack of empathy can be a kind of virtue in roles from bad-cop interrogator to corporate raider. He cautions that there is no biological marker for crime or criminal gene, and most people with a biological lack of empathy will not drift to crime.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: Put these topics from the chapter's final section in the order Goleman presents them.
items: The emotional cycle leading to child molestation
The perspective-taking treatment program
Faro's look at the men in the next car
The coolly calculating wife batterers
Hare's scrambled-words test
questions.explain: Goleman moves from molesters and their treatment to the psychopath, illustrated by Faro, then to the calculating batterers and Hare's evidence of a possible neural defect.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say about psychopaths?
options: They are charming yet completely without remorse
They are glib liars who manipulate their victims' emotions cynically
They show the normal fear response when about to receive a shock
They respond faster to emotional words than to neutral ones
questions.explain: Psychopaths are notorious for charm without remorse and for glib lying. Hare found they lack the normal fear response and do not respond faster to emotional words.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: Match each of Robert Hare's findings about psychopaths with what it showed.
pairs: Response to emotional words such as kill
No faster decisions and no distinctive brain-wave pattern
No sign of the fear that is normal before pain
No anxiety at the prospect of pain
Lack of concern about future punishment
No empathy or compassion for their victims' fear
questions.explain: Hare ties the psychopath's callousness to a pattern suggesting an irregularity in the amygdala and related circuits.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: Match each person in the final section with the role or reaction Goleman reports.
pairs: Felt a rush of remorse on seeing Nancy Kerrigan sobbing on television
Described crippling a mother and her baby with more pride than remorse
Vermont prison psychologist who developed perspective-taking therapy
Writer working on a book about the Crips and the Bloods
University of British Columbia psychologist who studied psychopaths
questions.explain: These figures illustrate both the power of empathy and its absence.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: Match each explanation for a lack of empathy in crime with the example Goleman gives.
pairs: Opportunistic lack of empathy as a virtue
A bad cop interrogator or a corporate raider
Dissociating from victims' feelings to do a job
Psychopaths' responses to emotional words and to shock
questions.explain: Goleman allows many routes to manipulativeness besides biology, while noting a possible neural basis in some psychopaths.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: Sort these findings by whether they describe psychopaths or ordinary people in Hare's research.

items.t: No faster decisions about emotional words
No distinctive brain wave to emotional words
No fear response when about to receive a shock
Decide faster whether an emotional word was scrambled
Distinctive brain wave to emotional words
Fear response when about to feel pain

questions.explain: Hare found psychopaths lack the responses most people show, suggesting disrupted circuits between the verbal cortex and limbic brain and an irregular amygdala.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: Sort these explanations for a lack of empathy by whether Goleman offers them as possible biological or non-biological accounts.

items.t: A neural defect in psychopaths
Disrupted circuits between the verbal cortex and limbic brain
No fear response before a shock
Intimidation has survival value in violent neighborhoods
Opportunistic lack of empathy as a virtue in some roles
Torturers learning to dissociate to do their job

questions.explain: Goleman notes that behavior as complex as crime has many plausible explanations that do not evoke a biological basis, alongside evidence of neural differences in some psychopaths.

questions.section: Life Without Empathy the Mind of the Molester, the Morals of the Sociopath
questions.q: Sort these parts of William Pithers' treatment by whether offenders take in victims' accounts or produce the victim's perspective themselves.

items.t: Reading accounts of crimes like theirs from the victim's view
Watching videotapes of victims describing the experience
Writing about their own offense from the victim's view
Reading that account to a group and answering as the victim
Reenacting the crime playing the victim

questions.explain: The program moves from receiving victims' stories to actively imagining and enacting the victim's experience.

questions.q: Which of the five domains of emotional intelligence, set out by Goleman in Chapter 3, does The Roots of Empathy take up?
questions.explain: Goleman's list assigns recognizing emotions in others, empathy, the fundamental people skill, to Chapter 7; the other domains go to Chapters 4, 6 and 8.
options: Recognizing emotions in others
Motivating oneself
Knowing one's emotions
Handling relationships

questions.q: Why does The Roots of Empathy open by returning to Gary, the alexithymic surgeon first met in Know Thyself (Chapter 4)?
questions.explain: Gary lacked insight into his own feelings and so could not read Ellen's; linking back to Chapter 4 makes the point that empathy builds on self-awareness.
options: To show that surgeons as a group tend to lack empathy
To show that empathy builds on self-awareness, so lacking one means lacking the other
To show that empathy is unrelated to knowing one's own feelings
To show that alexithymia can be cured by a loving partner

questions.q: Put these chapters of Part Two, The Nature of Emotional Intelligence, in the order Goleman presents them.
items: Know Thyself
Passion's Slaves
The Master Aptitude
The Roots of Empathy
The Social Arts
questions.explain: The chapters follow the domains of emotional intelligence: self-awareness, managing emotions, motivating oneself, empathy, and then handling relationships.

questions.q: True or false: The Roots of Empathy belongs to Part Three of the book, Emotional Intelligence Applied.
questions.explain: It belongs to Part Two, The Nature of Emotional Intelligence, which examines the basic abilities, such as reading another's feelings, before Part Three looks at relationships, work and health.

questions.q: What does the chapter that immediately follows The Roots of Empathy, The Social Arts, go on to examine?
questions.explain: In Goleman's scheme empathy leads to the domain of handling relationships, the art of managing emotions in others, taken up in The Social Arts.
options: How toxic emotions put physical health at risk
How the emotional brain was shaped by evolution
Handling relationships, which is largely skill in managing emotions in others
How schools can teach emotional literacy

questions.q: What does the word Roots in the chapter title The Roots of Empathy signal about the chapter's approach?
questions.explain: The chapter seeks where empathy comes from: its first signs in infants, attunement between parent and child, and the brain circuitry behind it, and then why it matters for morality.
options: It surveys the history of the word empathy across many languages
It argues that empathy is entirely a product of later schooling
It deals mainly with empathy among plants and animals in the wild
It traces empathy to its origins in infancy, in parent-child attunement and in the brain

questions.q: How does the order of sections in The Roots of Empathy build the chapter's argument?
questions.a: The chapter moves from origins to consequences. It traces how empathy unfolds in infancy and is shaped by parenting, attunement and misattunement, then its brain basis in the amygdala-cortical circuitry. It then shows why empathy matters, as the root of altruism and morality, and ends with what life without empathy looks like, in molesters, psychopaths and calculating batterers.

questions.q: The neurology section of The Roots of Empathy centers on the amygdala and its connections. Where earlier in the book was the amygdala's role in emotion laid out in detail?
questions.explain: Part One, especially Anatomy of an Emotional Hijacking, explained the amygdala as the emotional brain's sentinel; Chapter 7 builds on it to locate empathy's circuitry.
options: In Anatomy of an Emotional Hijacking (Chapter 2)
In Schooling the Emotions (Chapter 16)
In Managing with Heart (Chapter 10)
In Intimate Enemies (Chapter 9)

questions.q: True or false: Robert Levenson, whose study of married couples' physiology appears in The Roots of Empathy, reappears in Intimate Enemies (Chapter 9) with research on how husbands and wives handle marital squabbles.
questions.explain: In Chapter 9 Goleman cites Levenson's study of 151 long-married couples on how husbands find becoming upset in a disagreement more aversive than wives do.

questions.q: How does the chapter's material on attunement and misattunement in childhood look ahead to Part Four of the book?
questions.a: The chapter argues that countless small moments of attunement between parent and child shape the emotional expectations adults bring to relationships, and that neglect or abuse can dull or distort empathy. The Prologue's road-map says Part Four shows how the emotional lessons we learn as children at home and at school shape the emotional circuits. So attunement is an early example of the theme that childhood is critical for setting down emotional habits.

questions.q: Put these sections of The Roots of Empathy in the order the chapter presents them.
items: How Empathy Unfolds
The Well-Attuned Child
The Costs of Misattunement
The Neurology of Empathy
Empathy and Ethics
Life Without Empathy
questions.explain: The chapter traces empathy from infancy and parent-child attunement, through its costs and its brain basis, to its moral role and finally its absence.

questions.q: In Goleman's opening story of Len and Jay, what set off the episode in which Jay ends up comforting his older brother?
questions.explain: Five-year-old Len, losing patience with Jay's mess, bit him; when their mother scolded Len and made him put the blocks away, Len burst out crying and she refused to console him.
options: Len bit Jay over the Lego blocks, and their mother scolded Len, who then burst into tears
Jay broke Len's toy car, and their mother sent both boys to their room in tears
Len fell and hurt his knee, and their mother was too busy to come and console him
Jay knocked over Len's Lego tower, and Len cried until their mother smacked him

questions.q: Put Jay's attempts to calm his crying brother Len in the order Goleman describes them.
items: Pleading with Len directly to stop crying
Appealing to their mother on Len's behalf
Patting Len and reassuring him in soothing tones
Helping put the Lego blocks back in their bag
Showing Len a toy car to distract him
Threatening Len in their mother's voice of authority
questions.explain: Jay moves from a simple plea, to seeking an ally in his mother, to physical comfort, to a helping hand, to distraction, and finally to borrowing his mother's threat of a smack.

questions.q: Match each kind of tactic in Jay's repertoire to what Jay actually did with Len.
pairs: Calling to their mother to look at Len crying
Putting the Lego away in its bag for Len
Asking Len to look at a man inside a toy car
Warning Len that his bottom would be smacked
questions.explain: Goleman lists Jay's tactics as a plea, seeking an ally in his mother, physically comforting, lending a helping hand, distraction, threats and direct commands.

questions.q: Goleman says a toddler who uses a sibling's upset as a chance to torment them still shows a crucial emotional aptitude. What aptitude, and why does it matter?
questions.a: Even mean-spirited teasing shows the ability to know another's feelings and to act in a way that further shapes them. The same skills Jay used to soothe Len can be used to torment. That ability matters because managing emotions in someone else is “the core of the art of handling relationships.”

questions.q: What does Goleman say the Len and Jay episode reveals about a thirty-month-old's emotional abilities?
questions.a: It reveals remarkable emotional sophistication: in trying to soothe Len, Jay draws on a large repertoire of tactics, from a plea, to seeking an ally in his mother, to physical comfort, a helping hand, distraction, threats and commands. He probably learned these from how others treated him in his own distress, but what counts is that he can readily use them to manage someone else's emotions at such a young age.

questions.q: Goleman writes that being able to manage emotions in someone else is the core of the art of handling ____.
questions.explain: This is the chapter's central claim: the social arts are, at bottom, the skill of shaping other people's feelings.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say must ripen before a child can handle emotions in someone else?
options: Self-management
Empathy
Academic intelligence
Self-motivation
Verbal fluency
questions.explain: Handling emotions in someone else requires the ripeness of two other emotional skills, self-management and empathy. Self-motivation is a separate domain, and verbal or academic ability is not what Goleman names.

questions.q: Goleman writes that attunement to others demands a modicum of ____ in oneself.
questions.explain: To manage others' feelings a toddler must first reach a benchmark of self-control, damping down their own anger, distress and excitement.

questions.q: Sort these toddler behaviours by which of the two prerequisite skills for handling relationships each shows.

items.t: Waiting for a snack without wailing
Coaxing a parent instead of grabbing the toy
Showing patience in place of a tantrum
Getting upset because a brother is sobbing
Trying hard to cheer up a crying sibling
Noticing that a playmate is hurt

questions.explain: Goleman cites waiting without wailing, arguing or cajoling rather than using brute force, and patience instead of tantrums as early self-control; empathy, the root of compassion, is what drove Jay to cheer up Len.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman calls empathy, which drove Jay to try so hard to cheer up his brother, the root of compassion.
questions.explain: He writes that it was Jay's empathy, the root of compassion, that drove him to cheer up his sobbing brother Len.

questions.q: According to Goleman, what can happen to intellectually bright people who lack the social competences he calls people skills?
questions.explain: Goleman says it is precisely the lack of these skills that can cause even the brightest to founder in relationships. Hollow popularity is a different problem, that of the social chameleon who has social skill but little self-knowledge.
options: They become overly dependent on others to make their decisions for them
They founder in relationships, coming off as arrogant, obnoxious, or insensitive
They feel others' moods so keenly that they are swamped by distress
They succeed socially but feel empty and unsure of their true selves

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say social abilities allow a person to do?
options: Persuade and influence
Avoid ever feeling distressed
Shape an encounter
Raise their measured IQ
Mobilize and inspire others
questions.explain: These social abilities allow one to shape an encounter, mobilize and inspire others, thrive in intimate relationships, persuade and influence, and put others at ease. They do not raise IQ or remove one's own distress.

questions.q: Priya is the sharpest analyst on her team, yet colleagues dread meetings with her because she dismisses their ideas and ignores how they react. How would Goleman explain her problem?
questions.explain: Goleman says a lack of social competences can make even the intellectually brightest come off as arrogant or insensitive. Her problem is not intellect, and a chameleon would try too hard to please rather than dismiss people.
options: She has too little intellectual ability to understand her colleagues' ideas
She is a social chameleon who changes her views to suit whoever she is with
She lacks the people skills that make for effectiveness with others, despite her intellect
She has caught her colleagues' bad moods through emotional contagion

questions.q: Using the story of Jay and Len, explain why Goleman says handling another person's emotions depends on self-management and empathy.
questions.a: To soothe Len, Jay first needed a measure of calm in himself, since attunement to others demands some self-control over one's own distress and impulses. He also needed empathy, the root of compassion, which made him care about Len's tears and drove his many attempts to comfort him. Only with both skills in place can the art of relationships, managing emotions in others, develop.

questions.q: Paul Ekman uses the term ____ for the social consensus about which feelings can be properly shown when.
questions.explain: Display rules are the shared norms for showing feelings, and cultures vary greatly in them.

questions.q: In Ekman's study of Japanese students watching a horrific film of ritual circumcisions, when did the students' faces show vivid distress and disgust?
questions.explain: With an authority figure present, their faces showed only the slightest hints of reaction; when they believed they were alone, their faces twisted with anguish, dread and disgust.
options: When an authority figure was present and watching them closely
When they were asked afterward to describe the film to a classmate
When they watched the film together in a large group of students
When they thought they were alone, though a secret camera was taping them

questions.q: Which of these are basic kinds of display rules that Goleman describes?
options: Exaggerating what one feels
Substituting one feeling for another
Minimizing the show of emotion
Delaying a feeling until one is alone
Mirroring the feeling of the listener
questions.explain: Goleman names three basic display rules: minimizing, exaggerating by magnifying the expression, and substituting one feeling for another. Mirroring belongs to emotional contagion, not to display rules.

questions.q: Match each display rule to the example Goleman gives of it.
pairs: Japanese students' poker face in front of an authority figure
A six-year-old's quivering frown while complaining about being teased
False positive assurances where it is impolite to say no
questions.explain: The Japanese students masked their upset, the six-year-old magnified her expression to her mother, and in some Asian cultures a polite but false yes replaces a no.

questions.q: Sort these everyday situations by the display rule each person is following.

items.t: Keeping a blank face while the boss criticizes your report
Hiding nerves behind a calm look in a job interview
Barely reacting to bad news in front of a judge
Beaming and thanking an aunt for a sweater you dislike
Saying a plan sounds great when you think it will fail
Acting delighted about a friend's news that disappoints you

questions.explain: Minimizing damps down the show of a feeling, as the Japanese students did before authority; substituting puts a different, more acceptable feeling in place of the real one, as with a dreadful gift from Grandpa.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says children learn display rules mostly through explicit instruction, such as being told to smile and say thank you.
questions.explain: Explicit instruction plays a part, but Goleman says the education in display rules is more often through modeling: children learn to do what they see done.

questions.q: Goleman writes that in educating the sentiments, emotions are both the medium and the ____.
questions.explain: How a parent delivers a lesson about feelings teaches as much as the lesson's words do.

questions.q: In Goleman's example of Grandpa's dreadful birthday present, what happens when a cold, harsh parent hisses at the child to smile and say thank you, and what does it show?
questions.a: The child is likely to learn a different lesson from the one intended and respond to Grandpa with a frown and a curt, flat thank you, leaving him hurt by the mixed message. Taught warmly, the child would have smiled and Grandpa would have been happy, though misled. It shows that emotions are both the medium and the message, so the parent's own manner is part of what the child learns.

questions.q: Dana is upset that her manager has cancelled her project, but in the meeting she keeps her face neutral and says little. Which display rule is she following?
questions.explain: Like the Japanese students who masked their upset before an authority figure, Dana damps down her display. She does not put on a false cheerful feeling, which would be substituting.
options: Minimizing the show of emotion in front of someone in authority
Exaggerating her feeling to draw sympathy from her manager
Substituting a cheerful feeling for her real disappointment
Letting her feelings leak out through emotional contagion

questions.q: Why does Goleman say display rules are more than part of the lexicon of social propriety?
questions.a: Display rules dictate how our own feelings impact on everyone else, since emotional displays have immediate consequences for the person who receives them. To follow these rules well is to have optimal impact; to follow them poorly is “to foment emotional havoc.” How well one uses these strategies, and knows when to, is therefore one factor in emotional intelligence.

questions.q: Goleman describes actors as artists of the emotional ____, whose expressiveness evokes a response in their audience.
questions.explain: Some people are natural actors, but because the display rules we learn vary with our models, people differ greatly in their adeptness.

questions.q: Why, according to Goleman, do people differ so greatly in their adeptness at displaying emotion?
questions.a: Some people come into life as natural actors, whose expressiveness readily evokes a response in others. But display rules are learned, partly by instruction and more often by modeling, and the lessons vary according to the models a person has had. So people end up differing greatly in how well they use display rules and know when to use them.

questions.q: What did Ekman's study of Japanese students show about display rules?
questions.a: When the students watched a horrific film with an authority figure present, they followed the Japanese norm of minimizing distress before authority, showing only the slightest hints of reaction. When they believed they were alone, a secret camera caught vivid anguish, dread and disgust on their faces. The feelings were the same; what changed was the social rule about showing them.

questions.q: What happened when six monks walked calmly through a Vietnam War firefight, and what principle does Goleman draw from it?
questions.a: The monks walked straight along the berms toward the line of fire; nobody shot at them, and afterward the soldiers lost all will to fight and simply stopped for the day. Goleman says the power of their quietly courageous calm to pacify soldiers illustrates a basic principle of social life: emotions are contagious. The story is an extreme case of something that usually happens far more subtly.

questions.q: Goleman draws from the story of the monks in the firefight a basic principle of social life: emotions are ____.
questions.explain: The monks' calm spread to the soldiers, who stopped fighting; Goleman treats this as a dramatic case of emotional contagion.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says most emotional contagion is as dramatic and obvious as the monks' effect on the soldiers in Vietnam.
questions.explain: He calls the monks' tale an extreme; most emotional contagion is far more subtle, part of a tacit exchange that happens in every encounter.

questions.q: Goleman describes the way we transmit and catch moods as a subterranean ____ of the psyche, in which some encounters are toxic and some nourishing.
questions.explain: The image stresses that a hidden exchange of feeling goes on in every encounter, mostly below awareness.

questions.q: After paying for groceries, Tom leaves feeling vaguely unwelcome, though the cashier only said thank you in a flat, clipped way. How does Goleman's account explain this?
questions.explain: Goleman says the way a salesperson says thank you can leave us feeling ignored, resented, or welcomed. This tacit exchange of feeling happens at an almost imperceptible level in every encounter.
options: Tom was following a display rule that told him to feel resentful
Emotional signals pass subtly in every encounter, even in how a thank-you is said
The cashier deliberately set out to entrain Tom's mood as a leader would
Tom has dyssemia and so misread an entirely neutral remark

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman give as signs of the physical synchrony that mirrors emotional rapport?
options: Both people speak at exactly the same volume
Both shift in their chairs at the same moment
Each agrees with every point the other makes
Both rock in swivel chairs at the same rhythm
One person nods just as the other makes a point
questions.explain: The orchestration of movement he describes includes nodding on cue, shifting at the same moment, leaning forward as the other leans back, and rocking in rhythm. It is about timing of movement, not volume or agreement.

questions.q: Goleman writes that we are all part of each other's ____ for emotional change, for better or for worse.
questions.explain: Because moods pass between us, each person can soothe or unsettle others; those who can soothe others' feelings hold an especially valued social commodity.

questions.q: In the experiment in which two volunteers sat silently facing each other for two minutes, what happened to their moods?
questions.explain: Each pair had one highly expressive and one deadpan partner, and invariably the expressive partner's mood had been transferred to the more passive one, without a word spoken.
options: The mood of the deadpan partner calmed down the more expressive one
Both moods drifted toward neutral because neither person spoke
The mood of the more emotionally expressive partner transferred to the deadpan one
Their moods did not change, since no words passed between them

questions.q: Put the steps of the two-volunteer mood experiment in order.
items: Each volunteer fills out a checklist about current mood
The pair sit facing each other quietly, waiting
The experimenter returns two minutes later
Each volunteer fills out the mood checklist again
questions.explain: The design compares mood before and after two silent minutes together, which showed mood passing from the expressive to the deadpan partner.

questions.q: Goleman says we unconsciously imitate others' emotions through an out-of-awareness motor ____ of their facial expression, gestures and tone of voice.
questions.explain: Through this imitation people re-create in themselves the mood of the other person.

questions.q: Put the steps by which Goleman says one person's mood is caught by another in order.
items: Seeing someone's expression, gestures and tone
Unconsciously mimicking those nonverbal signs
Re-creating the other person's mood in oneself
questions.explain: Goleman calls this a low-key version of the Stanislavsky method: imitating the outward signs of a feeling evokes the feeling itself.

questions.q: What did Ulf Dimberg of the University of Uppsala find when people looked at a smiling or angry face?
questions.explain: The changes were evident through electronic sensors but typically not visible to the naked eye, showing how subtle the everyday imitation of feeling is.
options: Their faces visibly took on the opposite expression to the one they saw
Their faces showed no change unless they were told to copy the expression
Only people with dyssemia showed any change in their facial muscles
Their own facial muscles showed slight changes matching that mood, detectable by sensors

questions.q: True or false: When a lively, animated friend chats with a quiet, deadpan friend, Goleman's account predicts that the lively friend will mostly take on the quiet friend's mood.
questions.explain: Goleman says the direction of mood transfer is from the one who is more forceful in expressing feelings to the one who is more passive, so the quiet friend is the one more likely to catch the lively friend's mood.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say about people who are particularly susceptible to emotional contagion?
options: Sentimental commercials can move them to tears
They are better than others at masking their feelings
They may be more empathic than others
Cheerful people have little effect on their mood
Their autonomic nervous system is more easily triggered
questions.explain: Their innate sensitivity makes them more impressionable: sad commercials move them to tears, a chat with someone cheerful can buoy them, and they may be more empathic. They are more easily moved, not less.

questions.q: Match each researcher to the finding Goleman reports from them.
pairs: Cultures have display rules for which feelings can be shown when
Seeing a face shifts our own facial muscles toward that mood
Mood synchrony decides whether we feel an interaction went well
Close teacher-student movement coordination goes with good feeling
questions.explain: Ekman named display rules; Dimberg measured tiny facial changes; Cacioppo studied the subtle exchange of emotion; and Bernieri studied synchrony in classrooms.

questions.q: Sam's girlfriend has been depressed. They sit down to discuss a problem in their relationship, and without noticing, their postures and movements fall closely into step. What does the research Goleman cites predict about Sam?
questions.explain: In the study of depressed women and their partners, the more nonverbal synchrony, the worse the partners felt after the discussion. Synchrony transmits moods whether upbeat or down.
options: He will likely feel worse afterward, having caught her low mood
He will likely lift her mood, since synchrony only spreads good feelings
He will likely feel unaffected, since moods pass only through words
He will likely feel better, since closeness protects against bad moods

questions.q: Goleman concludes that coordination of moods is the essence of ____, the adult version of a mother's attunement with her infant.
questions.explain: Mood synchrony is what makes an encounter feel comfortable; it echoes the attunement Daniel Stern observed between mothers and infants.

questions.q: Match each term from Goleman's discussion of emotional contagion to its meaning.
pairs: A process, like the day-night cycle, that entrains biological rhythms
Out-of-awareness imitation of another's face, gestures and tone
Actors recalling past gestures to evoke a feeling again
Tightly coordinated movement that mirrors emotional rapport
questions.explain: Goleman uses the biological zeitgeber, literally time-grabber, as an image for the person who sets the emotional tone of an encounter.

questions.q: Goleman writes that emotional ____ is the heart of influence.
questions.explain: The person with more forceful expressivity or more power entrains the other's emotions, as a good speaker does with an audience.

questions.q: In each everyday encounter, sort the person by whether, on Goleman's account, their emotions are more likely to set the tone or to be caught.

items.t: A lively host telling a story at dinner
A boss who does most of the talking in a meeting
A stirring preacher addressing a congregation
A deadpan guest listening quietly at dinner
A junior employee watching the boss's face
A member of the congregation in the pews

questions.explain: Goleman says the person with the more forceful expressivity, or more power, entrains the other: dominant partners talk more, while the subordinate watches the other's face more, a setup for the transmission of affect.

questions.q: Maya and a new colleague find that, as they talk, one leans in as the other sits back and they nod in time with each other's points. What does Goleman's account suggest about their conversation?
questions.explain: Goleman says the degree of emotional rapport is mirrored by how tightly orchestrated people's movements are, usually out of awareness, and that a high level of synchrony means the people involved like each other.
options: One of them is likely a social chameleon putting on a false front
They likely feel real rapport, since tight physical coordination mirrors it
They are likely following display rules that hide their real feelings
They likely dislike each other and are mimicking to cover it up

questions.q: According to John Cacioppo, why are people who are poor at sending and receiving emotions prone to problems in their relationships?
questions.a: Cacioppo proposes that interpersonal effectiveness depends on how deftly people carry out emotional synchrony, attuning to others' moods or bringing others under the sway of their own. People poor at receiving and sending emotions miss this synchrony, so others feel uncomfortable with them, even if they cannot say exactly why. Since mood synchrony determines whether we feel an interaction went well, their encounters tend to feel off.

questions.q: When Reggie tripped and hurt his knee at preschool recess, what did Roger, the boy Thomas Hatch singles out, do?
questions.explain: Only Roger noticed Reggie's pain and tried to offer solace, even if all he could offer was rubbing his own knee, a small gesture showing a talent for rapport.
options: He ran to fetch a teacher and then kept on playing with the other boys
He laughed with the other boys and teased Reggie for crying over a scratch
He stopped running and, as Reggie calmed, rubbed his own knee, saying he had hurt it too
He organized the other boys to carry Reggie back inside to the classroom

questions.q: Thomas Hatch, who spotted Roger's interpersonal skill, is a colleague of Howard Gardner at ____, the school based on the concept of multiple intelligences.
questions.explain: Hatch and Gardner identify four components of interpersonal intelligence, of which Roger's talent is one.

questions.q: Match each of Hatch and Gardner's four components of interpersonal intelligence to its description.
pairs: Initiating and coordinating the efforts of a network of people
Preventing conflicts or resolving those that flare up
Empathy and recognizing and responding fittingly to feelings
Having insights about people's feelings, motives and concerns
questions.explain: Organizing is the leader's skill, negotiating the mediator's, personal connection is Roger's talent for empathy, and social analysis is insight into others' motives and concerns.

questions.q: Match each component of interpersonal intelligence to the kind of role Goleman says it suits.
pairs: Theater director, military officer or head of an organization
Diplomat, arbitrator or manager of takeovers
Therapist or counselor, or with literary talent a novelist
questions.explain: Each talent shows up in matching careers: leading, mediating, connecting with others, and understanding people deeply.

questions.q: Sort these children and adults by which component of interpersonal intelligence they most clearly show.

items.t: A girl who decides what game everyone will play
A boy who is chosen as team captain
A producer who coordinates a whole theater company
A child who settles arguments on the playing field
A lawyer who arbitrates a dispute between firms
A diplomat who heads off a quarrel between nations

questions.explain: Organizing groups is the leader's skill of initiating and coordinating; negotiating solutions is the mediator's talent for preventing or resolving conflicts.

questions.q: Which of Hatch and Gardner's components of interpersonal intelligence does Goleman identify as Roger's talent?
questions.explain: Goleman labels personal connection Roger's talent: empathy and connecting, which makes it easy to enter an encounter and respond fittingly to people's feelings.
options: Organizing groups
Negotiating solutions
Social analysis
Personal connection

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say about children who, like Roger, have a talent for personal connection?
options: They are most liked by their classmates
They tend to be best at reading emotions from facial expressions
They usually insist on being team captain
They easily enter into playing with others
They mostly prefer to play on their own
questions.explain: Such children get along with virtually everyone, easily enter into play, read facial emotions best and are most liked. Becoming team captain marks organizing groups, a different component.

questions.q: Two flatmates are fighting about chores, and Leo steps in, hears both sides, and finds a rota they both accept. Which of Hatch and Gardner's components of interpersonal intelligence is Leo showing?
questions.explain: Negotiating solutions is the talent of the mediator who prevents or resolves conflicts, the kind of child who settles arguments on the playing field.
options: Negotiating solutions
Organizing groups
Personal connection
Social analysis

questions.q: Nadia is the one friends ask when they want to understand why someone is acting oddly; she can usually tell what is really bothering a person and what they want. Which component of interpersonal intelligence does this best show?
questions.explain: Social analysis is the ability to detect and have insights about people's feelings, motives and concerns; at its best it makes for a good therapist or counselor.
options: Negotiating solutions
Social analysis
Organizing groups
Personal connection

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say people adept in social intelligence are able to do?
options: Read others' reactions and feelings astutely
Express the group's unspoken sentiment so as to guide it
Avoid all disputes so that none ever arise
Connect with people quite smoothly
Keep their own feelings completely hidden
questions.explain: Such people connect smoothly, read reactions, lead and organize, and handle the disputes that are bound to flare up, not avoid them altogether. They are natural leaders who can articulate the unspoken collective sentiment.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says socially intelligent people are emotionally nourishing: they leave other people in a good mood.
questions.explain: He describes them as the kind of people others like to be with because they leave others in a good mood and evoke the comment that they are a pleasure to be around.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say people who make an excellent social impression do?
options: Ignore the audience and simply say what they feel
Monitor their own expression of emotion
Continually fine-tune their social performance
Stay keenly attuned to how others are reacting
Let their feelings show without any filter
questions.explain: They monitor their own expression, watch how others react, and adjust their performance to have the desired effect; in that sense they are like skilled actors.
