questions.q: Mark Snyder studied people whose social skills make them first-rate social ____, champions at making a good impression.
questions.explain: Social chameleons seem to be whatever the people they are with seem to want.

questions.q: According to Mark Snyder, what is the sign that someone is a social chameleon, and why does this pattern arise?
questions.a: The sign is that they make an excellent impression yet have few stable or satisfying intimate relationships. The pattern arises when social skills outstrip the ability to know and honor one's own feelings, so that to be loved or liked the person becomes whatever others seem to want. The result is a hollow social success, popularity won at the cost of true satisfaction.

questions.q: The psychoanalyst Helena Deutsch called social chameleons the ____ personality, shifting personas with remarkable plasticity.
questions.explain: Such people pick up signals from those around them and change accordingly, living with a gap between public face and private reality.

questions.q: Which of these professions does Goleman say especially prize the impression-management traits of social chameleons?
options: Trial law
Diplomacy
Acting
Surgery
Accounting
questions.explain: He lists acting, trial law, sales, diplomacy and politics as professions where effective impression management is highly prized.

questions.q: Sort these behaviours by whether they mark a social chameleon or the emotional integrity Goleman contrasts with it.

items.t: Scanning others for what is wanted before replying
Acting like a different person with each group
Seeming friendly toward people one dislikes
Acting on one's deepest values despite the social cost
Provoking a confrontation to cut through denial
Using social polish in keeping with true feelings

questions.explain: Chameleons say one thing and do another to win approval; the capacity to be true to thine own self lets people act in accord with their deepest feelings and values, even at a social cost.

questions.q: Jess is liked by everyone at work; she agrees warmly with whoever she is talking to and is bubbly with one group and reserved with the next, yet she has no close, lasting friendships. Which pattern from Goleman's chapter does she fit?
questions.explain: Snyder's mark of the chameleon is making an excellent impression while having few stable or satisfying intimate relationships, and acting like very different people depending on whom one is with.
options: The social incompetent, who never learned the rudiments of interaction
The child with dyssemia, who cannot read nonverbal emotional signals
The social chameleon, whose social skill outstrips knowing her own feelings
The social analyst, who has deep insight into others' motives

questions.q: True or false: On Goleman's account, someone who deliberately calls out a family's denial about a problem, knowing it will cause an awkward scene, may be showing emotional integrity rather than poor social skill.
questions.explain: Goleman says being true to oneself could lead to deliberately provoking a confrontation to cut through duplicity or denial, a clearing of the air that a social chameleon would never attempt.

questions.q: Describe the four components of interpersonal intelligence that Hatch and Gardner identify.
questions.a: Organizing groups is the leader's skill of initiating and coordinating the efforts of a network of people. Negotiating solutions is the mediator's talent for preventing conflicts or resolving them. Personal connection, Roger's talent, is empathy and connecting with others, and social analysis is the ability to detect and have insights about people's feelings, motives and concerns.

questions.q: What kind of self-monitoring does Goleman say separates anchorless social chameleons from people who use their social polish well?
questions.a: It is the capacity to be true to thine own self, which allows a person to act in accord with their deepest feelings and values no matter what the social consequences. Social chameleons lack this anchor and simply live with the gap between public face and private reality. The healthier pattern balances being true to oneself with social skills, using them with integrity.

questions.section: The Making of a Social Incompetent
questions.q: What did Cecil, the bright translator in Lakin Phillips's case, confide was his real underlying problem?
questions.explain: Cecil came to therapy worried about his awkwardness around women, but the real problem was his fear that nothing he said would interest anyone, which compounded his lack of social graces.
options: He feared that he was secretly less intelligent than his colleagues
He believed that other people were deliberately trying to exclude him
He felt he could not understand people speaking in his own language
He feared that nothing he could say would be of any interest to anybody

questions.section: The Making of a Social Incompetent
questions.q: True or false: Cecil had felt socially at ease only when he was with his older brother, and once he left home his ineptitude was overwhelming.
questions.explain: His awkwardness went back to childhood; his older brother somehow eased things for him, and on leaving home he was socially paralyzed.

questions.section: The Making of a Social Incompetent
questions.q: What does psychologist Lakin Phillips propose was the source of Cecil's social plight?
questions.explain: Phillips says Cecil failed to learn as a child the rudiments of interaction that we begin teaching children from age two. Whether he was not taught or could not learn is unclear.
options: A failure in childhood to learn the most elementary lessons of social interaction
A lack of intelligence that kept him from following social conversation
A traumatic experience in adulthood that made him fear social contact
An inborn oversensitivity that made him catch everyone's moods

questions.section: The Making of a Social Incompetent
questions.q: Which of these does Lakin Phillips list among the elementary lessons Cecil could have been taught earlier?
options: To avoid eye contact with strangers
To speak directly to others when spoken to
To carry on a conversation, not give one-word replies
To argue firmly until others agree
To initiate social contact rather than always wait
questions.explain: Phillips's list also includes expressing gratitude, letting another go first through a door, waiting to be served, saying please and sharing.

questions.section: The Making of a Social Incompetent
questions.q: According to Goleman, what is the function of the unspoken rules of social harmony that Cecil never learned?
questions.explain: Goleman says the rules keep everyone at ease, since awkwardness spawns anxiety; failing to follow them creates waves and leaves disturbance in one's wake.
options: To mark out who has higher and lower status in a group
To keep everyone involved in a social exchange at ease
To stop people from showing any feelings at all in public
To help people win arguments without causing offense

questions.section: The Making of a Social Incompetent
questions.q: Ravi's cousin calls and talks on and on, ignoring Ravi's hints that he has to go, and steers every topic back to himself. How would Goleman classify this behavior?
questions.explain: Goleman's examples of the Cecils we all know include people who don't know when to end a conversation or call and who center conversation on themselves; these derailments bespeak a deficit in the building blocks of interaction.
options: A deliberate use of display rules to exaggerate feeling
An example of healthy emotional integrity and honesty
A deficit in the rudimentary building blocks of interaction
A sign of strong social analysis skills put to selfish use

questions.section: The Making of a Social Incompetent
questions.q: Which of these does Goleman give as habits of the socially graceless Cecils we have all known?
options: Being too shy to say anything at all
Not knowing when to end a conversation or phone call
Using overly formal manners with friends
Asking nosy questions
Talking about themselves without interest in anyone else
questions.explain: Goleman's list is of people oblivious to cues to say goodbye, centered on themselves, and intrusive. Shyness and formality are not what he describes.

questions.section: The Making of a Social Incompetent
questions.q: Psychologists have coined the term ____ for a learning disability in the realm of nonverbal messages.
questions.explain: The word comes from the Greek dys-, difficulty, and semes, signal.

questions.section: The Making of a Social Incompetent
questions.q: Match each area of dyssemia to an example of the problem in it.
pairs: Standing too close or spreading things into others' territory
Talking too shrilly or too flatly
Interpreting or using gestures and posture poorly
questions.explain: Goleman lists problems with personal space, body language, facial expressions, and prosody, the emotional quality of speech.

questions.section: The Making of a Social Incompetent
questions.q: One form of dyssemia is a poor sense of ____, the emotional quality of speech, so that a child talks too shrilly or flatly.
questions.explain: Prosody is one of several realms of nonverbal communication in which a child can have difficulty.

questions.section: The Making of a Social Incompetent
questions.q: True or false: Goleman says that when children do poorly in the nonverbal rules of interaction, playmates tend to see them as not very bright.
questions.explain: Poor language leads people to assume a child is not very bright; poor nonverbal skills lead playmates to see the child as strange and avoid them.

questions.section: The Making of a Social Incompetent
questions.q: Sort these difficulties a child might have by how Goleman says others tend to see such a child.

items.t: Using a very limited vocabulary
Making frequent grammar mistakes
Standing too close when talking
Touching others in ways that make them uneasy
Not knowing how to join a game gracefully
Speaking in an oddly flat tone

questions.explain: If children do poorly in language, people assume they are not bright or poorly educated; if they do poorly in the nonverbal rules of interaction, playmates see them as strange, or off, and avoid them.

questions.section: The Making of a Social Incompetent
questions.q: Put Stephen Nowicki's account of what happens to children who send the wrong emotional messages in order.
items: They send emotional signals they don't intend
Other people react to them in funny ways
They get rebuffed and don't understand why
They feel no control over how others treat them
They end up powerless, depressed and apathetic
questions.explain: Nowicki says such children constantly experience odd reactions and rebuffs they cannot explain, so they come to feel their actions have no impact, which leaves them “powerless, depressed, and apathetic.”

questions.section: The Making of a Social Incompetent
questions.q: Ben thinks he is just being friendly and excited, but other children react to him as if he is being aggressive, and he cannot work out why. How does Stephen Nowicki's account explain this?
questions.explain: Nowicki says that if you think you are acting happy but actually seem too hyper or angry, other kids get angry in turn and you don't realize why, since you cannot stop showing your expression, posture or tone.
options: Ben is following a display rule that tells him to exaggerate his feelings
Ben is a social chameleon who changes his manner to suit each group
Ben is catching the other children's anger through emotional contagion
Ben's facial and vocal signals come across as hyper or angry without his realizing it

questions.section: The Making of a Social Incompetent
questions.q: Why, according to Goleman, do socially awkward children also tend to suffer academically?
questions.a: The classroom is as much a social situation as an academic one, so a child who misreads others is as likely to misread and misrespond to a teacher as to another child. The resulting anxiety and bewilderment can themselves interfere with learning. Tests of nonverbal sensitivity show that children who misread emotional cues tend to do poorly in school compared with the potential their IQ suggests.

questions.section: The Making of a Social Incompetent
questions.q: True or false: Tests of children's nonverbal sensitivity show that those who misread emotional cues tend to do poorly in school compared with their academic potential as reflected in IQ tests.
questions.explain: Goleman cites this finding to show that social misreading has academic costs beyond being left out by playmates.

questions.section: The Making of a Social Incompetent
questions.q: What is dyssemia, and roughly how common does Goleman say it is?
questions.a: Dyssemia, from the Greek for difficulty with signals, is a learning disability in the realm of nonverbal messages. It can show up as a poor sense of personal space, poor use or reading of body language and facial expressions, or a poor sense of prosody. About one in ten children has one or more problems in this realm.

questions.section: The Making of a Social Incompetent
questions.q: According to Stephen Nowicki, why do children who can't read or express emotions well end up feeling powerless?
questions.a: Emotional communication is a constant subtext of everything we do, since we cannot stop showing our expression, posture or tone. Children who make mistakes in the messages they send keep getting odd reactions and rebuffs without knowing why. They come to feel they have no control over how others treat them and that their actions have no impact, which leaves them powerless, depressed and apathetic.

questions.q: In the study of second and third graders that Goleman cites, how often were even the most well-liked children rebuffed when trying to join a group at play?
questions.explain: Goleman uses the figure to show that being left out at a group's edge is a universal predicament; even the most popular children were rebuffed 26 percent of the time.
options: About 26 percent of the time
About 5 percent of the time
About 50 percent of the time
About 75 percent of the time

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says that the most popular children are almost never rejected when they try to join a group already at play.
questions.explain: Even the most popular children are sometimes rejected; the study he cites found the best-liked children rebuffed 26 percent of the time.

questions.q: Match each preschooler in Goleman's play-group dialogue to their part in it.
pairs: Sits down with the group and starts playing with the animals
Tells the newcomer she can't play and isn't liked today
Joins the attack, saying the group hates her today
questions.explain: The four-year-olds' exchange shows how brutally candid young children are about the emotional judgment in a rejection.

questions.q: What adult situation does Goleman compare to a child's anxiety on the threshold of joining a group at play?
questions.explain: Goleman says the child's anxiety is probably not much different from a grown-up's at a cocktail party, hanging back from a group who seem to be intimate friends.
options: Waiting outside a manager's office for an annual performance review
Hanging back from a happily chatting group of strangers at a cocktail party
Standing up to speak in front of a large audience for the first time
Meeting a romantic partner's parents for the very first time

questions.q: One researcher describes the moment at the threshold of a group as highly ____, quickly revealing differences in social skillfulness.
questions.explain: Because the moment is so momentous for a child, it shows clearly who has social skill and who lacks it.

questions.q: Six-year-old Mia wants to join two girls playing shop. According to the research Goleman reports, what matters most for whether she is accepted?
questions.explain: Goleman says what matters most is how well a child can enter the group's frame of reference. Suggesting a new game or pushing opinions early is exactly what unpopular children do.
options: How quickly she suggests a new and more exciting game for them to play
How confidently she states her own opinions about how to play shop
How well she enters their frame of reference, sensing what kind of play is in flow
How many toys she brings with her to share with the two girls

questions.q: Which of these are the two cardinal sins that Goleman says almost always lead to rejection when joining a group?
options: Trying to take the lead too soon
Imitating what another child is doing
Watching the group for too long before joining
Being out of synch with the frame of reference
Asking a question before committing to the play
questions.explain: Taking the lead too soon and being out of synch with the group's frame of reference almost always lead to rejection. Watching first, imitating and checking in are what skilled children like Roger do.

questions.q: A new employee joins a team that has been working together for months. Sort these moves by whether they match what Goleman says popular or unpopular children do when entering a group.

items.t: Spending time observing how the team works
Doing something that shows acceptance of their way
Waiting to be accepted before proposing changes
Changing the subject abruptly on day one
Offering strong opinions right away
Disagreeing with the others immediately

questions.explain: Popular children observe, show they accept what is going on, and wait for their status to be confirmed before taking initiative; unpopular ones push in with abrupt changes, opinions or disagreement.

questions.q: Put the steps of Roger's winning tactic for entering a group at play in order.
items: Observe what the others are doing
Imitate what another child is doing
Talk to the child and fully join the activity
questions.explain: Hatch observed that Roger first watched, then imitated, and only then talked and joined in fully, a sequence that keeps him in step with the group.

questions.q: Put the typical stages of a newcomer joining a group at play in the order Goleman describes them.
items: Simply watching for a time
Joining in very tentatively
Becoming more assertive in cautious steps
questions.explain: Typically newcomers watch, then join tentatively, and become more assertive only in very cautious steps.

questions.q: When Warren asked Roger whether he wanted to be in a helicopter or an airplane, Roger first asked whether Warren was in a helicopter. What does Thomas Hatch see in this?
questions.a: The seemingly innocuous question shows sensitivity to the other child's concerns and the ability to act on that knowledge in a way that keeps the connection. Hatch says Roger checks in with his playmate so that they and their play remain connected. Many other children simply get in their own helicopters or planes and fly away from each other, literally and figuratively.

questions.q: At her first meeting with a new book club, Grace interrupts to say the club's choice of novels is dull and proposes a new reading list. On Goleman's account, how is she likely to be received?
questions.explain: Pushing in, trying to change the subject too soon and disagreeing right away are what unpopular children do, and paradoxically these bids for attention lead to being ignored or rejected.
options: She is likely to be admired for showing confidence and initiative
She is likely to be accepted, since popular newcomers lead from the start
She is likely to be welcomed, since disagreement draws people closer
She is likely to be ignored or rejected for taking the lead too soon

questions.q: Eli arrives at a park where children are playing pirates. He watches for a while, then pretends to row like the others, and only after they include him does he suggest finding treasure. Which approach does this match?
questions.explain: Popular children observe the group, do something that shows they accept the play, and wait to have their status confirmed before suggesting what the group should do, as Roger did.
options: The popular children's approach of observing and accepting before taking initiative
The unpopular children's approach of pushing in to draw attention to oneself
The social chameleon's approach of becoming whatever others seem to want
The emotional judo approach of distracting others from what they are doing

questions.q: Why does Goleman call the way unpopular children try to join a group paradoxical?
questions.a: Unpopular children push their way in, change the subject too abruptly or too soon, offer their own opinions or disagree right away, all apparent attempts to draw attention to themselves. Paradoxically, this results in their being ignored or rejected. Popular children win acceptance by first observing and showing they accept what is going on.

questions.q: What strategy does Goleman suggest the data on anger and contagion point to for calming someone at the peak of rage?
questions.explain: Goleman suggests distracting the angry person, empathizing with his feelings and perspective, and drawing him into an alternative focus attuned to more positive feeling, a kind of emotional judo.
options: Match their anger forcefully so they feel heard, then withdraw in silence
Distract them, empathize with their perspective, then draw them into a more positive focus
Ignore them completely until their anger has burned itself out
Firmly order them to calm down, then explain why they are wrong

questions.q: Put the steps of the emotional judo Goleman suggests for calming an enraged person in order.
items: Distract the angry person
Empathize with their feelings and perspective
Draw them into a more positive alternative focus
questions.explain: The sequence comes from the data on self-regulation of anger and emotional contagion, and the old man on the Tokyo train enacts it.

questions.q: Goleman writes that if the test of social skill is calming distressing emotions in others, handling someone at the peak of rage is perhaps the ultimate measure of ____.
questions.explain: Calming an enraged person is the hardest case of the chapter's core skill, managing emotions in others.

questions.q: Match each person in Terry Dobson's story of the Tokyo train to their role.
pairs: An American aikido student ready to subdue the drunk
A man raging at passengers who had lost his wife
The old man in a kimono
A passenger who calmed the drunk by talking of sake
Taught that aikido is the art of reconciliation
questions.explain: Terry, one of the first Americans to study aikido in Japan in the 1950s, told Goleman the story; it was the tiny old man, not the martial artist, who defused the drunk.

questions.q: Terry Dobson's teacher told him that aikido is the art of ____.
questions.explain: The teacher added that whoever has the mind to fight has broken his connection with the universe, and that aikido studies how to resolve conflict, not start it.

questions.q: True or false: On beginning his lessons, Terry Dobson had agreed with his teacher never to pick a fight and to use his martial-arts skills only in defense.
questions.explain: That is why Terry saw the drunk's rampage as a legitimate chance to test his skills in real life.

questions.q: Just as the drunk laborer was about to attack Terry Dobson, what did the old man in a kimono do?
questions.explain: The shout had the cheery tone of someone who has come upon a fond friend; surprised, the drunk turned, and the old man waved him over with a lilting invitation.
options: He stood up between them and ordered the drunk to sit down at once
He grabbed the drunk's arm and pulled him away from Terry
He gave a joyous shout of Hey, as if greeting a fond friend, and beckoned the drunk over
He called out to the other passengers to help hold the drunk back

questions.q: Put these events of Terry Dobson's train story in order.
items: The drunk swings at a woman holding a baby
Terry stands up, slowly and deliberately
An old man gives a cheery shout of Hey
The old man asks what the drunk has been drinking
The drunk sobs out the story of losing his wife
The drunk lies along the seat, head in the old man's lap
questions.explain: The story moves from violent rage, through a confrontation narrowly avoided, to the old man's warm talk of sake and his garden, and finally to the drunk's grief and comfort.

questions.q: Which of these did the old man talk about with the drunk laborer on the Tokyo train?
options: Warming up sake each night with his wife
The aikido lessons he had once taken
Sitting on an old wooden bench in his garden
The persimmon tree in his backyard
The drunk's bad manners toward a foreigner
questions.explain: The old man spoke of sharing sake with his seventy-six-year-old wife on a garden bench and of his persimmon tree, an alternative, positive focus that softened the drunk.

questions.q: Sort these moments from Terry Dobson's train story by whether they belong to the readiness to subdue the drunk by force or to the old man's emotional judo.

items.t: Standing up slowly and with deliberation
Being ready to fell the drunk at his least violent move
Seeing a chance to test martial skills in real life
Greeting the drunk like a fond friend
Asking him what he had been drinking
Saying he too loves sake

questions.explain: Terry prepared to fight, while the old man surprised the drunk, warmly joined him in his interest and steered him toward pleasant thoughts, which led him from rage to grief and comfort.

questions.q: True or false: In Terry Dobson's story, Terry ended the drunk laborer's rampage by subduing him with an aikido move.
questions.explain: Terry never had to fight; the old man's warm talk of sake and his garden softened the drunk, who ended up sobbing with his head in the old man's lap.

questions.q: Why does Goleman call the old man's handling of the drunk on the Tokyo train emotional brilliance?
questions.a: The old man calmed a man at the peak of rage, which Goleman calls perhaps the ultimate measure of social mastery. He surprised and distracted the drunk with a cheerful greeting, connected with him over a shared love of sake, and drew him into a warm, positive focus on garden and wife, which let the man's grief surface. It is emotional judo, the fine art of influencing another's emotions, achieved without any force.

questions.q: A customer storms up to a help desk, shouting about a lost order. Using the strategy Goleman draws from the old man on the Tokyo train, how might the staff member calm him?
questions.a: Following the emotional judo Goleman describes, the staff member could first interrupt the rage with something unexpected and friendly, distracting the customer. Next they would empathize, acknowledging his frustration and seeing it from his side. Finally they would draw him into an alternative, more positive focus, such as what can be done now, attuning him to a calmer range of feeling instead of confronting him.

questions.q: A teenager comes home furious about a teacher. Her father first jokes warmly about the burnt dinner, then says he can see why she feels wronged, and then asks about the play she is rehearsing, which she loves. Which approach from Goleman's chapter is he using?
questions.explain: The father follows the sequence Goleman suggests for calming anger: distraction, empathy with her feelings and perspective, then an alternative focus attuned to positive feeling, as the old man did on the train.
options: Minimizing: masking his own feelings to keep her calm
Social chameleon behavior: becoming whatever she wants him to be
Entrainment by dominance: talking over her until she gives in
Emotional judo: distract, empathize, then shift to a more positive focus

questions.q: Which of Salovey's five domains of emotional intelligence, set out in Chapter 3, does Chapter 8, The Social Arts, cover?
questions.explain: Chapter 3 says the art of relationships is largely skill in managing emotions in others and that Chapter 8 looks at social competence and incompetence. Recognizing emotions in others, empathy, is Chapter 7's domain.
options: Handling relationships, the fifth domain
Recognizing emotions in others, the fourth domain
Managing emotions, the second domain
Motivating oneself, the third domain

questions.q: Why does The Social Arts come right after The Roots of Empathy and the chapters on managing one's own emotions?
questions.explain: Goleman says handling emotions in someone else requires two other emotional skills, self-management and empathy, which the preceding chapters covered, so relationships come last in Part Two.
options: Because social skill is the simplest emotional ability and must be learned first
Because handling others' emotions requires the ripeness of self-management and empathy
Because social skill replaces the need for empathy once a child is grown
Because the chapter is mainly about the brain anatomy behind empathy

questions.q: Put the chapters of Part Two, The Nature of Emotional Intelligence, in order.
items: When Smart Is Dumb
Know Thyself
Passion's Slaves
The Master Aptitude
The Roots of Empathy
The Social Arts
questions.explain: Part Two moves from the case for emotional intelligence through self-awareness, managing and motivating oneself, and empathy, ending with the social arts that build on all of them.

questions.q: Sort these chapters by the Part of the book they belong to.
groups: Part Two: The Nature of EI

items.t: The Roots of Empathy
The Social Arts
The Master Aptitude
Intimate Enemies
Managing with Heart
Mind and Medicine

questions.explain: The Social Arts closes Part Two; Part Three then shows the difference these abilities make in marriage, at work and for health.

questions.q: Match each of Salovey's domains of emotional intelligence to the chapter that covers it.
questions.explain: Chapter 3 maps the five domains onto Chapters 4 to 8, with handling relationships last.

questions.q: True or false: The Social Arts is the last chapter of Part Two, The Nature of Emotional Intelligence.
questions.explain: It follows The Roots of Empathy and is followed by Intimate Enemies, which opens Part Three, Emotional Intelligence Applied.

questions.q: Put the sections of Chapter 8, The Social Arts, in the order they appear.
items: Show Some Emotion
Expressiveness and Emotional Contagion
The Rudiments of Social Intelligence
The Making of a Social Incompetent
We Hate You: at the Threshold
Emotional Brilliance: a Case Report
questions.explain: The chapter moves from how we express and transmit feeling, to the components of social skill, to its failures, to the test of joining a group, and ends with a case of mastery.

questions.q: What does the chapter title The Social Arts signal about how Goleman treats social skill?
questions.a: Calling them arts presents social abilities as skills of handling relationships, chiefly the art of managing emotions in someone else, rather than as fixed traits. The plural reflects the several distinct abilities the chapter covers, from display rules and emotional contagion to organizing, negotiating, connecting and social analysis. Like any art, they ripen through childhood lessons and can be done badly or brilliantly.

questions.q: Why is it fitting that The Social Arts ends with Terry Dobson's story rather than with the cases of social failure?
questions.a: After showing the rudiments of social skill and what happens when they are missing, in Cecil, dyssemic children and rejected newcomers, Goleman closes with a picture of mastery. Calming a man at the peak of rage is, he says, perhaps the ultimate test of the core social skill, managing emotions in others. The story thus caps both the chapter and Part Two with what fully developed emotional intelligence can do.

questions.q: How does the Prologue, Aristotle's Challenge, describe the purpose of Part Two, which The Social Arts concludes?
questions.explain: The Prologue says Part Two shows that flair, including the ability to handle relationships smoothly. The other descriptions belong to Parts Four, Five and Three.
options: Showing how childhood lessons at home and school shape the emotional circuits
Exploring the hazards awaiting those who fail to master the emotional realm
Seeing how neurological givens play out in the basic flair for living called emotional intelligence
Examining how emotional skills help in marriage, at work and for health

questions.q: According to the remark Goleman attributes to Sigmund Freud, which two capacities mark full maturity?
questions.explain: Freud told his disciple Erik Erikson that loving and working are the twin marks of maturity, and Goleman uses this to introduce why emotional intelligence matters in marriage.
options: The capacities to love and to work
The capacities to reason and to remember
The capacities to marry and to parent
The capacities to feel and to forgive

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says the yearly divorce rate in the United States has kept climbing sharply, which is why newlyweds face the greatest risk.
questions.explain: The yearly rate has more or less leveled off; what has climbed is the risk of divorce for a given newly married couple, so the risk has shifted to newlyweds.

questions.q: For American couples who began marriage in 1990, the projected chance of eventual divorce was close to ____ percent.
questions.explain: Goleman cites a projection of close to 67 percent, up from about 10 percent for marriages begun in 1890.

questions.q: Put these groups of American newlyweds in order from the lowest to the highest eventual divorce rate Goleman reports.
items: Couples wed in 1890
Couples wed in 1920
Couples wed in 1950
Couples wed in 1970
Couples wed in 1990
questions.explain: The figures rise from about 10 percent for 1890, to about 18 percent for 1920, 30 percent for 1950, fifty-fifty for 1970 and close to 67 percent for 1990.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman name as social pressures that once kept couples together even in miserable marriages?
questions.explain: He lists stigma and wives' economic dependence as the fading glue; skills and therapy are not part of that argument.
options: The stigma surrounding divorce
The economic dependence of wives on husbands
Couples' skill at reading each other's faces
Therapists' success at repairing marriages
Parents' lessons about handling anger

questions.q: Why does Goleman argue that emotional intelligence matters more for marriage as social pressures against divorce fade?
questions.a: Some of the rising divorce risk may come from weaker pressures such as stigma and wives' economic dependence rather than from a decline in emotional intelligence. But once those pressures no longer hold couples together, the emotional forces between wife and husband are what decide whether the marriage survives.

questions.q: What does Goleman call the biggest breakthrough in understanding what holds a marriage together or tears it apart?
questions.explain: Sophisticated physiological measures reveal adrenaline surges, blood pressure jumps and fleeting facial microemotions that the couple themselves usually miss.
options: Large surveys of divorced couples about what went wrong
Physiological measures that track a couple's emotional shifts moment to moment
Long interviews with couples at the start of therapy
Statistics on divorce rates for different decades

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says the hidden biological subtext revealed by physiological measures is something couples themselves can typically perceive.
questions.explain: He says it is a level of emotional reality typically imperceptible to, or disregarded by, the couple themselves.

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: In the restaurant scene Goleman describes, what common pattern in distressed couples does the young woman chasing the young man epitomize?
questions.explain: The woman pummeling a retreating back and demanding he be nice captures the engage-withdraw pattern marital therapists see in distressed couples.
options: He demands attention while she retreats into silence
Both partners attack each other with equal force
She seeks to engage while he withdraws
She leaves the conflict while he pursues her to apologize

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: Marital therapists find distressed couples in a pattern in which she seeks to engage and he ____.
questions.explain: By the time couples reach the therapy office, his complaint is about her unreasonable demands and hers is about his indifference.

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: True or false: In the study of children's friendships Goleman cites, three-year-olds say about half their friends are of the opposite sex, while by age seven almost no boys or girls name an opposite-sex best friend.
questions.explain: The share falls from about half at three, to about 20 percent at five, to almost none by seven, so boys and girls inhabit separate social universes.

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: Put these ages in order from the age at which children report the most opposite-sex friends to the age at which they report the fewest.
items: Three-year-olds
Five-year-olds
Seven-year-olds
questions.explain: About half of three-year-olds' friends are of the opposite sex, about 20 percent at five, and almost none at seven.

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: Parents discuss emotions more with daughters than with sons in general, with the exception of which emotion?
questions.explain: Goleman notes that parents talk about emotions, except anger, more with daughters; mothers do give sons more detail on the causes and consequences of anger.
options: Fear
Sadness
Joy
Anger

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: Match each way parents treat daughters and sons with what the research found.
pairs: More emotion words are used with daughters
A wider range of emotions is displayed to daughters
More detail about the emotional state itself
More detail about its causes and consequences
questions.explain: Girls are exposed to more information about emotions; with sons, the extra detail on anger is probably a cautionary tale.

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: According to Brody and Hall, why are girls more skilled than boys at using words to explore their emotions?
questions.explain: Faster language development lets girls articulate feelings and use words in place of physical fights, whereas boys may become largely unconscious of emotional states.
options: Girls develop facility with language more quickly, so they get more practice articulating feelings
Girls are punished less often for expressing anger in words
Girls have more emotionally expressive mothers than boys do
Girls spend more time than boys playing in large groups

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: What do Leslie Brody and Judith Hall propose about language and the emotional differences between girls and boys?
questions.a: They propose that girls develop language faster than boys, which makes them more experienced at putting feelings into words and at using words instead of physical fights. Boys, for whom verbalizing feelings is de-emphasized, may become largely unconscious of their emotional states, in themselves and in others.

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: By age thirteen, what difference between the sexes in handling anger does Goleman report?
questions.explain: At ten the sexes are about equally overt; by thirteen girls pick up artful aggression while boys, by and large, simply stay confrontational and are oblivious to the covert strategies.
options: Boys are more adept at covert tactics, while girls confront openly
Girls are more adept at covert tactics like ostracism and gossip, while boys keep confronting openly
Girls stop being aggressive, while boys turn to indirect vendettas
Both sexes shift equally to gossip, but boys do it more subtly

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: Sort these behaviors by whether Goleman says they typify girls or boys at around age thirteen when angry.

items.t: Ostracizing a rival
Spreading vicious gossip
Running indirect vendettas
Confronting openly when angry
Staying oblivious to covert strategies

questions.explain: Girls become adept at artful aggressive tactics; boys continue being confrontational and miss the covert strategies.

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: True or false: Goleman reports that at age ten, girls are far more likely than boys to be overtly aggressive.
questions.explain: At age ten roughly the same percent of girls as boys are overtly aggressive; the telling difference emerges at thirteen.

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: Sort these features of childhood play by whether Goleman ties them to girls' games or boys' games.

items.t: Small, intimate groups
Emphasis on minimizing hostility
Play stops to help a hurt child
Larger groups
Emphasis on competition
A hurt child is expected to get out of the way

questions.explain: Girls emphasize cooperation and care; boys emphasize competition, and the game goes on.

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: When a child is hurt and cries during a group game, what does Goleman say typically happens among girls?
questions.explain: Among girls the game stops for the hurt child; a hurt boy is expected to stop crying and get out of the way.
options: The hurt girl is asked to leave so play can continue
The group quickly assigns someone to replace her
The game stops while everyone gathers around to help
The girls ignore the crying until she calms down

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: Carol Gilligan says boys take pride in a lone, tough-minded independence, while girls see themselves as part of a ____ of connectedness.
questions.explain: Boys are threatened by challenges to independence, girls by a rupture in their relationships.

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: Match each researcher with the point Goleman draws from that person's work in this part of the chapter.
pairs: Boys prize independence, girls see a web of connectedness
Men and women expect different things from a conversation
Girls' faster language growth helps them voice feelings
For wives, intimacy means talking things over
questions.explain: Each researcher supplies one piece of the picture of separate emotional worlds for men and women.

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: In Deborah Tannen's view as Goleman reports it, what do men and women want and expect from a conversation?
questions.explain: Tannen's point is that differing perspectives lead to very different expectations of talk.
options: Women want to solve problems quickly, while men want to air feelings
Both want agreement, but men value it more
Men want emotional connection, while women want to talk about things
Men are content to talk about things, while women seek emotional connection

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say the research shows, on average, about women compared with men?
questions.explain: Hundreds of studies show women read nonverbal cues better and feel more intensely, and it is generally easier to read feelings from a woman's face.
options: They experience the whole range of emotions with greater intensity and volatility
They are less skilled at reading emotion from tone of voice
They are less expressive as they go through elementary school
They are harder to read facially than men
They are more empathic when reading unstated feelings from nonverbal cues

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: True or false: Goleman says that among very young children, boys are already less facially expressive than girls.
questions.explain: He says there is no difference in facial expressiveness among very young boys and girls; boys become less expressive, girls more so, through the elementary-school grades.

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: Goleman concludes that women typically come into marriage groomed for what role?
questions.explain: Because of their schooling in emotions, women arrive with more appreciation of how vital the task of managing emotion is to keeping a relationship going.
options: Emotional manager
Peacemaker between the extended families
Keeper of the household finances
Judge of the couple's disagreements

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: In the study of 264 couples Goleman cites, what mattered most to women's, but not men's, satisfaction with their relationship?
questions.explain: Good communication was the most important element for women, not for men.
options: Having a fair division of household work
The sense that the couple has good communication
Having plenty of time for shared activities
Agreeing about how to raise children

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: Ted Huston observes that husbands often say, 'I want to do things with her, and all she wants to do is talk.' What does this show about the couple's different views of closeness?
questions.explain: Huston found wives treat talking, especially about the relationship, as intimacy, while husbands, especially in more traditional couples, found closeness in doing things like gardening together.
options: Wives want less closeness than husbands do after the wedding
Husbands want to talk about the relationship but wives avoid it
Wives define intimacy as talking things over, while husbands often find closeness in shared activity
Both want the same closeness but disagree on how often

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: What did Huston find about how much husbands talked with their wives in ways that met the wives' wish for intimacy?
questions.explain: During courtship the men were much more willing to talk in such ways, but after marriage, especially in more traditional couples, they did so less and less.
options: Husbands avoided such talk both during courtship and in marriage
Husbands talked more once married because they felt secure
Husbands and wives talked equally in all stages
Husbands were willing before the wedding but spent less and less time doing it as marriage went on

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: Goleman says that men tend to be a bit ____ about the state of their marriage, with a rosier view than their wives of almost everything.
questions.explain: In one study men viewed lovemaking, finances, in-law ties and how well they listened more rosily than their wives did.

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: Why does Goleman say a wife often has to be all the sadder for her husband to notice her feelings?
questions.explain: Men's relative lack of skill at reading facial expressions slows their noticing, let alone their raising of the question of what is wrong.
options: Women are more sensitive to sadness on a man's face than men are to sadness on a woman's
Men are taught to ignore all emotions except anger
Wives usually hide their sadness to avoid conflict
Men are more likely to be sad themselves in marriage

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: True or false: Goleman says specific issues such as how often a couple has sex, how to discipline children and how much debt to carry are what chiefly make or break a marriage.
questions.explain: He says how a couple discusses such sore points matters more for the marriage than the specific issues themselves.

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: According to Goleman, what is key to marital survival with regard to grievances?
questions.explain: Men and women have to overcome innate gender differences in approaching rocky emotions, or emotional rifts can eventually tear the relationship apart.
options: Making sure each partner wins roughly half of the arguments
Having reached an agreement about how to disagree
Avoiding any discussion of money or sex
Letting the more emotional partner decide

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: Maya wants to talk over how they have been getting along, but her husband Sam suggests they do some gardening together instead. Which idea from this chapter best explains the mismatch?
questions.explain: Huston's finding is that for wives intimacy is talking, while many husbands feel close simply doing things together such as gardening.
options: Sam has been flooded and is trying to stonewall
Maya is using contempt to signal her anger
Wives tend to equate intimacy with talking things over, while husbands tend to find closeness in doing things together
Sam is offering a practical solution too early

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: At a school sports day, five-year-old Ben falls during a boys' game and his teammates tell him to move aside so they can keep playing, while at a nearby girls' game the play stops when a girl cries. Which idea does the contrast illustrate?
questions.explain: Gilligan's point is that boys take pride in lone, tough-minded independence while girls see themselves as part of a web of connectedness.
options: Girls become adept at covert tactics earlier than boys
Boys have faster language growth than girls
Boys express emotion more freely than girls in early childhood
Boys prize independence and keep the game going, while girls feel threatened by a rupture in connection

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: Why does Goleman say the specific issues couples argue about matter less than how they discuss them, and how does the emotional gender gap come into this?
questions.a: Issues like sex, discipline and money do not make or break a marriage; how a couple discusses such sore points does. Because men and women learn different emotional skills in childhood, they must overcome those innate differences and reach an agreement about how to disagree, or emotional rifts can tear the relationship apart.

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: Describe how boys' and girls' separate emotional upbringing helps explain the pattern in which she seeks to engage and he withdraws.
questions.a: Boys and girls grow up in separate social worlds and are taught different lessons about emotions. Girls become skilled at reading and expressing feelings and arrive in marriage as emotional managers, while boys learn to minimize vulnerability and hurt, so wives push to talk things over while husbands pull back.

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: What does Goleman say about the different views of the marriage that husbands and wives often hold, and what is the result when a wife wants to raise a problem?
questions.a: Husbands tend to be rosy about the marriage and averse to emotional confrontation, while wives are attuned to trouble spots and more vocal about complaints. Combined with men's weaker skill at reading facial emotion, wives often find their husbands trying to wiggle out of discussing troubling things.

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: Goleman says Brody and Hall found that boys, for whom putting feelings into words is de-emphasized, may become what?
questions.explain: Boys' lack of verbal practice with feelings leaves them less aware of emotion in themselves and others.
options: Largely unconscious of their emotional states, in themselves and in others
Unusually skilled at disguising their feelings from others
More aggressive than girls at every age
Better at resolving conflict through games

questions.section: His Marriage and Hers: Childhood Roots
questions.q: Goleman says girls become adept at reading both verbal and nonverbal emotional signals, while boys become adept at minimizing emotions to do with vulnerability, guilt, fear and ____.
questions.explain: The contrast in schooling in the emotions fosters very different skills in girls and boys.

questions.q: In the dry-cleaning exchange between Fred and Ingrid, what did Goleman use the couple to show?
questions.explain: Goleman reports that the painfully caustic exchange came from a couple who divorced within a few years, which makes it an example of a predictive fault line.
options: How a healthy couple airs a small complaint without hostility
How caustic an interchange recorded in Gottman's laboratory could be, from a couple who later divorced
How a stonewalling husband protects himself from conflict
How a wife's cooperative request ends in agreement

questions.q: John Gottman, a psychologist at the University of ____, ran the laboratory where couples' conversations were videotaped and microanalyzed.
questions.explain: Gottman has done perhaps the most detailed analysis ever of the emotional glue and corrosive feelings in marriage.

questions.q: True or false: In one study, Gottman could predict which couples seen in his lab would divorce within three years with 94 percent accuracy.
questions.explain: Goleman calls this a precision unheard of in marital studies.

questions.q: Which of these were part of Gottman's method of studying couples' conversations?
questions.explain: The combination yields what Goleman likens to an emotional X-ray of the marriage.
options: Each partner separately narrating secret thoughts while watching the videotape
Questionnaires given to the couple's children
Daily diaries kept by each spouse at home
Interviews with the spouses' parents
Sensors recording the slightest changes in physiology
Second-by-second analysis of facial expressions using Paul Ekman's system

questions.q: Put the steps of a Gottman lab session in the order Goleman describes them.
items: Couple talks while sensors record physiology
Conversation is videotaped
Each partner separately watches the tape
Partner narrates secret thoughts from the heated moments
questions.explain: The conversation is recorded first; afterward each partner comes separately and narrates what they secretly thought during the heated moments.

questions.q: According to Gottman, what is an early warning signal that a marriage is in danger?
questions.explain: In a healthy marriage partners can voice complaints; harsh criticism turns the complaint into an attack on the spouse's character.
options: Frequent small disagreements about money
A wife's occasional tears
Harsh criticism
A husband's time away on work trips

questions.q: In the shoe-shopping story, what makes Pamela's remark to Tom a personal criticism rather than a complaint?
questions.explain: Goleman says it is a critique of the person, not the deed, even though Tom had apologized.
options: She criticizes him in front of their daughter
She raises the matter after he has already apologized
She says nothing about how his lateness affected her
She turns his lateness into a verdict on his character, calling him thoughtless and self-centered

questions.q: Match each kind of statement with the example Goleman gives.
pairs: When you forgot my clothes, it made me feel you do not care
You are always so selfish and uncaring
Mockery, insults, a sneer or rolling the eyes
Going blank and answering with a stony silence
questions.explain: A complaint names the action and the feeling; criticism attacks the person; contempt adds mockery or disgust signals; stonewalling is withdrawal.

questions.q: Sort these statements by whether they are a complaint or a personal criticism in Goleman's sense.

items.t: When you were late, I felt unimportant
I was upset that the dishes were left out
I felt worried when you did not call
You are so thoughtless and self-centered
You always screw things up
You never think of anyone but yourself

questions.explain: A complaint names a specific action and the speaker's feeling, an expression of basic emotional intelligence; criticism launches a global attack on the person.

questions.q: Why does a harsh personal criticism usually backfire, according to Goleman?
questions.explain: Those feelings make a defensive response more likely than steps to improve things.
options: It leaves the recipient feeling ashamed, disliked, blamed and defective, which invites defensiveness rather than improvement
It makes the recipient angry enough to take action at once
It lets the recipient realize the criticism is exaggerated and ignore it
It shows the recipient how strongly the speaker feels, so the recipient calms down

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says personal criticisms become more likely the more a husband or wife feels their complaints go unheard or ignored.
questions.explain: He says such attacks, perhaps understandably, grow likelier when complaints seem to fall on deaf ears.

questions.q: Gottman says a particularly destructive emotion, often expressed through mockery, insult, a sneer or eye rolling, is ____.
questions.explain: Contempt comes easily with anger and is conveyed by tone of voice, expression and words.

questions.q: Which muscle's contraction does Goleman call the facial signature of contempt?
questions.explain: The mouth corner is pulled to the side, usually the left, while the eyes roll upward.
options: The brow lowerer, which knits the eyebrows
The dimpler, which pulls the corners of the mouth to the side
The jaw clencher, which tightens the chin
The cheek lifter, which raises the corners of the eyes

questions.q: True or false: When one spouse flashes the facial expression of contempt, the other spouse's heart rate typically rises by two or three beats per minute.
questions.explain: Goleman describes this as a hidden, tacit emotional exchange that takes its toll.

questions.q: Which of these health problems does Goleman say a wife is more prone to if her husband regularly shows contempt?
questions.explain: Gottman found a range of health problems in wives whose husbands show contempt regularly.
options: Chronic back pain
Long-lasting insomnia
Frequent colds and flus
Bladder and yeast infections
Gastrointestinal symptoms

questions.q: If a wife's face shows disgust, a near cousin of contempt, four or more times within a fifteen-minute conversation, the couple is likely to separate within ____ years.
questions.explain: Goleman calls it a silent sign of likely separation.

questions.q: Why does Goleman compare emotional volleys such as contempt and disgust to smoking and high cholesterol?
questions.explain: An occasional show of contempt will not undo a marriage; it is the intensity and persistence that matter.
options: Like them, they cause damage only after many decades
Like them, a single occurrence is enough to doom a marriage
Like them, they are risk factors: the more intense and prolonged, the greater the danger
Like them, they are easy to prevent by changing habits

questions.q: Put these in the order of the escalating chain Goleman describes in a marriage heading for divorce.
items: Habitual criticism
Contempt or disgust
Defensiveness or counterattack
questions.explain: Harsh criticism and contempt come first, and the hostile thinking behind them leads to attacks that leave the partner defensive or ready to counterattack.

questions.q: Why does Goleman say habitual criticism and contempt are danger signs?
questions.explain: Such negative and hostile thinking leads to attacks that put the other person on the defensive.
options: They show the couple is too busy to talk
They prove one partner is hiding something
They reveal the couple has poor physical health
They indicate a silent judgment for the worse about the partner, who is constantly condemned in thought

questions.q: How does Goleman connect the fight-or-flight response to ways a spouse can respond to an attack?
questions.explain: He calls the fight route a fruitless shouting match and the flight route, retreat into stony silence, potentially more pernicious.
options: Fighting back means lashing out in anger, while fleeing can mean retreating into stony silence
Fighting back is always the more harmful response
Fleeing means leaving the house for good
Both arms mean attacking, but at different volumes

questions.q: True or false: Goleman describes stonewalling as the ultimate defense, in which the person goes blank and withdraws from the conversation.
questions.explain: It sends a powerful message of icy distance, superiority and distaste.

questions.q: In the marriages heading for trouble where Gottman saw stonewalling, who stonewalled in 85 percent of the cases?
questions.explain: Stonewalling showed up mainly in marriages heading for trouble.
options: The wife, in response to a husband who refused to talk
The husband, in response to a wife who attacked with criticism and contempt
Both partners, in alternation
The husband, in response to a wife's silence

questions.q: Wendell answers every criticism from his wife Rosa by staring at the table and saying nothing, however long she goes on. Which concept from the chapter does this describe?
questions.explain: Going blank with a stony expression and silence is Gottman's stonewalling; it cuts off any chance of working out disagreements.
options: Mirroring
Detoxified self-talk
Stonewalling
Flooding in her

questions.q: Tessa says to her partner, 'I was hurt when you cancelled dinner without telling me.' Which description from Gottman's distinction fits what she did?
questions.explain: A complaint states what is upsetting, criticizes the action rather than the person and says how it made the speaker feel.
options: A personal criticism that attacks his character
An expression of contempt
A stonewalling reply
A complaint that names the action and her feeling

questions.q: Explain how Goleman distinguishes a complaint from a personal criticism, and why the difference matters.
questions.a: A complaint states specifically what upset the speaker, criticizes the action rather than the person and says how it felt, which is assertive emotional intelligence. A personal criticism uses a specific grievance to launch a global attack on the spouse, leaving the recipient ashamed, blamed and defective and thus likelier to be defensive than to improve.

questions.q: How did Gottman study couples in his laboratory, and what did he achieve with the results?
questions.a: He videotaped couples talking, recorded their physiology with sensors, and analyzed facial expressions second by second with Ekman's system. Each partner later narrated secret thoughts while watching the tape, which gave an emotional X-ray of the marriage. In one study he predicted which couples would divorce within three years with 94 percent accuracy.

questions.q: What are contempt and disgust in Gottman's findings, and how do they harm a marriage?
questions.a: Contempt is a destructive emotion shown in mockery, insult, a sneer or eye rolling, and disgust is its near cousin. A husband's regular contempt raises his wife's risk of illness, and a wife's disgust four or more times in fifteen minutes signals likely separation within four years. They are risk factors that signal a silent negative judgment of the spouse.

questions.q: Why does Goleman call stonewalling devastating, and who mostly does it?
questions.a: Stonewalling means going blank and withdrawing from the conversation, which sends a message of icy distance, superiority and distaste. As a habitual response it cuts off all possibility of working out disagreements. In troubled marriages it was the husband in 85 percent of cases, answering a wife's criticism and contempt.

questions.q: In the Martin and Melanie episode, what do the two parallel conversations illustrate?
questions.explain: Beck reports the spoken and silent conversations as an example of thinking that can poison a marriage.
options: That the real emotional exchange is shaped by the silent thoughts behind the spoken words
That a mild request can calm an angry spouse
That couples argue mainly about child care
That a wife's yielding always ends the argument

questions.q: Aaron Beck, the founder of ____ therapy, reported the story of Martin and Melanie.
questions.explain: Beck is the founder of cognitive therapy, and his work is used here for toxic thoughts.

questions.q: Beck calls the fleeting, background assumptions about oneself and others that shape the exchange ____ thoughts.
questions.explain: They reflect our deepest emotional attitudes.

questions.q: Match each partner in the Martin and Melanie story with the background thought Goleman gives.
pairs: He is always bullying me with his anger
She has no right to treat me like this
How Melanie feels in the marriage
How Martin feels in the marriage
questions.explain: Melanie feels like an innocent victim and Martin feels righteous indignation; these are typical of troubled marriages.

questions.q: Sort these thoughts by whether Goleman's template would class them as the pessimistic or the optimistic view of a spouse.

items.t: He is selfish and always will be
That is just the way he was brought up and he will never change
He could not care less how I feel
He has been thoughtful in the past
Maybe something is bothering him at work
This is a bad moment that can change

questions.explain: The pessimistic view treats the partner as inherently and permanently flawed; the optimistic view sees a bad moment due to changeable circumstances.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says automatic distressing thoughts become self-confirming because the partner who feels victimized scans for acts that confirm the view and discounts acts of kindness.
questions.explain: Kind acts get reinterpreted as feeble attempts to deny victimizing, leaving the other spouse in a no-win situation.

questions.q: Why is the spouse of a partner who feels like an innocent victim in a no-win situation?
questions.explain: The victim keeps ruminating on grievances while not recalling anything that disconfirms the victim view.
options: Her kind acts are always ignored by everyone else
Even kind acts can be reinterpreted through the negative lens and dismissed
His victim feelings fade as soon as she acts kindly
He refuses to discuss any of her actions

questions.q: Goleman says thoughts that maintain or alleviate marital distress follow the pessimistic and optimistic template from Chapter 6. Whose work does that template come from?
questions.explain: The general template for thoughts that maintain or alleviate distress follows Seligman's outlooks outlined in Chapter 6.
options: Paul Ekman's
Ted Huston's
Martin Seligman's
Carol Gilligan's

questions.q: Which of these are features of the pessimistic view of a spouse that Goleman describes?
questions.explain: The pessimistic view writes off the spouse as irredeemably flawed; the optimistic view blames changeable circumstances.
options: The partner has been thoughtful in the past
The partner is inherently flawed in a way that cannot change
The flaw guarantees misery
The bad moment is taken as proof of lasting character
The partner may simply be having a bad mood

questions.q: A husband snaps at his wife one evening. Which thought does Goleman give as an example of the optimistic view?
questions.explain: The optimistic view sees a bad moment as due to circumstances that can change, so the second attitude soothes.
options: He is selfish and self-absorbed and will always be that way
He expects me to wait on him hand and foot
I should do whatever he says to avoid a fight
He is being demanding now, but he has been thoughtful before; maybe something at work is bothering him

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says partners who take the pessimistic stance recover from emotional hijackings more readily than those free of distress-triggering views.
questions.explain: The reverse is true: pessimistic partners are extremely prone to hijackings and stay disturbed once the episode begins.

questions.q: Put these steps in the order Goleman describes the cycle that follows when partners take the pessimistic stance.
items: Pessimistic thinking about the partner
Easy emotional hijacking
Criticism and contempt
Defensiveness and stonewalling
questions.explain: Pessimism makes hijackings likelier and so resort to criticism and contempt, which heightens defensiveness and stonewalling.

questions.q: What did the Indiana University psychologists find about the thinking of violent husbands?
questions.explain: Goleman adds that men who are sexually aggressive with dates misread them in a similar way.
options: They think like schoolyard bullies, reading hostile intent into neutral actions and using it to justify violence
They think too little about their wives' wishes at all times
They misjudge rare cases of real hostility as friendly
They think carefully before each outburst of violence

questions.q: Violent husbands are particularly threatened by perceived slights, rejection or public ____ by their wives.
questions.explain: Goleman points back to Chapter 7's finding on such men when discussing triggers for violence.

questions.q: What are automatic thoughts in Beck's account, and how do they make a troubled marriage worse?
questions.a: Automatic thoughts are fleeting, background assumptions about oneself and others that reflect our deepest emotional attitudes. In troubled marriages they take the form of innocent-victim or righteous-indignation thoughts that feed anger and hurt. Because they are self-confirming, the person scans for confirming acts, ignores kindness and easily suffers an emotional hijacking.

questions.q: Contrast the pessimistic and optimistic ways a spouse can interpret the other's bad behavior, and say what each leads to.
questions.a: The pessimistic view takes the partner as inherently flawed in a way that will never change, guaranteeing misery. The optimistic view sees the bad moment as due to changeable circumstances and recalls past thoughtfulness, which soothes. Pessimists are more prone to hijackings, criticism and contempt.

questions.q: What does Goleman say about the thinking of men who are physically violent to their wives, and what triggers it?
questions.a: They think like schoolyard bullies, reading hostile intent into neutral acts and using that to justify violence. They are threatened by perceived slights, rejection or public embarrassment, and a thought such as that she is going to leave sets off a hijacking in which they respond impulsively with incompetent behavioral responses.

questions.section: Flooding: the Swamping of a Marriage
questions.q: Gottman uses the term ____ for the susceptibility to frequent emotional distress in which a spouse is swamped by dreadful, out-of-control feelings.
questions.explain: Flooded husbands or wives are overwhelmed by their partner's negativity and their own reaction to it.

questions.section: Flooding: the Swamping of a Marriage
questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say happen to a person who is flooded?
questions.explain: Flooded people want things to stop, or want to run or strike back; flooding is a self-perpetuating emotional hijacking.
options: They cannot hear without distortion
They find it hard to organize their thinking
They fall back on primitive reactions
They become unusually calm and analytical
They respond with greater clarity than usual

questions.section: Flooding: the Swamping of a Marriage
questions.q: True or false: Goleman says every person floods at the same level of provocation, such as a spouse's mild criticism.
questions.explain: Some people have high thresholds and easily endure anger and contempt, while others are triggered the moment a spouse makes a mild criticism.

questions.section: Flooding: the Swamping of a Marriage
questions.q: Flooding begins at about ____ beats per minute above a person's resting heart rate.
questions.explain: Goleman gives the technical description of flooding as a heart rate rise from calm levels.

questions.section: Flooding: the Swamping of a Marriage
questions.q: Once the heart rate reaches ____ beats per minute, the body is pumping adrenaline and other hormones that keep distress high for some time.
questions.explain: This can happen easily during moments of rage or tears.

questions.section: Flooding: the Swamping of a Marriage
questions.q: Match each figure with what Goleman reports about it in the discussion of flooding.
pairs: 10, 20 or even 30 beats in one heartbeat
How far the rate can jump at hijacking
questions.explain: The heart rate figures show how the moment of hijacking is visible in the body.

questions.section: Flooding: the Swamping of a Marriage
questions.q: What does Goleman say about how fast heart rate can rise at the moment of emotional hijacking?
questions.explain: The jump comes with tense muscles, hard breathing and a swamp of fear and anger that seems inescapable.
options: It climbs by about one beat per minute each minute
It can jump 10, 20 or even 30 beats per minute within a single heartbeat
It drops quickly as adrenaline is secreted
It rises only after several minutes of anger

questions.section: Flooding: the Swamping of a Marriage
questions.q: Sort these statements by whether they describe occasional flooding or continual flooding in a marriage.

items.t: A natural result of fights now and then
Most husbands and wives experience it from time to time
One partner is always on guard for an emotional assault
One partner is hypervigilant for any sign of insult
Even a gentle remark is overreacted to

questions.explain: Goleman says intense moments are natural; the problem begins when one spouse feels flooded almost continually.

questions.section: Flooding: the Swamping of a Marriage
questions.q: Put these steps in the order Goleman gives for how a hypervigilant, flooded husband spirals from one small remark.
items: Wife says that they have got to talk
Husband thinks she is picking a fight again
Flooding is triggered
Recovery from arousal becomes harder
Innocuous exchanges look sinister
questions.explain: The cycle feeds itself: the physiological arousal makes it easier to see harmless exchanges in a sinister light, triggering flooding all over again.

questions.section: Flooding: the Swamping of a Marriage
questions.q: When the flooded partner starts leading parallel lives and feeling alone within the marriage, Gottman finds the next step is all too often ____.
questions.explain: Talking things over seems useless, so the partners try to soothe their feelings on their own.

questions.section: Flooding: the Swamping of a Marriage
questions.q: Put these developments in the order Goleman describes after continual flooding sets in.
items: Small issues become major battles
Problems seem severe and impossible to fix
Talking things over seems useless
Partners lead parallel lives
Divorce
questions.explain: Flooding sabotages attempts to work things out, so the couple withdraws into isolation, which Gottman finds often ends in divorce.

questions.section: Flooding: the Swamping of a Marriage
questions.q: Why does Goleman call continual flooding the most dangerous turning point for a marriage?
questions.a: A continually flooded partner comes to think the worst of the spouse almost all the time, reads everything negatively and sees every problem as severe and impossible to fix. Because flooding itself sabotages attempts to work things out, talking seems useless, the couple lead parallel lives and feel alone, and the next step is often divorce.

questions.section: Flooding: the Swamping of a Marriage
questions.q: What does flooding look like physiologically and psychologically, according to Goleman?
questions.a: It is marked by a rise of about ten beats per minute above resting heart rate, and at about 100 beats the body is pumping adrenaline that keeps distress high. Muscles tense, breathing seems hard, and the person feels swamped by fear and anger, cannot take the other's viewpoint and cannot reason calmly.

questions.section: Flooding: the Swamping of a Marriage
questions.q: According to Goleman, what does the cycle of criticism, contempt, defensiveness, stonewalling, distressing thoughts and flooding reflect?
questions.explain: Goleman says the tragic consequences of deficits in emotional competences are self-evident in this trajectory.
options: A mismatch of the couple's intelligence quotients
A temporary difference in how the sexes talk
A disintegration of self-awareness, self-control, empathy and the abilities to soothe each other and oneself
A lack of social pressure to stay married

questions.section: Flooding: the Swamping of a Marriage
questions.q: Which of these emotional competences does Goleman say disintegrate when a couple is caught in the cycle toward divorce?
questions.explain: The cycle reflects a disintegration of emotional self-awareness and self-control, of empathy and the abilities to soothe each other and oneself.
options: Emotional self-awareness
Self-control
Empathy
Motivation to earn
Facility with language
Physical fitness

questions.section: Flooding: the Swamping of a Marriage
questions.q: Sort these ideas by whether Goleman's account ties them to the start of the cycle toward divorce or to its end.

items.t: Harsh criticism
Contempt
Defensiveness
Continual flooding
Parallel lives
Feeling alone within the marriage

questions.explain: Criticism and contempt start the reverberating cycle; continual flooding then leads to isolation and, often, divorce.

questions.q: Robert Levenson at the University of California at Berkeley studied ____ couples in long-lasting marriages and found that husbands found marital upset unpleasant.
questions.explain: Even after thirty-five or more years of marriage, husbands uniformly found it aversive to become upset during a disagreement, while wives did not mind it much.

questions.q: Which of these did Levenson's findings show about husbands compared with wives?
questions.explain: More men than women react to a spouse's criticism with flooding, and they take longer to recover.
options: They take longer to recover physiologically
They are less likely to react with flooding to criticism
They recover from flooding faster than wives
They flood at a lower intensity of negativity
They secrete more adrenaline once flooded

questions.q: What possibility does Goleman suggest about the stoic, Clint Eastwood type of male imperturbability?
questions.explain: Because men flood more easily, calm can serve as protection.
options: It shows men feel little emotion
It is a skill men learn from women
It proves men are less sensitive to negativity
It may be a defense against feeling emotionally overwhelmed

questions.q: Gottman proposes that men stonewall mainly to protect themselves from ____.
questions.explain: Once men started stonewalling, their heart rates dropped about ten beats per minute, bringing subjective relief.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman reports that when husbands began stonewalling, their wives' heart rates dropped along with their own.
questions.explain: The paradox is that the husbands' rates fell by about ten beats while the wives' shot up to levels signaling high distress.

questions.q: Goleman calls the pattern in which each sex seeks comfort in opposing gambits, men avoiding confrontation and women seeking it, a limbic ____.
questions.explain: Men want to avoid emotional confrontations as fervently as their wives feel compelled to seek them.

questions.q: Put the steps of the escalating cycle Goleman describes in the order they occur, starting with the wife raising a grievance.
items: Wife raises a grievance
Husband is reluctant to engage
