Wife criticizes more intensely
Husband becomes defensive or stonewalls
Wife adds contempt
questions.explain: Her role as emotional manager meets his withdrawal; she ups the volume, criticizes, then adds contempt, while he defends or stonewalls and ends up flooded.

questions.q: Why, according to Goleman, are women more likely to criticize their husbands?
questions.explain: The asymmetry arises from wives pursuing their role as emotional managers.
options: As emotional managers, wives press to resolve grievances and raise the volume when husbands withdraw
Wives enjoy conflict more than husbands do
Wives are less empathic than husbands
Wives were taught to hide complaints in girlhood

questions.q: Why do men stonewall, and what does it do to their wives?
questions.a: Men flood at lower levels of negativity and take longer to recover, so they stonewall to protect themselves; Gottman found their heart rates dropped about ten beats per minute, a relief. But then the wives' heart rates shot up to levels of high distress, so each sex seeks comfort in opposing ways.

questions.q: Describe how the wife's criticism and the husband's stonewalling feed each other in the cycle Goleman describes.
questions.a: As the wife sees her husband withdraw she ups the volume and starts to criticize; when he becomes defensive or stonewalls, she feels frustrated and adds contempt. He then falls into innocent-victim or righteous-indignation thoughts that trigger flooding, so he stonewalls more, which floods her and sends the cycle spinning out of control.

questions.q: Match each finding to its source or emphasis in this part of the chapter.
pairs: Husbands found marital upset aversive, wives did not
Men stonewall to protect against flooding
Male imperturbability may be a defense against overwhelm
Each sex seeks comfort in opposing gambits
questions.explain: Each of these appears in the section on men's vulnerability to flooding.

questions.q: What general advice does Goleman give men about a wife's grievance?
questions.explain: Aired grievances take pressure off, whereas simmering ones build to an explosion.
options: Respond by leaving the room until she calms down
Do not sidestep conflict, since raising a grievance may be an act of love to keep the relationship healthy
Treat her anger as a sign the marriage is failing
Agree with her at once to end the discussion

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman advise husbands to do when a wife raises a complaint?
questions.explain: Wives want their feelings heard and respected, and more often than not calm down once they are.
options: Offer a practical solution right away
Dismiss minor complaints as petty
Realize anger or discontent is not necessarily a personal attack
Stay with her through the heat of anger
Acknowledge her feelings as valid even if disagreeing

questions.q: Goleman says a wife's emotions are often simply ____, emphasizing the strength of her feelings about the matter.
questions.explain: Anger or discontent is not synonymous with personal attack.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman advises husbands to offer a practical solution early in the discussion because that shows they care.
questions.explain: Offering a solution too early short-circuits the discussion and may be heard as dismissing her feelings as inconsequential.

questions.q: Alma tells her husband Raj she is upset that he never tells her when plans change, and Raj immediately says she should just set up a shared calendar. According to the chapter's advice, what would have helped more?
questions.explain: More important to a wife is feeling heard; she may take early advice as a dismissal of her feelings.
options: Agreeing that he is thoughtless and promising to change
Leaving the room until she calms down
Letting her know he hears and empathizes with her feelings before suggesting anything
Telling her that her tone is the real problem

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman advise wives to do?
questions.explain: An angry personal attack will almost certainly make him defensive or stonewalling, which escalates the fight.
options: Wait for him to bring up problems first
Complain about what the husband did, not who he is
Avoid expressing contempt
Reassure him of her love when making complaints
Raise the volume until he responds

questions.q: What is Goleman's advice to husbands about a wife's complaints, and what does it do for the marriage?
questions.a: Husbands should not sidestep conflict but see that her grievance may be an act of love, and that her anger underlines how strongly she feels rather than attacking him. By staying with her, empathizing and acknowledging her feelings without offering a solution too early, they help her feel heard and respected, and she calms down.

questions.q: What advice does Goleman give wives, and why is it parallel to his advice to husbands?
questions.a: Wives should make a purposeful effort to complain about what the husband did, not criticize him as a person or express contempt, and should put the complaint in the context of reassuring him of her love. It parallels the men's advice because both aim to avoid the defensiveness, stonewalling and escalation that follow personal attacks.

questions.q: Why does grievance-airing matter according to Goleman, and how can a husband misread a wife's anger?
questions.a: Grievances that simmer build in intensity until they explode, whereas aired and worked-out grievances take the pressure off. A husband may misread her anger as a personal attack, when it is often simply an underliner emphasizing how strongly she feels.

questions.q: Match each person with the advice Goleman gives.
pairs: Hear the complaint and empathize before offering solutions
Complain about the deed, not the person
Learn to calm down (and calm the partner), empathize and listen well
A husband who sees his wife's anger
Treat it as an underliner of strong feeling, not a personal attack
questions.explain: The marital advice is parallel for both partners but targets each one's typical weak point.

questions.q: Sort these responses by whether the chapter's advice recommends them for husbands or for wives.

items.t: Stay with her through the heat of anger
Acknowledge her feelings as valid even if you disagree
Avoid offering a solution too early
Complain about the action, not the person
Avoid expressing contempt
Reassure him of your love

questions.explain: Husbands are told to engage and empathize; wives are told to complain without attacking.

questions.q: Which of these do couples in lasting marriages tend to do when they argue?
questions.explain: Goleman adds that feeling heard is often exactly what the aggrieved partner is after, so an act of empathy is a masterly tension reducer.
options: Stick to one topic
Give each partner the chance to state a point of view at the outset
Show each other that they are being listened to
Bring up old grievances to show a pattern
Leave the room whenever feelings run high

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman name as the handful of emotional competences that help a couple settle disagreements?
questions.explain: These make possible the healthy disagreements, or good fights, that let a marriage flourish.
options: Empathy
Listening well
Winning each argument decisively
Choosing the right topics to fight about
Being able to calm down and calm your partner

questions.q: Which of these are forms of defensiveness that Goleman says have no place in open communication?
questions.explain: Open communication has no bullying, threats or insults, and none of the innumerable forms of defensiveness.
options: Counterattacking with a criticism
Repeating the complaint back in your own words
Acknowledging the emotion behind the complaint
Making excuses
Denying responsibility

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman describe as ways of validating a partner?
questions.explain: Validation can be offered even without agreeing, and it helps soothe your spouse or build up emotional capital.
options: Agreeing with every point the partner makes
Waiting for the partner to apologize first
Conveying that you are listening and can acknowledge the emotions being expressed
Taking responsibility or apologizing when you are in the wrong
Offering compliments when there is no fight going on

questions.q: Counting the pulse for ____ seconds and multiplying by four gives the pulse rate in beats per minute.
questions.explain: The baseline is taken while calm; a rise of more than about ten beats signals the beginning of flooding.

questions.q: One method for effective emotional listening, commonly used in marital therapy, repeats a partner's complaint back in your own words and is called ____.
questions.explain: The partner mirroring checks that the restatement is on target and tries again until it is right.

questions.q: Put these steps of the pulse-monitoring method in the order Goleman describes.
items: Take a baseline pulse while calm
Check the carotid pulse every five minutes or so during the argument
Count for fifteen seconds and multiply by four
Notice a rise of more than ten beats above baseline
Take a twenty-minute break before resuming
questions.explain: A rise of about ten beats signals flooding, and a twenty-minute break gives the body time to recover from the arousal.

questions.q: Put the steps of mirroring in the order Goleman gives.
items: One partner makes a complaint
The other repeats it back in her own words with the feelings
She checks that the restatement is on target
If it is not, she tries again until it is right
questions.explain: The effect of being mirrored accurately is feeling understood and in emotional attunement.

questions.q: Match each part of Goleman's remedy for marital fights with its purpose.
pairs: Soothing distressed feelings and recovering from flooding
Catching and challenging harsh thoughts about the partner
Hearing the message past the anger and keeping complaints specific
Overlearning the responses before a crisis hits
questions.explain: These four strategies together are a small remedial education in emotional intelligence.

questions.q: Match each part of Ginott's XYZ formula for a complaint with its content.
pairs: The action: when you did this
What I would rather you did instead
questions.explain: Haim Ginott's formula keeps a complaint to a specific action rather than escalating to a personal attack.

questions.q: Match each person or case with the point Goleman makes in the section on the good fight.
pairs: An object lesson in how not to resolve differences
Catch and challenge thoughts rather than being enraged by them
The XYZ formula for a complaint
questions.explain: Goleman opens with a violent dispute over a football game and then turns to constructive methods.

questions.q: Sort these features of arguments by whether they mark healthy marriages or marriages that end in divorce.

items.t: Sticking to one topic
Attempts to de-escalate tension
Showing the partner they are heard
Absence of attempts to de-escalate
Fixation on the specifics of the issue
Not hearing implicit peace offerings

questions.explain: Repair mechanisms are the crucial difference between the fights of couples who thrive and those who eventually divorce.

questions.q: Sort these responses to a spouse's angry complaint by whether they are defensive or nondefensive.

items.t: Ignoring the complaint
Immediately rebutting it
Answering with a criticism of your own
Saying okay, go ahead and finish
Repeating the complaint back to check you heard it
Saying that you see the other is upset

questions.explain: Defensiveness treats a complaint as an attack; nondefensive listening hears the message and responds without reacting to the hostility.

questions.q: Sort these thoughts by whether they are toxic slogans to catch or reframed thoughts Goleman recommends.

items.t: I am not going to take this anymore
I do not deserve this kind of treatment
He does not care, he is always so selfish
He does sometimes show he cares, even though this upset me
He has done many thoughtful things, though this was not one of them

questions.explain: Challenging the harsh thought with evidence reframes it and opens the possibility of change and positive resolution.

questions.q: What do repair mechanisms do in a marital fight, and how are they absent in couples who end up divorcing?
questions.a: Repair mechanisms are simple moves such as keeping the discussion on track, empathizing and reducing tension, working like an emotional thermostat that stops feelings from boiling over. Couples who eventually divorce most notably lack attempts by either partner to de-escalate the tension.

questions.q: A couple notices both partners shouting and their heart rates rising. Using Goleman's advice, what should they do and why for twenty minutes rather than five?
questions.a: They should stop and take a time-out, since nothing gets resolved during a hijacking and the ability to hear and think clearly dissolves. Twenty minutes is needed because physiological recovery is gradual and, as in Chapter 5, residual anger triggers more anger; a five-minute break may feel long enough but is not.

questions.q: How does detoxifying self-talk work in Goleman's account?
questions.a: It means monitoring harsh thoughts such as I do not deserve this treatment, realizing you need not believe them, and deliberately recalling evidence that puts them in question. A wife who thinks he is always selfish can remind herself of thoughtful things he has done and reframe the thought, which opens the way to change rather than fostering anger and hurt.

questions.q: Why does Goleman say these strategies must be overlearned and practiced even in calm times?
questions.a: In the heat of confrontation the emotional brain engages the response routines learned earliest in life, and memory and response are emotion-specific, so reactions tied to calmer times are hard to recall. Responses practiced until automatic have a better chance of appearing in crisis, so they should be rehearsed in non-stressful encounters as well as in the heat of battle.

questions.q: Goleman places this chapter at the start of Part Three, Emotional Intelligence Applied. Why does it fit there, after the chapters on empathy and the social arts?
questions.a: Part Two described the nature of emotional intelligence, including self-control, empathy and handling relationships. Part Three applies these abilities to see how they can preserve, or their lack corrode, our most prized relationships, and marriage is the first and most intimate case before work and health.

questions.q: What does the chapter title Intimate Enemies signal, and how does the chapter's order of sections develop it?
questions.a: The title signals that those closest to us can become sources of hostility when emotional skills fail. The chapter moves from childhood roots of the gender gap, to Gottman's fault lines of criticism, contempt and stonewalling, to toxic thoughts and flooding, then men's vulnerability, advice for each sex and finally the skills of a good fight.

questions.q: Name two earlier chapters this chapter explicitly draws on and say how each is used.
questions.a: It draws on Chapter 5 for the point that residual anger triggers more anger, so a longer break is needed to calm down. It draws on Chapter 6 for Seligman's pessimistic and optimistic outlooks, and on Chapter 7 for empathy requiring physiological attunement and for the violent husbands who are threatened by rejection.

questions.q: Goleman's road-map places this chapter in Part ____, titled Emotional Intelligence Applied.
questions.explain: Part Three examines how emotional abilities preserve or corrode relationships, and the role they play at work and in health.

questions.q: The chapter that comes right before this one in the book is Chapter 8, titled The ____ Arts.
questions.explain: Chapter 8 deals with social competence and incompetence, the skills of handling relationships, before Part Three applies them.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say Part Three examines?
questions.explain: The brain is Part One's subject, and childhood lessons are Part Four's; Part Three covers relationships, work and health.
options: How childhood lessons at home and school shape the emotional circuits
How emotional abilities can preserve or corrode our most prized relationships
How market forces are putting a premium on emotional intelligence at work
How toxic emotions put physical health at risk
How the brain's emotional architecture explains hijackings

questions.q: Which of these ideas from earlier in the book does this chapter explicitly build on?
questions.explain: The chapter cross-refers to Chapters 5, 6 and 7 to explain how calming down, thinking and empathy work in a marriage.
options: Chapter 5's point that residual anger triggers more anger
Chapter 6's pessimistic and optimistic outlooks
Chapter 7's point that empathy needs physiological attunement
Chapter 12's account of the family crucible
Chapter 16's plan for schooling the emotions

questions.q: Put these Parts of the book in the order the table of contents gives.
items: The Emotional Brain
The Nature of Emotional Intelligence
Emotional Intelligence Applied
Windows of Opportunity
Emotional Literacy
questions.explain: This chapter sits in the third of five Parts, after the foundations and before the discussion of childhood.

questions.q: Put these topics in the order this chapter takes them up.
items: Childhood roots of his and hers
Gottman's marital fault lines
Toxic thoughts
Flooding
Men as the vulnerable sex
Marital advice and the good fight
questions.explain: The chapter moves from why men and women differ to how marriages fail and then to how couples can protect themselves.

questions.q: Match each chapter to its link with this chapter's argument.
pairs: Source of the idea that residual anger triggers more anger
Source of Seligman's pessimistic and optimistic outlooks
Source of the idea that empathy needs physiological attunement
questions.explain: This chapter applies earlier ideas to marriage.

questions.q: Match each Part of the book to its theme.
questions.explain: Chapter 9 opens Part Three, which turns from describing emotional intelligence to showing it at work in life.

questions.q: Sort these topics by whether they belong to marriage in this chapter or to the later work and health chapters of Part Three.
groups: Work and health in later chapters

items.t: Stonewalling
Mirroring a partner's complaint
Gottman's prediction of divorce
Market forces that reward emotional intelligence at work
Toxic emotions as a health risk like chain-smoking

questions.explain: Part Three applies emotional intelligence first to relationships, then to work and health.

questions.q: In Goleman's opening story of the 1978 crash near Portland, Oregon, why did pilot Melburn McBroom's copilots say nothing as the fuel ran low?
questions.explain: The copilots feared McBroom's temper so much that they stayed silent even as disaster loomed. The failure was emotional and social, not one of noticing or of formal rules.
options: They had not noticed the fuel gauges while watching the landing gear
They assumed McBroom had already radioed for an emergency landing
They were so afraid of his wrath that they kept silent
Airline rules at the time barred copilots from questioning the captain

questions.q: True or false: Goleman reports that in about half of airline crashes, pilots make mistakes that better crew teamwork could have prevented.
questions.explain: The figure he gives is 80 percent of airline crashes, which is why pilot training now stresses teamwork and communication.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say airline pilot training now emphasizes, along with technical prowess, after crashes like McBroom's?
questions.explain: Training now stresses teamwork, open communication, cooperation, listening and speaking one's mind, the rudiments of social intelligence. Deference to the captain is exactly what doomed McBroom's crew.
options: Teamwork and cooperation
Open lines of communication and listening
Strict deference to the captain's judgment
Speaking one's mind
Faster memorization of emergency checklists

questions.q: Goleman writes that the cockpit is a ____ of any working organization.
questions.explain: The cockpit is a small-scale version of any workplace; elsewhere the same emotional failings simply lack the dramatic reality check of a crash.

questions.q: Which of these signs does Goleman say reveal the hidden cost of low emotional intelligence in a workplace?
questions.explain: Without a crash to expose them, emotional deficiencies show up as lower productivity, missed deadlines, mistakes and mishaps, and people leaving for friendlier workplaces.
options: Decreased productivity
An increase in missed deadlines
An exodus of employees to more congenial settings
A rise in the number of meetings
Higher spending on office equipment

questions.q: True or false: In the 1970s study of executives, many feared that feeling empathy or compassion for those they worked with would put them in conflict with their organizational goals.
questions.explain: That fear is what the study found. Goleman replies that their hard decisions would likely just have been delivered more humanely.

questions.q: According to Harvard psychologist Shoshona Zuboff, as quoted by Goleman, who symbolizes the corporate future?
questions.explain: Zuboff contrasts the jungle-fighter boss, who stands for where the corporation has been, with the interpersonally skilled virtuoso, who stands for its future.
options: The virtuoso in interpersonal skills
The manipulative, jungle-fighter boss
The technical specialist who works alone
The manager who rules through a rigid hierarchy

questions.q: A management consultant sums up for Goleman how emotional upset impairs work, saying that stress makes people ____.
questions.explain: The line echoes Chapter 6: when emotionally upset, people cannot remember, attend, learn or decide clearly, at work as anywhere else.

questions.q: How does Goleman define leadership in his chapter on emotional intelligence at work?
questions.explain: He states that leadership is not domination but the art of persuading people toward a common goal, which depends on emotional skills.
options: Domination of a team through clear authority
Technical expertise that earns automatic respect
Keeping emotional distance so hard decisions can be made
The art of persuading people to work toward a common goal

questions.q: A junior nurse notices a surgeon is about to give the wrong dose but says nothing, because the surgeon is known for exploding at anyone who questions him. Which story in Goleman's chapter on work does this most closely mirror?
questions.explain: As with McBroom's crew, an intimidating boss silences the people who could prevent a disaster. That is the cockpit-as-microcosm point.
options: The vice president who mocked the engineer's software plan
Melburn McBroom's copilots staying silent as the fuel ran out
The Bell Labs middle performer waiting for unreturned calls
The Denny's waitresses ignoring black customers

questions.q: After a heated argument with a colleague, Raj sits at his desk for an hour unable to focus on a report or remember what he was about to write. Which point from Goleman's chapter on work explains this?
questions.explain: Goleman carries Chapter 6's finding into the workplace: agitation disrupts memory, attention, learning and decision-making.
options: People can only enter flow when they are slightly angry
Emotional upset keeps people from remembering, attending, learning or deciding clearly
Criticism received in private is more upsetting than public criticism
Group IQ falls when one member is too eager to take part

questions.q: Shoshona Zuboff tells Goleman that the rigid corporate hierarchy began breaking down in the 1980s under the twin pressures of globalization and information ____.
questions.explain: Zuboff names globalization and information technology as the twin pressures that broke the hierarchy which had rewarded the jungle-fighter boss.

questions.q: Put in order the stages of corporate history that Shoshona Zuboff describes to Goleman.
items: Managerial domination of a rigid corporate hierarchy
The manipulative jungle-fighter boss is rewarded
Globalization and information technology break down the hierarchy
The virtuoso in interpersonal skills becomes the corporate future
questions.explain: Zuboff traces a long period of managerial domination that rewarded the jungle fighter, the 1980s breakdown of that hierarchy, and the rise of interpersonal skill as the future.

questions.q: Put the events of Goleman's account of Melburn McBroom's flight in order.
items: McBroom notices a problem with the landing gear
He circles the field in a holding pattern, fiddling with the mechanism
The fuel gauges approach empty while his copilots stay silent
The plane crashes, killing ten people
The crash becomes a cautionary tale in pilot safety training
questions.explain: The story runs from the landing-gear problem and the obsessive holding pattern, through the crew's fearful silence, to the crash and its later use in training.

questions.q: Sort these into what Goleman lists as benefits of emotional skill at work versus costs of emotional deficiency at work.

items.t: Being attuned to the feelings of those we deal with
Handling disagreements so they do not escalate
Getting into flow states while working
Recognizing our deepest feelings about our work
Mistakes and mishaps
Missed deadlines
Employees leaving for more congenial settings

questions.explain: The benefits are the basic emotional competences applied to work; the costs are the hidden signs of low emotional intelligence that show up on the bottom line.

questions.q: Match each source in the opening of Goleman's chapter on work to the point it makes.
pairs: An intimidating boss can silence the people who could avert disaster
Managers felt work needed their heads but not their hearts
The jungle-fighter boss is the past; the interpersonal virtuoso the future
questions.explain: Each source supports the opening case: emotional failings are costly, old attitudes are outmoded, and upset impairs thinking at work.

questions.q: Why does Goleman argue that the 1970s executives' view that work needs heads but not hearts is now outmoded?
questions.a: He calls such attitudes a luxury of a former day: a new competitive reality is putting emotional intelligence at a premium in the workplace and marketplace. As Zuboff explains, globalization and information technology broke down the rigid hierarchy that rewarded the manipulative jungle-fighter boss, so interpersonal skill is now the corporate future. And even hard decisions would likely be delivered more humanely by managers with empathy.

questions.q: What does the story of Melburn McBroom's crash show about workplaces in general, and why are such problems usually less visible elsewhere?
questions.a: The cockpit is a microcosm of any organization: an intimidating boss whose crew fear his wrath can produce disaster because no one speaks up. In most workplaces there is no dramatic reality check like a crash, so miserable morale, intimidated workers and arrogant bosses go largely unnoticed by outsiders. Their costs show up instead as lower productivity, missed deadlines, mistakes and staff leaving.

questions.q: Put the events of Goleman's story of the software engineer and the sarcastic vice president in order.
items: The engineer presents his team's months of work
The vice president mocks the specifications as ridiculous
The meeting breaks up, leaving bitterness and anger
The engineer broods for two weeks and thinks of leaving
The engineer asks the vice president what he was trying to accomplish
The vice president, astonished, apologizes
questions.explain: The story moves from the presentation and the sarcastic put-down, through the engineer's demoralized brooding, to his careful inquiry and the vice president's belated apology.

questions.q: True or false: In Goleman's story of the software engineer, the vice president later admitted he had thought the software plan was worthless.
questions.explain: The vice president actually thought the plan was promising but needed more work. He meant his remark as a throwaway line and had no idea how devastating it was.

questions.q: In Goleman's story, how did the demoralized software engineer finally approach the vice president who had mocked his plan?
questions.explain: He reminded the vice president of the meeting and its effect, then made a carefully worded inquiry that assumed a goal other than embarrassment, which opened the way to the apology.
options: He demanded a public apology in front of his whole team
He complained to the vice president's superiors in a formal memo
He resubmitted the plan without mentioning the earlier meeting
He asked what the vice president had meant to accomplish, assuming it was not just to embarrass him

questions.q: In its original sense in systems theory, ____ meant the exchange of data about how one part of a system is working, so any part heading off course could be corrected.
questions.explain: Goleman borrows the systems-theory meaning of feedback: one part affects all others, so information about how each part works keeps the whole on track.

questions.q: Because everyone in a company is part of the system, Goleman calls feedback the ____ of the organization.
questions.explain: Feedback is the lifeblood because it lets people know whether their work is going well or needs fine-tuning, upgrading or redirecting.

questions.q: Why does Goleman say that criticism is one of the most important tasks a manager has, and why do so many managers handle it badly?
questions.a: Feedback is the lifeblood of an organization: it tells people whether their work is on track or needs to be changed, and without it problems only grow. Yet criticism is also one of the most dreaded and put-off tasks, and many managers, like the sarcastic vice president, have poorly mastered the art of feedback. How criticism is given and received goes a long way toward determining people's satisfaction with their work and colleagues.

questions.q: Match each workplace pattern in Goleman's chapter on work to its marriage counterpart from his chapter on couples.
pairs: An employee quitting or being fired
An employee avoiding all contact with the manager
Criticism voiced as a personal attack
Complaint turned into ad hominem attack with contempt
The XYZ statement of a grievance
questions.explain: Goleman maps Gottman's marriage findings onto work: attacks, defensiveness and stonewalling, ending in the business equivalent of a divorce, and the same remedy of a specific, XYZ-style complaint.

questions.q: In the Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute experiment on criticism, volunteers were asked to create an ad for a new ____ and then received a prearranged critique.
questions.explain: The shampoo-ad task let researchers give one group a considerate, specific critique and another a threatening, blaming one.

questions.q: Which of these are features of the common destructive workplace criticism Goleman describes?
questions.explain: Destructive criticism is blanket, harsh and one-way. Being face to face and specific are features of the artful critique instead.
options: A generalized rather than specific complaint
A harsh, sarcastic, angry tone
No chance for the person to respond
Delivery face to face and in private
A focus on one significant incident

questions.q: From the vantage point of emotional intelligence, what is wrong with a blanket, sarcastic criticism like You're screwing up?
questions.a: It displays ignorance of the feelings it will trigger in the person who receives it. Those feelings, helplessness and anger, have a devastating effect on the person's motivation, energy and confidence in doing the work. Because it gives no chance to respond and no suggestion for doing better, it undermines the very performance it was meant to improve.

questions.q: Which of these reactions did employees most often show, in the survey of managers recalling times they blew up and made a personal attack?
questions.explain: Employees reacted as attacked spouses do: defensiveness, excuses, dodging responsibility and stonewalling. Nothing in the survey suggests attacks spurred harder work.
options: Becoming defensive
Making excuses or evading responsibility
Working harder to prove the manager wrong
Stonewalling by avoiding the manager
Asking calmly for specific examples

questions.q: Goleman suggests that employees attacked by an angry manager, if their physiology were measured, would probably show the ____ that reinforces thoughts of innocent victimhood.
questions.explain: He borrows Gottman's term from the marriage research: flooding keeps the attacked person locked in thoughts of victimhood or righteous indignation.

questions.q: In the study of 108 managers and white-collar workers that Goleman cites, how did inept criticism rank as a reason for conflict on the job?
questions.explain: Inept criticism came out ahead of all of those other sources of conflict, which is why Goleman treats the art of the critique as central.
options: Ahead of mistrust, personality struggles, and disputes over power and pay
Behind disputes over pay but ahead of personality struggles
Last among the causes, well behind mistrust and power disputes
Equal with mistrust, and behind personality struggles

questions.q: True or false: In the Rensselaer experiment, the harsh critique included threats and blamed the person's innate deficiencies, such as a possible lack of talent.
questions.explain: One prearranged critique was considerate and specific; the other threatened and blamed innate shortcomings, suggesting someone else should do the job.

questions.q: Which of these were effects on volunteers who got the harsh, blaming critique in the Rensselaer experiment?
questions.explain: The attacked volunteers became tense, angry and antagonistic, wanted to stonewall, tried less hard and, most damaging, no longer felt capable. None responded by trying harder.
options: They said they would refuse to cooperate with the critic on future projects
They no longer felt capable of doing well
They tried harder to win the critic's approval
They wanted to avoid contact with the critic
They asked for more detailed feedback

questions.q: In the Rensselaer experiment, what does Goleman single out as perhaps the most damaging effect of the harsh, personal critique, and why does it matter?
questions.a: Beyond making people tense, angry and unwilling to cooperate, the attack left them so demoralized that they stopped trying as hard and, most damaging, said they no longer felt capable of doing well. That loss of felt capability attacks the motivation needed to improve, so the criticism defeats its own purpose; the personal attack was devastating to their morale.

questions.q: Put in order the cycle J. R. Larson describes when a boss delays criticism.
items: An employee's performance problem develops slowly
The boss keeps his feelings to himself
The boss's frustration builds up
The boss blows up with sarcasm and old grievances
The employee takes it as an affront and gets angry in return
questions.explain: Larson traces how silence lets frustration build into an explosion, which the employee experiences as an affront, so the attack backfires.

questions.q: Goleman says an artful critique focuses on what a person has done and can do, rather than reading a mark of ____ into a job poorly done.
questions.explain: A character attack, as Larson notes, puts the person on the defensive so they are no longer receptive to how to do better.

questions.q: How does Goleman link the artful critique to his earlier account of optimism?
questions.explain: The basic belief behind optimism is that setbacks come from circumstances we can change, so criticism aimed at character rather than actions destroys hope and effort.
options: Optimists need harsher criticism because they discount bad news
Criticism works best when it is followed immediately by praise
People who think failure comes from an unchangeable deficit lose hope, while optimists see setbacks as changeable
Pessimists respond better to criticism of their character than of their actions

questions.q: Levinson's advice to be specific echoes the advice to couples about the ____ statement of a grievance.
questions.explain: Like the XYZ statement, a good critique says exactly what the problem is, what is wrong with it or how it feels, and what could be changed.

questions.q: Match each of Harry Levinson's rules for the art of the critique to what it asks of the critic.
pairs: Pick a significant incident and say what was done well, poorly and how to change it
Point to a way to fix the problem
Give the critique face to face and in private
Be attuned to the impact of what you say and how you say it
questions.explain: Levinson's four rules cover content (specific, with a solution), setting (in person, in private) and empathy for the person receiving it.

questions.q: Levinson notes that specificity is just as important for ____ as for criticism, since the vague kind teaches little.
questions.explain: He says vague praise has little effect and that you cannot learn from it; the art of the critique is entwined with the art of praise.

questions.q: True or false: Levinson advises giving criticism by memo when it is awkward, because a written message is more carefully considered.
questions.explain: He warns that a memo makes the communication too impersonal and robs the receiver of a chance to respond or ask for clarification; critiques work best face to face and in private.

questions.q: Sort these features into Goleman's destructive criticism versus his artful critique.

items.t: Calls the person stupid or incompetent
Saved up until the critic boils over
Blanket, generalized complaint
Sent at a distance to spare the critic discomfort
Names a significant, specific incident
Suggests how to fix the problem
Given face to face and in private
Attuned to its impact on the receiver

questions.explain: Destructive criticism attacks character, is delayed, vague and distant; the artful critique, following Levinson, is specific, solution-focused, in person and sensitive.

questions.q: Sort Levinson's advice into advice for the person giving criticism versus the person receiving it.

items.t: Offer a solution
Deliver it face to face and in private
Pick a significant incident
Treat it as information about how to do better
Watch for the impulse toward defensiveness
Ask to resume later if it gets too upsetting
See it as a chance to solve the problem with the critic

questions.explain: Levinson's rules for critics are specificity, solutions, presence and sensitivity; his counsel for receivers is to take it as information, avoid defensiveness, cool down if needed and collaborate.

questions.q: A supervisor tells a struggling new hire, You're just not cut out for this kind of work. According to Goleman's chapter on work, what is the likely result?
questions.explain: A remark about innate unfitness reads character into poor work. When people believe failure comes from an unchangeable deficit, they lose hope and stop trying.
options: The new hire feels challenged and works harder to prove the supervisor wrong
The new hire gets clear guidance on which tasks to improve first
The new hire becomes more optimistic because the problem is now named
The new hire concludes the failure is an unchangeable deficit, loses hope and stops trying

questions.q: For months a team lead notices that Priya's reports contain the same errors but says nothing; then one day he explodes and lists every mistake she has ever made. What would J. R. Larson say went wrong?
questions.explain: Larson says problems develop slowly; giving criticism early lets the employee correct the problem, while bottled-up frustration erupts in the worst, biting form.
options: He should have waited even longer, until he was completely calm
He was right to collect all the errors so the criticism was complete
He should have given the criticism early, before his frustration built up
He should have praised her work to balance out the criticism

questions.q: Midway through a tough performance review, Tom feels his face burning and an urge to argue back. Following Levinson's advice for people receiving criticism, what should he do?
questions.explain: Levinson tells receivers to watch for defensiveness and, if it gets too upsetting, to ask to resume later after cooling down, so the criticism can be used as information.
options: Defend each point immediately so the criticism does not go on record
Ask to resume the meeting later, after he has absorbed the message and cooled down
Agree with everything quickly to end the meeting sooner
Insist that the criticism be sent to him in writing instead

questions.q: Dreading an awkward talk, a manager sends a team member a short email listing his complaints about her project. Which of Levinson's rules for the critique does this most clearly break?
questions.explain: Be present means giving critiques face to face and in private; doing it at a distance, as by memo, is too impersonal and denies the person a chance to respond.
options: Be present
Be specific
Offer a solution
Be sensitive

questions.q: Which of these comments to a colleague who gave a weak sales pitch follow the art of the critique as Goleman and Levinson describe it?
questions.explain: The good comments name a specific incident, say what went well or badly and point to a fix. The others attack character, stay vague, or give no way forward.
options: Your opening slide on pricing confused the client; leading with their problem might work better
Honestly, you just don't have a head for sales
Your demo of the product was clear; the pricing section lost them, so let's rework it together
Something about the pitch was off, but I can't say what
That was a disaster; we'll talk about it some other time

questions.q: Lena wants to praise a junior colleague's work in a way that helps him grow. Based on Levinson's advice, what should she do?
questions.explain: Levinson says specificity matters as much for praise as for criticism, since vague praise has little effect, and that praise, like critique, works best face to face.
options: Send a brief Great job! note to the whole team
Wait until his annual review so the praise carries more weight
Tell him in person exactly which part of his work was strong and why
Praise him in general terms so he does not become complacent

questions.q: Using Goleman's example, explain why the vice president's sarcastic remark and the artful alternative he could have given have opposite effects on the engineer.
questions.a: The sarcastic remark was a contemptuous dismissal that gave no specifics and no way forward, so it left the engineer humiliated, helpless and thinking of quitting. The artful version would have named the real difficulty, that the plan would take too long and escalate costs, and asked him to rework the specifications. Instead of creating helplessness, anger and rebellion, it holds out the hope of doing better and suggests the beginning of a plan.

questions.q: Why does Goleman conclude his discussion of criticism with the phrase As with marriage, so with work?
questions.a: The same emotional dynamics operate in both settings: criticism voiced as personal attack provokes defensiveness, stonewalling and feelings of being unfairly treated, ending in divorce or its business equivalent, quitting or firing. And the remedies match too: Levinson's advice to be specific mirrors the XYZ complaint, and his counsel to receivers echoes advice to couples on handling complaints without permanent damage.

questions.q: A manager plans to tell a designer, This is sloppy work. Using Levinson's rules, describe how she should give the criticism instead and why.
questions.a: She should be specific, naming the particular part of the design that falls short, what was done well and what was done poorly, and offer a solution or a way to fix it. She should say it face to face and in private, and be sensitive to how it will land. That keeps the focus on what the designer did and can do, not on character, so he stays receptive rather than defensive.

questions.q: Put the events of Goleman's Denny's account in order.
items: Waitresses ignore a group of black customers
Sylvia Skeeter confronts them and complains to the manager
The manager shrugs it off and Skeeter quits
Hundreds come forward to testify to a pattern of prejudice
A $54 million class-action settlement is reached
Every employee must attend sessions on a multiracial clientele
questions.explain: The single incident leads to wider testimony, the class-action settlement, and finally company-wide training on the advantages of a multiracial clientele.

questions.q: Which of these were among the plaintiffs in the class-action suit against Denny's that Goleman describes?
questions.explain: The suit included the Secret Service agents on their way to provide security for President Clinton and the girl in a wheelchair in Tampa. The other cases are not in Goleman's account.
options: Seven African-American Secret Service agents kept waiting for breakfast
A black girl with paralyzed legs who waited two hours for her food after a prom
A group of black soldiers refused service at a base restaurant
A black city council member asked to leave a branch

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman give as pragmatic reasons, beyond human decency, for companies to train employees to act without prejudice?
questions.explain: Goleman's three reasons are the shifting face of the workforce and customers, the needs of international companies, and the creative fruit of diversity. He says training does not eliminate deep prejudice.
options: White males are becoming a minority in the workforce
International companies need people who can turn appreciation of diverse cultures into competitive advantage
Diversity can heighten collective creativity and entrepreneurial energy
Diversity training reliably eliminates deep-seated prejudice
Diverse workforces need fewer managers

questions.q: True or false: Goleman cites a survey of several hundred American companies finding that more than three quarters of new employees were nonwhite.
questions.explain: That survey illustrates the shifting face of the workforce, a shift largely mirrored in the changing pool of customers.

questions.q: Psychiatrist Vamik Volkan grew up in a Turkish family on the island of ____, then bitterly contested between Turks and Greeks.
questions.explain: Volkan's childhood memories of rumors about Greek neighbors show how hostile biases are passed down to each new generation.

questions.q: Goleman calls prejudices a kind of emotional ____ that occurs early in life, which makes them hard to eradicate entirely.
questions.explain: Because prejudice is emotional learning laid down early, it persists even in adults who believe it is wrong; for the same reason, relearning is possible but slow.

questions.q: What does social psychologist Thomas Pettigrew mean when he says the emotions of prejudice are formed in childhood while the beliefs used to justify it come later?
questions.a: Prejudice starts as feeling learned in the family, and the intellectual justifications are added afterward. Later in life it is far easier to change one's beliefs than one's deep feelings. So Southerners who no longer believe in prejudice against blacks may still feel squeamish shaking hands with a black person, because the feelings are left over from childhood learning.

questions.q: Maya believes engineers are socially awkward. When she meets a charming, outgoing engineer, she decides he must be the rare exception, and later recalls mainly the awkward ones. What does Goleman's chapter on work say explains this?
questions.explain: This is the neutral mental dynamic Goleman describes that makes stereotypes of all kinds self-confirming, as with the warm Englishman explained away as unusual.
options: Stereotypes are self-confirming: people recall fitting cases and discount those that challenge them
Prejudice is formed by beliefs first and feelings later
Group IQ falls when members do not share their talents
Covert bias appears only in hiring decisions

questions.q: Which of these are examples Goleman gives of covert bias by people who disavow racist attitudes?
questions.explain: Covert bias shows up in ambiguous situations with a rationale other than prejudice, as in hiring and coaching. The Denny's incidents were open discrimination.
options: A white senior manager rejecting a black applicant as not quite right for the job while hiring a similar white one
Giving a briefing and helpful tips to a white salesman but neglecting to do so for a black or Hispanic salesman
Waitresses openly ignoring black customers while glaring at them
Locking a restaurant's doors when black customers approach

questions.q: Sort these examples from Goleman's chapter on work into open discrimination versus covert bias.

items.t: Demanding advance payment from black customers only
Denying black customers the free birthday meal
Locking the doors and claiming to be closed
Rejecting a black applicant whose background is said to be not quite right
Coaching a white salesman but not a Hispanic one before a call
Acting with bias in ambiguous situations while denying any bigotry

questions.explain: The Denny's policies were blatant acts against black customers; covert bias is practiced by people who say they feel no bigotry and give some other rationale.

questions.q: Which of these discriminatory practices does Goleman say some Denny's managers suggested?
questions.explain: Goleman lists advance payment, denial of free birthday meals, and locking the doors. Higher prices and separate seating are not in his account.
options: Demanding payment for meals in advance from black customers only
Denying black customers the widely advertised free birthday meals
Locking the doors and claiming to be closed when black customers were coming
Charging black customers higher menu prices
Seating black customers in a separate section

questions.q: Goleman argues that turning a blind eye to acts of bias lets discrimination thrive: to do nothing, in this context, is an act of ____ in itself.
questions.explain: Inaction is not neutral: it lets the virus of prejudice spread unopposed.

questions.q: What does Goleman say is more to the point than diversity training courses, or perhaps essential to their working at all?
questions.explain: Biases may not budge, but acts of prejudice can be quashed if the climate is changed through an active stance against discrimination from top management down.
options: Hiring only managers who have no personal prejudices
Requiring every employee to repeat the training each year
Keeping employees of different groups in separate teams
Decisively changing a group's norms by actively opposing any act of discrimination, from the top down

questions.q: What did one study find happened when people in a group heard someone make ethnic slurs?
questions.explain: Hearing slurs led others to make them too, which is why naming bias or objecting on the spot matters; saying nothing serves to condone it.
options: Others in the group usually objected on the spot
It led others in the group to do the same
It had no measurable effect on the others
The others became more tolerant out of sympathy

questions.q: In a team meeting, a coworker makes an offensive joke about an ethnic group and a few people laugh. According to Goleman, what is the most effective response?
questions.explain: Naming bias or objecting on the spot sets a climate that discourages it, while silence condones it. The objection works best when given like an artful critique, so it is heard without defensiveness.
options: Say nothing at the time to avoid embarrassing the coworker
Object to it on the spot, framed with the finesse of an effective criticism
Report it anonymously months later in an annual survey
Respond with an equally cutting joke about the coworker

questions.q: True or false: Suppose a department head overhears a slur in the break room and lets it pass without comment. By Goleman's account, this sends staff the tacit message that such acts are okay.
questions.explain: Those in authority play a pivotal role: their failure to condemn bias sends the tacit message that it is acceptable, while a reprimand shows bias has real consequences.

questions.q: Goleman names ____, a stance that encourages empathy and tolerance, as an active ingredient in diversity courses.
questions.explain: When people understand the pain of those who feel discriminated against, they are more likely to speak out against it.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says that simply putting people of different groups together reliably lowers intolerance.
questions.explain: He says it does little or nothing, pointing to school desegregation cases in which intergroup hostility rose rather than fell.

questions.q: Sort these features into Goleman's inept diversity courses versus the more effective ones.

items.t: Promises too much and raises false expectations
Creates an atmosphere of confrontation
Relies on a single day, video or weekend
Sets an explicit, organization-wide rule that bias is out-of-bounds
Encourages silent bystanders to voice objections
Uses perspective-taking to build empathy

questions.explain: Inept courses can heighten tensions between groups; effective ones set a clear ground rule, empower bystanders and encourage perspective-taking.

questions.q: What lesson does Goleman draw from school desegregation about how stereotypes can be broken down?
questions.a: Simply putting groups together does little: when students fail to mix socially and form hostile cliques, negative stereotypes intensify. But when they work together as equals toward a common goal, as on sports teams or in bands, their stereotypes break down. The same can happen naturally at work when people of different backgrounds work together as peers over the years, which is why sustained camaraderie matters more than a one-time workshop.

questions.q: Sort these into what Goleman sees as realistic versus unrealistic goals for corporate diversity programs.

items.t: Changing a group's norms for showing prejudice
Making it known that bigotry will not be tolerated
Encouraging bystanders to voice objections
Uprooting deeply held prejudices in one workshop
Quickly erasing long-held stereotypes
Lowering intolerance just by mixing groups

questions.explain: Goleman says it is more practical to suppress the expression of bias than to eliminate the attitude, since stereotypes change very slowly, if at all.

questions.q: After a merger, two departments with different backgrounds eye each other with suspicion. Based on Goleman's chapter on work, which step would most likely break down their stereotypes over time?
questions.explain: Sustained camaraderie and daily effort toward a common goal by peers is what Goleman says can relearn prejudice; one-time workshops and mere proximity do little.
options: Holding one intensive diversity workshop for both departments
Seating both departments together in one open-plan office
Asking each department to list its complaints about the other
Forming mixed teams that work as equals on shared goals over months and years

questions.q: Match each person in Goleman's discussion of diversity to the point associated with them.
pairs: Childhood rumors keep ethnic hatreds alive across generations
Feelings of prejudice are harder to change than beliefs
Management turned a blind eye to staff discrimination
Slights or insults are not tolerated in any way
Quit after her manager shrugged off ignored black customers
questions.explain: Volkan and Pettigrew explain the roots of prejudice; Relman, the IBM executive and Skeeter illustrate tolerated versus confronted acts of bias.

questions.q: Match each problem in Goleman's discussion of workplace prejudice to the remedy he points to.
pairs: Managers turning a blind eye to discrimination
An active stance against bias from the top down
An explicit ground rule that encourages them to object
An offensive joke in a meeting
Naming it as bias on the spot
Sustained camaraderie toward a common goal over time
questions.explain: Each remedy targets what can change: norms and actions now, and deep feelings slowly through relearning among peers.

questions.q: Why does Goleman argue that companies should aim at zero tolerance for acts of bias rather than trying to eliminate prejudiced attitudes?
questions.a: Prejudices are emotional learning formed early in life, so stereotypes change very slowly, if at all, and a one-time course will not uproot them. What can be changed is what people do about their biases. By decisively changing group norms, with leaders actively opposing even low-key acts of discrimination, a company can quash acts of prejudice even when biases do not budge.

questions.q: Why are prejudices so hard to eradicate, even in adults who believe they are wrong?
questions.a: Prejudices are emotional learning laid down early in life, while the beliefs that justify them come later; it is far easier to change beliefs than deep feelings. Stereotypes are also self-confirming, since people remember cases that fit and discount those that do not. So people may sincerely disavow racism yet still act with covert bias in ambiguous situations.

questions.q: What greater opportunity than battling prejudice does Goleman say a diverse workforce offers?
questions.a: Stopping at fighting prejudice misses the creative and entrepreneurial possibilities of diversity. A working group of varied strengths and perspectives, if it can operate in harmony, is likely to reach better, more creative and more effective solutions than the same people working in isolation. This leads into his discussion of group IQ, where harmony is the key.

questions.q: A store manager says, I can't change what my staff privately believe about other groups, so there is nothing I can do about bias. How would Goleman answer?
questions.a: He would agree that long-held biases cannot easily be weeded out, but say that what people do about them can be changed. The manager should set an explicit rule that bias is out-of-bounds, object to even low-key acts on the spot, and follow through with reprimands, because silence from those in authority condones bias. Over time, staff working together as equals toward common goals may also relearn their prejudices.

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: Peter Drucker coined the term ____ workers for people whose productivity is marked by adding value to information.
questions.explain: Drucker's knowledge workers, such as market analysts, writers or programmers, have specialized expertise and depend on coordination within a team.

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: True or false: Goleman expected that by the end of the century a third of the American workforce would be knowledge workers.
questions.explain: He gives that projection to show how central coordinated, team-based knowledge work is becoming.

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: Goleman writes that if the organizational chart is the skeleton of an organization, its human touch points are its central ____ system.
questions.explain: Meetings, e-mail, teleconferences, work teams and informal networks are the living connections through which work is actually shared.

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: How does Goleman define a group's group IQ?
questions.explain: Group IQ is the sum of everyone's talents and skills, and how well the group performs depends on how high it is. Its key ingredient is not average academic IQ.
options: The sum total of the talents and skills of all those involved
The average academic IQ of the group's members
The IQ of the group's most talented member
The group's score on a joint intelligence test

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: Goleman concludes that the key to a high group IQ is social ____.
questions.explain: Social harmony, all else being equal, makes one group talented and productive and another with equal members do poorly.

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: In Robert Sternberg and Wendy Williams's study of group intelligence, what challenge were the groups given?
questions.explain: The groups devised an ad campaign for a fictitious sweetener. The shampoo ad belongs to the Rensselaer criticism experiment.
options: Creating an ad for a new shampoo
Designing electronic switches for telephone systems
Creating an advertising campaign for a fictitious sugar substitute
Planning a training course for airline pilots

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: Which of these did Sternberg and Williams find dragged down a group's performance on their creative task?
questions.explain: Over-eager members lacked the social sense of what is apt in give-and-take, and non-participants were dead weight. A talented member helped, at least in harmonious groups.
options: Members who were too eager, controlling or domineering
Dead weight: members who did not participate
Having one particularly talented member
Members bringing different kinds of talent

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: In Sternberg and Williams's study, how did having a particularly talented member affect groups?
questions.explain: Harmony lets a group take full advantage of its most talented members; emotional and social static from fear, anger or rivalry keeps people from offering their best.
options: It helped all groups equally, whatever their level of friction
It hurt harmonious groups by making others less involved
It made no difference compared with the group's average ability
It helped harmonious groups, while groups with friction were far less able to capitalize on it

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: A manager can staff a project with either five brilliant rivals who resent one another or five solid performers who work well together. On Goleman's account of group IQ, which team is likely to produce better work, all else being equal?
questions.explain: The key to a high group IQ is social harmony; groups with emotional static from rivalries or resentments cannot draw on their members' full abilities.
options: The brilliant rivals, because group IQ is the average of members' IQ
The brilliant rivals, because competition drives creativity
The harmonious team, because friction keeps a group from using its members' talent
Neither, because group performance depends only on its leader

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: In the study of star performers at Bell Labs, what distinguished the stars from average engineers?
questions.explain: All the engineers were at the top on academic IQ tests; what set the stars apart was emotional IQ, not academic talent.
options: Their much higher scores on academic IQ tests
Their emotional IQ, including self-motivation and working informal networks into ad hoc teams
Their more advanced degrees from top universities
Their preference for working alone on hard problems

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: Put in order the steps of Kelley and Caplan's study of Bell Labs star engineers.
items: Managers and peers nominate the top 10 to 15 percent as stars
Stars are compared with others on cognitive and social measures
Few meaningful differences in innate ability turn up
Detailed interviews reveal different work strategies
Rapport with a network of key people emerges as crucial
questions.explain: Nomination came first, then a comparison that showed surprisingly little difference, then interviews that exposed the stars' interpersonal strategies.

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: In Kelley and Caplan's Bell Labs study, why did star performers rarely get stuck the way the middle performer did with his technical problem?
questions.explain: The middle performer called gurus and waited while calls went unreturned. Stars do the work of building networks in advance, so they almost always get a faster answer.
options: They built reliable networks before they needed them, so their calls got fast answers
They knew enough to solve technical problems without help
They had official authority to demand answers from experts
They avoided taking on problems outside their specialty

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: Ana, newly hired, spends her first months having coffee with people in IT, legal and finance, though no project yet needs them. When a crisis hits, she pulls them into a quick team and solves it in a day. Which finding from Goleman's chapter on work does this illustrate?
questions.explain: Like the Bell Labs stars, Ana cultivated relationships in advance and could turn her informal network into an instant ad hoc team.
options: Group IQ is the average IQ of a team's members
Formal organization charts handle unexpected problems best
Bell Labs stars build reliable networks before they need them
Expertise networks and trust networks are the same thing

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: Match each of the three varieties of informal network Goleman describes to what it tracks.
pairs: Which people are turned to for advice
Who is trusted with secrets, doubts and vulnerabilities
questions.explain: Goleman distinguishes the three; stars often have thick connections in all of them.

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: True or false: Goleman reports that being a main node in an expertise network strongly predicts being someone colleagues trust with their secrets and doubts.
questions.explain: There is virtually no relationship between being an expert and being trusted with secrets, doubts and vulnerabilities.

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: Dev, the most technically brilliant engineer in his group, is promoted to manager. He checks every line his team writes and people stop telling him about problems. On Goleman's account, what is Dev lacking?
questions.explain: Like the micromanager Goleman describes, Dev ranks high on expertise but low on trust, which undermines his ability to manage and cuts him out of informal networks.
options: A place in the trust network, which expertise alone does not bring
Expertise, since his team no longer asks him for advice
A higher academic IQ than his team members
A position in the formal organizational chart

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: Match each finding from Sternberg and Williams's study of group intelligence to its effect.
pairs: Members too eager to take part
Were too controlling and lowered the group's performance
Acted as dead weight on the group
A talented member in a harmonious group
A talented member in a group with friction
Was far less able to help the group
questions.explain: The study showed that harmony, not raw ability, decides how much of its members' talent a group can use.

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: Sort these into what Goleman says about the formal organization versus informal networks.

items.t: Set up to handle easily anticipated problems
Mapped on the organizational chart, the skeleton
Kick in when unexpected problems arise
Form every time colleagues communicate
Skip entire functions to get things done

questions.explain: The formal organization handles what can be foreseen; informal networks, highly adaptive, take over when the unexpected happens.

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: Sort the forms of organizational savvy shown by Bell Labs stars into social skills versus self-management and initiative.

items.t: Building consensus
Seeing things from customers' or teammates' perspective
Persuasiveness
Promoting cooperation while avoiding conflicts
Taking on responsibilities beyond the stated job
Regulating their time and work commitments well

questions.explain: Goleman lists coordination, consensus, perspective-taking, persuasion and cooperation as social skills, and separately notes the stars' initiative and self-management; all are aspects of emotional intelligence.

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: Match each researcher in Goleman's discussion of organization savvy to their contribution.
pairs: Introduced the idea of group intelligence
Studied star performers at Bell Labs
questions.explain: Drucker frames the shift to team-based knowledge work, Sternberg and Williams show that harmony drives group IQ, and Kelley and Caplan show that networking makes stars.

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: Put the steps of Goleman's argument in his section on organization savvy and group IQ in order.
items: Knowledge work makes teams the unit of work
Group IQ depends above all on social harmony
Stars work informal networks into ad hoc teams
Corporations should boost their collective emotional intelligence
questions.explain: He moves from the rise of team-based knowledge work, to harmony as the key to group IQ, to the Bell Labs stars' networking, to his closing call for collective emotional intelligence.

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: Why does Goleman think emotional intelligence will become increasingly valued as more people become knowledge workers?
questions.a: Knowledge workers' expertise is highly specialized, so their productivity depends on their efforts being coordinated as part of a team; as Drucker says, teams become the work unit rather than the individual. Emotional intelligence is the set of skills that help people harmonize. So as knowledge work spreads, the ability to work together smoothly becomes a central workplace asset.

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: What is group IQ, and what did Sternberg and Williams find is the single most important factor in raising it?
questions.a: Group IQ is the sum total of the talents and skills of everyone in a group, and how well the group does its task depends on how high it is. Sternberg and Williams found the key was not average academic IQ but the group's ability to create internal harmony. Harmony lets a group use the full talent of its members, while emotional static from fear, anger, rivalry or resentment keeps people from offering their best.

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: According to Goleman, why do informal networks matter so much for on-the-job success?
questions.a: Many tasks depend on calling on a loose network of fellow workers, which in effect lets a person form ad hoc teams tailored to each problem. The informal organization is especially critical for unexpected problems the formal one is not set up to handle. Bell Labs stars succeeded because they built rapport with key people before they needed them, and the strongest have thick connections in communications, expertise and trust networks alike.

questions.section: Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
questions.q: How does Goleman use the Bell Labs findings to close his chapter on work, and what does he urge corporations to do?
questions.a: He sees Bell Labs as a sign of the future of all corporate life, where emotional intelligence matters ever more in teamwork, cooperation and learning to work together. As knowledge-based services and intellectual capital become central, improving how people work together is a major way to leverage that capital and gain a competitive edge. So, to thrive if not survive, corporations should boost their collective emotional intelligence.

questions.q: In which Part of Emotional Intelligence does the chapter Managing with Heart appear?
questions.explain: Managing with Heart belongs to Part Three, which looks at the difference emotional intelligence makes in relationships, work and health.
options: Part Two, The Nature of Emotional Intelligence
Part Four, Windows of Opportunity
Part Five, Emotional Literacy
Part Three, Emotional Intelligence Applied

questions.q: Put the chapters of Part Three, Emotional Intelligence Applied, in the book's order.
items: Intimate Enemies
Managing with Heart
Mind and Medicine
questions.explain: Part Three moves from marriage, to the workplace, to physical health, matching the Prologue's road-map of relationships, work and health.

questions.q: In the Prologue's road-map of Part Three, which theme corresponds to the chapter Managing with Heart?
questions.explain: The Prologue says Part Three covers relationships, work and health; Managing with Heart is the work chapter. Childhood lessons belong to Part Four.
options: How emotional abilities can preserve or corrode our most prized relationships
How market forces reshaping work life put a premium on emotional intelligence for on-the-job success
How toxic emotions put physical health at as much risk as chain-smoking
How childhood lessons at home and school shape the emotional circuits

questions.q: True or false: In Managing with Heart, Goleman explicitly links workplace stress back to his earlier review, in Chapter 6, of how agitation disrupts thinking.
questions.explain: He says all the effects of agitation on thinking reviewed in Chapter 6 operate at work too, and quotes a consultant: “Stress makes people stupid.”

questions.q: Put in order the three applications of emotional intelligence that Goleman announces and then treats in Managing with Heart.
items: Airing grievances as helpful critiques
Creating an atmosphere where diversity is valued
Networking effectively
questions.explain: He announces critique, diversity and networking in that order, and his three sections follow it: Criticism Is Job One, Dealing with Diversity, and Organization Savvy and the Group IQ.

questions.q: Match each part of Goleman's chapter Managing with Heart to the job it does in the chapter.
pairs: The opening on McBroom and Zuboff
Argues that emotional skill now pays at work
Shows how to air grievances as helpful critiques
Shows how to make diversity valued, not a source of friction
Organization Savvy and the Group IQ
Shows how harmony and networking raise performance
questions.explain: The opening makes the general case; each section then tracks one application of emotional intelligence.

questions.q: What does the title Managing with Heart signal about Goleman's argument in the chapter?
questions.explain: The title answers the 1970s executives who thought work needed heads but not hearts; Goleman argues a new competitive reality puts emotional intelligence at a premium.
options: That managers should let their feelings decide every business choice
That the old view of work as needing heads but not hearts is outmoded
That kindness matters more at work than competence
That emotional intelligence matters at home but not at work

questions.q: Which of these ideas from earlier chapters does Goleman reuse in Managing with Heart?
questions.explain: He leans on the marriage chapter for stonewalling, flooding and the XYZ complaint, and on Chapter 6 for the optimistic belief about setbacks. The marshmallow test and temperament are not used here.
options: Gottman's findings on stonewalling and flooding in married couples
The XYZ statement of a grievance
The belief behind optimism that setbacks come from changeable circumstances
The marshmallow test of delayed gratification in four-year-olds
The idea that temperament is set by inborn shyness

questions.q: Why does Goleman's chapter on work lean so heavily on the preceding chapter on marriage?
questions.a: He argues that the emotional dynamics of marriage operate in the workplace in similar forms. Criticism voiced as personal attack triggers defensiveness, stonewalling and flooding, ending in the business equivalent of divorce, quitting or firing, and the remedies, such as a specific XYZ-style complaint and treating criticism as information, are the same. Placing work right after marriage lets him show the same emotional skills at stake in a new arena: as with marriage, so with work.

questions.q: How does Managing with Heart support the book's larger claim that emotional intelligence can matter more than IQ?
questions.a: At Bell Labs, engineers who were all at the top on academic IQ tests differed in output because of emotional IQ: stars motivated themselves and worked informal networks into ad hoc teams, while academic talent did not predict productivity. Likewise, Sternberg and Williams found group IQ depends on harmony, not average academic IQ. The chapter thus applies the book's thesis to work, as the Prologue promised for Part Three.

questions.q: Why, according to Goleman, are we so emotionally fragile when we are ill?
options: Pain directly damages the brain circuits that keep our moods steady
Doctors usually deliver frightening news in a deliberately blunt way
Sickness bursts the illusion of invulnerability on which our mental well-being partly rests
Illness lowers the rational intelligence we normally use to calm ourselves
questions.explain: Goleman says our well-being rests partly on feeling invulnerable; serious illness attacks the premise that our private world is safe, so we suddenly feel weak and helpless.

questions.q: Goleman says that our mental well-being is based in part on the illusion of ____, an illusion that serious sickness bursts.
questions.explain: Illness attacks the premise that our private world is safe and secure, which is why fear is only a thought away in the land of the sick.

questions.q: Goleman distinguishes disease, the medical disorder, from ____, the patient's experience of disease, which modern medicine has tended to overlook.
questions.explain: Medicine has defined its mission as curing disease while overlooking illness, the patient's lived and emotional experience of being sick.

questions.q: By going along with medicine's focus on disease, patients, Goleman says, join a quiet ____ to ignore how they are reacting emotionally to their medical problems.
questions.explain: Patients collude with the medical model by ignoring or dismissing their own emotional reactions as irrelevant to the course of the illness.

questions.q: Beyond the humanitarian argument, what scientific case does Goleman make for treating patients' emotions as part of medicine?
options: Treating emotional state reliably cures serious disease without the need for medication
Patients who are emotionally supported are much less likely to sue their doctors
Across many cases, treating emotional state adds an average margin of benefit in prevention and treatment
Treating emotional state lets hospitals replace costly drugs with cheaper therapy
questions.explain: He claims a margin of medical effectiveness, not a cure: not in every case, but on average across hundreds of cases there is enough benefit to make emotional intervention standard.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman argues that people can cure themselves of even the most serious disease by making themselves happy or thinking positive thoughts.
questions.explain: He calls this attitude-will-cure-all idea an equally unproductive ideology that breeds confusion and can make the sick feel guilty; the truth, he says, lies between the extremes.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say have resulted from the attitude-will-cure-all rhetoric about illness?
