options: Widespread confusion about how far illness can be affected by the mind
Making people feel guilty for having a disease, as if it were a moral lapse
Doctors refusing to prescribe drugs to patients who seem cheerful
A medical model that denies the mind can influence the body at all
questions.explain: Goleman blames the cure-all rhetoric for confusion and for making the sick feel guilty. Denying any mind-body influence is the opposite error, belonging to the traditional medical model.

questions.q: What two opposing ideologies about mind and illness does Goleman set his chapter between, and where does he place the truth?
questions.a: On one side is a medical model that dismisses entirely the idea that mind influences body in any consequential way, so patients' emotions are treated as irrelevant. On the other is the attitude-will-cure-all notion that positive thinking can cure even pernicious disease, or that people are to blame for falling ill. Goleman says “The truth lies somewhere between these extremes,” and aims to sort the scientific data to show how far emotions really matter for health.

questions.q: A patient just told she needs a scan to rule out a tumor keeps asking the receptionist to repeat where the scan room is. Which idea from Goleman's opening best explains this?
options: In the land of the sick, fear can swamp rational processing of even simple information
Patients who ask many questions are usually trying to delay unpleasant tests
Receptionists rarely give directions clearly enough for anyone to follow
Frequent repetition is a normal sign of memory loss in older patients
questions.explain: Goleman describes needing a simple instruction repeated three or four times after hearing cytology; in illness emotions reign and fear is a thought away, crowding out clear thinking.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it belongs to disease, in Goleman's sense, or to illness.
groups: Illness: the patient's experience of disease

items.t: A tumor that is growing in the bladder
A bacterial infection of the kidney
A narrowed coronary artery
Panic on hearing the word cancer
Feeling helpless and alone in a hospital bed
Worry about whether the treatment will work

questions.explain: Disease is the biological disorder that medicine has defined its mission around; illness is the patient's emotional experience of it, which Goleman says medicine tends to overlook.

questions.q: Match each view of mind and illness in Goleman's introduction to its consequence.
pairs: Patients' emotional reactions are treated as irrelevant to the illness
Patients may feel guilty, as if illness showed moral lapse
The truth lies between the extremes, sorted through scientific data
questions.explain: Goleman sets his chapter between a medicine that ignores the mind and a rhetoric that overstates it.

questions.section: The Body's Mind: How Emotions Matter for Health
questions.q: Put the stages of Robert Ader's rat experiment in order.
items: Rats were given a T-cell-suppressing drug along with saccharin-flavored water
Later the rats were given the flavored water alone, without the drug
Their T-cell counts still fell in response to the flavored water
Some of the rats got sick and died
questions.explain: The immune system had learned to suppress T cells in response to the taste of saccharin alone, a learned response once thought impossible outside the brain.

questions.section: The Body's Mind: How Emotions Matter for Health
questions.q: Why was Robert Ader's 1974 finding about rats and saccharin such a shock to medicine?
questions.a: The prevailing wisdom was that only the brain and central nervous system could respond to experience by changing how they behaved, and that the brain and immune system were separate entities that could not influence each other. There was thought to be no pathway linking the brain centers monitoring taste with the bone marrow that makes T cells. Ader's rats showed the immune system learning, which opened the study of the many ways the nervous and immune systems communicate.

questions.section: The Body's Mind: How Emotions Matter for Health
questions.q: Neuroscientist Francisco Varela calls the immune system the body's ____, because it defines the body's own sense of self.
questions.explain: Varela's phrase is the body's brain: immune cells decide what belongs within the body and what does not, attacking what they fail to recognize.

questions.section: The Body's Mind: How Emotions Matter for Health
questions.q: The leading-edge field that studies the links between the immune system and the central nervous system is called ____, or PNI.
questions.explain: Psychoneuroimmunology grew out of Ader's discovery; its very name joins mind, the neuroendocrine system and the immune system.

questions.section: The Body's Mind: How Emotions Matter for Health
questions.q: Match each part of the name psychoneuroimmunology to what it stands for.
pairs: The neuroendocrine system, covering nerves and hormones
questions.explain: Goleman explains that the field's name itself acknowledges the links among mind, the neuroendocrine system and the immune system.

questions.section: The Body's Mind: How Emotions Matter for Health
questions.q: In David Felten's animal experiments, what happened when nerves were removed from the lymph nodes and spleen before a viral challenge?
options: Immune response to the virus became dangerously excessive
The animals produced extra stress hormones instead
Immune response to the virus dropped hugely
Immune response was unchanged, showing the nerves were idle
questions.explain: Without those nerve endings the immune system did not respond properly, so Felten concluded the nervous system is essential for proper immune function.

questions.section: The Body's Mind: How Emotions Matter for Health
questions.q: What did David Felten conclude from removing nerves from the lymph nodes and spleen of animals, and why does it matter for Goleman's argument?
questions.a: With those nerves removed, the animals' immune response to a virus dropped hugely, so Felten concluded that the immune system cannot respond properly without its nerve connections. The nervous system therefore not only connects to the immune system but is essential for its proper function. This gives a direct physical pathway through which emotions, which strongly affect the autonomic nervous system, can influence immunity.

questions.section: The Body's Mind: How Emotions Matter for Health
questions.q: Which of these does Goleman list among the hormones released during stress arousal that hamper immune cells?
options: Cortisol
Prolactin
Beta-endorphin
Insulin
Thyroxine
questions.explain: Goleman lists the catecholamines, cortisol, prolactin and the natural opiates beta-endorphin and enkephalin. Insulin is mentioned only as something the autonomic nervous system regulates.

questions.section: The Body's Mind: How Emotions Matter for Health
questions.q: Why, presumably, does stress suppress immune resistance, according to Goleman?
options: Because stress hormones directly destroy immune cells in the bone marrow
To prevent the immune system from attacking the body during an injury
Because the brain shuts off the spleen whenever the heart rate rises
To conserve energy for the more immediate emergency that matters most for survival
questions.explain: Goleman suggests the suppression is a conservation of energy that prioritizes the immediate emergency; it is usually temporary, but constant and intense stress can make it long-lasting.

questions.section: The Body's Mind: How Emotions Matter for Health
questions.q: Sort each detail by whether it comes from Robert Ader's work or David Felten's work.

items.t: Saccharin-flavored water
T-cell counts falling without the drug
The immune system shown to learn
Electron-microscope views of nerve endings
Nerves removed from lymph nodes and spleen
Autonomic nerves touching macrophages

questions.explain: Ader's 1974 rat study showed a learned immune response to flavored water; his colleague Felten then found the nerve-to-immune-cell contacts and showed they are needed for proper immune response.

questions.section: The Body's Mind: How Emotions Matter for Health
questions.q: A friend insists that feelings cannot possibly affect the immune system because nerves and immune cells are separate systems. Which finding from Goleman's chapter most directly answers this?
options: Cohen's finding that stressed people catch colds more often after exposure
Pennebaker's finding that writing about trauma reduces health-center visits
Felten's discovery that autonomic nerve endings directly contact and signal to immune cells
Spiegel's finding that support groups lengthen survival with breast cancer
questions.explain: The friend's claim is about anatomy, and Felten found the physical meeting point where nerves talk to immune cells. The other findings show health effects but not the pathway itself.

questions.section: The Body's Mind: How Emotions Matter for Health
questions.q: Through what two routes does Goleman say emotions can reach the immune system?
questions.a: One route is direct: David Felten found synapse-like contacts where autonomic nerve endings abut lymphocytes and macrophages, so nerves can signal immune cells and are essential to a proper immune response. The other is hormonal: stress releases catecholamines, cortisol, prolactin and natural opiates, which hamper immune cells, at least temporarily and possibly long-term if stress is constant and intense.

questions.section: The Body's Mind: How Emotions Matter for Health
questions.q: Robert Ader discovered that the immune system, like the brain, could ____.
questions.explain: Rats learned to suppress T cells in response to saccharin-flavored water alone, which overturned the belief that only the brain and central nervous system could learn from experience.

questions.section: The Body's Mind: How Emotions Matter for Health
questions.q: Put the steps of David Felten's investigation of nerves and immunity in order.
items: Noted that emotions strongly affect the autonomic nervous system
Detected contacts where autonomic nerve endings abut immune cells
Removed nerves from the lymph nodes and spleen of animals
Challenged the immune system with viruses and saw a huge drop in response
questions.explain: Felten moved from the nervous-system link to a physical contact point, then showed by removing the nerves that the contact is essential for immune response.

questions.section: The Body's Mind: How Emotions Matter for Health
questions.q: Put the effect of stress on immune resistance in order, from first to last.
items: Stress arousal releases hormones such as cortisol and epinephrine
The hormones surge through the body
Immune cells are hampered in their function
If stress is constant and intense, the suppression may become long-lasting
questions.explain: Goleman says immune resistance is suppressed while the hormones surge, presumably to prioritize the immediate emergency, and prolonged stress can make this lasting.

questions.section: The Body's Mind: How Emotions Matter for Health
questions.q: Match each researcher to the idea or finding Goleman credits to him.
pairs: Autonomic nerve endings talk directly to immune cells
The immune system is the body's brain, defining its sense of self
questions.explain: Ader showed learning in the immune system, Felten found a physical nerve link to it, and Varela described its role in defining self from non-self.

questions.section: The Body's Mind: How Emotions Matter for Health
questions.q: Match each term to its meaning in Goleman's account of the body's mind.
pairs: Immune cells misidentify and attack the body's own cells
Epinephrine and norepinephrine, released in stress
The field studying links among mind, nervous and hormone systems, and immunity
questions.explain: These terms come from Goleman's explanation of how the immune system recognizes self and how stress hormones and the nervous system influence it.

questions.section: The Body's Mind: How Emotions Matter for Health
questions.q: Sort each detail by whether it belongs to the nerve pathway or the hormone pathway linking emotions to immunity.

items.t: Synapse-like contacts between nerve terminals and immune cells
Neurotransmitters released onto lymphocytes and macrophages
Removing nerves from the spleen weakened response to a virus
Surges of cortisol during stress arousal
Epinephrine and norepinephrine hampering immune cells
Prolactin and natural opiates released in stress

questions.explain: Felten's work shows a direct nervous link to immune cells, while stress hormones act through the bloodstream to suppress immune function.

questions.q: Why, according to Goleman, do many physicians remain skeptical that emotions matter clinically?
options: It is not always clear that the immune changes caused by stress are large enough to make a medical difference
Most studies have found that stress has no measurable effect on immune cells
The studies linking emotion and health have been done only on animals
Emotional states cannot be measured reliably enough to include in research
questions.explain: Many studies show stress and negative emotion weaken immune cells, but the doubt is whether the size of those changes reaches clinical significance.

questions.q: Why, according to Goleman and the surgeon Camran Nezhat, do extremely frightened patients do worse in surgery?
questions.a: Panic and anxiety raise blood pressure, and veins distended by pressure bleed more profusely when cut. Excess bleeding is among the most troublesome surgical complications and can even lead to death. Nezhat adds that very scared patients also have more infections and complications and a harder time recovering, so it is much better if they are calm.

questions.q: The most compelling data on emotion and health, Goleman says, come from a mass analysis combining results from ____ smaller studies.
questions.explain: The meta-analysis pooled 101 studies covering several thousand men and women and confirmed that perturbing emotions are bad for health, to a degree.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman list as diseases whose risk was doubled in the 101-study analysis of distressing emotions?
options: Asthma
Arthritis
Peptic ulcers
Diabetes
Influenza
questions.explain: The analysis named asthma, arthritis, headaches, peptic ulcers and heart disease, each representing a broad category of disease. Diabetes and influenza were not on that list.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says the doubled disease risk from distressing emotions makes them as toxic a risk factor as smoking or high cholesterol are for heart disease.
questions.explain: He uses the comparison to show the size of the effect: distressing emotions are a major threat to health, on a par with these familiar risk factors.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says the 101-study analysis shows that everyone with chronic distressing feelings will fall prey to disease more easily.
questions.explain: He stresses it is a broad statistical link that by no means indicates everyone with such feelings will more easily fall ill.

questions.q: Which of these are the big three emotions whose medical effects Goleman examines in detail?
options: Anger
Anxiety
Depression
Shame
Jealousy
questions.explain: Goleman singles out anger, anxiety and depression as the big three, examining each in turn for its specific medical significance.

questions.q: In the Stanford anger-recall study, a drop in pumping efficiency of 7 percent or more is regarded by cardiologists as a sign of a myocardial ____, a dangerous drop in blood flow to the heart.
questions.explain: Some angry patients showed a drop of 7 percent or more, the range cardiologists treat as a sign of myocardial ischemia.

questions.q: What has replaced the failed theory that a hurried, high-pressure Type-A personality is at great risk of heart disease?
options: The finding that anxiety is the main risk in both sexes
The finding that relaxed people neglect their heart health
The finding that it is hostility that puts people at risk
The finding that perfectionism damages the coronary arteries
questions.explain: The Type-A idea did not hold up, but from it emerged a new finding: hostility is the dangerous ingredient.

questions.q: Goleman reports that the old idea that a hurried, high-pressure ____ personality is at great risk of heart disease has not held up.
questions.explain: The Type-A theory failed, but out of it came the finding that hostility specifically is what puts people at risk.

questions.q: True or false: In Redford Williams's study of physicians, being prone to anger was a stronger predictor of dying young than smoking, high blood pressure and high cholesterol.
questions.explain: Williams found hostility scores in medical school outpredicted these standard risk factors for early death.

questions.q: Put Peter Kaufman's explanation of how habitual anger can lead to coronary artery disease in order.
items: A young person gets angry again and again
Each episode raises heart rate and blood pressure
Turbulent blood flow causes microtears in the coronary vessel
Plaque develops at the microtears
Over decades, faster plaque buildup leads to coronary artery disease
questions.explain: Kaufman describes repeated stress on the heart from each angry episode, microtears from turbulent flow, and plaque building faster over some thirty years.

questions.q: How does Peter Kaufman explain the way a twenty-year-old who repeatedly gets angry might develop coronary artery disease?
questions.a: Each episode of anger adds stress to the heart by raising heart rate and blood pressure. Repeated over and over, the turbulence of blood flowing through the coronary artery can cause microtears in the vessel, where plaque develops. A habitually faster heart rate and higher blood pressure may, over thirty years, speed plaque buildup and so lead to coronary artery disease. Kaufman adds that it is not yet clear whether anger causes early disease, worsens existing disease, or both.

questions.q: Match each study of anger and the heart to its finding.
pairs: Most aggressive, hostile men had the most second heart attacks
Easily angered men were three times likelier to die of cardiac arrest
Harvard study of over 1,500 heart-attack patients
Anger more than doubled cardiac arrest risk for about two hours
High hostility in medical school meant seven times the risk of death by fifty
questions.explain: Each study points the same way: anger and hostility raise heart risk, and the effect is especially lethal in people who already have heart disease.

questions.q: In the Harvard study of heart-attack patients, being angry more than doubled the risk of cardiac arrest, and the heightened risk lasted for about ____ after the anger was aroused.
questions.explain: Patients described their emotional state in the hours before their attacks; the anger-linked risk lasted about two hours.

questions.q: What caveat do the Yale researchers add about anger and death from heart disease?
options: Anger only matters for people who already have high cholesterol
The link disappears once age and smoking are taken into account
Anger raises the risk only in women, not in men
Any intense negative emotion that regularly floods the body with stress hormones may raise the risk
questions.explain: They suggest the culprit may be intense negative emotionality of any kind, though overall the strongest links between emotion and heart disease are to anger.

questions.q: What paradox does Goleman describe about expressing or suppressing anger, and how does Redford Williams resolve it?
questions.a: Completely suppressing anger in the heat of the moment can magnify the body's agitation and may raise blood pressure, yet, as Chapter 5 showed, ventilating anger every time simply feeds it. Williams resolves this by concluding that whether anger is expressed matters less than whether it is chronic. An occasional display of hostility is not dangerous; the danger is hostility so constant that it defines an antagonistic personal style.

questions.q: True or false: Redford Williams concludes that whether anger is expressed or held in matters more for health than whether it is chronic.
questions.explain: Williams concludes the reverse: chronic hostility is what matters, and an occasional display of anger is not dangerous to health.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman describe as marks of the antagonistic personal style that makes hostility dangerous to health?
options: Repeated feelings of mistrust and cynicism
A propensity to snide comments and put-downs
Bouts of temper and rage
An occasional display of anger at a real wrong
Feeling briefly irritated when a plan falls through
questions.explain: The danger comes when hostility is so constant it defines a style of mistrust, cynicism, put-downs and rage; an occasional display of anger is not dangerous.

questions.q: Which of these elements of emotional intelligence does Goleman say Redford Williams's anger program teaches?
options: Mindfulness of anger as it begins to stir
The ability to regulate anger once it has begun
Empathy, seeing things from the other person's view
Venting anger fully whenever it is felt
Holding all feelings in until they pass
questions.explain: Like the Stanford program, it teaches awareness, regulation and empathy. Venting feeds anger and total suppression magnifies agitation, so neither is taught.

questions.q: Stuck in a traffic jam, Ravi starts fuming about the careless driver who must have caused it. What would Redford Williams's program teach him to do?
options: Search for a benign explanation and substitute a reasonable thought for the hostile one
Shout out his frustration in the car so the anger is released
Keep perfectly still and push all feeling out of his mind
Plan a complaint so the anger has a useful outlet later
questions.explain: The program has patients replace cynical thoughts with reasonable ones, as with looking for a benign reason when an elevator is delayed rather than blaming an imagined thoughtless person.

questions.q: A heart patient keeps noticing the same cynical thought about a coworker's motives coming back during the day. In Redford Williams's program, what should he do after jotting it down?
options: Confront the coworker at once to clear the air
Short-circuit the thought by saying or thinking Stop
Keep the thought to himself and ignore its return
Write a full account of every past grievance
questions.explain: Patients jot down cynical or hostile thoughts as they notice them, and if the thoughts persist they cut them off by saying or thinking Stop, then substitute reasonable thoughts.

questions.q: Redford Williams told Goleman that the antidote to hostility is to develop a more ____ heart.
questions.explain: Williams adds that motivation is all it takes, and people are ready to try once they see hostility can lead to an early grave.

questions.q: Following Redford Williams's view of anger and health, sort each pattern by its health risk.

items.t: Making snide put-downs of coworkers day after day
Assuming most people are out to cheat you
Flying into a rage at small frustrations every week
Getting angry once at an unfair bill, then letting it go
Voicing annoyance at a rude remark and moving on

questions.explain: Williams says an occasional display of hostility is not dangerous; the risk comes when mistrust, cynicism, put-downs and rage become a constant style.

questions.q: A friend with heart disease says he just bottles up his anger so it can't hurt his heart. Using Goleman's chapter, what would you tell him?
questions.a: Completely suppressing anger in the moment can actually magnify the body's agitation and may raise blood pressure, so bottling it up is not the safe choice. Venting every time is no answer either, since it feeds anger. What matters is whether hostility is chronic, and that habit can change: anger-control training that teaches noticing anger as it stirs, regulating it, and empathy cut second heart attacks by 44 percent in one Stanford group.

questions.q: Goleman says that in modern life anxiety is more often out of proportion and out of ____, arising in situations we must live with or that are conjured by the mind.
questions.explain: Out of proportion and out of place: the distress is triggered by things that are not real dangers we need to confront.

questions.q: Which of these effects of stress did Bruce McEwen note in his 1993 review of the stress-disease link?
options: Speeding the metastasis of cancer
Increasing vulnerability to viral infections
Worsening or triggering an asthma attack
Lowering cholesterol in the blood
Strengthening the memory for stressful events
questions.explain: McEwen listed compromised immunity that can speed metastasis, viral vulnerability, atherosclerosis, diabetes effects and asthma; he also noted damage to the hippocampus and so to memory, not strengthening.

questions.q: Bruce McEwen says evidence is mounting that the nervous system is subject to wear and ____ as a result of stressful experiences.
questions.explain: McEwen's phrase sums up how sustained stress gradually damages the nervous system itself.

questions.q: Why does Goleman say prospective studies give stronger evidence linking stress to illness than direct assays of immune strength?
options: They measure immune cells far more precisely than laboratory assays can
They test only people who are already ill, so effects are easier to see
They follow healthy people through rising distress, weakened immunity and then actual illness
They rely on doctors' judgments rather than patients' own reports
questions.explain: Immune assays show weakening but leave unclear whether it is clinically significant; prospective studies track the whole sequence from distress to the onset of illness.

questions.q: In Sheldon Cohen's study, people were exposed to a cold virus after their life stress was assessed. What did he find?
options: 27 percent of the least stressed caught cold, against 47 percent of the most stressed
Nearly everyone caught cold, whatever their stress level
47 percent of the least stressed caught cold, against 27 percent of the most stressed
Stress made no difference, but age strongly predicted colds
questions.explain: The more stress in people's lives, the more likely they were to catch cold: direct evidence that stress itself weakens the immune system.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says Sheldon Cohen's colds study is considered a landmark because it revealed something nobody had suspected.
questions.explain: It may confirm what everyone already suspected; it counts as a landmark because of its scientific rigor.

questions.q: In the study of married couples who logged daily hassles, why was the three-to-four-day gap between upsets and colds significant?
questions.a: Colds and upper-respiratory infections tended to appear three or four days after an especially intense batch of upsets such as marital fights. That lag is precisely the incubation time for many common cold viruses. This suggests that people exposed to a virus while they were most worried and upset were especially vulnerable to it, linking stress to infection.

questions.q: Which of these groups showed reactivation of the herpes virus under stress, according to Goleman?
options: Medical students during year-end exams
Recently separated women
People caring for a family member with Alzheimer's disease
Retirees in their first year of retirement
Parents of newborn babies
questions.explain: Herpes reactivation, tracked by antibody levels in the blood, was found in exam-stressed medical students, recently separated women and Alzheimer's caregivers.

questions.q: Goleman says jobs are high in strain when they combine high-pressure performance demands with little or no ____ over how to get the job done.
questions.explain: High demands plus little control is the predicament that gives bus drivers, for example, a high rate of hypertension.

questions.q: Using Goleman's definition of a job high in strain, sort these workers.

items.t: A bus driver held to a tight timetable in heavy traffic
An assembly-line worker under quota with no say over the pace
A call-center agent with strict targets who must follow a fixed script
A freelancer with heavy deadlines who decides how and when to work
A librarian with modest demands who plans her own day

questions.explain: Strain means high performance demands together with little or no control over the work; lacking either ingredient, a job falls outside Goleman's definition.

questions.q: Why are relaxation techniques used clinically for illnesses such as heart disease, arthritis, asthma and chronic pain?
options: They cure the underlying disease by strengthening the immune system
They replace the need for medication in most chronic illness
They make patients more willing to accept painful tests
They directly counter the physiological arousal of stress that worsens symptoms
questions.explain: To the degree symptoms are worsened by stress, helping patients relax and handle turbulent feelings can offer some reprieve.

questions.q: Dana notices that she comes down with a cold a few days after almost every week of fights at home. Which finding in Goleman's chapter best fits her pattern?
options: Heart patients' pumping efficiency fell when they recalled angry incidents
Bus drivers have high rates of hypertension because of job strain
Couples who logged daily hassles got colds three or four days after intense upsets
Optimistic bypass patients recovered faster from surgery
questions.explain: The married-couples study found colds followed intense batches of upsets by three or four days, the incubation time of many cold viruses.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says the evidence clearly shows that depression speeds the course of cancer.
questions.explain: He says the evidence that melancholy affects the course of cancer is as yet mixed, though depression seems to worsen many other conditions.

questions.q: In the study of patients with kidney failure on dialysis, how did depression lead to death, according to Goleman?
questions.a: Patients diagnosed with major depression were most likely to die within two years, and depression was a stronger predictor of death than any medical sign. Here the route was not biological but attitudinal: depressed patients were much worse at complying with their medical regimens, for example cheating on their diets, which put them at higher risk.

questions.q: In the study of dialysis patients, Goleman says the route connecting depression to death was not biological but ____, since depressed patients failed to follow their regimens.
questions.explain: Depressed dialysis patients cheated on their diets and neglected their regimens, so the link ran through attitude and behavior.

questions.q: Match each study of depression in medical patients to its finding.
pairs: 12 of the 13 who were depressed died within the first year
Patients discharged after a first heart attack in Montreal
The seriously depressed had five times the death rate within six months
The depressed stayed about eight days longer in hospital
Top 10 percent of users of medical services
Treating major depression cut disabled days from 79 to 51 a year
Middle-aged adults tracked for twelve years
The most severely depressed had four times the heart-disease death rate
questions.explain: Across these studies depression worsens outcomes once illness has begun, and in some, treating it brings measurable gains.

questions.q: Which of these did the study of elderly women with hip fracture find about those who were depressed on admission?
options: They stayed in hospital an average of eight days longer
They were only a third as likely ever to walk again
They needed more surgery on the fracture
They recovered faster once they returned home
questions.explain: Depressed women stayed eight days longer and were a third as likely to walk again; those who also got psychiatric help needed less physical therapy and had fewer rehospitalizations.

questions.q: True or false: Among the heaviest users of medical services, treating mild depression cut disabled days from 62 a year to just 18.
questions.explain: For those treated for mild depression disabled days fell from 62 to 18 a year; for major depression they fell from 79 to 51.

questions.q: After hip surgery, an elderly relative eats little and seems listless, and staff put it down to the operation. Based on Goleman's chapter, what is the main risk?
options: The listlessness proves the surgery has failed and must be redone
Untreated depression mistaken for physical symptoms could slow her recovery
Low appetite after surgery always signals a hidden infection
Paying attention to her mood will distract staff from her hip
questions.explain: Goleman warns that depression's symptoms are easily mistaken for other illness, and depressed hip-fracture patients stayed longer and walked again less often; treating the depression helped.

questions.q: What did the Stanford study of heart patients recalling an angry incident show, and why might it understate the damage?
questions.a: While the patients, all first-heart-attack survivors, recounted incidents that made them mad, their hearts' pumping efficiency dropped by five percentage points, and in some by 7 percent or more, a sign of myocardial ischemia. The drop did not appear with anxiety or physical exertion. The patients said they were only about half as angry as during the original event, so a real angry encounter would likely hamper the heart even more.

questions.q: Why does Goleman call Sheldon Cohen's cold-virus study a landmark, and what did it find?
questions.a: Cohen assessed how stressed people were and then deliberately exposed them to a cold virus, so he could follow stress forward to illness rather than guess from immune measurements. Among those with little stress 27 percent caught a cold, against 47 percent of those with the most stressful lives. Goleman calls it direct evidence that stress itself weakens the immune system, valued for its scientific rigor.

questions.q: Why does depression in medically ill patients so often go untreated, and what may that cost them?
questions.a: Symptoms such as loss of appetite and lethargy are easily mistaken for signs of other diseases, especially by physicians with little training in psychiatric diagnosis. The depression, like that of the weepy breast-cancer patient, then goes unnoticed and untreated. Goleman says that failure may add to the risk of death in severe disease.

questions.q: What does the study of elderly women with hip fracture show about depression and its treatment?
questions.a: Women who were depressed on admission stayed an average of eight days longer than comparable patients and were only a third as likely ever to walk again. Those who also got psychiatric help for their depression needed less physical therapy to walk again and had fewer rehospitalizations in the following three months. This supports Goleman's point that depression worsens a sickness once it has begun and that treating it pays medically.

questions.q: Put the steps of Sheldon Cohen's colds experiment in order.
items: Assessed how much stress people felt in their lives
Exposed them to a cold virus
Checked who actually came down with a cold
Found more colds among the most stressed, 47 percent against 27 percent
questions.explain: Because stress was measured before exposure, the study shows distress preceding illness, which is why Goleman rates it highly.

questions.q: Put the steps of the anger-reduction method Goleman describes for heart patients in the order he gives them.
items: Jot down cynical or hostile thoughts as they are noticed
If the thoughts persist, short-circuit them by saying Stop
Substitute reasonable thoughts for cynical ones in trying situations
In frustrating encounters, see things from the other person's perspective
questions.explain: The program builds mindfulness of anger, then regulation, then empathy, which Goleman calls a balm for anger.

questions.q: Match each researcher to the stress study Goleman attributes to him.
pairs: Exposed people to a cold virus after assessing their life stress
Reviewed the stress-disease link and noted wear and tear on the nervous system
Monitored blood ATP in volunteers put through an anxiety-riddled lab ordeal
questions.explain: Each study is used by Goleman as evidence that stress and anxiety have measurable physical effects.

questions.q: Match each statistic to the study Goleman reports it from.
pairs: Seven times as likely to have died by fifty
Physicians with the highest hostility scores in medical school
Three times more likely to die of cardiac arrest
Easily angered heart-attack survivors in the Yale study
Five and a half times more likely to have the cancer
Colorectal cancer patients reporting severe on-the-job aggravation
Seriously depressed patients after a first heart attack in Montreal
questions.explain: Each number is the main result of a study Goleman uses to show the medical toll of anger, job strain or depression.

questions.q: Sort each finding by whether Goleman links it to anger and hostility or to anxiety and fear.

items.t: Heart pumping efficiency dropped when recalling an angry incident
Hostility scores matched the severity of coronary artery disease
Being angry more than doubled cardiac arrest risk for about two hours
Women with a second heart attack showed crippling phobias
Platelet ATP, heart rate and blood pressure rose under lab stress
Women stopped driving or quit jobs after a first heart attack

questions.explain: Goleman finds anger is the emotion most damaging to the heart, with anxiety and fear the more deadly emotions for women who have had a heart attack.

questions.q: Sort each study by whether it is about colds or herpes.

items.t: Volunteers exposed to a cold virus at a research unit in Sheffield
Couples keeping daily checklists of marital upsets
Cases tracked three or four days after intense upsets
Medical students facing year-end exams
Recently separated women
Caregivers of family members with Alzheimer's disease

questions.explain: Goleman uses these studies to show that stress lets infections take hold, with latent herpes reactivated and colds more likely.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: How does Goleman summarize the different medical effects of anger and anxiety on the one hand and depression on the other?
questions.a: Both anger and anxiety, when chronic, can make people more susceptible to a range of disease. Depression may not make people more vulnerable to becoming ill, but it does seem to impede medical recovery and heighten the risk of death, especially in frailer patients with severe conditions. Together the evidence for adverse medical effects from these emotions is compelling.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: Goleman says that if chronic emotional distress is toxic, the opposite range of emotion can be ____, to a degree.
questions.explain: Toxic versus tonic: positive emotions give a subtle edge, though Goleman stresses they are not curative on their own.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: True or false: Goleman says laughter or happiness alone can turn the course of a serious disease.
questions.explain: He says the reverse: positive emotion is not curative, and its edge is subtle, detectable only in studies with large numbers of people.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: True or false: In the study of 122 heart-attack patients, mental outlook predicted survival better than any medical risk factor, including the damage done to the heart.
questions.explain: Outlook beat heart damage, artery blockage, cholesterol and blood pressure as a predictor of survival.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: Why does Goleman say hope is especially telling in paralysis from spinal injury?
questions.a: This medical tragedy typically involves a man paralyzed in his twenties by an accident who will remain so for the rest of his life. How he reacts emotionally has broad consequences for whether he makes the efforts that might bring him greater physical and social functioning. In the study, the more hopeful patients gained greater mobility than others with similar injuries.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: Which of these explanations does Goleman offer for why optimism or pessimism might affect health?
options: Pessimism may lead to depression, which interferes with immune resistance
Pessimists may neglect their health, smoking and drinking more and exercising less
The physiology of hopefulness may itself help the body fight disease
Optimists may inherit stronger immune systems from their parents
Optimists may receive more attention and better care from doctors
questions.explain: Goleman offers these three possibilities and calls the first an unproven speculation; he does not mention inheritance or better treatment by doctors.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: True or false: Goleman presents the theory that pessimism leads to depression, which then weakens the immune system, as a proven mechanism.
questions.explain: He calls it an unproven speculation at present, one of several possible explanations.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: Two men have suffered first heart attacks with similar damage. One expects to recover and get back to work; the other is sure he is finished. Based on the study of 122 heart-attack patients, what would Goleman predict?
options: The pessimist is at greater risk of dying in the following years
Their risks are equal, since the damage to their hearts is the same
The optimist is at greater risk because he will push himself too hard
Only their cholesterol levels will tell which is at greater risk
questions.explain: Outlook predicted survival better than any medical risk factor, including heart damage; 21 of the 25 most pessimistic men died, against 6 of the 25 most optimistic.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: Goleman reports that smoking increases mortality risk by a factor of just 1.6, while social isolation does so by a factor of ____.
questions.explain: Isolation's factor of 2.0 makes it a greater health risk than smoking, as a 1987 report in Science concluded.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: True or false: Goleman reports that social isolation is harder on women than on men.
questions.explain: Isolation is harder on men: isolated men were two to three times likelier to die, isolated women one and a half times.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: Why might social isolation affect men's health more than women's, according to Goleman?
options: Women usually live alone less often than men do
Women's relationships tend to be emotionally closer, so a few ties comfort them more
Men are more likely to smoke when they are lonely
Women's immune systems are less affected by stress hormones
questions.explain: A few strands of emotionally close ties may comfort a woman more than the same number of friendships comforts a man.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: Arjun lives alone and sees few friends, but he is content and talks openly with his sister every week. Is he at the medical risk Goleman links to isolation?
options: Probably not, since the risk lies in feeling cut off with no one to turn to
Yes, because living alone is itself the main risk factor
Yes, because seeing few friends doubles the risk of death
Only if he also smokes or has high blood pressure
questions.explain: Goleman says solitude is not isolation; many people who live alone are content and healthy. The risk is the subjective sense of being cut off.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: Sort these people by whether they face the medical risk Goleman links to social isolation.

items.t: A widower who feels he has no one to share his feelings with
An office worker surrounded by colleagues but with nobody to confide in
A man who has drifted from all his friends and feels cut off
A writer who lives alone by choice and feels content and supported
A retiree living alone who phones close friends daily

questions.explain: The risk is the subjective sense of being cut off with no one to turn to, not living alone or seeing few people.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: Why does Goleman suggest self-help groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous have added value?
options: They replace the need for medical treatment of addiction
They can serve as surrogate communities as modern social ties fall away
They are cheaper for health plans than psychotherapy
They teach members to avoid all close relationships
questions.explain: With isolation bred by solitary TV-watching and the decline of clubs and visits, such groups can act as surrogate communities.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: Put the stages of the 1993 Swedish study of men from Goteborg in order.
items: All men in the city born in 1933 were offered a free medical exam
752 men came for the exam and reported their life stresses
Seven years later the men were contacted again
It emerged that 41 of them had died in the meantime
questions.explain: The study followed the 752 examined men for seven years, then compared deaths with the stress and support they had reported.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: Which of these were among the stressful events counted in the Swedish Goteborg study?
options: Serious financial trouble
Being forced out of a job
Going through a divorce
Moving to a new city
The birth of a child
questions.explain: The study counted events such as financial trouble, job insecurity or loss, legal action and divorce; three or more in a year predicted death better than blood pressure or cholesterol.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: True or false: In the Swedish Goteborg study, men with a dependable web of intimacy showed no relationship at all between high stress and death rate.
questions.explain: Having people to turn to and talk with protected them from the deadly impact of life's rigors.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: What does the Swedish study of men from Goteborg show about stress and close relationships?
questions.a: Men who reported intense emotional stress, such as financial trouble, job loss, legal action or divorce, had three times the death rate of calmer men over seven years, and three or more such troubles predicted death better than medical indicators like blood pressure or cholesterol. Yet among men with a dependable web of intimacy, such as a wife and close friends, there was no relationship at all between stress and death rate. Having people who offer solace, help and suggestions buffered them against stress.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: John Cacioppo told Goleman that the more significant a relationship is in your life, the more it matters for your ____.
questions.explain: Cacioppo says the people you see day in and day out are crucial for your health, which is why bad relationships take a toll.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: Whose findings does Goleman present as scientific corroboration of Robin Hood's advice that a flow of words eases a sorrowful heart?
options: James Pennebaker's
David Spiegel's
John Cacioppo's
Redford Williams's
questions.explain: Pennebaker showed in a series of experiments that getting people to put their most troubling thoughts into words has a beneficial medical effect.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: Which of these benefits followed James Pennebaker's writing exercise?
options: Enhanced immune function
Significant drops in health-center visits over the next six months
Improved liver enzyme function
Lower blood cholesterol
Faster healing of broken bones
questions.explain: Pennebaker found better immune function, fewer health-center visits, fewer days off work and even improved liver enzymes.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: True or false: In James Pennebaker's experiments, people had to hand in what they wrote about their troubles to the researchers.
questions.explain: What people wrote could be kept entirely to themselves if they liked; the benefit came from the writing itself.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: True or false: In James Pennebaker's studies, those whose writing showed the most turbulent feelings had the greatest improvements in immune function.
questions.explain: The most emotionally turbulent writers gained the most in immune function.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: Put the healthiest way of writing about troubling feelings, as found by James Pennebaker, in order.
items: Express a high level of the troubling feelings, such as sadness, anxiety or anger
Over the next several days, weave the experience into a narrative
Find some meaning in the trauma or travail
questions.explain: The healthiest pattern starts with strong feeling and moves over days to a story that makes sense of the experience, much as in psychotherapy.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: Why, according to Goleman, do Pennebaker's findings help explain why medical patients given psychotherapy often fare better?
options: Psychotherapy distracts patients so they notice symptoms less
Exploring troubles in therapy resembles the unburdening and meaning-making that writing provides
Therapists can prescribe stronger drugs than other doctors
Patients in therapy keep more doctor's appointments than others
questions.explain: Expressing feelings and finding meaning in them is akin to what happens in psychotherapy, which may be one reason therapy alongside medical treatment helps.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: Since a painful breakup, Leena keeps going over it in her head. Which approach drawn from James Pennebaker's research would Goleman's chapter suggest?
options: Writing about it for fifteen to twenty minutes a day for several days, letting the feelings out and then making sense of it
Refusing to think about it at all until the feelings fade by themselves
Telling as many people as possible about it in a single long evening
Writing one brief neutral summary of the facts without any feelings
questions.explain: Pennebaker's healthiest pattern pairs open expression of troubling feelings with building a narrative and finding meaning over several days.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: What did David Spiegel find about women with advanced metastatic breast cancer who attended weekly support groups?
options: They reported less pain but survived no longer
They survived twice as long as women facing the disease on their own
They survived about ten percent longer than others
They needed less chemotherapy but survived as long
questions.explain: Spiegel himself was stunned: group members survived twice as long as women with the same disease who faced it alone.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: In David Spiegel's study, women with metastatic breast cancer who attended the groups lived on average ____ additional months, against nineteen for those who did not.
questions.explain: Thirty-seven months against nineteen: a gain in life expectancy beyond the reach of any medication.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: Why were David Spiegel's support groups so important to the women with advanced breast cancer, and what does the result suggest?
questions.a: All the women got standard medical care; the difference was that group members could unburden themselves with others who understood and would listen to their fears, pain and anger. Often this was the only place they could be open, because other people in their lives dreaded talking about the cancer and their death. They lived about thirty-seven months on average against nineteen, a gain Goleman says is beyond any medication, so emotional support has real clinical power.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: True or false: In David Spiegel's study, the women who did not attend the support groups received less medical care than those who did.
questions.explain: All the women received standard medical care; the only difference was that some also attended the groups.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: How does Goleman separate solitude from isolation, and why does the difference matter for health?
questions.a: Solitude is not isolation: many people who live alone or see few friends are content and healthy. The medical risk lies in the subjective sense of being cut off from people with no one to turn to, which studies of more than thirty-seven thousand people found doubles the chances of sickness or death. So what counts is felt emotional connection, not simply how much company a person has.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: What did the heart-attack study of 122 men reveal about optimism, and what explanations does Goleman offer?
questions.a: Eight years on, 21 of the 25 most pessimistic men had died against 6 of the 25 most optimistic, and outlook predicted survival better than any medical risk factor. Goleman offers several possible explanations: pessimism might lead to depression that undermines immune resistance (unproven), pessimists neglect their health habits, or the physiology of hopefulness might itself help the body fight disease.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: Why does Goleman say David Spiegel's support-group result was so remarkable?
questions.a: Women with advanced metastatic breast cancer who attended weekly groups lived on average thirty-seven additional months against nineteen for those who did not, though all received standard medical care. The groups let them unburden fears, pain and anger that others in their lives dreaded hearing. Goleman stresses that the gain in life expectancy was beyond the reach of any medication, and a new drug with that effect would have companies battling to make it.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: In James Pennebaker's experiments, people wrote about their most troubling thoughts for fifteen to twenty minutes a day over about ____ days.
questions.explain: The method was simple: a few minutes of private writing a day over five or so days, with what people wrote kept to themselves if they liked.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: Match each researcher to the finding Goleman reports.
pairs: Writing about troubling thoughts boosted immune function
Weekly support groups doubled survival in advanced breast cancer
Roommates who disliked each other had more colds and doctor visits
questions.explain: All three studies show that how people share, or fail to share, their feelings with others affects health.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: Match each figure to the finding Goleman gives it for.
pairs: Two-year survival of bone marrow transplant patients with strong against little emotional support
Deaths among the most pessimistic and most optimistic men after eight years
Average survival of women with and without breast-cancer support groups
Mortality risk factor of smoking against social isolation
questions.explain: These paired figures are Goleman's evidence that emotional ties and outlook influence survival as much as medical risks.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: Sort each relationship by whether Goleman presents it as protecting health or harming it.

items.t: A dependable web of intimacy of wife and close friends
Two or more people to rely on after a heart attack
Weekly meetings with others who understand a cancer diagnosis
Roommates who dislike each other
Marital arguments
Feeling cut off with no one to turn to

questions.explain: Goleman shows that both the quality and the number of relationships matter, buffering stress when good and weakening immunity when bad.

questions.section: The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
questions.q: Sort each detail by whether Goleman ties it to optimistic or pessimistic people.

items.t: Only 6 of the 25 died within eight years of a first heart attack
Faster recovery with fewer complications after bypass surgery
Spinal-injury patients gained more physical mobility
21 of the 25 died within eight years of a first heart attack
Smoke and drink more and exercise less
Careless about health habits

questions.explain: Goleman shows outlook predicting survival and recovery, with possible explanations including health habits.

questions.section: Bringing Emotional Intelligence to Medical Care
questions.q: During Goleman's kidney X-ray test, who finally asked the nephrologist whether he had seen signs of cancer?
options: Goleman himself
A nurse running the machine
Goleman's own doctor by phone
A physician friend who had come with him
questions.explain: Shaken and dazed, Goleman could not ask the one question on his mind; his companion, himself a physician, asked for him.

questions.section: Bringing Emotional Intelligence to Medical Care
questions.q: In a study of patients in waiting rooms, each had three or more questions for the physician, but on average only ____ of them had been answered when they left.
questions.explain: Goleman says his own inability to ask his question is repeated a thousand times a day, and unanswered questions feed fear.

questions.section: Bringing Emotional Intelligence to Medical Care
questions.q: Which of these does Goleman say unanswered questions lead to in patients?
options: Uncertainty and fear
Catastrophizing
Balking at treatment they don't fully understand
Greater trust in the physician
Faster recovery from surgery
questions.explain: Unanswered questions feed uncertainty, fear and catastrophizing, and lead patients to resist treatment regimes they do not understand.

questions.section: Bringing Emotional Intelligence to Medical Care
questions.q: Ahead of a hospital appointment Mei has three worries she wants to raise. According to Goleman's chapter, what kind of help would make her likely to leave with three answers?
options: A short program that teaches patients to be effective questioners with their physicians
A longer appointment slot booked through the hospital
Bringing a relative to speak to the doctor on her behalf
A sedative to keep her calm while the doctor talks
questions.explain: Goleman describes programs that, in a few minutes, teach patients to question effectively, so that three questions in mind become three answers.

questions.section: Bringing Emotional Intelligence to Medical Care
questions.q: How much sooner did patients recover from surgery when hospitals gave them presurgery instruction to ease their fears?
options: A few hours sooner
About two weeks sooner
No sooner, but with less pain
Two to three days sooner
questions.explain: Presurgery instruction that eased fears and discomforts cut recovery by an average of two to three days.

questions.section: Bringing Emotional Intelligence to Medical Care
questions.q: Which of these were part of the presurgery instruction some hospitals gave patients?
options: Teaching relaxation techniques
Answering their questions well in advance of surgery
Telling them days ahead what they would experience in recovery
Giving sedatives the night before so they could not worry
Keeping details of recovery from them to avoid alarm
questions.explain: The programs helped patients assuage fears by relaxation, early answers and frank preparation for recovery, the opposite of keeping them in the dark.

questions.section: Bringing Emotional Intelligence to Medical Care
questions.q: What does Jon Kabat-Zinn's Stress Reduction Clinic at the University of Massachusetts Medical Center offer patients?
options: A weekend retreat on positive thinking
A ten-week course in mindfulness and yoga
Weekly group therapy for cancer patients
A low-fat diet and exercise plan
questions.explain: The course stresses mindfulness of emotional episodes as they happen and a daily practice of deep relaxation; tapes of it are shown on hospital televisions.

questions.section: Bringing Emotional Intelligence to Medical Care
questions.q: What did patients with severe heart disease achieve after a year of Dr. Dean Ornish's program?
options: They actually reversed the buildup of artery-clogging plaque
They avoided all further heart attacks for ten years
They lowered their blood pressure but not their plaque
They needed only half the usual bypass surgery
questions.explain: The program, combining relaxation, yoga and a low-fat diet, reversed plaque in patients sick enough to warrant bypass, and Ornish says relaxation is among its most important parts.

questions.section: Bringing Emotional Intelligence to Medical Care
questions.q: Dr. Herbert Benson's term for the physiological opposite of stress arousal is the relaxation ____.
questions.explain: Kabat-Zinn's and Ornish's programs both use the relaxation response to counter the stress arousal behind many medical problems.

questions.section: Bringing Emotional Intelligence to Medical Care
questions.q: Goleman calls for ____ care, recognizing that the relationship between physician and patient is itself a factor of significance.
questions.explain: Relationship-centered care values an empathic doctor or nurse who can listen and be heard.

questions.section: Bringing Emotional Intelligence to Medical Care
questions.q: Which of these basic tools of emotional intelligence does Goleman say medical education should include?
options: Self-awareness
Empathy
The art of listening
Competitive drive
Emotional detachment
questions.explain: Goleman names self-awareness and the arts of empathy and listening as the tools that would foster relationship-centered care.

questions.section: Bringing Emotional Intelligence to Medical Care
questions.q: Match each step toward emotionally intelligent medical care to its described benefit.
pairs: Recovery two to three days sooner
Computer searches of the medical literature
Patients become more equal partners in decisions
Three questions in mind become three answers
questions.explain: Each step addresses an emotional reality of illness, such as fear, helplessness or uncertainty, and brings a practical gain.

questions.section: Bringing Emotional Intelligence to Medical Care
questions.q: How does Goleman use his own experience of the kidney X-ray test to show what is missing from medical care?
questions.a: After an hour and a half of testing, the kidney specialist barely introduced himself and never returned to tell him the results. Shaken and dazed, Goleman could not ask the one question he cared about, whether there were signs of cancer; his physician friend had to ask, and got a curt reply. Goleman says this is repeated a thousand times a day, and unanswered questions feed uncertainty, fear and catastrophizing, showing how patients' emotional needs go unmet.

questions.section: Bringing Emotional Intelligence to Medical Care
questions.q: A hospital wants to give bedridden patients something better than soap operas on their room televisions. What does Goleman's chapter describe some hospitals doing?
options: Showing recordings of support-group meetings for cancer patients
Showing instructional tapes from Kabat-Zinn's mindfulness and relaxation course
Showing lectures on the latest medical research about their illness
Showing comedy programs to raise patients' spirits through laughter
questions.explain: Hospitals made tapes from Kabat-Zinn's course available on patients' televisions, which Goleman calls a far better emotional diet than soap operas.

questions.section: Bringing Emotional Intelligence to Medical Care
questions.q: What practical steps does Goleman describe for helping patients cope with surgery and hospital stays?
questions.a: Some hospitals give presurgery instruction that teaches relaxation techniques, answers questions well in advance and tells patients days ahead exactly what recovery will involve, and patients recover two to three days sooner. Others have designed rooms so family members can stay and care for patients as at home. Patients can also be given fuller information and taught in a few minutes to be effective questioners with their physicians.

questions.section: Bringing Emotional Intelligence to Medical Care
questions.q: How do Jon Kabat-Zinn and Dean Ornish use relaxation in treating patients?
questions.a: Kabat-Zinn's Stress Reduction Clinic offers a ten-week course in mindfulness and yoga, stressing awareness of emotional episodes as they happen and a daily practice of deep relaxation. Ornish's heart-disease program combines relaxation, yoga and a low-fat diet, and after a year it reversed artery-clogging plaque in severe cases. Both draw on Herbert Benson's relaxation response, the physiological opposite of stress arousal.

questions.section: Bringing Emotional Intelligence to Medical Care
questions.q: Why does Goleman say patients leaving the doctor's office often remain emotionally unmet, and what follows from it?
questions.a: In a study of waiting-room patients, each had an average of three or more questions to ask but only about one and a half were answered. Unanswered questions feed uncertainty, fear and catastrophizing, and lead patients to balk at treatment regimes they do not fully understand. His own silent worry about cancer during the kidney test illustrates how common this is.

questions.section: Bringing Emotional Intelligence to Medical Care
questions.q: Put the events of Goleman's kidney X-ray test in order.
items: A routine checkup spotted blood in his urine
He was injected with radioactive dye while a physician friend sat with him
A kidney specialist hurried in briefly, then left to scan the X-rays
His friend asked the specialist about cancer, and got a curt No abnormalities
questions.explain: Goleman uses the episode to show a patient too shaken to ask the one question he cared about, and a specialist too rushed to volunteer the answer.

questions.section: Bringing Emotional Intelligence to Medical Care
questions.q: Match each person or program to the approach Goleman describes.
pairs: Ten-week course in mindfulness and yoga at a stress reduction clinic
Heart-disease program with relaxation, yoga and low-fat diet that reversed plaque
The relaxation response, the physiological opposite of stress arousal
Relatives stay with patients, cooking and caring for them as at home
questions.explain: Each is an example of widening medicine to deal with the emotional realities of illness.

questions.section: Bringing Emotional Intelligence to Medical Care
questions.q: Sort each step by whether it mainly gives patients information or teaches relaxation and mindfulness.

items.t: A computer search of the medical literature on a patient's condition
A short program on being an effective questioner
Telling patients days ahead what recovery will involve
Kabat-Zinn's ten-week mindfulness and yoga course
Instructional tapes on patients' televisions
Relaxation training in Ornish's heart program

questions.explain: Goleman lists both informing patients and teaching relaxation as ways for medicine to attend to emotional realities of illness.

questions.q: What is the first of the two large implications Goleman draws from the findings on emotions and health?
options: Positive thinking should replace standard medical treatment
Doctors should screen every patient for psychiatric illness
Helping people manage upsetting feelings is a form of disease prevention
Hospitals should hire more psychologists than physicians
questions.explain: Because the toxicity of chronic upsetting emotions is on a par with smoking, helping people handle them is prevention; the second implication concerns attending to patients' psychological needs.

questions.q: Goleman says helping people handle chronic upsetting emotions could have a medical payoff as great as what?
options: Vaccinating children against measles
Lowering everyone's cholesterol
Building more hospitals
Getting heavy smokers to quit
questions.explain: Since chronic toxic emotions are on a par with smoking cigarettes, managing them better could pay off as much as heavy smokers quitting.

questions.q: Which of these groups does Goleman suggest as high-payoff targets for teaching emotion management as disease prevention?
options: Children
People reaching retirement age
At-risk groups such as the very poor and single working mothers
Medical students
Professional athletes
questions.explain: Children can make the skills lifelong habits, retirees' emotional well-being shapes whether they decline or thrive, and at-risk groups live under extraordinary daily pressure.

questions.q: Why does Goleman suggest teaching emotion management to people reaching retirement age?
questions.a: He calls it a high-payoff preventive strategy because emotional well-being is one factor that determines whether an older person declines rapidly or thrives. Since chronic upsetting emotions are as toxic as smoking, helping older people handle them could protect their health.

questions.q: Goleman calls emotional care, an opportunity too often lost in today's medicine, a blind ____ for medicine.
questions.explain: Despite mounting data, many physicians dismiss the evidence as trivial, anecdotal or fringe, so emotional care remains a blind spot.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says that as medicine becomes more responsive to the imperatives of business, humane and sensitive care is becoming easier to find.
questions.explain: He says the changing culture of medicine is making such care increasingly difficult to find, so humane medicine is becoming endangered.

questions.q: In the study of elderly hip-fracture patients at Mt. Sinai and Northwestern, what did therapy for depression added to orthopedic care achieve?
options: Patients needed no further surgery, saving about a million dollars
Patients reported more satisfaction but stayed just as long
Patients left hospital about two days earlier, saving $97,361 in all
Patients left a week earlier but needed more home care
questions.explain: Treating depression shortened stays by two days on average, and total savings for the hundred or so patients were $97,361, part of the business case for humane medicine.

questions.q: Which of these reasons does Goleman give, in the chapter's last section, for adopting a more emotionally attentive medicine?
options: It can save money by speeding healing or delaying sickness
It makes patients more satisfied and more loyal to their health plans
Medical ethics may demand it
It reduces the number of lawsuits against doctors
It shortens the training needed to become a doctor
questions.explain: Goleman argues from business advantage, patient satisfaction in a competitive marketplace, and ethics, quoting a JAMA editorial; lawsuits and training are not part of his case.

questions.q: In the chapter's last section, put Goleman's supporting arguments for humane medicine in the order he presents them.
items: A business advantage: treating distress can save money
Patient satisfaction and loyalty in a competitive marketplace
Medical ethics, as argued in a JAMA editorial
questions.explain: Goleman moves from money to satisfaction and finally to ethics, saying it would be unethical not to treat factors like depression and isolation.

questions.q: What did the Journal of the American Medical Association editorial conclude about psychological factors such as depression and social isolation in heart patients?
options: It would be unethical not to start trying to treat them
They are too poorly measured to guide treatment
They matter only for patients who refuse surgery
They should be left to psychiatrists, not cardiologists
questions.explain: Since these factors mark the coronary patients at highest risk, the editorial said not treating them would be unethical.

questions.q: Goleman closes the chapter with a patient's words to his surgeon: compassion is not mere hand holding, it is good ____.
questions.explain: The closing quote sums up the chapter: caring for feelings is part of effective treatment, not a mere courtesy.

questions.q: A health-plan manager wonders whether paying for depression treatment for elderly hip-fracture patients could ever pay for itself. Which finding in Goleman's chapter speaks most directly to this?
options: Spiegel's support groups doubled survival with breast cancer
Cohen found stressed people were likelier to catch colds
Optimistic bypass patients had fewer complications
Patients given therapy for depression left hospital two days early, saving $97,361
questions.explain: The Mt. Sinai and Northwestern study directly measured savings from treating depression in hip-fracture patients, part of Goleman's business case for humane care.

questions.q: Sort each step by which of Goleman's two large implications it serves.

items.t: Teaching children basic emotional intelligence skills
Teaching emotion management to people nearing retirement
Helping single working mothers handle chronic stress
Treating depression alongside orthopedic care
Offering support groups to patients with advanced cancer
Easing patients' fears before surgery

questions.explain: The first implication is prevention for the healthy and at-risk; the second is caring for the emotional needs of people who are already patients.

questions.q: What final conclusion does Goleman draw about medical care that neglects patients' feelings?
questions.a: He says medical care that neglects how people feel as they battle a chronic or severe disease is no longer adequate, and that medicine should take more methodical advantage of the link between emotion and health. What is now the exception should become mainstream, so caring medicine is available to all. At the least it would make medicine more humane, and for some it could speed recovery.

questions.q: What business and ethical arguments does Goleman give for a more humane medicine?
questions.a: Treating emotional distress can save money: hip-fracture patients given depression therapy left hospital two days earlier, saving about $97,000 across roughly a hundred patients. Such care also raises patient satisfaction, which matters when patients can choose among health plans. Finally, a JAMA editorial argued it would be unethical not to start treating factors like depression and social isolation in heart patients at highest risk.

questions.q: Goleman's first large implication is that helping people better manage upsetting feelings is a form of disease ____.
questions.explain: Because chronic anger, anxiety, depression, pessimism and loneliness are as toxic as smoking, handling them better could pay off medically like getting smokers to quit.

questions.q: Put the target groups Goleman suggests for teaching emotion management in the order he lists them.
items: Children
People reaching retirement age
At-risk populations such as the very poor and single working mothers
questions.explain: Each group is a high-payoff target for prevention: children so skills become lifelong habits, older people so they thrive, and high-pressure populations so they cope with daily stress.

questions.q: Match each argument for humane medicine to the evidence Goleman gives.
pairs: Toxic emotions are on a par with smoking as a health risk
Hip-fracture patients given depression therapy left hospital two days earlier
Pleasing experiences translate into loyalty when patients choose health plans
A JAMA editorial called it unethical not to treat depression and isolation
questions.explain: Goleman builds a prevention, business and ethical case for treating patients' emotions as part of medicine.

questions.q: In which Part of Goleman's book does the chapter Mind and Medicine appear?
options: Part Two, The Nature of Emotional Intelligence
Part Three, Emotional Intelligence Applied
Part Four, Windows of Opportunity
Part Five, Emotional Literacy
questions.explain: Mind and Medicine is the last chapter of Part Three, which shows what difference emotional intelligence makes in key areas of life.

questions.q: In the Prologue's road map, Goleman says Part Three will show that toxic emotions put our physical health at as much risk as what?
options: Chain-smoking
Heavy drinking
Poor diet
Lack of sleep
questions.explain: The Prologue promises that Part Three will show how toxic emotions put health at as much risk as chain-smoking, which this chapter's data support.

questions.q: Put the chapters of Part Three, Emotional Intelligence Applied, in order.
items: Intimate Enemies
Managing with Heart
Mind and Medicine
questions.explain: Part Three applies emotional intelligence to marriage, then the workplace, then health and medical care.

questions.q: What does the chapter after Mind and Medicine, opening Part Four, turn to?
options: How emotions affect success at work and in teams
How emotional lessons learned in childhood at home shape emotional abilities
How the amygdala can hijack the thinking brain
How schools can teach emotional literacy programs
questions.explain: Part Four, Windows of Opportunity, begins with The Family Crucible, moving from what emotional intelligence does in adult life to how it is shaped in childhood.

questions.q: Why does Mind and Medicine make a fitting close to Part Three of Goleman's book?
questions.a: Part Three examines key differences emotional intelligence makes in life, first in close relationships (Intimate Enemies), then at work (Managing with Heart). Mind and Medicine extends this to physical health, showing that toxic emotions are as risky as chain-smoking while emotional balance and support protect health, and arguing that medical care itself needs emotional intelligence. It completes the case that emotional skills matter across the main areas of life before the book turns to how they are learned.

questions.q: What does the title Mind and Medicine signal about the chapter's theme?
options: That mental illness should be treated with medicine rather than therapy
That doctors need higher IQs to make good diagnoses
That emotions affect physical health and should be part of medical care
That the brain is the body's most important organ
questions.explain: The chapter traces how emotions influence the body and disease, then argues medicine should attend to patients' feelings.

questions.q: Put the main sections of the chapter Mind and Medicine in order.
items: The Body's Mind: How Emotions Matter for Health
Toxic Emotions: The Clinical Data
The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
Bringing Emotional Intelligence to Medical Care
Toward a Medicine That Cares
questions.explain: The chapter moves from biological pathways to clinical evidence of harm and benefit, then to practical changes and broad implications.

questions.q: Match each section of the chapter Mind and Medicine to its role in the argument.
