pairs: Shows the biological pathways linking emotions and immunity
Gives evidence that anger, anxiety and depression harm health
The Medical Benefits of Positive Feelings
Shows how optimism, hope and close ties protect health
Bringing Emotional Intelligence to Medical Care
Describes practical changes hospitals and doctors can make
Draws two large implications for prevention and patient care
questions.explain: Goleman builds from mechanism to evidence to practice to policy.

questions.q: Why does Goleman begin the body of the chapter with Ader's and Felten's research before presenting clinical data?
options: To show that emotions matter only in laboratory animals, not in patients
To prove that positive thinking can cure serious disease
To argue that the immune system controls the emotions
To establish a physical pathway by which emotions can affect the body before showing their clinical effects
questions.explain: Showing that brain and immune system communicate answers the old belief they were separate, making the later statistics on emotion and disease plausible.

questions.q: When Goleman says venting anger every time it is felt simply feeds it, which earlier chapter does he point back to?
options: Chapter 1, on what emotions are for
Chapter 7, on empathy
Chapter 5, on managing emotions
Chapter 9, on marriage
questions.explain: He explicitly recalls Chapter 5 (Passion's Slaves), where ventilating anger was shown to feed it rather than release it.

questions.q: A later chapter on families refers back to Mind and Medicine. What link does it make?
options: Children of emotionally adept parents have lower stress hormones, which may augur better physical health
Children who are bullied later develop heart disease in middle age
Parents who are optimistic recover faster from surgery
Children who write about trauma have fewer doctor visits
questions.explain: The Family Crucible notes these children are more relaxed biologically, a pattern that might well mean better health later, as shown in Chapter 11.

questions.q: How does the Camus epigraph, in which a doctor says suffering taught him, prepare the reader for Goleman's chapter?
options: It suggests that doctors should be stricter with complaining patients
It argues that physical pain is the main cause of depression
It claims that only sick people can become good doctors
It points to the emotional side of illness that a caring medicine must understand
questions.explain: The chapter argues medicine must attend to the suffering and feelings of illness, not just disease, and ends on compassion as good medicine.

questions.q: How does the chapter Mind and Medicine move from evidence to prescription?
questions.a: It opens by rejecting both the mind-body-blind medical model and the attitude-will-cure-all view, then presents the biology linking nervous and immune systems. Next it gives clinical data showing anger, anxiety and depression harm health, and that optimism, hope, relationships and emotional support help. Only then does it prescribe practical changes in medical care and two broad implications: emotion management as prevention, and attending to patients' psychological needs.

questions.q: Put the three sub-parts of the section on positive feelings in the order they appear.
items: The price of pessimism and advantages of optimism
The medical value of relationships
The healing power of emotional support
questions.explain: The section moves from an individual's outlook, to the protection of close ties, to the benefit of unburdening feelings with others.

questions.q: In the Hooven and Gottman study, why did researchers have parents teach their child a new video game?
options: The session served as a revealing barometer of the parents' emotional style toward the child
It tested how quickly the child could master a new skill without parental help
It measured how much the parents knew about video technology
It showed which parent was more skilled at teaching the child
questions.explain: The task looked innocuous but exposed how patient or overbearing parents were, so it worked as a gauge of emotional style rather than of skill or knowledge.

questions.q: According to the University of Washington research, what was true of couples who handled feelings well in their marriage?
options: They were less likely to involve their children in emotional matters at all
They were also the most effective at helping their children with emotional ups and downs
They relied on professional coaches to teach their children emotional skills
They were more effective with children only once the children reached adolescence
questions.explain: The team found that emotional competence between partners went together with emotional competence in guiding the children.

questions.q: Which parenting style treats a child's emotional upset as trivial and something to wait out?
options: Being too laissez-faire
Being contemptuous
Ignoring feelings altogether
Acting as an emotional coach
questions.explain: Parents who ignore feelings see upset as a bother that will blow over and miss the chance to teach emotional competence. Laissez-faire parents, by contrast, notice the feelings but accept any way of handling them.

questions.q: A mother sees her son shove a friend in anger. She says that whatever way he handles his anger is fine with her, and offers him a cookie to cheer up. Which style from the chapter does this show?
options: Ignoring feelings altogether
Being contemptuous
Acting as an emotional coach
Being too laissez-faire
questions.explain: She notices the feeling, accepts even hitting as a way of handling it, and soothes with a bribe, which marks the laissez-faire style. She does not ignore the feeling, nor does she show an alternative response as a coach would.

questions.q: A boy starts to explain his side of a quarrel, and his father snaps at him not to talk back and sends him to his room. Which parenting style does this illustrate?
options: Being contemptuous and showing no respect for the child's feelings
Ignoring feelings altogether
Being too laissez-faire
Acting as an emotional coach
questions.explain: Harsh criticism and punishment of a child who tries to speak is the contemptuous style. A coach would take the feelings seriously and try to understand what is upsetting the child.

questions.q: Why does the author say parents need some emotional intelligence of their own to be effective emotional coaches?
options: Coaching only works if parents have been coached themselves as children
A parent who is tuned out of his own sadness cannot help a child tell apart different kinds of sadness
Children copy only the emotions that parents display openly
Parents need it mainly to avoid arguing in front of the child
questions.explain: The example is a father who cannot help his son distinguish grieving a loss, sadness at a sad movie, and sadness for someone cared about. Coaching rests on the parent's grasp of the basics.

questions.q: When IQ was held constant, what did the University of Washington team find about five-year-olds whose parents were good emotional coaches?
options: They had higher IQ scores by third grade
They needed less teaching of reading in kindergarten
They had higher math and reading achievement scores in third grade
They had equal scores to other children but fewer behavior problems
questions.explain: Even with IQ controlled, good coaching predicted better third-grade achievement, which the author uses to argue for teaching emotional skills to prepare children for learning.

questions.q: Which physical difference did the research find in children of emotionally adept parents?
options: Faster growth of the brain in the first years
Higher levels of stress hormones that helped them cope
Better coordination in handling games and toys
Lower levels of stress hormones and other signs of emotional arousal
questions.explain: These children were more relaxed biologically, a pattern the author links to possibly better physical health if sustained through life.

questions.q: In Brazelton's test with an eight-month-old, what does a baby who is hopeful about life do?
options: Plays with a block, drops it to see whether you will retrieve it, then finishes the task and looks up expecting praise
Puts the two blocks together at once and then looks away
Ignores the blocks until the adult shows her again and again
Pushes the blocks away and waits for the adult to finish the task
questions.explain: The hopeful baby explores, expects help, completes the task and looks for approval, a sign that she expects to succeed.

questions.q: What does Brazelton say about babies from bleak, chaotic or neglectful homes who show a hangdog look?
options: They cannot understand the instruction because of poor coordination
They can understand and do the task but act as though they already expect to fail
They refuse the task out of defiance toward the adult
They finish faster than other babies to avoid disapproval
questions.explain: The problem is not ability: they have the understanding and the coordination, yet their demeanor signals expected failure.

questions.q: According to the report from the National Center for Clinical Infant Programs, what best predicts a child's success in school?
options: A large fund of facts learned before school begins
A precocious ability to read
Emotional and social measures such as self-assurance and knowing how to rein in impulses
The child's IQ measured at age four
questions.explain: The report says school success depends less on facts or early reading than on traits like being self-assured, able to wait, follow directions and get along.

questions.q: A five-year-old lets a classmate go first on the swing, then takes his turn and plays happily with the group. Which of the seven ingredients of readiness to learn does this best show?
options: Intentionality, the wish to have an impact and persist
Curiosity, the sense that finding out is pleasurable
Relatedness, the sense of being understood by adults
Cooperativeness, balancing his own needs with those of others in group activity
questions.explain: Taking turns and fitting one's wants to the group is the report's definition of cooperativeness. The other ingredients concern effectiveness, discovery and being understood.

questions.q: What does the author mean by giving children a "Heart Start"?
options: Early care that provides the emotional equivalent of what Head Start programs give
A program that teaches infants to read before kindergarten
A medical screening of children's hearts and stress responses
A school curriculum on emotions for preschoolers
questions.explain: Heart Start names the kind of care parents and preschool teachers give that prepares a child emotionally for school, as Head Start does educationally.

questions.q: What does the first baby, comforted at 3 A.M. by a mother who is glad to see her, learn?
options: That nighttime crying is the best way to earn attention
That people can be trusted to notice her needs and that she can be effective in getting help
That her mother's moods decide whether her needs are met
That she should expect to cope with distress alone
questions.explain: The calm, affectionate response teaches trust and a sense of effectiveness, tying to Erikson's idea of basic trust.

questions.q: In the survey of maltreated children, which group did the worst of all?
options: The physically abused children
The children of drug-abusing parents
The neglected children
The children who were verbally criticized
questions.explain: Simple neglect, the studies found, can be more damaging than outright abuse. Neglected children were the most anxious, inattentive and apathetic.

questions.q: Why does the author say the first three or four years of life are so important for emotional learning?
options: The brain stops changing after age four so later lessons cannot help
Children at that age copy only what their parents say aloud
Children first notice other people's feelings at that age
The toddler's brain grows to about two thirds its full size and learning comes more readily than it later will
questions.explain: Brain growth and complexity are at their fastest then, though the author adds that later experience can remedy some damage.

questions.q: In the study of 870 children followed from age eight to thirty, what was found about the most belligerent children?
options: They were the most likely to drop out and by thirty to have a record of violent crime
They were the least likely to have children of their own
They became more peaceful once they were parents
They were more often boys than girls who later had violent children
questions.explain: Quick-to-fight children had worse outcomes in school and in crime, and their own children showed the same troublemaking in grade school.

questions.q: How did the parents of the aggressive children discipline them?
options: Rarely, because they feared making their children angry
Arbitrarily, so that punishment depended on the parent's mood and not on what the child had done
Consistently, with the same fixed penalty for each offense
Gently, but only when other adults were watching
questions.explain: Bad moods brought severe punishment while good moods let mayhem pass, which breeds worthlessness, helplessness and a sense that threats are everywhere.

questions.q: In the day-care observation of abused toddlers, how did the abused children react in the twenty-seven instances where another child was hurt or upset?
options: Most responded with concern but were too young to help
About half comforted the child and half ignored her
None showed the least concern; they responded with fear, anger or a physical attack
They copied the nonabused children and tried to console her
questions.explain: By contrast five of nine nonabused toddlers showed concern, sadness or empathy in the twenty-three incidents they faced.

questions.q: The title "The Family Crucible" and the opening call family life an intimate cauldron. What does this signal about the chapter?
options: Families are mainly sources of conflict that children must escape
Emotional skills are fixed at birth by temperament
Schools are the main source of emotional lessons
Home is where children first learn, through repeated small exchanges, how to feel and respond
questions.explain: The author calls family life our first school for emotional learning, so the chapter shows what that school teaches.

questions.q: How does the final section of Chapter 12 point toward the next chapter?
options: It ends by saying trauma leaves a lasting imprint on the brain and that even savage imprints can be mended
It promises that abused children will recover without any help
It turns to the question of how schools should teach emotions
It moves from childhood to the emotional lives of adults at work
questions.explain: The closing note that harsh imprints can be mended sets up the following chapter on trauma and emotional relearning.

questions.q: True or false: Hooven and Gottman found that couples who were more emotionally competent with each other were also the most effective in helping their children with their feelings.
questions.explain: The team's microanalysis linked emotional competence in the marriage to effective handling of the child's emotional ups and downs.

questions.q: True or false: Laissez-faire parents fail to notice how their child feels.
questions.explain: They do notice the feelings; the fault is that they accept any way of handling them, even hitting, and rarely offer an alternative.

questions.q: True or false: When IQ was held constant, the advantage in third-grade math and reading for children of good emotional coaches disappeared.
questions.explain: The advantage remained with IQ held constant, which is why the author sees emotional skill as a help to learning.

questions.q: True or false: In Brazelton's block test, the hangdog babies understood the instruction and had the coordination to follow it.
questions.explain: The babies could do the task; what differed was their expectation of failure.

questions.q: True or false: Studies find that simple neglect is less damaging to children than outright abuse.
questions.explain: The studies found that neglect can be more damaging than outright abuse; neglected children did worst in the survey.

questions.q: True or false: In the study of aggressive children, mothers who had been aggressive as girls were as harshly punitive as fathers who had been aggressive as boys.
questions.explain: The pattern held whether the aggressive child had been the father or the mother.

questions.q: True or false: In the day-care observation, some of the abused toddlers responded to a crying child with concern.
questions.explain: Not one of the abused toddlers showed the least concern in the instances where they could have done so.

questions.q: True or false: Chapter 12 presents family life as the first school for emotional learning, with lessons beginning in infancy.
questions.explain: The chapter argues that emotional learning starts in life's earliest moments and shapes the outlook children carry onward.

questions.q: Which of these are emotionally inept parenting styles named in the chapter?
options: Ignoring feelings altogether
Being too laissez-faire
Being contemptuous
Acting as an emotional coach
questions.explain: The fourth is the positive alternative: coaches take feelings seriously and help the child find better responses.

questions.q: Which of these were found in children of emotionally adept parents?
options: Lower levels of stress hormones
Being better liked by peers
Better ability to soothe themselves
Higher inherited intelligence
questions.explain: The benefits were emotional, biological, social and cognitive, but the chapter does not claim they had higher inherited intelligence.

questions.q: Which of these are among the seven ingredients of the capacity to learn?
options: Curiosity
Self-control
Capacity to communicate
Obedience to teachers
Precocious reading ability
questions.explain: The seven are confidence, curiosity, intentionality, self-control, relatedness, communication and cooperativeness; obedience and early reading are not listed.

questions.q: Which of these did the National Center for Clinical Infant Programs report name as signs of school readiness?
options: Being able to wait and follow directions
Expressing needs while getting along with other children
Knowing how to rein in the impulse to misbehave
A large fund of facts
Fluent early reading
questions.explain: The report stresses emotional and social measures over facts or early reading.

questions.q: Which lessons does the baby soothed by a loving mother take in?
options: People can be trusted to notice her needs
She can be effective in getting help
Her efforts to get solace will fail
No one really cares
questions.explain: The last two are what the second baby, met by a tense and irritable mother, comes to feel.

questions.q: Which of these were true of the neglected children in the survey of maltreated children?
options: They were the most anxious and apathetic
They were alternately aggressive and withdrawn
They repeated first grade at a rate of 65 percent
They did better than the physically abused children
questions.explain: Neglected youngsters did the worst of all, so the last statement is the reverse of the finding.

questions.q: Which of these describe the aggressive children when they became parents?
options: They disciplined with arbitrary, relentless severity
They took little interest in their children's lives
They modeled violence for their children
They deliberately wanted their children to suffer
questions.explain: The author says they were not necessarily mean-spirited or ill-wishing; they were repeating the parenting they had received.

questions.q: How did the abused toddlers react to a crying child in the day-care study?
options: With fear
With anger
With a physical attack
With concern
questions.explain: Concern, sadness or empathy was the reaction of the nonabused toddlers, not of the abused ones.

questions.q: Which earlier chapters does Chapter 12 look back on to support its argument?
options: Chapter 6 on the marshmallow test
Chapter 7 on empathy in infancy
Chapter 11 on emotions and health
Chapter 10 on managing with heart
Chapter 4 on gut feeling
questions.explain: The chapter cites the marshmallow finding, the attunement of infancy and the link between stress and health; it does not draw on the workplace or gut-feeling chapters.

questions.q: The author calls family life our first ____ for emotional learning.
questions.explain: Family life is described as the first school for emotional learning.

questions.q: Parents who take a child's upset seriously and help find positive ways to soothe it act as an emotional ____.
questions.explain: These parents use the upset as a chance to coach.

questions.q: The author says anger is so often prompted by first feeling ____.
questions.explain: This is one of the sophisticated insights an adept parent can teach.

questions.q: Carole Hooven and John Gottman did their research at the University of ____.
questions.explain: Their team at the University of Washington followed the families.

questions.q: Four-year-olds who resisted grabbing a ____ went on to have much higher SAT scores fourteen years later.
questions.explain: This Chapter 6 finding is recalled to show early emotional control predicts later achievement.

questions.q: Brazelton's diagnostic test for a baby's outlook toward life uses two ____ that the baby must put together.
questions.explain: The baby's handling of the blocks shows hopefulness or expected failure.

questions.q: The ability to balance one's own needs with those of others in group activity is called ____.
questions.explain: It is the seventh of the report's key ingredients.

questions.q: Erik Erikson put the first lessons of infancy in terms of "basic ____" versus basic mistrust.
questions.explain: The loving and the tense nighttime scenes show how trust or mistrust takes form.

questions.q: In the survey of maltreated children, ____ percent of the neglected ones had to repeat first grade.
questions.explain: The neglected youngsters did worst of all.

questions.q: In the first three or four years, the toddler's brain grows to about ____ of its full size.
questions.explain: This period is when emotional learning comes most readily.

questions.q: The longitudinal study of upstate New York children followed ____ children from age eight to thirty.
questions.explain: It showed how aggression passes from generation to generation.

questions.q: Martin seemed to lack the most primitive empathy, the instinct to stop ____ against someone who is hurt.
questions.explain: He kept hitting the sobbing girl despite her screams.

questions.q: After Chapter 11 on health, Chapter 12 turns to the ____ as the place where emotional lessons first take shape.
questions.explain: The title The Family Crucible names the family as the setting for early emotional learning.

questions.q: Put in order the steps of an emotional coach, from first to last.
items: Take the child's feelings seriously
Try to understand exactly what is upsetting the child
Help the child find positive ways to soothe the feelings
questions.explain: The coach first takes the upset seriously, then works out its cause, then helps with a better response.

questions.q: Order the actions of a hopeful baby in Brazelton's block test.
items: Picks up a block and mouths it
Rubs it in her hair
Drops it over the side to see if you will retrieve it
Completes the task of putting the blocks together
Looks up expecting to be told how great she is
questions.explain: The baby explores and tests the adult before finishing and looking for approval.

questions.q: Order what happens in the night scene with the tense mother and the crying baby.
items: Mother abruptly picks him up and tells him to be quiet
Baby tenses and stops nursing
Mother says to stop eating if that is all he wants
Mother puts him back in the crib and leaves
Baby cries until he falls asleep exhausted
questions.explain: The mother's tension is passed to the baby and the exchange ends with him left alone.

questions.q: Order the cycle that makes family life a school for aggression.
items: Parent is disciplined with arbitrary severity as a child
Child grows up aggressive and defiant
Adult repeats harsh, capricious discipline with own children
Children carry the violent model to school and the playground
questions.explain: The study shows the pattern repeating from one generation to the next.

questions.q: Order the stages in the life of the most belligerent children in the study of 870 children.
items: Quick to start fights at age eight
Drop out of school
By thirty, a record for violent crimes
Their own children act as troublemakers in grade school
questions.explain: The troublemaking continued into the next generation.

questions.q: Order how Martin's home taught him to respond to a child who keeps crying.
items: A quick consoling gesture
Nasty looks and shouts
Hitting
Outright beating
questions.explain: The author suggests Martin mirrors the escalation he learned at home.

questions.q: Put the sections of Chapter 12 in the order they appear.
items: Heart Start
Getting the Emotional Basics
How to Raise a Bully
Abuse the Extinction of Empathy
questions.explain: The chapter moves from the early emotional readiness of babies to the effects of harsh discipline and then of abuse.

questions.q: Match each parenting style to its description.
pairs: Treats the upset as trivial and waits for it to pass
Notices feelings but accepts any way of handling them
Harsh criticism and punishment, no respect for the child's feelings
Takes the child's feelings seriously and offers better ways to cope
questions.explain: Each style differs in how the parent responds to a child's feelings.

questions.q: Match each person or group to the part they play in the chapter.
pairs: Research team that watched parents and children with a video game
Harvard pediatrician with a block test of a baby's outlook
Described basic trust versus basic mistrust
National Center for Clinical Infant Programs
questions.explain: Each source supports a different step of the chapter's argument.

questions.q: Match each figure to what it describes.
pairs: Age of the baby in Brazelton's block test
SAT advantage for four-year-olds who resisted the marshmallow
Children in some states who must repeat first grade
Key ingredients of the capacity to learn
questions.explain: These figures anchor the case that emotional readiness shapes school success.

questions.q: Match each early experience to its effect.
pairs: Worst outcomes of the maltreated children surveyed
Can impair the brain's learning centers
questions.explain: The chapter ties early care to emotional outlook and to intellectual development.

questions.q: Match each group or feature to what the study found.
pairs: Dropped out and had violent crime records by thirty
Breeds worthlessness, helplessness and fear of threats
Repeating the style modeled by their own parents
questions.explain: The study shows a passing-down of aggression through harsh parenting.

questions.q: Match each abused toddler to what he or she did.
pairs: Turned pats on a crying girl into pounding
Froze in terror at a distant crying child
Patted a smaller child tenderly, then hit harder and harder
Made a ferocious face at a crying child
questions.explain: Each shows a lack of empathy or fear in the face of distress.

questions.q: Match each ingredient of readiness to learn to its meaning.
pairs: A sense of control and mastery of body, behavior and world
The sense that finding out is positive and pleasurable
Wish and capacity to have an impact and persist
Ability to modulate one's own actions in age-appropriate ways
Engaging with others through being understood and understanding
questions.explain: These are five of the seven ingredients on the report's list.

questions.q: Sort each parent response into the right group.

items.t: Asks whether the child is angry because a friend hurt his feelings
Suggests playing alone with a toy instead of hitting
Yells at a child for trying to tell his side
Says that however the child handles the storm is fine
Uses a bribe to stop the child being sad
Waits for the child's upset to blow over

questions.explain: Coaches understand the upset and suggest better responses; the other styles ignore, excuse or punish.

questions.q: Sort each advantage of emotionally adept parenting into social or cognitive.

items.t: More popular with peers
Seen by teachers as more socially skilled
Fewer behavioral problems such as rudeness
Better able to pay attention
Higher third-grade math and reading scores
More effective learners

questions.explain: The chapter separates social advantages from cognitive ones.

questions.q: Sort each sign into the baby who is hopeful or the baby who expects to fail.

items.t: Drops the block to see if you will retrieve it
Looks up bright-eyed, expecting praise
Has had a dose of approval and encouragement
Shows a hangdog look
Comes from a bleak, chaotic or neglectful home
Acts as if saying: I'm no good

questions.explain: Both babies can do the task; their expectations differ.

questions.q: Sort each detail into the calm mother or the tense mother.

items.t: Gazes affectionately at the baby
Says she is happy to see her
Baby drifts back to sleep
Stares stonily ahead while nursing
Puts the baby in the crib and stalks out
Baby squirms and stiffens

questions.explain: The two scenes show opposite emotional messages.

questions.q: Sort each item into a cause in the home or a result in the child.

items.t: Punishment based on the parent's mood
A violent model of aggressiveness
Parents repeating how they were raised
Feelings of worthlessness and helplessness
A sense that threats are everywhere
A combative, defiant posture toward the world

questions.explain: The home life produces the child's defensive stance.

questions.q: Sort each reaction to a crying child into abused toddlers or nonabused toddlers.

items.t: Fear
Anger
A physical attack
Concern
Sadness
Empathy

questions.explain: Not one abused toddler showed concern, while five of nine nonabused toddlers did.

questions.q: Name the three emotionally inept parenting styles and say how each treats a child's feelings.
questions.a: Ignoring feelings treats a child's upset as trivial and waits for it to pass. Laissez-faire parents notice the feeling but accept any way of handling it, even hitting, and soothe with bargains or bribes. Contemptuous parents show no respect for the feelings and respond with harsh criticism and punishment.

questions.q: What did the video game session reveal about parents, and what lesson might Leslie take from it?
questions.a: The session worked as a barometer of the parents' emotional style: overbearing parents lost patience and put the child down, while patient ones let her work it out. Leslie, ignored in her tears, may conclude that no one cares about her feelings. Repeated over childhood, such moments teach lessons that can shape a life.

questions.q: What does an emotional coach do, and what must parents have to do it well?
questions.a: A coach uses a child's upset to understand exactly what is troubling the child and to help the child find positive ways to soothe the feelings. To do this a parent needs a fairly good grasp of the rudiments of emotional intelligence, for example being able to tell apart different kinds of sadness.

questions.q: Describe the range of benefits found in children whose parents are emotionally adept.
questions.a: They get along better with parents and handle and soothe their own emotions better, with lower stress hormones. They are better liked by peers, rated as more socially skilled, with fewer behavior problems. They also pay attention better, and with IQ held constant score higher in third-grade math and reading.

questions.q: Describe Brazelton's block test and what it shows about the two kinds of babies.
questions.a: Brazelton gives an eight-month-old two blocks and shows how to put them together. A hopeful baby explores the blocks, watches for the adult to retrieve one, completes the task and looks for praise. A baby from a bleak or neglectful home can do it too but looks hangdog, expecting to fail.

questions.q: Why does the National Center for Clinical Infant Programs report treat emotional skills as central to school success?
questions.a: It finds that school success is predicted less by facts or early reading than by emotional and social traits such as self-assurance, impulse control, waiting, following directions and getting along. Almost all poorly performing students lack one or more of these elements. Readiness depends on knowing how to learn.

questions.q: List at least four of the seven ingredients of the capacity to learn and explain why they count as emotional intelligence.
questions.a: The seven are confidence, curiosity, intentionality, self-control, relatedness, capacity to communicate and cooperativeness. Each concerns how a child feels about himself and others and manages impulses and relationships, not a body of facts. They are formed by the early care the author calls a Heart Start.

questions.q: Contrast the two nighttime scenes with a crying two-month-old and the lessons each baby learns.
questions.a: In the first, the mother comes in warmly and the baby nurses and drifts to sleep, learning that people notice her needs and that she can get help. In the second, a tense mother is curt and leaves the baby crying, so he learns no one cares and efforts to get solace fail. Repeated over years, such exchanges build basic trust or mistrust.

questions.q: How does the chapter compare neglect with abuse, and what evidence does it give?
questions.a: The author says simple neglect can be more damaging than outright abuse. In a survey of maltreated children, the neglected did worst: most anxious, inattentive and apathetic, alternately aggressive and withdrawn. Of them 65 percent had to repeat first grade.

questions.q: Why are the first three or four years so important for emotional learning?
questions.a: The toddler's brain grows to about two thirds its full size and develops in complexity faster than it ever will again. Key learning, emotional learning above all, comes more readily then. Severe stress can impair learning centers, so early lessons have a profound effect, though later experience can partly remedy them.

questions.q: How is aggressiveness passed from one generation to the next in the 870-child study?
questions.a: The most belligerent children were disciplined with arbitrary, relentless severity and as parents did the same, while otherwise ignoring their children. They also modeled aggression for the children to copy at school. The parents were not necessarily mean-spirited; they were repeating the style modeled for them.

questions.q: Why does capricious discipline lead children to a combative posture toward the world?
questions.a: Punishment comes from how the parent feels, not from what the child did, so a bad mood brings severity and a good mood lets mayhem pass. This breeds feelings of worthlessness and helplessness and a sense that threats may strike at any time. Seen in light of that home life, a combative, defiant posture makes sense.

questions.q: Describe the day-care study of abused toddlers and its finding.
questions.a: Nine abused toddlers were compared with nine nonabused ones from equally poor, high-stress homes. Five of nine nonabused toddlers showed concern, sadness or empathy at another child's distress, but in twenty-seven instances not one abused toddler did. They showed fear, anger or physical attack, treating others as they had been treated.

questions.q: Why does the author conclude that abuse warps empathy, and what does he say about the brain in moments of crisis?
questions.a: Abused children like Martin meet a crying playmate with hitting, mirroring home where crying led to shouts and beatings. In moments when passions run high the limbic centers dominate, and the habits the emotional brain has learned repeatedly take over. So abused toddlers respond like miniature versions of their abusive parents.

questions.q: How does Chapter 12 build on the ideas of Chapters 6 and 7?
questions.a: It recalls the marshmallow test from Chapter 6, where early impulse control predicted later success, as support for emotional skills being the foundation of learning. It also recalls Chapter 7, where empathy begins in infancy through parental attunement and toddlers console crying playmates. Chapter 12 shows how family life gives or withholds those lessons.

questions.q: In the chapter's opening story, what was the game some Cleveland Elementary children called Purdy?
options: A school-run drill teaching children how to hide from an armed intruder
A game invented by teachers to help children talk about the shooting
A play reenactment by survivors of the schoolyard shooting, in which the villain massacres children and then himself
A video game popular in the neighborhood before the shooting took place
questions.explain: Goleman presents Purdy as the macabre reenactment by survivors of the February 1989 shooting. It appeared spontaneously in their play, which the book later treats as a way children begin to heal.

questions.q: The gunman at Cleveland Elementary sprayed bullets at the playground for ____ minutes before turning a pistol on himself.
questions.explain: The shooting lasted seven minutes, yet it was seared into the children's memories for months afterward.

questions.q: True or false: In the Purdy game, the story always ends with the children helpless as the gunman survives.
questions.explain: Sometimes the children changed the ending so that they kill Purdy. The book later reads this as a way of gaining mastery over a moment of helplessness.

questions.q: A man survives a car crash caused by a skidding truck. Months later he flinches and grips the wheel whenever any car, even a slow one, brakes hard nearby. Which idea from the chapter best explains this?
options: His amygdala has been damaged so it can no longer respond to danger
He is consciously choosing to dwell on the crash as a way of coping
He has dissociated from the crash and cannot recall any of it
The traumatic memory has become a mental hair trigger that sounds an alarm at the slightest hint of the dreaded moment
questions.explain: Goleman says traumatic memories become mental hair triggers, ready to sound an alarm at the least hint that the dread moment will recur. The man's reaction is excess alarm, not lost alarm or a deliberate choice.

questions.q: Sort these reactions of the Cleveland Elementary children by whether they show guarding against danger or intrusion of the memory.

items.t: Hovering beside the classroom doors at recess
Posting a designated child as lookout
Avoiding areas where children had died
Trying to sleep with eyes open to avoid dreams
Nightmares repeating the shooting
Hearing shots in a swinging tetherball chain
Fright at the announcement of St. Patrick's Day

questions.explain: Hypervigilance and avoidance are ways of watching for or steering clear of danger, while nightmares and false alarms are the memory breaking into awareness.

questions.q: Match each person in the chapter's opening to who or what they are.
pairs: The gunman, who had attended Cleveland Elementary himself years earlier
The school principal to whom a frantic girl cried that she heard shots
A child psychiatrist who specializes in PTSD in children
A Cambodian refugee whose three sons wanted toy machine guns
questions.explain: These are the people through whom the chapter introduces the Stockton shooting and its aftermath.

questions.q: Why does Goleman say violent acts are more pernicious than natural catastrophes like hurricanes?
options: Violence always involves more physical injury than natural disasters do
Victims of violence feel they were intentionally selected as targets, which shatters assumptions about the safety of the interpersonal world
Natural catastrophes are over so quickly that they cannot form memories
Victims of violence receive less sympathy and support from others
questions.explain: A hurricane leaves assumptions about people's trustworthiness untouched, whereas violence turns the social world into a place where people are potential threats.

questions.q: Goleman says the symptoms of PTSD are, in effect, signs of an overaroused ____.
questions.explain: The amygdala, the brain's emotional alarm center, keeps vivid memories of the trauma intruding on awareness.

questions.q: A man was struck on the back of the head without seeing his attacker and afterward walked directly in front of an old lady on the street. What does Goleman use this to show?
options: Victims of violence typically become more trusting of the elderly
Trauma memories fade fastest when the attacker was never seen
Fear of attack is learned only from watching other people be attacked
Human cruelties stamp memory with a template that regards with fear anything vaguely similar to the assault
questions.explain: The man used the old lady as protection against another blow from behind. His fear generalized to the whole situation, not just the attacker.

questions.q: In the study of Holocaust survivors, about ____ percent said they thought about the Holocaust almost daily even after a half century.
questions.explain: The study shows how the imprint of horror in memory can last a lifetime.

questions.q: True or false: Nearly fifty years after the death camps, nearly three quarters of the Holocaust survivors studied still became anxious at reminders such as a uniform or a knock at the door.
questions.explain: The haunting memories were still alive close to fifty years later, with reminders such as dogs barking or smoke rising from a chimney provoking anxiety.

questions.q: Why does Goleman say the hair-trigger phenomenon is a hallmark of emotional trauma of all kinds, and what examples does he give?
questions.a: Any traumatizing event, such as a fire, accident, earthquake, hurricane, rape, mugging, or repeated physical abuse in childhood, can implant trigger memories in the amygdala. Afterward the person fears anything vaguely similar to the original event. The mugged woman who feared elevators and the survivors who fear a knock at the door show how reminders set off alarm.

questions.q: What does the study of Holocaust survivors show about how long traumatic imprints can last, and what symptoms does it report?
questions.a: Close to fifty years after the camps, haunting memories were still alive in the survivors: nearly three quarters became anxious at reminders, about 60 percent thought of the Holocaust almost daily, and among those with active symptoms as many as eight in ten still had repeated nightmares. The imprint of horror in memory can last a lifetime.

questions.q: A boy who watched a house fire now panics at the smell of any smoke, even from a barbecue. Which idea from the chapter explains this best?
options: The boy has learned that all fires are equally dangerous by reasoning it through
His neocortex is flooding the amygdala with too much information
The boy is exaggerating his fear to get attention
A trigger memory implanted in the amygdala sounds the alarm at anything vaguely similar to the original event
questions.explain: Any traumatizing event, including a fire, can implant trigger memories in the amygdala. The memory fires at the least hint of the dreaded moment.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman name as traumatizing events that can implant trigger memories in the amygdala?
options: A fire or an auto accident
A natural catastrophe such as an earthquake or hurricane
Being raped or mugged
Failing a school examination
Being laid off from a job
questions.explain: Hundreds of thousands of people each year endure such disasters. Ordinary setbacks are not on his list.

questions.q: Why does Goleman say violence is more damaging to a person's world view than a natural catastrophe?
questions.a: In a hurricane, victims do not feel singled out, so their assumptions about people's trustworthiness stay intact. Victims of violence feel they were intentionally selected as the target of malevolence, which shatters those assumptions. In an instant the social world becomes dangerous, a place where people are potential threats.

questions.q: Put the events around the Purdy game in the order they happened.
items: Patrick Purdy fires on the playground during recess
Purdy shoots himself
The Purdy game spontaneously appears in the children's play
Goleman visits the school five months later
questions.explain: The shooting came first, then the play, then the visit.

questions.q: Match each statistic in the Holocaust survivors study to what it describes.
pairs: Thought about the Holocaust almost daily after half a century
As many as eight in ten
Of those with active symptoms, suffered repeated nightmares
Became anxious at reminders such as a uniform or a knock at the door
questions.explain: These figures come from the study of survivors close to fifty years after the camps.

questions.q: Match each reminder at Cleveland Elementary to how the school reacted.
pairs: The announcement of St. Patrick's Day
Fright spread as children thought it honored the killer
An ambulance siren to the rest home
Everything halted as the kids listened to see if it would stop
A frantic girl yelled that she heard shots
A rumor spread of a monster called Bloody Virgin Mary
questions.explain: Each shows how a small similar detail revived the memory.

questions.q: Sort these effects by whether they come from natural catastrophes or from violence by others.

items.t: Trust in people stays untouched
Victim is not singled out
Victim feels intentionally selected as a target
Social world becomes dangerous
People seen as potential threats

questions.explain: Violence by others shatters assumptions about safety of the interpersonal world.

questions.q: Goleman says PTSD represents a perilous lowering of the neural ____ for alarm.
questions.explain: With the setpoint lowered, the person reacts to life's ordinary moments as though they were emergencies.

questions.q: True or false: The brain changes of PTSD can arise only from a single overwhelming episode, not from years of cruelty.
questions.explain: Findings are typically based on single episodes, but similar results can come from cruelties inflicted over years, as with children who are abused.

questions.q: Dennis Charney says the same biological impact can follow combat, torture, childhood abuse, or a one-time hurricane. What is the common feature?
options: The stress was uncontrollable
The stress lasted for more than a year
The victim was physically wounded
The event was caused by another person
questions.explain: Charney puts it as: “All uncontrollable stress can have the same biological impact.” The operative word is uncontrollable.

questions.q: The element that makes a given event subjectively overwhelming and so can trigger PTSD is ____.
questions.explain: People who feel they can exert some control, however minor, fare far better emotionally than those who feel utterly helpless.

questions.q: Two passengers survive the same bus crash. One tries to open the emergency door for others, while the other thinks, I'm dead, and freezes. According to the chapter, which is more susceptible to PTSD, and why?
options: The helper, because taking action increases exposure to the danger
Both equally, because the event was identical for each
Neither, because PTSD requires repeated rather than single events
The frozen passenger, because feeling that there is nothing to be done is when the brain change begins
questions.explain: Krystal contrasts a person who defends himself with one who thinks he is dead: the helpless one is more susceptible.

questions.q: True or false: In the laboratory rat studies, the rat that could press a lever to stop the shocks for both cages showed the stress-induced brain changes, while the helpless rat did not.
questions.explain: It was the helpless rat that showed the stress-induced brain changes, even though both rats received exactly the same amount of shock.

questions.q: Describe the paired-rat experiment and what Goleman says it shows about PTSD.
questions.a: Two rats in separate cages receive identical mild shocks, but only one cage has a lever that stops the shock for both. Over days and weeks both get the same total shock, yet only the helpless rat shows the stress-induced brain changes. This shows that helplessness is the wild card in triggering PTSD, which helps explain why children shot at on the playground were so vulnerable.

questions.q: Put the stages of the Vietnam veteran's flashback in the order they occur in his account.
items: A storm front passes and thunder crackles
He wakes instantly, frozen in fear
He feels himself back at his guard post in Vietnam
He sees what is left of his buddy Troy
The next thunderclap makes him jump so much that he falls to the floor
questions.explain: The account moves from the thunder to the instant reliving of the combat memory and ends with a second clap throwing him to the floor.

questions.q: Which of these bodily reactions does the Vietnam veteran report in his flashback?
options: Freezing hands while sweat pours from his body
The hairs on the back of his neck standing on end
A damp sulfur smell
A sense of calm after waking
A feeling that the danger is long past
questions.explain: The memory is relived with vivid bodily detail and fear, not calm or reassurance.

questions.q: What does Charney mean when he says victims of devastating trauma 'may never be the same biologically'?
questions.a: Charney says that uncontrollable stress of any kind, whether combat, torture, repeated childhood abuse, or a single hurricane or accident, can produce the same biological impact. The brain's chemistry is altered by a single instance of overwhelming terror. Goleman adds that this is why such memories become so indelible.

questions.q: After the same flood, Sam, who climbed to a roof and helped pull neighbors up, copes well, while Lee, swept away and sure he would die, develops PTSD. Which idea from the chapter explains the difference?
options: Feeling helpless, with nothing one can do, is the wild card that makes an event overwhelming
Sam had a larger amygdala than Lee
Lee received a larger amount of danger than Sam
Natural disasters only traumatize people who are alone
questions.explain: Even minor control exerted in a catastrophe leaves people far better off than feeling utterly helpless.

questions.q: A cyclist is hit by a car and lies pinned, unable to move or call out. Another cyclist hit in the same way rolls clear and phones for help. Using the chapter, which is more at risk of PTSD and why?
questions.a: The pinned cyclist is more at risk, because Goleman identifies helplessness as the wild card that makes an event subjectively overwhelming. People who exert some control, however minor, fare far better. The lab rats with no lever showed the brain changes while those who could stop the shocks did not.

questions.q: Put the causal chain from helplessness to the setpoint of PTSD in order.
items: A life-threatening event occurs and the person feels helpless
The brain change begins
The neural setpoint for alarm is lowered
Ordinary moments are met as though they were emergencies
questions.explain: Krystal says feeling there is nothing you can do is when the brain change begins.

questions.q: Match each experiment or observation to what it showed.
pairs: Paired rats, one with a lever
Helplessness is the wild card in triggering stress-induced brain changes
More left prefrontal activity meant faster recovery from learned fear
Clapping behind a person with too much CRF
The startle response does not habituate
High opioid levels raise tolerance for pain
questions.explain: Each result supports a different strand of the chapter's account.

questions.q: Sort these by whether they make PTSD more likely or less likely.

items.t: Feeling utterly helpless
Thinking I'm dead
Feeling life is in danger with no escape
Knowing how to defend oneself and acting
Exerting even minor control
A lever that stops the shock

questions.explain: Feeling in control protects, helplessness makes the event subjectively overwhelming.

questions.q: The structure that regulates the brain's secretion of the catecholamines adrenaline and noradrenaline is the locus ____.
questions.explain: This structure is closely linked to the amygdala and other limbic structures.

questions.q: True or false: The catecholamine surge that mobilizes the body for emergency also stamps memories with special strength.
questions.explain: That is part of why emotionally charged moments become indelible memories.

questions.q: Charles Nemeroff says that too much ____ makes you overreact.
questions.explain: He gives the example of a Vietnam vet with PTSD flooded by the same feelings as in the original trauma when a car backfires in a parking lot.

questions.q: At a fireworks show, one friend jumps at the first bang but barely notices the fourth. Another friend, who is a trauma survivor with too much CRF, jumps just as hard at the fourth bang as the first. What does the chapter call the second friend's failure?
options: A failure to habituate, because the startle response is overactive
A failure to dissociate, because memory is blocked
A failure of extinction, because the amygdala lost its fear
A failure of mourning, because the loss was not accepted
questions.explain: Nemeroff describes the clapping test: most people stop startling by the third or fourth repetition, but people with too much CRF do not habituate.

questions.q: Which of these PTSD symptoms does Goleman attribute to the hyperactive opioid system?
options: Anhedonia, the inability to feel pleasure
A general emotional numbness
Dissociation, including not remembering crucial minutes of the event
An exaggerated startle response
Extra-large surges of adrenaline at reminders
questions.explain: The startle response and adrenaline surges belong to the CRF and catecholamine changes. The opioid changes bring numbing.

questions.q: Match each brain system changed in PTSD to its effect.
pairs: Extra-large surges of adrenaline and noradrenaline at reminders of the trauma
Oversecretion of the main stress hormone, producing an overactive startle response
Numbing of feeling, including anhedonia and emotional indifference
questions.explain: Goleman describes three sets of changes: catecholamines, CRF, and opioids.

questions.q: True or false: People close to someone with PTSD may experience the emotional numbness as a lack of empathy.
questions.explain: Anhedonia and numbness can leave the person cut off from life or from concern about others' feelings.

questions.q: According to the chapter, why does one person exposed to a catastrophe develop PTSD while another does not?
options: The person who recovers has a larger neocortex that blocks all fear
The person who develops PTSD always faced more violent circumstances
An amygdala already primed to find danger, as by earlier stress, raises its alarm to a higher pitch when real danger comes
PTSD appears only in those who did not talk about the event right away
questions.explain: Animals exposed to even mild stress when young were far more vulnerable to trauma-induced brain changes later.

questions.q: When the amygdala takes on a new setpoint, Goleman says all of life is on the verge of becoming an ____.
questions.explain: Even an innocent moment is then susceptible to an explosion of fear run amok.

questions.q: Sort these PTSD changes by whether they raise alarm or blunt feeling.

items.t: Extra-large catecholamine secretion
Oversecreted CRF
Failure to habituate to repeated startle
Flashbacks at the sound of a car backfiring
Inability to feel pleasure
Heightened tolerance for pain
Not remembering crucial minutes of the event

questions.explain: The catecholamine and CRF changes make the person jumpy and reactive, while the opioid changes numb feeling.

questions.q: Why does Goleman say the short-term advantages of PTSD's neural changes become lasting problems?
questions.a: Under duress it is adaptive to be vigilant, aroused, ready for anything, impervious to pain, and indifferent to disturbing events. But when the brain changes so that these states become predispositions, the person is like a car stuck in perpetual high gear. The new setpoint makes all of life seem to be on the verge of an emergency.

questions.q: Name the three sets of limbic changes Goleman describes in PTSD and say what each leads to.
questions.a: The locus ceruleus and catecholamine system becomes hyperreactive, producing extra-large doses of adrenaline and noradrenaline at reminders. The limbic-pituitary circuit oversecretes CRF, leading to overreaction and a startle response that does not habituate. The opioid system becomes hyperactive, numbing feeling and causing anhedonia, emotional numbness, and possibly dissociation.

questions.q: A veteran with PTSD sits through his daughter's wedding feeling nothing and seems indifferent to the people around him. Which PTSD change does Goleman link to this?
options: The oversecretion of CRF, which exaggerates the startle response
The hyperreactive catecholamine system, which marks memories strongly
The hyperactive opioid system, which numbs feelings and produces anhedonia
The prefrontal cortex's suppression of the amygdala
questions.explain: Endorphin changes produce a numbing of certain feelings, including the inability to feel pleasure and a sense of being cut off from others.

questions.q: A teenager who was mildly bullied at an early age is far more shaken by a car accident than classmates who were never bullied. What idea from the chapter fits?
options: An amygdala primed by earlier stress raises its alarm to a higher pitch when real danger comes
Bullying numbs the opioid system so the teenager feels more
The teenager's neocortex had grown larger from the early stress
The earlier bullying protected against later trauma
questions.explain: Animals exposed to even mild stress when young were far more vulnerable to trauma-induced brain changes later.

questions.q: Which limbic structures does Goleman say are closely linked to the locus ceruleus and the amygdala?
options: The hippocampus
The hypothalamus
Other limbic structures with circuitry extending into the cortex
The cerebellum
The spinal cord
questions.explain: The locus ceruleus and amygdala are linked with other limbic structures such as the hippocampus and hypothalamus.

questions.q: Explain how the hyperactive opioid system changes feeling in PTSD.
questions.a: The opioid system secretes endorphins, the brain's own morphine, which raise tolerance for pain; battlefield surgeons noted wounded soldiers needed less narcotic. In PTSD the system becomes hyperactive and numbs certain feelings, causing anhedonia and emotional numbness that others may see as lack of empathy. It may also lead to dissociation, such as being unable to remember crucial parts of the event.

questions.q: Put the steps of a PTSD reaction to a reminder in order, as with the Cleveland children and the siren.
items: A siren like those heard after the shooting sounds
The locus ceruleus secretes extra-large doses of catecholamines
The body is mobilized for an emergency
The child panics though there is no real threat
questions.explain: The reminder hyperactivates the catecholamine system.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning in the chapter.
pairs: Being continually on guard against a repetition of the terror
Inability to remember crucial minutes, hours, or days of the event
A harmless thing becoming dreaded through association with something frightening
questions.explain: These terms appear in Goleman's account of PTSD and of acquired fear.

questions.q: What does Goleman say the CRF clapping test reveals?
options: People with too much CRF cannot hear sudden noise
People with too much CRF startle only the first time
Most people stop startling by the third or fourth clap, but people with too much CRF respond as much to the fourth as to the first
All people respond equally to each repetition
questions.explain: People with too much CRF do not habituate.

questions.q: Psychologists call the process by which something harmless becomes dreaded through association with something frightening ____ conditioning.
questions.explain: In laboratory animals the fears induced this way can last for years.

questions.q: A woman is stung by wasps in her garden and avoids it. Over several weeks she sits there calmly with no stings and her fear fades. Which idea in the chapter does this match?
options: PTSD, in which spontaneous relearning never occurs
Ordinary fear conditioning subsides with time through natural relearning, when the feared thing is met without anything truly scary
Dissociation, in which the memory is blocked from awareness
The opioid numbing of feeling after trauma
questions.explain: Goleman's example is a child chased by a snarling shepherd who loses her fear by playing with a friendly dog.

questions.q: True or false: Charney describes extinction of a learned fear as a passive fading that needs no active learning.
questions.explain: He says extinction “appears to involve an active learning process,” which is impaired in people with PTSD.

questions.q: Charney says extinction of fear appears to involve an active ____ process.
questions.explain: The impairment of this process leads to the abnormal persistence of emotional memories.

questions.q: According to Charney, what happens in the brain when PTSD lifts?
options: The prefrontal cortex actively suppresses the amygdala's command to respond with fear
The original fear is erased from the amygdala
The thalamus stops sending signals to the amygdala
The locus ceruleus permanently stops secreting catecholamines
questions.explain: The relearning is cortical. The original fear does not go away completely.

questions.q: Put the steps of ordinary fear conditioning and natural recovery in order.
items: Something harmless is paired with something frightening
The person comes to dread the harmless thing
The feared thing is met again with nothing truly scary
The fear gradually subsides
questions.explain: Natural relearning happens when the feared object is encountered without the original threat.

questions.q: In overcoming acquired fear, the ____ is critical, though the amygdala is key in acquiring it.
questions.explain: Goleman contrasts the amygdala's role in learning fear with the neocortex's role in overcoming it.

questions.q: Why does PTSD fail to fade the way an ordinary conditioned fear does?
questions.a: Normally a conditioned fear fades through natural relearning when the feared thing is met again without anything truly scary, as with the child who plays with a friendly dog. In PTSD the brain changes are so strong that an amygdala hijacking occurs at anything reminiscent of the trauma, strengthening the fear pathway. The feared thing is never paired with calm, and the active learning of extinction is impaired.

questions.q: Which of these describe Davidson's experiment on acquired fear?
options: People first learned an aversion to a loud noise
People with more left prefrontal activity got over the fear faster
It served as a lower-key parallel of PTSD
People with more amygdala damage got over the fear faster
It used pairs of rats with a lever
questions.explain: It suggested a cortical role in letting go of learned distress. The lever experiment belongs to the helplessness research.

questions.q: A survivor of a bombing panics at fireworks every July and has never once felt calm around them. Why, by Charney's account, will the fear not fade by itself?
options: Fear of fireworks is an inborn reaction that cannot be unlearned
The neocortex has stopped receiving any information about the fireworks
Each reminder triggers a hijacking that strengthens the fear pathway, so the feared thing is never paired with calm
He should be exposed only once, which is not enough to relearn
questions.explain: Spontaneous relearning fails because the amygdala never experiences the reminder together with a feeling of calm.

questions.q: Which of these does Charney say about the extinction of a learned fear?
options: It appears to involve an active learning process
It is impaired in people with PTSD
Its impairment leads to abnormal persistence of emotional memories
It happens passively without any new learning
It erases the fear from the amygdala
questions.explain: The fear stays in the amygdala and is suppressed by the cortex; it is not erased.

questions.q: What did Davidson's experiment on learned aversion to a loud noise suggest about getting over fear?
questions.a: People first learned an aversion to a loud noise, a lower-key parallel of PTSD. Those with more activity in the left prefrontal cortex got over the acquired fear more quickly. This suggests the cortex plays a role in letting go of learned distress, consistent with Charney's view that relearning is cortical.

questions.q: Put Charney's account of why PTSD fear persists in order.
items: Something vaguely reminiscent of the trauma appears
An amygdala hijacking occurs
The fear pathway is strengthened
The feared thing is never paired with calm
The amygdala never relearns a milder reaction
questions.explain: Each hijacking strengthens the fear pathway, so no relearning can happen.

questions.q: Sort these by whether they concern acquiring a fear or overcoming it.

items.t: Amygdala hijacking at a reminder
Thalamus-amygdala-prefrontal pathway
Fear strengthened by each reminder
Prefrontal cortex suppressing the amygdala
Left prefrontal activity in Davidson's study
Extinction as an active learning process

questions.explain: The amygdala is key in acquiring fear, and the neocortex is critical in overcoming it.

questions.q: The good news, says Goleman, is that traumas as profound as those causing PTSD can heal, and the route to healing is through ____.
questions.explain: The emotional circuitry can be reeducated.

questions.q: Which are the two avenues of healing Goleman sees in the Purdy game?
options: The memory repeats in a context of low anxiety, which desensitizes it
The children give the tragedy a better outcome, boosting their sense of mastery
The children are praised by adults for playing it
The children are prevented from talking about the event
The children's play removes the memory
questions.explain: Both routes work through safe, repeated replay, not through suppression or adult approval.

questions.q: The Chowchilla children, kidnapped in 1973, were held in a buried bus for ____ hours.
questions.explain: Lenore Terr found them still reenacting the ordeal in play five years later.

questions.q: Match each Barbie game described by Terr to what it reflects.
pairs: Washing a Barbie over and over
A girl who hated the feeling of other children's urine on her skin
Barbie goes somewhere and returns safely, which is the point
The doll suffocates, echoing the buried bus
questions.explain: These games show that the kidnapping was still replayed in the children's play.

questions.q: One child needs only one or two replays of a visit to the dentist, but another keeps replaying a kidnapping for years in a grim, monotonous ritual. What explains the difference, according to Terr?
options: The second child has an unusually poor memory
The first child is avoiding the memory instead
Dentist visits are never traumatic
The more overwhelming the trauma, the more endless repetitions the child needs
questions.explain: If the trauma is minor, once or twice may be enough; if it is overwhelming, a child needs endless repetitions.

questions.q: True or false: If a child's trauma is minor, such as going to the dentist, replaying it once or twice may be enough.
questions.explain: Only overwhelming trauma needs endless repetition.

questions.q: The emotional brain is attuned to the mode Freud called the primary ____.
questions.explain: This is the mode of metaphor, story, myth, and the arts.

questions.q: Describe the drawing of the five-year-old boy treated by Spencer Eth and what it shows about art in therapy.
questions.a: The boy had hidden under a blanket while his mother was beaten to death, and he was reluctant to talk. Eth asked him to draw anything, and he drew a race-car driver with strikingly large eyes, which Eth took to refer to the boy's own peeking at the killer. Hidden references to the trauma almost always appear in such children's art, so Eth uses drawing as the opening gambit, and drawing itself begins the mastery of the trauma.

questions.q: What do the Holocaust survivor findings suggest about whether the brain changes of PTSD are permanent?
questions.a: About three quarters had active symptoms after a half century, but a quarter of those once troubled no longer had them. Those still symptomatic showed the catecholamine-related changes typical of PTSD, while the recovered showed none. Goleman concludes that the changes are not indelible and that the emotional circuitry can be reeducated through relearning.

questions.q: After a frightening ambulance ride, a six-year-old stages game after game in which her teddy bear is rushed off and always gets home safe. How would Terr's account read this play?
options: As a voluntary replay that lets her rethink the ordeal and master it, heading off the need to dam it up
As a sign she has become numb to the ordeal
As a sign her memory of the ride has been lost
As a sign she should be discouraged from playing such games
questions.explain: Terr saw children use fantasy and play to recall and rethink ordeals, as in the Traveling Barbie game where the doll returns safely.

questions.q: A frightened child asked to draw anything produces a house with one huge locked door and tiny watching windows. How would Spencer Eth view the drawing?
options: The drawing proves the child has no traumatic memory
The drawing is a test of artistic ability
The drawing should be set aside, since only speech counts in therapy
Hidden references to the traumatic scene almost always appear in such children's art, so it may open the way to talk about the horror
questions.explain: Eth uses drawing as the opening gambit because the potent memories intrude in the art just as in thoughts, and drawing begins mastery of the trauma.

questions.q: True or false: A girl who keeps replaying a terrifying event in her doll games, as the Chowchilla girls did with Barbie dolls, is in Terr's view using play to rethink the ordeal rather than damming it up.
questions.explain: Voluntary replays through fantasy and play seem to head off the need to dam up memories that burst through later as flashbacks.

questions.q: What did Terr conclude about why children replay trauma in play, and how many repetitions are needed?
questions.a: Terr believes children less often become numb because they use fantasy, play, and daydreams to recall and rethink their ordeals. Voluntary replays seem to head off damming up potent memories that later burst through as flashbacks. A minor trauma may need only once or twice, but an overwhelming one needs endless repetitions in a grim, monotonous ritual.

questions.q: Sort these examples by whether they come from spontaneous play or from Spencer Eth's therapy.

items.t: Children kill Purdy in the game
Washing a Barbie over and over
Traveling Barbie returns safely
Drawing a race-car driver with huge eyes
Playing games to build rapport
Narrative becoming free-flowing

questions.explain: The first three are children's own games; the rest are steps in the therapy with the five-year-old.

questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: Put Herman's three stages of recovery in order.
items: Attaining a sense of safety
Remembering the trauma and mourning the loss
Reestablishing a normal life
questions.explain: Safety must come first so that relearning can proceed.

questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: Another early step is to help patients regain some sense of ____ over what is happening to them.
questions.explain: This directly unlearns the lesson of helplessness that the trauma itself imparted.

questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: After a robbery, a man feels helpless. His therapist helps him arrange for neighbors to check on him and to call the police when needed. Which part of the chapter's account does this match?
options: Retelling the story in as much vivid detail as possible
Regaining a sense of control as an early step, which unlearns the lesson of helplessness
Mourning what was lost
Reeducating the amygdala through art
questions.explain: Irene likewise mobilized friends and family to buffer her from her stalker and got the police to intervene.

questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: Which of these does Goleman name as ways to help patients feel less at the mercy of their emotional alarms?
options: Antidepressants that act on the serotonin system
Beta-blockers such as propranolol
Relaxation techniques
Stimulants that raise arousal
Opioid painkillers
questions.explain: Medications and relaxation can counter some effects of PTSD and open a window for relearning.

questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: According to Herman, what pace should retelling of the trauma ideally follow?
options: As fast as possible so the memory is exhausted
One short telling, never repeated
Whatever pace the patient's family prefers
The pace of people who recover naturally, as an inner clock alternates intrusive memories with weeks or months of respite
questions.explain: The alternation of reimmersion and respite allows spontaneous review and relearning.

questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: True or false: Herman says the therapist should keep retelling at full intensity even if it triggers overwhelming fears.
questions.explain: The therapist should ease the pace to keep reactions within a bearable range that will not disrupt relearning.

questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: The goal of retelling is to put the entire memory into ____.
questions.explain: That includes dissociated parts and the patient's own reactions.

questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: Put the stages of the five-year-old boy's therapy with Spencer Eth in order.
items: He draws a picture of a race-car driver with large eyes
He and Eth play games and build rapport
He retells the murder in a stereotyped, repeated way
His narrative becomes free-flowing and his nightmares less frequent
He talks only about daily life in his new home
questions.explain: The boy's recovery moved from rapport to retelling to daily life as the hold of the trauma faded.

questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: The decline in the boy's nightmares was, says Eth, an indication of some “trauma ____.”
questions.explain: Eth used the phrase as the boy's narrative opened up and his body relaxed.

questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: What purpose does mourning serve in Herman's account?
options: It proves the trauma was the patient's fault
It replaces the need for retelling
It marks the ability to let go of the trauma to some degree and look ahead
It keeps the memory vivid forever
questions.explain: Instead of being perpetually captured by the past, patients can begin to hope and rebuild.

questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: Which losses does Herman say patients may need to mourn?
options: The death of a loved one
Regret over some step not taken to save someone
The shattering of confidence that people can be trusted
The end of the therapist's treatment
The loss of the chance to forget
questions.explain: Mourning accompanies the retelling of painful events.

questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: Which of these are signs that a trauma has largely been overcome, per Herman?
options: Physiological symptoms reduced to a manageable level
Being able to bear the feelings tied to the memories
No longer having memories erupt at uncontrollable moments
Never having to think about the event again
Complete disappearance of all aftereffects
questions.explain: Herman notes aftereffects or occasional recurrences often persist.

questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: What is especially significant as a sign of recovery?
options: Being able to revisit trauma memories voluntarily and to put them aside like any other memory
Being unable to recall the event at all
Having no emotional response to any reminder
Having talked about the event with everyone you know
questions.explain: Memory no longer erupts at uncontrollable moments.

questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: Sort these elements by whether they belong to Herman's stage of regaining safety or to retelling and mourning.

items.t: Learning that jumpiness is part of PTSD
Mobilizing friends and family as a buffer
Taking propranolol
Learning relaxation techniques
Recounting every sordid detail of the event
Putting sensory details and feelings into words
Grieving a loved one who died
Easing the pace when the retelling overwhelms

questions.explain: Safety work calms the circuits; retelling and mourning reconstruct the memory in safety.

questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: Match each step of recovery to what it does for the emotional brain.
pairs: Calms the easily triggered circuits so relearning is possible
Brings the memory under neocortical control
Lets the person let go of the trauma and look ahead
Brings trusting relationships and a belief system that finds meaning
questions.explain: These are Herman's steps as Goleman presents them.

questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: Describe Herman's three stages of recovery and say what the emotional brain learns at each.
questions.a: First comes safety: understanding symptoms, regaining control, medication, and relaxation calm the circuits enough to allow relearning. Second comes remembering and mourning: retelling the trauma in words in the safety of therapy teaches the circuitry that security can coexist with the memory, and mourning lets go of it. Third, the person reestablishes a normal life with trusting relationships and a belief system that finds meaning.

questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: What does the Irene case show about the first stage of recovery?
questions.a: Irene, stalked and harassed after an attempted rape, had PTSD symptoms and felt a prisoner in her own house. She mobilized friends and family as a buffer and got the police to intervene, which regained control and unlearned the helplessness the trauma taught. This is Herman's first step of attaining safety.

questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: What are the markers of success in reeducating the emotional brain after trauma?
questions.a: Physiological symptoms drop to a manageable level and the person can bear the feelings tied to the memories. Trauma memories no longer erupt at uncontrollable moments but can be revisited voluntarily and put aside like any other memory. The person rebuilds a life with strong trusting relationships and a belief system that finds meaning.
