questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: Match each researcher to what the chapter credits them with.
pairs: Three stages of recovery from trauma
Traumatic games among children such as in Chowchilla
Extinction of fear as an active learning process
Left prefrontal cortex as a damper on distress
questions.explain: Each is cited for a different strand of the chapter's account of trauma and relearning.

questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: A patient with PTSD begins retelling her assault and soon becomes flooded with overwhelming fear. According to Herman, what should the therapist do?
options: Insist she continue at full intensity to exhaust the memory
Ease the pace to keep her reactions within a bearable range so relearning is not disrupted
End therapy until the memory fades by itself
Switch to mourning the loss and drop the retelling for good
questions.explain: For intractable PTSD, retelling can sometimes trigger overwhelming fears, and the pace should be adjusted accordingly.

questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: Months after a crash, Ana can think about it when she chooses and then put it aside as she would any other memory. Which of Herman's signs does this show?
options: Complete disappearance of all physiological symptoms
Trauma memories no longer erupt at uncontrollable moments but can be revisited voluntarily and set aside
Total loss of the memory of the crash
A stronger belief that the world is dangerous
questions.explain: Herman says especially significant is being able to revisit trauma memories voluntarily and to put them aside.

questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: True or false: A man who feels guilt over a step he did not take to save a friend in an accident should, per Herman, expect mourning of such regret to be part of recovery.
questions.explain: Herman lists regret over some step not taken to save someone among the losses patients mourn while retelling.

questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: A woman who survived a mugging seeks help for PTSD. Which of these would the chapter support as part of her recovery?
options: Learning that her jumpiness and nightmares are symptoms of PTSD
Finding ways to regain some sense of control, such as friends who form a buffer
Retelling the mugging in vivid detail once she feels safe with a trusted therapist
Forcing a full retelling at maximum pace even if it overwhelms her
Never discussing the mugging again
questions.explain: Safety and control come first, then retelling at a bearable pace.

questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: Why does Herman want retelling of the trauma to proceed at a particular pace, and what does that pace imitate?
questions.a: The ideal pace mimics people who recover naturally without PTSD, in whom an inner clock doses them with intrusive memories alternating with weeks or months when they remember little. This alternation of reimmersion and respite allows spontaneous review and relearning. If retelling triggers overwhelming fears, the therapist should ease the pace so reactions stay bearable.

questions.section: Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
questions.q: Put the work of retelling the trauma in order.
items: The therapist builds safety and trust
The patient retells the event vividly
Sensory details and feelings are put into words
The memory comes more under neocortical control
Security is experienced alongside the memory
questions.explain: Retelling happens in the harbor of safety and transforms the memory.

questions.q: According to LeDoux, what does therapy do?
options: It erases emotional learning from the amygdala
It teaches the neocortex how to inhibit the amygdala, suppressing the propensity to act while a subdued basic emotion remains
It prevents the amygdala from reacting at all
It strengthens the amygdala's control over the neocortex
questions.explain: LeDoux says: “Once your emotional system learns something, it seems you never let it go.”

questions.q: After successful psychotherapy, what remains is a ____ reaction, a remnant of the original sensitivity.
questions.explain: The prefrontal cortex can brake the amygdala but cannot keep it from reacting in the first place.

questions.q: According to Goleman, what can we control about emotional outbursts?
options: Whether they occur at all
How long they last
When they occur
How strong they are in the first instant
questions.explain: We cannot decide when we have outbursts, but a quicker recovery may be a mark of emotional maturity.

questions.q: Two coworkers feel a flash of anger at the same criticism. One calms down in minutes; the other stews all day. By the chapter's reasoning, which shows greater emotional maturity?
options: The second, because deep feeling shows maturity
Neither, because outbursts show immaturity
The first, because they never felt anger
The first, because quicker recovery from outbursts is one mark of emotional maturity
questions.explain: We have more control over how long outbursts last than over whether they begin.

questions.q: Which two changes did Luborsky's patients show over long-term therapy?
options: Their emotional reaction to triggering events became less distressing
Their overt responses became more effective at getting what they wanted
Their underlying wish or fear disappeared
The initial twinge of feeling vanished
They stopped having relationship conflicts
questions.explain: The underlying wish or fear and the initial twinge did not change.

questions.q: By the end of therapy the patients had only ____ as many negative emotional reactions as at the start.
questions.explain: They were also twice as likely to get the positive response they wanted.

questions.q: A man in therapy for years still feels a pang of fear of rejection when his partner is late, but now responds calmly and asks directly what happened. Which finding does this fit?
options: Therapy removes the sensitivity that underlies the reaction
Therapy has had no effect on the patient
The tendency for the reaction to be triggered stays, but the response after it changes
The patient has dissociated from his fear
questions.explain: What changes in therapy is mainly the responses once an emotional reaction is triggered.

questions.q: Match each pattern in Luborsky's studies to its outcome.
pairs: Created a backlash of anger or coldness in the other person
Withdrawing in self-defense from an anticipated slight
Left the other person miffed by the seeming rebuff
Emotional reaction less distressing and responses more effective
The underlying wish or fear and the initial twinge of feeling
questions.explain: Therapy altered responses, not the root sensitivity.

questions.q: What did Luborsky's studies show about what changes and what does not change in psychotherapy?
questions.a: Patients' emotional reaction to triggering events became less distressing and their responses more effective, so they had half as many negative reactions and were twice as likely to get the response they wanted. What did not change was the underlying wish or fear and the initial twinge of feeling. In brain terms, the limbic circuitry still sends the alarm while the prefrontal cortex has learned a healthier response.

questions.q: Explain LeDoux's conjecture about how therapy changes emotional patterns and what remains afterward.
questions.a: LeDoux holds that once the emotional system learns something it is never let go; therapy teaches the neocortex to inhibit the amygdala. The propensity to act is suppressed while the basic emotion remains in subdued form, a vestigial reaction. So we cannot stop the amygdala from reacting but can control how long an outburst lasts.

questions.q: What does Goleman mean by saying 'Emotional learning is lifelong'?
questions.a: Even the deepest implanted habits of the heart learned in childhood can be reshaped. The limbic circuitry may still send alarm signals, but the prefrontal cortex and related zones can learn a new, more healthy response. Traumatic and ordinary emotional wounds alike can be healed through relearning.

questions.q: A man who was chronically ignored by his parents as a child now is overly demanding with his partner, driving her away. How does the chapter place such patterns?
options: Only true trauma such as PTSD can affect adult relationships
They are conscious choices which therapy cannot change
They show a deficiency in the neocortex that cannot be treated
Ordinary childhood travails, short of trauma, still imprint the emotional brain and distort intimate relationships later
questions.explain: Neglect and rejection may never reach the fever pitch of trauma but leave their imprint, and psychotherapy is the task of healing such scars.

questions.q: Which feelings does the chapter say Luborsky's patients felt flooded by during their ill-fated encounters?
options: Hopelessness and sadness
Resentment and anger
Guilt and self-blame
Elation and triumph
Boredom
questions.explain: These upsetting feelings flooded the patients when their wishes and fears were activated.

questions.q: Why does Goleman say a quicker recovery from emotional outbursts may be a mark of emotional maturity?
questions.a: The prefrontal cortex can refine or put the brakes on the amygdala's impulse but cannot keep it from reacting in the first place. So we cannot decide when outbursts happen but we have more control over how long they last. Therefore recovering sooner is where growth in emotional control shows.

questions.q: Put the elements of a patient's ill-fated encounter in Luborsky's analysis in order.
items: A deep wish or fear is activated in a relationship
The patient responds in a self-defeating way
The other person reacts with a backlash or a rebuff
The patient feels flooded by upsetting feelings
questions.explain: The conflict triggers a habitual response, which provokes the other person and floods the patient.

questions.q: Sort these by whether long-term therapy changed them in Luborsky's studies.

items.t: Distress of the emotional reaction
Effectiveness of the patient's response
Number of negative reactions
Chance of getting the desired response
The underlying wish or fear
The initial twinge of feeling

questions.explain: Therapy changed responses but not the root sensitivity.

questions.q: What does the chapter title pair of Trauma and Emotional Relearning signal about the chapter's message?
options: Trauma permanently destroys emotional intelligence
Only children can relearn after trauma
Even the most extreme emotional imprinting can be healed through relearning
Trauma is best treated with medication alone
questions.explain: Goleman concludes that the emotional circuitry can be reeducated and that emotional learning is lifelong.

questions.q: How does this chapter build on Chapter 2, Anatomy of an Emotional Hijacking?
options: It uses the hijacking circuit to explain why traumatic memories are so indelible and why PTSD sufferers overreact
It disproves the hijacking account of Chapter 2
It shifts to discussing only the neocortex
It applies the hijacking idea to groups at work
questions.explain: The more brutal the events that trigger the amygdala hijacking, the more indelible the memory.

questions.q: Put the chapter's sections in the order they appear.
items: Horror Frozen in Memory
PTSD as a Limbic Disorder
Emotional Relearning
Reeducating the Emotional Brain
Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
Psychotherapy as an Emotional Tutorial
questions.explain: The chapter moves from how trauma is imprinted to how it is healed and then to ordinary therapy.

questions.q: Why does the chapter explain the limbic changes of PTSD before it turns to relearning?
options: To argue that nothing can be done about PTSD
To show that medication is the only treatment
To describe the symptoms in children only
To show what has gone wrong in the emotional brain before explaining how it can be retrained
questions.explain: The limbic changes explain why relearning fails spontaneously and why recovery must begin by calming the circuits.

questions.q: Why does the chapter end with psychotherapy as an emotional tutorial?
options: To show that psychotherapy is the same as trauma treatment
To show that the logic of healing trauma applies to the more muted emotional scars most people carry
To argue that therapy cures all emotional reactions
To move on to the topic of children's play
questions.explain: If PTSD can be healed, so can the quieter scars, and this is where emotional intelligence comes into play.

questions.q: True or false: The Prologue says brain circuitry is extraordinarily malleable and that temperament is not destiny, which fits Chapter 13 coming just before Chapter 14, Temperament Is Not Destiny.
questions.explain: Chapter 13 shows that even trauma can be relearned, and the theme of malleability carries on into Chapter 14.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter concludes that therapy erases the amygdala's reaction so that the old trigger no longer fires.
questions.explain: It concludes that the trigger tendency remains and what changes is the response after it.

questions.q: The chapter's discussion of traumatic memory builds on the amygdala hijacking from Chapter ____.
questions.explain: Chapter 2 is Anatomy of an Emotional Hijacking.

questions.q: How does Chapter 13's closing message connect to the Prologue's account of the book's journey?
questions.a: The Prologue says the brain circuitry involved in emotion is extraordinarily malleable and that childhood is a critical time for setting emotional habits. Chapter 13 shows from trauma and therapy that even deeply implanted habits of the heart can be reshaped, so emotional learning is lifelong. This supports the book's later hope of teaching emotional skills.

questions.q: Match each chapter to its connection to Chapter 13, Trauma and Emotional Relearning.
pairs: Anatomy of an Emotional Hijacking, the source of the hijacking idea
The Family Crucible, the chapter just before this one
Temperament Is Not Destiny, the chapter just after this one
Schooling the Emotions, the last chapter of the book
questions.explain: The chapter reuses the hijacking account from the start of the book and sits in the middle of the later chapters.

questions.q: Sort the chapter's sections by whether they show how trauma harms the brain or how learning repairs it.

items.t: Horror Frozen in Memory
PTSD as a Limbic Disorder
Reeducating the Emotional Brain
Emotional Relearning and Recovery From Trauma
Psychotherapy as an Emotional Tutorial

questions.explain: The first two describe imprinting; the last three describe recovery.

questions.q: According to Goleman, whose work gives the clearest answer to whether a biologically given temperament can be changed by experience?
options: Jerome Kagan, a developmental psychologist at Harvard
Richard Davidson, a psychologist at the University of Wisconsin
John Gottman, a psychologist at the University of Washington
Thorsten Wiesel, a neuroscientist who studied vision
questions.explain: Goleman turns to Kagan's long study of shy and bold children. Davidson, Gottman and Wiesel appear later for other points.

questions.q: In Kagan's follow-up of toddlers observed at twenty-one months and again in kindergarten, what happened to the two groups?
options: Most of the timid children had become outgoing, and a few outgoing children had become timid
None of the outgoing children became timid, while two thirds of the timid ones were still reticent
All of the timid children stayed timid, and a third of the outgoing children turned shy
Both groups shifted at random, so early behaviour told researchers almost nothing
questions.explain: Early boldness was stable, and most early timidity persisted, which is why Kagan treats the pattern as temperament.

questions.q: A toddler is finicky about new foods, reluctant to approach unfamiliar animals and clings to her mother around strangers. Which description from the chapter fits her?
options: Melancholy, the type Davidson links to greater right frontal activity
Bold, the type with a very high threshold for amygdala arousal
Behaviorally inhibited, the type Kagan finds in about 15 to 20 percent of children
Upbeat, the type that bounces back from every setback
questions.explain: Kagan describes behaviorally inhibited infants as timid about anything unfamiliar, including new foods, animals and people.

questions.q: Goleman says temperament is not something the child simply chooses. What does he mean by calling it a given?
options: It is learned from parents during the first year
It appears only once the child starts school
It is set by the first serious fear a child has
It is present at birth, part of the genetic lottery
questions.explain: The chapter opens by defining temperament as the background murmur of moods that marks our basic disposition, present from birth.

questions.q: Where does Kagan locate the difference between cautious Tom and bold Ralph?
options: In how easily a neural circuit centered on the amygdala is aroused
In how fast the left and right frontal lobes mature
In how many neurons the brain loses through pruning
In how much practice each boy had meeting strangers
questions.explain: Kagan proposes that Tom was born with an easily aroused amygdala circuit, while Ralph's threshold for arousal is much higher.

questions.q: A young woman who was very shy as a child is exposed in a lab to harsh smells, and her heart rate stays raised much longer than her outgoing peers'. What does Goleman say this suggests?
options: Her frontal lobes have been pruned too heavily
Surging norepinephrine keeps her amygdala excited and her sympathetic nervous system aroused
Her mother held her too long when she cried as a baby
Her left frontal lobe is more active than her right
questions.explain: Prolonged heart rate is read as a sign of a sensitive amygdala kept excited by norepinephrine.

questions.q: What did direct brain probes find in the unusually timid cats Kagan used as part of his evidence?
options: The frontal lobes were smaller than in bold cats
The caudate nucleus was overactive at all times
Portions of the amygdala were unusually excitable, especially at a threatening howl
The visual cortex had too few synapses from one eye
questions.explain: The cats' pattern of fearfulness resembles the timid children's, and their amygdala responded strongly to a threatening howl from another cat.

questions.q: Why does the cats' timidity show itself at about one month of age?
options: That is when the cats are first separated from their mothers
That is when pruning removes their curiosity
That is when the left frontal lobe becomes active
That is when the amygdala has matured enough to take control of approach and avoidance circuitry
questions.explain: Goleman links this to human babies, whose stranger fear appears at eight or nine months, when the equivalent maturation occurs.

questions.q: What does Kagan suspect timid children may have inherited?
options: Chronically high levels of norepinephrine or other chemicals that activate the amygdala
Too little activity in the left prefrontal area
An unusually slow-maturing vagus nerve
A shortage of neurons in the visual cortex
questions.explain: Such chemicals lower the amygdala's threshold of excitability, so it is more easily triggered.

questions.q: Why does Kagan treat a timid child's silence as a barometer of timidity?
options: He thinks silent children have damaged speech centers
He speculates it reflects a circuit linking the forebrain, amygdala and limbic structures that control vocalizing
He believes silence shows a child is calmly observing and not afraid
He finds silent children have a faster resting heart rate than anyone else
questions.explain: The same circuits are said to make us choke up under stress, so the timid child falls silent before novelty or a perceived threat.

questions.q: In the study of 754 sixth and seventh graders, what was the onset of panic episodes closely tied to?
options: Starting a new school
The loss of a parent
Puberty
Parental overprotection
questions.explain: Girls with few signs of puberty reported no attacks, while about 8 percent of those who had gone through puberty reported panic.

questions.section: Nothing Bothers Me: The Cheerful Temperament
questions.q: According to Davidson, what brain pattern marks people who are by temperament cheerful?
options: Greater activity in the right frontal lobe than the left
Equal activity in both frontal lobes
Greater activity in the amygdala than the frontal lobes
Greater activity in the left frontal lobe than the right
questions.explain: Left-side dominance goes with delight in people and bouncing back from setbacks; right-side dominance goes with negativity.

questions.section: Nothing Bothers Me: The Cheerful Temperament
questions.q: A man sees catastrophe in the smallest thing, is prone to funks and moods, and distrusts a world he sees as full of dangers. Which pattern did Davidson find in people like him?
options: Relatively more activity in the right frontal area
Relatively more activity in the left frontal area
An unusually high threshold for amygdala arousal
Unusually early pruning of frontal synapses
questions.explain: Davidson's right-frontal group matched a negative personality-test pattern, which Goleman compares to Woody Allen's comic roles.

questions.section: Nothing Bothers Me: The Cheerful Temperament
questions.q: In Davidson's film-clip experiment, how did the right-hemisphere, somber volunteers respond?
options: They enjoyed the happy clips most and barely noticed the surgery film
They found happy clips only mildly amusing but felt extreme fear and disgust at the surgery film
They reacted strongly to both kinds of clip
They reacted weakly to both kinds of clip
questions.explain: The cheerful group showed the opposite pattern: minimal reaction to the surgery and delight at the upbeat films.

questions.section: Nothing Bothers Me: The Cheerful Temperament
questions.q: What did Davidson find when he measured frontal-lobe activity in infants about ten months old?
options: Greater left-side activity went with crying when the mother left
Frontal activity could not be linked to any behaviour
Greater right-side activity went with crying when the mother left the room
Frontal activity predicted which infants would later be shy with peers
questions.explain: Of dozens of infants, every one who cried had more right-sided activity, which suggests the cheerful-melancholy dimension is present within the first year.

questions.section: Nothing Bothers Me: The Cheerful Temperament
questions.q: A woman has previously suffered clinical depression. According to Davidson's findings, what would her brain activity most likely show compared with people never depressed?
options: More activity in the left frontal lobe and less on the right
Less activity in the amygdala and more in the caudate nucleus
No difference, since depression has no link to frontal activity
Less activity in the left frontal lobe and more on the right
questions.explain: Davidson found this pattern in people with a history of depression and in patients newly diagnosed.

questions.q: Roughly what share of infants born with an overexcitable amygdala had lost their timidness by kindergarten?
options: About one in three
About one in ten
About one in two
Nearly all of them
questions.explain: This is why Goleman says that temperament is not destiny.

questions.q: In Kagan's home observations, what distinguished the protective mothers of timid six-month-olds?
options: They left their infants alone when the babies cried
They held their fretful infants longer during upsets than during calm periods
They held their infants only when the infants were calm
They let their infants cry until they stopped on their own
questions.explain: The protective mothers soothed the upset infants for longer, rather than helping them learn to master such moments.

questions.q: A father firmly says no and blocks his one-year-old from crawling toward a dangerous object, again and again. What does Kagan speculate the infant gains?
options: A lasting fear of the objects around the house
Protection from every frustration and anxiety
Repeated small doses of uncertainty that rehearse meeting the unexpected
Faster pruning of the amygdala
questions.explain: Manageable doses are just right for a fearful child to learn the lesson of coping with surprises on their own.

questions.q: A mother's toddler cries at a new playgroup. Which approach fits what Kagan found helped timid children become bolder?
options: Take the child home and avoid new groups until she is older
Pick the child up each time she fusses to head off distress
Say nothing and expect the child to outgrow it on her own
Lovingly put gentle pressure on the child to cope and be more outgoing
questions.explain: Parents who helped fearful children learn to adapt, with gentle pressure, tended to raise children who were less timid by kindergarten.

questions.q: What marked the timid four-year-olds who had shaken off their timidity by age ten?
options: Higher social competence such as cooperating, sharing and forming close friendships
Greater physical strength than their classmates
Parents who shielded them from social situations
Slower brain maturation than other timid children
questions.explain: Those whose temperament changed little were instead more emotionally unskilled, falling apart under stress or overreacting to frustration.

questions.q: Why did socially skilled but shy children spontaneously outgrow their timidity?
options: Their amygdala stopped producing norepinephrine
Their skill brought a succession of positive experiences with other children
Their parents sent them to special schools
They avoided other children until they were older
questions.explain: Even if tentative with a new playmate, once the ice was broken they shone, and repeated social success made them more sure of themselves.

questions.q: What does the process of pruning do in the developing brain?
options: It adds new neurons to the most-used circuits
It permanently closes the window for any learning
It removes less-used neuronal connections and strengthens the most-used ones
It keeps every connection a child is born with
questions.explain: Children are born with many more neurons than the mature brain keeps, and pruning improves the signal-to-noise ratio.

questions.q: A child has one eye taped closed for several months before age six, and the eye is later restored. What does Goleman's account of the critical period for vision predict?
options: That eye will see normally, because the eye itself was healthy
That eye will become better than the open eye
Both eyes will lose vision for detail
That eye's vision for detail will be impaired
questions.explain: Hubel and Wiesel showed that synapses from a closed eye dwindle during the critical period, so too few circuits remain to interpret its signals.

questions.q: In the experiments on rich and poor rats, what was found after months of living in the different cages?
options: The rich rats had more complex synaptic networks, heavier brains and better maze-solving
The poor rats had heavier brains and learned mazes faster
Both groups had identical circuitry, but the rich rats were calmer
The rich rats had fewer synapses because of pruning
questions.explain: The experiment is a vivid demonstration of experience shaping the developing brain.

questions.q: What was the remarkable finding about obsessive-compulsive patients treated with behavior therapy?
options: Their caudate nucleus activity stayed unchanged although symptoms eased
Their caudate nucleus activity fell as much as in patients treated with fluoxetine
Their symptoms eased only in patients who also took fluoxetine
Their prefrontal activity rose above normal
questions.explain: Experience in therapy changed brain function and relieved symptoms as effectively as the drug.

questions.q: Why should a parent not expect a fourteen-year-old's emotional self-control to be fully built yet?
options: The limbic system does not mature until after twenty
The sensory areas are the last parts of the brain to mature
The frontal lobes keep developing until about sixteen to eighteen
The frontal lobes finish maturing during early childhood
questions.explain: Goleman calls the frontal lobes the seat of emotional self-control, understanding and artful response, and they are among the slowest areas to mature.

questions.q: Between ten and eighteen months, what is the orbitofrontal area forming connections to do?
options: Begin the first stranger fear in the baby
Complete the pruning of the visual cortex
Raise the baby's resting blood pressure
Become a key on/off switch for distress by linking to the limbic brain
questions.explain: Goleman reports the speculation that an infant who is soothed countless times builds stronger circuitry for controlling distress.

questions.q: How does Chapter 14 begin, in relation to the chapter before it on emotional relearning?
options: It moves from changing learned emotional patterns to asking whether inborn temperament can change
It moves from inborn temperament to the cost of emotional illiteracy
It repeats the case for relearning trauma through therapy
It begins the book's account of how emotions evolved
questions.explain: The chapter's first lines say 'so much for' learned patterns and turn to responses that are givens of our genetic endowment.

questions.q: The prologue says Part Four, Windows of Opportunity, shows that childhood and adolescence are critical for what?
options: Choosing a lifelong emotional temperament
Setting down the essential emotional habits that govern our lives
Learning to read facial expressions
Building the physical structures of the amygdala
questions.explain: Chapter 14 supports this by arguing that temperament is not destiny and that childhood lessons sculpt the emotional circuits.

questions.q: True or false: Kagan finds that from birth about 15 to 20 percent of children are behaviorally inhibited.
questions.explain: This is the group of infants who are timid about anything unfamiliar.

questions.q: True or false: About two in five infants have the timid temperament and about one in five the bold one.
questions.explain: It is the other way around: about one in five infants is timid and about two in five are bold, at least at birth.

questions.q: True or false: In Kagan's follow-up from toddlerhood to kindergarten, none of the outgoing children had become timid.
questions.explain: Boldness proved stable, while two thirds of the timid children stayed reticent.

questions.q: True or false: Kagan proposes that people like Tom have a much higher threshold for amygdala arousal than people like Ralph.
questions.explain: It is Ralph, the bold boy, whose nervous system has the higher threshold; Tom's circuit is easily aroused.

questions.section: Nothing Bothers Me: The Cheerful Temperament
questions.q: True or false: A baby of about ten months with more right-sided than left-sided frontal activity was likely to cry when its mother left the room.
questions.explain: Davidson found the correlation virtually 100 percent among the dozens of infants tested.

questions.section: Nothing Bothers Me: The Cheerful Temperament
questions.q: True or false: Davidson found that people with greater activity in the right frontal lobe are by temperament cheerful and quick to bounce back.
questions.explain: Greater left frontal activity goes with cheerfulness; right-side dominance goes with negativity and sour moods.

questions.q: True or false: A mother who always holds her timid infant for longer when upset than when calm is, by Kagan's findings, helping the child grow bolder.
questions.explain: Kagan's team found that this protective approach abetted fearfulness by depriving the child of chances to learn to cope.

questions.q: True or false: In the obsessive-compulsive study, behavior therapy reduced caudate nucleus activity as much as fluoxetine did.
questions.explain: The finding showed that experience can change brain function as effectively as medication.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says that once childhood is over, the brain stops changing, so emotional habits cannot be altered at all.
questions.explain: He says the brain remains plastic throughout life, though not to the spectacular extent seen in childhood, and emotional habits remain malleable with sustained effort.

questions.q: True or false: In the rich and poor rat experiments, the poor rats had sparser neuronal circuitry than the rich rats.
questions.explain: The rich rats' brains had more complex synaptic networks and were heavier.

questions.q: True or false: Chapter 14 follows a chapter about changing learned emotional patterns by asking whether an inborn temperament can be changed too.
questions.explain: The chapter opens by moving from learned responses to those that are givens of genetic endowment.

questions.q: True or false: In the prologue's road-map, Part Four argues that temperament fixes a person's emotional abilities for life.
questions.explain: The prologue says the brain circuitry is extraordinarily malleable and that childhood lessons shape it, so temperament is not destiny.

questions.q: Temperament can be defined in terms of the ____ that typify our emotional life.
questions.explain: Goleman defines temperament as the background murmur of feelings that mark our basic disposition.

questions.q: The developmental psychologist who studied shy and bold children at Harvard is Jerome ____.
questions.explain: Kagan's studies of timid children are the main evidence of the chapter.

questions.q: Kagan's four temperamental types are timid, bold, upbeat and ____.
questions.explain: Each type is said to rest on a different pattern of brain activity.

questions.q: Kagan calls the roughly 15 to 20 percent of children who are timid about anything unfamiliar behaviorally ____.
questions.explain: They are finicky about new foods and wary of strangers.

questions.q: From birth, timid infants' hearts beat ____ than other infants' in response to strange or novel situations.
questions.explain: This is among the evidence for a more reactive neural circuitry in timid children.

questions.q: Kagan believes the difference between Tom and Ralph lies in the excitability of a neural circuit centered on the ____.
questions.explain: Tom's circuit is easily aroused, while Ralph's has a higher threshold.

questions.q: About one in ____ housecats shows a pattern of fearfulness akin to that of timid children.
questions.explain: These cats draw away from novelty and attack only the smallest rodents.

questions.q: Kagan postulates that timid children may have inherited chronically high levels of ____ or other brain chemicals that activate the amygdala.
questions.explain: That would give the amygdala a low threshold of excitability.

questions.section: Nothing Bothers Me: The Cheerful Temperament
questions.q: Richard Davidson works at the University of ____.
questions.explain: His work links cheerful and melancholy temperament to left and right prefrontal activity.

questions.section: Nothing Bothers Me: The Cheerful Temperament
questions.q: People who are by temperament cheerful have greater activity in the ____ frontal lobe than in the right.
questions.explain: Right-sided dominance goes with negativity and moodiness.

questions.q: Kagan's view that human qualities can change is summed up in his words that no human quality is beyond ____.
questions.explain: Although he adds that timidity seems slightly harder to change than others, probably because of its physiological basis.

questions.q: The childrearing philosophy that seems to have helped fearful children become braver was that they should learn to ____ to life's small struggles.
questions.explain: The protective philosophy, by contrast, seems to have abetted fearfulness.

questions.q: Through a process known as ____, the brain loses neuronal connections that are less used.
questions.explain: Pruning improves the signal-to-noise ratio by removing extraneous synapses.

questions.q: The Nobel Prize-winners who showed a critical period for vision development in cats and monkeys were Thorsten Wiesel and David ____.
questions.explain: Closing one eye during the critical period made the synapses from that eye dwindle.

questions.q: In the study of obsessive-compulsive patients, behavior therapy lowered activity in the ____ nucleus, just as fluoxetine did.
questions.explain: The caudate nucleus is described as a key part of the emotional brain.

questions.q: John Gottman says parents modify their children's ____ tone by coaching them emotionally.
questions.explain: Vagal tone measures how easily triggered the vagus nerve is.

questions.q: A parent who calmly talks a child through feelings and alternatives to hitting is, in Gottman's terms, modifying the child's ____ tone.
questions.explain: The vagus nerve helps prime the fight-or-flight response, so coaching helps suppress it.

questions.q: Chapter 14 belongs to the part of the book titled “____ of Opportunity”.
questions.explain: The part title signals that childhood and adolescence are critical for setting down emotional habits.

questions.q: Which of these are among the four temperamental types Kagan posits?
options: Timid
Upbeat
Volatile
Placid
questions.explain: Kagan's four types are timid, bold, upbeat and melancholy. Volatile and placid are not on his list.

questions.q: Which of these does Kagan cite as signs of higher reactivity in timid children?
options: Higher resting blood pressure
Greater dilation of the pupils
Talking less around unfamiliar people
Lower norepinephrine markers in the urine
questions.explain: Timid children show higher norepinephrine markers, not lower ones.

questions.q: Which of these are traits of behaviorally inhibited children?
options: Finickiness about new foods
Reluctance to approach new animals
Proneness to guilt and self-reproach
Eagerness to explore new places
questions.explain: Eagerness to explore is the mark of the bold child.

questions.section: Nothing Bothers Me: The Cheerful Temperament
questions.q: Which of these describe the people with strong left frontal activity in Davidson's experiment?
options: Sociable and cheerful
A strong sense of self-confidence
A lower lifetime risk of depression
Suspicious of a world full of dangers
questions.explain: Suspicion of a dangerous world belongs to the right-frontal group.

questions.q: Which of these marked timid four-year-olds who had shaken off their timidity by ten?
options: Being cooperative with other children
Being empathic and prone to sharing
Overreacting to minor frustration with anger
Being able to develop close friendships
questions.explain: Overreacting with anger marked the timid children whose temperament changed little.

questions.q: Which of these were found among timid four-year-olds whose temperament changed little over six years?
options: Crying and falling apart under stress
Trouble delaying gratification
Being oversensitive to criticism
Developing close friendships
questions.explain: Close friendships marked the children who outgrew timidity.

questions.q: Which of these were found among the protective mothers of timid infants?
options: Holding infants longer during upsets than calm periods
Being lenient and indirect in setting limits
Blocking the child's actions and insisting on obedience
Helping infants learn to master moments of upset
questions.explain: Firm limits and helping infants master upset belonged to the other mothers.

questions.q: Which of these studies did Goleman use to show experience shaping the brain?
options: Eye closure in cats and monkeys
Rich and poor rats
Behavior therapy for obsessive-compulsive disorder
Davidson's film clips of a gorilla and surgery
questions.explain: The film-clip study showed differences in temperament, not experience shaping the brain.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman name as critical childhood experiences for emotional circuitry?
options: Dependable, responsive parents
Guidance in handling distress and impulse
Practice in empathy
Early academic tutoring
questions.explain: Academic tutoring is not among the experiences he lists.

questions.q: Which of these are true of the frontal lobes?
options: They are the seat of emotional self-control and artful response
They continue to develop into late adolescence
They finish maturing in early childhood
They finish maturing by puberty
questions.explain: The sensory areas mature in early childhood and the limbic system by puberty, but the frontal lobes keep developing.

questions.q: Which of these are part of the emotional coaching Gottman describes?
options: Talking with children about their feelings
Not being critical and judgmental
Problem-solving about emotional predicaments
Shielding children from every upset
questions.explain: Coaching means helping children understand and cope with feelings, not shielding them.

questions.q: Which of these are true of Chapter 14's place in the book?
options: It follows the chapter on trauma and emotional relearning
It comes before the chapter on the cost of emotional illiteracy
It comes before the chapter on empathy's roots
It comes before the prologue
questions.explain: The chapter sits in Part Four, after Chapter 13 and before Chapter 15; the Roots of Empathy is Chapter 7.

questions.q: Put these steps of Kagan's study of toddlers in the order they happened.
items: Toddlers watched at twenty-one months in free play
Some are noticed hanging back and clinging
Same children observed again in kindergarten
Two thirds of the timid ones are still reticent
questions.explain: The follow-up came almost four years after the first observations.

questions.q: Put these in the order of Kagan's account of how a timid child reacts to something new.
items: Child meets something unfamiliar
Easily excited amygdala circuit fires
Sympathetic nervous system is aroused
Child hangs back and falls silent
questions.explain: The amygdala circuit and norepinephrine sit between the novelty and the shy behaviour.

questions.q: Put these developmental milestones in the order they occur in a human life.
items: Stranger fear appears, at eight or nine months
Orbitofrontal soothing circuit forms, at ten to eighteen months
Critical period for vision ends, at six years
Frontal lobes finish maturing, at sixteen to eighteen
questions.explain: The orbitofrontal connections form during infancy, and the frontal lobes keep developing into late adolescence.

questions.q: Put these in order to show how the protective strategy backfires, in Kagan's account.
items: Parent shields the timid toddler from upset
Child misses chances to learn to calm himself
Prefrontal circuits do not learn alternatives to fear
Fearfulness is strengthened through repetition
questions.explain: The strategy deprives the toddler of the lesson and so leaves the tendency to fearfulness unchallenged.

questions.q: Put these in order to show what Kagan thinks a firm limit teaches a baby.
items: Baby crawls toward an intriguing object
Mother warns him away
Baby faces a mild uncertainty
Repeated hundreds of times, he learns to handle surprise
questions.explain: The interruption is a small dose of uncertainty that the infant rehearses over the first year.

questions.q: Put these in order for Hubel and Wiesel's experiments on cats and monkeys.
items: One eye is kept closed in the first months
Synapses from that eye dwindle
The closed eye is reopened after the critical period
The animal is functionally blind in that eye
questions.explain: The eye itself was fine, but too few circuits to the visual cortex remained.

questions.q: Put these in order for the behavior therapy given to obsessive-compulsive patients.
items: Patient is exposed to the object of the obsession
Patient is not allowed to perform the compulsion
Patient learns to question the fears behind it
Compulsions fade over months, with lower caudate activity
questions.explain: Exposure, blocked ritual and questioning fears together led to improvement.

questions.q: Put these in order to show how self-soothing is learned, in the speculation Goleman reports.
items: Infant cries
Caretaker holds and rocks the infant until calm
Countless repeated episodes of being soothed
Stronger connections for controlling distress form
questions.explain: Biological attunement helps the child later learn to soothe himself.

questions.q: Put these chapters in the order they appear in the book.
items: The Family Crucible
Trauma and Emotional Relearning
Temperament Is Not Destiny
The Cost of Emotional Illiteracy
questions.explain: They run from Chapter 12 to Chapter 15.

questions.q: Match each researcher with the work Goleman describes in this chapter.
pairs: Timid-to-bold temperament and the overexcitable amygdala
Cheerful versus melancholy temperament and left versus right frontal activity
Critical period for vision in cats and monkeys
Emotional coaching and children's vagal tone
questions.explain: Each researcher supplies one strand of the chapter's argument.

questions.q: Match each brain structure with the role it has in the chapter.
pairs: Left versus right activity marks cheerful versus melancholy temperament
Activity fell in OCD patients after therapy
Becomes a key on/off switch for distress
Regulates the heart and signals the amygdala from the adrenals
questions.explain: Each structure is tied to the section where it appears.

questions.section: Nothing Bothers Me: The Cheerful Temperament
questions.q: Match each temperament with the brain pattern the chapter links to it.
questions.explain: Kagan's pair rests on the amygdala, Davidson's on the frontal lobes.

questions.q: Match each person with how Goleman portrays them.
pairs: Among the most timid at every measurement from age two
One of the boldest and most outgoing at every age
Laughed at her fall after a stroke and said at least she could walk
questions.explain: Tom and Ralph are Kagan's two contrasting boys, while June is Goleman's own example of a cheerful temperament.

questions.q: Match each figure with what it refers to.
pairs: Fearful infants who had lost their timidness by kindergarten
Girls past puberty who reported panic
questions.explain: These figures come from different parts of the chapter.

questions.q: Match each age with the event Goleman describes.
pairs: Orbitofrontal connections for soothing form rapidly
questions.explain: Each age marks a stage in brain or behaviour development.

questions.q: Match each experience with its effect on the brain.
pairs: Keeping one eye closed in early life
Leaves an imprint on the emotional circuitry
questions.explain: Experience sculpts the brain in each case, for better or worse.

questions.q: Match each parenting style with the result Goleman reports.
pairs: Holding a fretful infant longer than a calm one
Setting firm limits with direct commands
Putting gentle pressure on a shy child
Marks children less timid by kindergarten
questions.explain: The first is the protective approach; the others are the helpful ones.

questions.q: Match each section of Chapter 14 with its job in the argument.
pairs: Shows the biology behind inborn shyness
Adds a second temperament dimension, cheerful versus melancholy
Shows that experience can change a temperament
Shows why childhood habits set so firmly
questions.explain: The chapter moves from biology, to change, to why the brain can change and why childhood matters.

questions.q: Sort these traits by whether they describe Tom (the timid boy) or Ralph (the bold boy).

items.t: Tense and stiff at thirteen, biting his lip
Troubled by nightmares of monsters
Relaxed and talkative at thirteen
Had only two short-lived fears
Broke into a sweat approaching playmates
Sociable and popular

questions.explain: Tom is the shy type; Ralph was among the boldest at every age.

questions.section: Nothing Bothers Me: The Cheerful Temperament
questions.q: Sort these by whether they go with greater left or greater right frontal activity.

items.t: Takes delight in people and in what life presents
Bounces back from setbacks
Prone to funks and moodiness
Suspicious of a world fraught with dangers
Strong self-confidence
History of clinical depression

questions.explain: Left dominance goes with cheerfulness, right with negativity and depression.

questions.q: Sort these by whether they belong to the protective mothers or the mothers who taught their children to adapt.

items.t: Held fretful infants longer than calm ones
Lenient and indirect in setting limits
Gave firm limits and direct commands
Helped infants master moments of upset
Believed they should shield toddlers from what upset them
Blocked the child's action and insisted on obedience

questions.explain: The protective approach was linked to fearfulness; the adapt approach to bravery.

questions.q: Sort these by whether they belong to timid children who outgrew timidity or those who did not.

items.t: Cooperative and getting along with others
Empathic, giving and sharing
Crying and falling apart under stress
Trouble delaying gratification
Overly sensitive to criticism
Developed close friendships

questions.explain: Emotional competence predicted who shook off timidity.

questions.q: Sort these by whether the evidence is from Kagan's work or Davidson's work.

items.t: Excitable amygdala in timid cats
Heart rate racing at twenty-one months
Gorilla and surgery film clips
Infants crying when mother left the room
Higher norepinephrine markers in urine
Frontal activity in people with depression

questions.explain: Kagan studied boldness and timidity; Davidson studied cheerful and melancholy temperament.

questions.q: Sort these by whether they show biology shaping temperament or experience reshaping the brain.

items.t: Racing heart in timid infants from birth
Excitable amygdala in timid cats
Frontal activity predicting infants' crying
Poor-cage rats with sparse circuitry
Synapses lost from a closed eye
Lower caudate activity after behavior therapy

questions.explain: The first three belong to inborn differences; the others show experience altering circuits.

questions.q: Sort these by whether the brain area has matured by puberty or keeps developing into late adolescence.

items.t: Sensory areas
Limbic system
Visual circuits (critical period of six years)
Frontal lobes
Seat of emotional self-control
Regulatory circuits of the emotional brain

questions.explain: The frontal lobes continue developing until sixteen to eighteen.

questions.q: Sort these by whether they help or harm a child's emotional circuitry.

items.t: Dependable, responsive parents
Practice in empathy
Emotional coaching
Neglect or abuse
A self-absorbed, indifferent parent
Capricious yelling and hitting

questions.explain: Experiences with parents shape the circuits for better or for worse.

questions.q: What question does Chapter 14 pose about temperament, and what does Kagan's toddler study suggest?
questions.a: The chapter asks whether a biologically given emotional set can be changed by experience, or whether an innately shy child can become a confident adult. Kagan observed toddlers at twenty-one months and again in kindergarten, finding that none of the outgoing children became timid while two thirds of the timid ones were still reticent, so early temperament is fairly stable but not entirely.

questions.q: Describe behaviorally inhibited children as Kagan portrays them, including how they turn out.
questions.a: About 15 to 20 percent of children are born behaviorally inhibited, timid about anything unfamiliar. They are finicky about new foods, shy of strangers, prone to guilt and anxious in social situations. As adults they tend to be wallflowers, afraid of public speaking or performing.

questions.q: How does Kagan explain the difference between Tom and Ralph in terms of the brain?
questions.a: Kagan believes it lies in the excitability of a neural circuit centered on the amygdala. Tom was born with a neurochemistry that makes this circuit easily aroused, so he avoids the unfamiliar and feels anxiety, while Ralph has a much higher threshold for amygdala arousal and is outgoing and exploratory.

questions.q: What evidence from cats and from physiological measures supports Kagan's view of timidity?
questions.a: About one in seven housecats has a timid pattern, and direct probes find that portions of their amygdala are unusually excitable. In timid children Kagan finds higher heart rate, blood pressure, pupil dilation and urinary norepinephrine markers, which suggests chronically high norepinephrine keeps the amygdala easily triggered.

questions.q: What did the study of 754 sixth and seventh graders show about timid teenagers and panic?
questions.a: Forty-four of them had already suffered at least one panic episode or several preliminary symptoms, usually set off by ordinary alarms like a first date or big exam. Those who were timid by temperament and unusually frightened by new situations were the ones affected, and the onset was tied to puberty. The episodes signal greater risk of developing panic disorder later.

questions.section: Nothing Bothers Me: The Cheerful Temperament
questions.q: What did Davidson find about left and right frontal activity and temperament?
questions.a: People with more activity in the left frontal lobe than the right are by temperament cheerful, sociable and confident, bounce back from setbacks, and have a lower risk of depression. Those with more right frontal activity are given to negativity, sour moods and worry, and people with a history of depression show this right-sided pattern too.

questions.section: Nothing Bothers Me: The Cheerful Temperament
questions.q: Describe Davidson's film-clip experiment and the evidence that this dimension of temperament appears early.
questions.a: Volunteers watched amusing clips and a distressing surgery film. The right-hemisphere somber people felt extreme fear and disgust at the surgery and only mild amusement at the happy clips, while the cheerful group reacted minimally to the surgery and delighted in the upbeat films. In infants of about ten months, right-sided frontal activity predicted crying when the mother left, suggesting the pattern is present in the first year.

questions.section: Nothing Bothers Me: The Cheerful Temperament
questions.q: Why, according to Goleman, are people with a morose temperament not doomed to brooding?
questions.a: Even if the basic dimension is laid down at or near birth, the emotional lessons of childhood can amplify or mute an innate predisposition. The brain is highly plastic in childhood, so experiences have a lasting effect on how neural pathways are sculpted.

questions.q: How did the mothers of timid babies who grew bolder differ from the mothers of those who stayed fearful?
questions.a: Some mothers believed in protecting timid toddlers from what upset them, while others helped their children learn to cope. The protective mothers held fretful babies longer during upsets and were lenient and indirect in setting limits. The other mothers were firm and direct, and their children became braver.

questions.q: Why, in Kagan's speculation, does firmness reduce a fearful child's fearfulness?
questions.a: When a mother interrupts the baby's crawl toward an intriguing object, the baby meets a mild uncertainty. Repeated hundreds of times in the first year, this gives continual rehearsals of meeting the unexpected in manageable doses. Loving parents who do not rush to soothe every upset let the child learn to manage such moments alone.

questions.q: A friend always picks up her timid baby the moment he fusses, to protect him. Using the chapter, what would you say?
questions.a: Kagan found that protecting highly reactive infants from frustration in the hope of a benevolent outcome tends to exacerbate their uncertainty and produce the opposite effect. The baby loses the chance to learn to calm himself and master small fears, and at the neural level his fearfulness may be strengthened by repetition. Gentle pressure to cope and be outgoing seems to help instead.

questions.q: What role does social competence play in whether a timid child outgrows timidity?
questions.a: Timid four-year-olds who shook off the trait by ten were cooperative, empathic, giving and good at friendships. Their skill brought a succession of positive social experiences, and repeated social success made them more sure of themselves. Those whose temperament changed little fell apart under stress, overreacted and struggled in relationships.

questions.q: A parent says a shy toddler was born that way, so nothing can be done. How would the chapter respond?
questions.a: Goleman says fearfulness and other temperaments may be biological givens, but we are not limited to a specific emotional menu by inherited traits, since there is a range of possibility within genetic constraints. About one in three overexcitable infants had lost timidness by kindergarten, and the right experiences can tame the amygdala. Kagan puts it this way: “no human quality is beyond change.”

questions.q: What is pruning, and why does it matter for the argument that experience shapes the brain?
questions.a: Children are born with more neurons than the mature brain keeps, and pruning removes the less-used connections while strengthening the most-used circuits. It is constant and quick, so experience, particularly in childhood, sculpts the brain, which is why temperament is not destiny.

questions.q: What do the Hubel and Wiesel vision studies and the rich and poor rats show?
questions.a: Hubel and Wiesel showed a critical period in the first months of life: when one eye was kept closed, synapses from it dwindled, and after the period the animal was functionally blind in that eye, though the eye itself was fine. In the rat studies, rich cages produced more complex synaptic circuits, heavier brains and better maze-solving than barren cages. Both show experience shaping the developing brain.

questions.q: Why is the obsessive-compulsive disorder study so important to Goleman's argument?
questions.a: Patients treated with behavior therapy, who were exposed to the object of the compulsion without performing it and learned to question their fears, improved. A PET scan showed their caudate nucleus activity fell as much as that of patients treated with fluoxetine. Experience, in the form of relearning, changed brain function and symptoms as effectively as the drug.

questions.q: Why does Goleman call childhood a crucial window for emotional habits?
questions.a: The frontal lobes, the seat of emotional self-control, keep developing until sixteen to eighteen, so habits repeated through childhood and the teen years help mold their circuitry and become set in the brain's wiring. Habits acquired then are harder to change later. Experiences such as responsive parents, guidance with distress and practice in empathy, or neglect and abuse, leave lasting imprints.

questions.q: How do infant soothing and Gottman's work on vagal tone illustrate parents' effect on emotional circuitry?
questions.a: Between ten and eighteen months the orbitofrontal area forms connections that make it an on/off switch for distress, and an infant repeatedly soothed may build stronger circuits for later self-soothing. Gottman found that parents who coach children emotionally, by talking about feelings, avoiding criticism and problem-solving, change their children's vagal tone, so they better suppress the fight-or-flight activity.

questions.q: How does Chapter 14 build its argument from its opening question to its closing point about parents?
questions.a: It opens by asking whether biological temperament can be changed, then shows the biology of timidity and of cheerful versus melancholy temperament. It next shows that experience can tame the overexcitable amygdala, then explains why with brain pruning and critical windows, and closes by urging nurturing of emotional skills in childhood so remedial therapy is less needed.

questions.q: How does the title Temperament Is Not Destiny fit into Part Four, Windows of Opportunity, and the prologue's road-map?
questions.a: The prologue says genetic heritage gives emotional setpoints, but the brain circuitry is malleable, so temperament is not destiny. Part Four shows how lessons learned at home and at school shape the emotional circuits, making childhood and adolescence critical for setting essential emotional habits. Chapter 14 provides the biological case for that claim, before later chapters turn to the costs of emotional illiteracy and to schooling the emotions.

questions.q: How does Goleman read the Brooklyn school shooting in which Khalil Sumpter killed two older boys?
options: As a sign of a desperate need for lessons in handling emotions and settling disagreements peaceably
As proof that schools need armed guards stationed in every hallway
As an isolated tragedy caused by one unusually troubled boy
As the result of weak academic standards in mathematics and reading
questions.explain: Goleman treats the shooting as one example of emotional illiteracy, not an isolated event or a security failure, and says the standard curriculum is not addressing that deficiency.

questions.q: According to the chapter's opening statistics, what is the most common cause of disability among teenagers?
options: Injuries from shootings
Mental illness
Drug and alcohol addiction
Complications of teen pregnancy
questions.explain: Goleman lists mental illness as the leading cause of disability among teenagers, alongside depression symptoms in up to a third of them.

questions.q: Goleman calls the United States a ____ of world trends, so its figures on troubled youth are meant to signal where others may be heading.
questions.explain: A bellwether is a leader whose direction others follow, which is why American statistics are used as a warning.

questions.q: True or false: In the chapter's opening statistics, the suicide rate for teenagers quadrupled over two decades while teen murder rates tripled.
questions.explain: It was the other way round: teen murder rates quadrupled (mostly through shootings) and the teen suicide rate tripled.

questions.q: Match each opening statistic about American youth with the change the chapter reports.
pairs: Heroin and cocaine use among African-American youth
Rose to 13 times the level of twenty years earlier
Heroin and cocaine use among white youth
questions.explain: These are the figures Goleman gives to show that the problems of youth are worsening, and worst of all for inner-city African-American youth.

questions.q: Sort each of these opening statistics into the kind of trouble it describes.

items.t: The highest juvenile arrest rate for violent crimes ever recorded
Teen murder rates quadrupled, mostly through shootings
The number of children under fourteen who are murder victims tripled
Symptoms of depression affect up to a third of teenagers
Depression among girls doubles at puberty
Eating disorders in teenage girls have skyrocketed

questions.explain: The first three are violence statistics; the last three describe the emotional and psychiatric troubles of adolescence.

questions.q: What new deficiency do educators discover in this chapter's opening, and why does Goleman say it is going unaddressed?
questions.a: They are realizing that besides lagging math and reading scores, children suffer from emotional illiteracy. It is not addressed because the standard school curriculum focuses on raising academic standards, which a Brooklyn teacher summed up as caring more about reading and writing than about whether children will be alive next week.

questions.q: What did the national sample of American children aged seven to sixteen show when the mid-1970s were compared with the end of the 1980s?
options: A sharp rise in violence alone, with other indicators unchanged
An improvement in attention but a decline in friendships
A steady worsening across many indicators, with no single problem standing out
A worsening that affected only children living in poverty
questions.explain: Parents' and teachers' ratings showed all indicators creeping in the wrong direction; no one problem stood out.

questions.q: Why does Goleman say the individual problems in the national comparison matter even though none of them alone raises eyebrows?
options: Each one is individually a clinical disorder needing treatment
Together they show that schools are the main cause of the decline
They prove that American children are worse off than children anywhere else
Taken together they signal a sea change, a new toxicity seeping into childhood and sweeping deficits in emotional competence
questions.explain: He reads the group of ordinary-looking problems as a barometer of a broad decline in emotional competences, not as separate crises.

questions.q: In the chapter's international comparison, which countries rated children at about the level American children had reached in 1976?
options: The Netherlands, China and Germany
Australia, France and Thailand
Canada, Japan and Italy
Britain, India and Brazil
questions.explain: Those three were comparable to 1976 America in the 1980s, while Australia, France and Thailand had children in worse shape than current U.S. levels.

questions.q: What did Goleman find about how the decline in emotional skills related to family income?
options: Only children in poverty showed a decline over the decades
Poor children had the worst record, but rich, middle-class and poor children all slid at about the same rate
Wealthy children declined fastest because of busy parents
Middle-class children were protected by their families' resources
questions.explain: No children are exempt: the rate of deterioration for poor children was no worse than for middle-class or wealthy ones.

questions.q: A school board member argues that the decline in children's emotional skills is a problem of poor inner-city neighborhoods and does not concern the wealthy suburbs. Which finding in the chapter most directly contradicts this view?
options: The rate of children getting psychological help tripled
Teachers rated children in other countries as no better than American children
Children from every income group showed the same steady slide in emotional competence
Both parents working long hours is now commonplace
questions.explain: The decline cuts across ethnic, racial and income groups, so wealthier districts are not exempt.

questions.q: What does Goleman mean by comparing the alarming statistics to the canary in the coal miner's tunnel?
options: They show that a few sensitive children suffer first while the rest are fine
They prove the danger is limited to isolated mining-town communities
They show that the situation is already beyond repair
They are an early warning of a deeper problem, before everyday difficulties blossom into outright crises
questions.explain: The canary's death warns of too little oxygen; the statistics warn of trouble that is also visible in subtler day-to-day problems.

questions.q: The share of American children with emotional problems serious enough to need help but who did not get it nearly doubled, from about 9 percent in 1976 to ____ percent in 1989.
questions.explain: The threefold rise in children receiving help was possibly a good sign, but the near doubling of untreated children was a bad one.

questions.q: The Cornell developmental psychologist who warned that even strong families are falling apart without good support systems is Urie ____.
questions.explain: Bronfenbrenner made an international comparison of children's well-being and said the next generation, particularly males, is at stake.

questions.q: True or false: The national comparison of children's emotional condition between the mid-1970s and the late 1980s relied on parents' and teachers' assessments.
questions.explain: It was based on parents' and teachers' assessments of children aged seven to sixteen, not on the children's own reports.

questions.q: Which of these are among the four groups of problems that grew worse in the national sample of children?
options: Withdrawal or social problems
Anxious and depressed
Delinquent or aggressive
Eating and sleeping problems
Substance abuse problems
questions.explain: The four groups were withdrawal/social problems, anxious/depressed, attention/thinking problems, and delinquent/aggressive; eating, sleeping and substance problems were not among them.

questions.q: Sort each of these children's problems into the group where the national comparison placed it.

items.t: Preferring to be alone
Needing to be perfect
Feeling unloved
Being secretive
Lying and cheating
Having a hot temper
Destroying other people's things
Teasing a lot

questions.explain: The first four come from the withdrawal and anxious-depressed lists; the last four come from the delinquent-aggressive list.

questions.q: According to Goleman, how do economic pressures on families erode children's emotional competence, even when parents mean well?
questions.a: Global competition to drive down labor costs leaves families financially besieged, with both parents working long hours, more single-parent homes, children left to their own devices or the TV, and some day care amounting to neglect. All this erodes the countless small, nourishing exchanges between parent and child that build emotional competences.

questions.q: What point does Goleman make by describing the bully Jimmy, who was in jail for assault by sixteen?
options: Flagrant aggression in childhood marks emotional and other troubles to come
Bullies are usually unpopular only because of their size
Most aggressive children outgrow their behavior by adolescence
Bullies come mainly from wealthy and permissive families
questions.explain: Jimmy illustrates that being so flagrantly aggressive in childhood is a mark of troubles ahead, backed by many studies of its lifelong legacy.

questions.q: What kind of family life does Goleman say typically surrounds aggressive children?
options: Parents who give in to every demand
Parents who alternate neglect with harsh and capricious punishment
Parents who are consistently strict but warm
Parents who are overinvolved in the child's friendships
questions.explain: That pattern may make the children somewhat paranoid or combative.

questions.q: What one perceptual flaw unites angry children, whether bullies or withdrawn outcasts?
options: They fail to notice when someone is truly being hostile
They overestimate how much other children like them
They perceive slights where none were intended and imagine peers to be more hostile than they are
They cannot tell one emotion from another in their own bodies
questions.explain: An innocent bump is seen as a vendetta, so they attack in return and are then shunned, which isolates them further.

questions.q: In the experiment where bullies watched a video of a boy who drops his books and then tries to hit those who laugh, how did the bullies judge the scene?
options: They saw the boy who struck out as the aggressor and the laughers as innocent
They judged the whole scene as an accident with no one to blame
They saw the boy who dropped his books as having provoked the laughter
They saw the boy who struck out as justified and the boy who knocked into him as the more combative
questions.explain: The bullies read hostility into the knock and treated the retaliation as justified, a perceptual bias toward threat.

questions.q: An aggressive boy playing checkers sees his partner move a piece out of turn. What does Goleman say he is likely to do?
options: Interpret it as cheating at once, without checking whether it was an innocent mistake, and accuse or hit
Point out the mistake politely and move on
Quietly withdraw from the game
Laugh it off with a joke
questions.explain: His presumption is malevolence rather than innocence, and hostile perception is entwined with automatic aggression.

questions.q: Why do aggressive children's alternatives such as politeness and joking shrink over time?
options: Teachers punish them whenever they try to joke
The more they react with automatic aggression, the more automatic it becomes and the less they use other responses
They never learned any alternatives from other children
Their parents forbid them from using humor
questions.explain: Practice makes the hostile reaction an overlearned habit, narrowing the repertoire.

questions.q: In the Montreal kindergarten study, how did the children rated highest for hostility and trouble making at age five compare by their early teens?
options: They were about as likely as others to have broken the law
They were about half as likely to have been drunk
They were about three times as likely as others to have committed acts such as beating someone up, shoplifting or using a weapon in a fight
They were three times as likely to be in special-education classes
questions.explain: Their drift toward delinquency showed up early, before they reached fourteen.

questions.q: How does impulsivity compare with IQ as a predictor of later delinquency in ten-year-old boys?
options: IQ is about three times as powerful as impulsivity
They are equally good predictors
Neither predicts delinquency reliably
Impulsivity is almost three times as powerful a predictor as IQ
questions.explain: Boys heading for delinquency do tend to have lower IQ scores, but impulsivity is more directly the cause.

questions.q: What did the study of fourth-grade girls who were 'bad' but not unpopular find about their later lives?
options: About 40 percent had a child by the end of high school, three times the school average
Most became violent criminals in adolescence
Nearly all dropped out of school by ninth grade
They were no different from the other girls in their schools
questions.explain: Goleman sums up the contrast: antisocial teenage girls do not get violent, they get pregnant.

questions.q: Eleven-year-old Marcus is bumped in a crowded hallway, instantly concludes it was deliberate, and shoves the other boy. Which idea from the chapter best explains his reaction?
options: A lack of intelligence that makes him fail his schoolwork
A perceptual bias that assumes hostility, followed by automatic aggression
Peer pressure from an outcast group he has joined
Hyperactivity that makes him unable to sit still
questions.explain: Aggressive children jump to a presumption of threat without checking what is actually going on, and then leapfrog to action.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says that all angry, aggressive children are bullies.
questions.explain: Some are withdrawn social outcasts who overreact to teasing or perceived unfairness; what they share is the perceptual flaw of seeing slights.

questions.q: True or false: Within two or three hours of a first playground contact with a bully, other children already say they dislike him.
questions.explain: Aggressive children rely on force and bluster, and pay a quick social price.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman argues that growing up in poverty or a high-crime neighborhood makes a life of violent crime inevitable.
questions.explain: He lists such factors as risks but says none of them makes a life of violent crime inevitable.

questions.q: The psychologist who has followed hundreds of boys into young adulthood and said the antisocial acts of a five-year-old may be prototypic of those of the delinquent adolescent is Gerald ____.
questions.explain: Patterson's long-term following of boys supports the continuity of aggression from age five to adolescence.

questions.q: Up to ____ of first graders who are disruptive, disobedient and unable to get along with others become delinquents in their teen years.
questions.explain: Studies following preschoolers into their teens found this.

questions.q: Children who learn a coercive style at home, which the author glosses as ____, are often written off by teachers who spend too much time keeping them in line.
questions.explain: Such children waste classroom time defying rules, and their academic failure is obvious by about third grade.

questions.q: Put these stages of the prototypical pathway to violence and criminality in the order they typically occur.
items: Aggressive and hard to handle in first and second grade
Poor impulse control makes them poor students
Academic failure is obvious by about third grade
Rejected by peers by fourth or fifth grade and drawn to other outcasts
Drop out and drift into petty crimes in high school
questions.explain: The path runs from early aggression through school failure and peer rejection to an outcast group and delinquency.

questions.q: Match each study or finding about aggressive children with what it showed.
pairs: About three times the delinquent acts by the early teens
Fourth-grade girls who were bad but popular
40 percent had a child by high-school graduation
Almost three times as strong a delinquency predictor as IQ
Disruptive first graders followed into their teens
questions.explain: Each result shows how early aggression or poor impulse control points toward later trouble.

questions.q: Sort each of these into whether it describes aggressive children or most other children by second grade.

items.t: Read an innocent bump as a vendetta
Rely more and more on force and bluster
Jump to accusation, yelling and hitting
Begin to learn negotiation and compromise
Settle playground disagreements without fighting
Develop a modicum of self-control

questions.explain: By second grade most children are learning self-control and compromise, while aggressive children fall back on force.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman name as other factors that can put a child at risk of violence and criminality?
options: Being born in a high-crime neighborhood
Coming from a family under high levels of stress
Living in poverty
Being an only child
Attending a large school
questions.explain: He lists neighborhood, family stress and poverty, but says none makes violent crime inevitable.

questions.q: Which of these are traits of angry, isolated children according to the chapter?
options: They see themselves as victims of unfair treatment
They are highly sensitive to injustice
In the heat of anger they can think of only one way to react
They readily negotiate to settle disputes
They underestimate other children's hostility
questions.explain: They perceive more hostility than exists, feel wronged, and see lashing out as the only reaction.

questions.q: Explain how the hostile perceptual bias of aggressive children turns into a cycle of social isolation.
questions.a: They see neutral acts as threats and respond with automatic aggression. Other children then dislike and shun them, and the bullies themselves feel victimized, which isolates them further and pushes them toward other outcasts. Goleman notes that these children are emotionally vulnerable with a low threshold for upset and that once upset their thinking is muddled.

questions.q: Describe the typical path from an aggressive first grader to a teenage delinquent as Goleman lays it out.
questions.a: A child who is aggressive and hard to handle in first and second grade has poor impulse control, is a poor student by third grade and is shunted aside. By fourth or fifth grade the child is rejected by peers, joins other outcasts, and greatly increases truancy, drinking and drug taking. In high school this group tends to drop out and drift into petty crimes such as shoplifting, theft and drug dealing.

questions.q: Why does Goleman say impulsivity matters more than IQ in the drift toward delinquency?
