questions.a: Boys heading for delinquency do tend to have lower IQ scores, but impulsivity in ten-year-old boys is almost three times as powerful a predictor of later delinquency as IQ. Poor impulse control also leads to poor schooling and defiance of rules, so it is more directly the cause.

questions.q: What mind-set did a study find in violent juvenile offenders and aggressive high-school students?
options: They plan violent acts carefully, weighing the consequences first
They feel guilty about fights but cannot stop themselves
They jump to conclusions about the other person's hostility without seeking information, and the costs of a violent solution never cross their mind
They believe adults will always protect them from harm
questions.explain: Their aggression is justified by beliefs that violence is acceptable when angry and that backing down shows cowardice.

questions.q: How was the Duke University anger-control program for grade-school troublemakers structured?
options: A full school year of daily lessons for the whole class
A single weekend workshop with parents
Weekly counseling for the boys' families lasting two years
Forty-minute training sessions twice a week for six to twelve weeks
questions.explain: The sessions taught the boys to reinterpret cues, take others' perspectives and control anger.

questions.q: What is the key skill for anger control taught in the Duke program?
options: Monitoring their feelings, noticing body sensations such as flushing or tensing, and taking them as a cue to stop and think
Suppressing anger completely so it never shows
Telling a teacher whenever another child bothers them
Avoiding all situations where teasing might occur
questions.explain: The boys learn to treat early physical signs of anger as a signal to consider what to do next rather than strike out.

questions.q: Three years later, how did boys who had been through the Duke training compare with equally aggressive boys who had not?
options: They were the same in class but less likely to be arrested
They were less disruptive in class, felt better about themselves and were less likely to drink or take drugs
They were more popular but just as disruptive
They did better in math but had worse self-esteem
questions.explain: Lochman also found that the longer they had been in the program, the less aggressive they were as teenagers.

questions.q: Why do the Duke boys practice alternatives in role-playing scenes such as being taunted on a bus?
options: Role-playing replaces the need for anyone to learn anger control
It lets the boys practice hitting without real harm
Cool-headed responses such as walking away or counting to ten are not automatic in the heat of the moment, so they must be rehearsed
It teaches them to avoid public transportation
questions.explain: Rehearsal lets them try friendly responses that preserve dignity while avoiding hitting, crying or running away in shame.

questions.q: True or false: The Duke program taught boys that some social cues they took as hostile were in fact neutral or friendly.
questions.explain: Reinterpreting such cues was one of the program's lessons, along with perspective taking and anger control.

questions.q: True or false: Lochman found that the longer boys had been in the program, the less aggressive they were as teenagers.
questions.explain: The trained boys became less aggressive in proportion to time in the program.

questions.q: One belief that justifies aggression for violent youths is, 'If you back down from a fight everyone will think you're a ____.'
questions.explain: Such beliefs are part of the mind-set that keeps aggressive youths on the path to trouble.

questions.q: The Duke University psychologist who helped design the anger-control program and spoke to Goleman about it is John ____.
questions.explain: Lochman also compared the trained boys with untrained ones three years later.

questions.q: Which of these were taught in the Duke University program for aggressive boys?
options: Seeing that some cues they read as hostile were neutral or friendly
Taking the perspective of other children
Enacting scenes such as being teased to practice anger control
Memorizing school discipline rules
Avoiding all contact with other aggressive boys
questions.explain: The program combined reinterpreting cues, perspective taking and anger control practice through role-play.

questions.q: Put in order the steps the Duke program teaches a boy to follow as he starts to get angry.
items: Notice body sensations such as flushing or muscle tensing
Take them as a cue to stop
Consider what to do next
Choose a calmer alternative such as walking away or counting to ten
questions.explain: The body's signals come first and serve as the trigger for stopping and choosing a non-violent response.

questions.q: How does the Duke program change what an aggressive boy does when another boy bumps him in a hallway?
questions.a: Instead of assuming the bump was deliberate and striking out, he learns to see that some cues are neutral, to think of how the other child sees it, and to notice his body's anger signals. He can then respond with a calm alternative, like staring and telling the other boy not to do it again and walking away, which keeps control and self-esteem without a fight.

questions.q: What does Goleman say about why the aggressive boys in the Duke program were receptive to the training?
questions.a: Many such boys are unhappy that they lose their temper so easily, so they welcome learning to control it. They practice cool-headed alternatives in role-played situations so they can choose friendly responses that preserve their dignity.

questions.q: What was the focus of the Columbia University treatment that lifted sixteen-year-old Dana's depression?
options: Medication to lift her mood while her relationships stayed the same
Family therapy aimed at her parents' marriage
Academic tutoring to help her catch up at her new school
Remedial lessons in basic emotional skills such as developing friendships, asserting limits and expressing feelings
questions.explain: The treatment was in essence a remedial tutorial in some of the most basic emotional skills, and her depression lifted.

questions.q: Depressed children often cannot label their feelings accurately and show instead a sullen ____, impatience and crankiness, especially toward parents.
questions.explain: This makes it harder for parents to give support, setting off a downward spiral of arguments and alienation.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says the tendency to depression in the young is due entirely to genetic destiny.
questions.explain: Some is genetic, but some seems due to reversible pessimistic habits of thought.

questions.q: Which of these were difficulties for Dana before her depression?
options: Not knowing how to end an unsatisfying relationship
Holding back from starting conversations with girls at her new school
Not knowing how to avoid getting sexually involved with a boy right away
Failing most of her classes
Constant quarrels with a younger sibling
questions.explain: Her problems were relationship skills: ending relationships, setting limits on sexual closeness and starting conversations.

questions.q: Sort each of these into the area of emotional competence in which new research finds deficits in depressed young people.

items.t: Not knowing how to develop a friendship
Not knowing how to assert limits on closeness
Not knowing how to express feelings to others
Treating a bad grade as a lasting personal flaw
Reacting to a social rejection with pessimism
Magnifying small defeats into hopelessness

questions.explain: The chapter pinpoints two areas: relationship skills, and a pessimistic way of reading life's small defeats.

questions.q: Why does the typical behavior of a depressed child toward parents make the problem worse?
questions.a: Depressed children are often unable or unwilling to talk about their sadness and cannot label feelings accurately, so they show sullen irritability and anger, especially toward parents. That makes it harder for parents to give the emotional support the child needs, producing constant arguments and alienation.

questions.q: Put these in the order of the downward spiral Goleman describes between a depressed child and parents.
items: Child cannot label sadness accurately
Child shows irritability and anger toward parents
Parents find it harder to give support and guidance
Constant arguments and alienation follow
questions.explain: Unlabeled sadness comes out as anger, which pushes away the support the child needs.

questions.section: A Cost of Modernity: Rising Rates of Depression
questions.q: Which comparison does Goleman use to describe the rise of depression in the millennial years?
options: An Age of Melancholy, as the twentieth century became an Age of Anxiety
An Age of Reason, following the Age of Enlightenment
An Age of Isolation, following an Age of Industry
An Age of Violence, following an Age of Melancholy
questions.explain: He sees a modern epidemic of depression spreading with the adoption of modern ways around the world.

questions.section: A Cost of Modernity: Rising Rates of Depression
questions.q: For Americans born after 1955, how does the lifetime likelihood of major depression compare with that of their grandparents?
options: It is about the same, but the cases are more severe
In many countries it is three times or more greater
It is roughly half
It is about equal but starts later
questions.explain: Each generation worldwide has faced higher risk, and the greatest increases are among the young.

questions.section: A Cost of Modernity: Rising Rates of Depression
questions.q: What happened to depression in Beirut according to the worldwide study of more than thirty-nine thousand people?
options: It fell during civil war because people were united
It did not rise at all, unlike in other places
The upward trend tracked political events, rocketing during periods of civil war
It rose only among the very old
questions.explain: Troubled political times raised rates, though the overall upward trend holds apart from political events.

questions.section: A Cost of Modernity: Rising Rates of Depression
questions.q: Seligman explains the rise in depression partly by a waning of religion, community and extended-family supports. Why would that matter?
options: It removes the need for children to learn social skills
It increases the number of setbacks people face
It makes people less aware of their feelings
It removes resources that buffer against setbacks, so a failure is more easily seen as lasting and all-tainting
questions.explain: A larger perspective, like religious belief, lets a lost job feel like a temporary defeat.

questions.section: A Cost of Modernity: Rising Rates of Depression
questions.q: Two people lose their jobs. One has a strong sense of a larger perspective in religion and community; the other has only a sense of individual self-reliance. By Seligman's reasoning, which is more prone to a lasting sense of hopelessness?
options: The second, who lacks buffers and may magnify the failure to taint everything
The first, because faith makes setbacks seem larger
Neither, because job loss never causes depression
Both equally, because beliefs have no effect
questions.explain: Seligman says larger beliefs make a job loss just a temporary defeat.

questions.section: A Cost of Modernity: Rising Rates of Depression
questions.q: Among Americans born before 1905, only about ____ percent had a major depression over a lifetime.
questions.explain: For those born since 1955, about 6 percent had been depressed by age twenty-four.

questions.section: A Cost of Modernity: Rising Rates of Depression
questions.q: The psychologist from the University of Pennsylvania who blamed the ascendance of individualism for a loss of buffers against setbacks is Martin ____.
questions.explain: His theory centers on a waning of religion, community and extended-family support.

questions.section: A Cost of Modernity: Rising Rates of Depression
questions.q: True or false: According to the worldwide study, the upward trend in depression appeared only in generations that came of age in politically troubled times.
questions.explain: Troubled generations had higher rates, but the overall upward trend holds apart from any political events.

questions.section: A Cost of Modernity: Rising Rates of Depression
questions.q: True or false: Dr. David Kupfer said that parental indifference is not a direct cause of depression but sets up a vulnerability.
questions.explain: He suggested early emotional stressors may affect neuron development, producing depression decades later under great stress.

questions.section: A Cost of Modernity: Rising Rates of Depression
questions.q: Match each expert with the explanation he offered for the rise of depression.
pairs: Erosion of the nuclear family, with less time for children and less contact with extended family
After industrialization nobody was home, creating growing parental indifference and vulnerability
Individualism and waning religion and community removed buffers against setbacks
questions.explain: Each expert pointed to a different social change behind the epidemic.

questions.section: A Cost of Modernity: Rising Rates of Depression
questions.q: Which of these places did the worldwide study of more than thirty-nine thousand people include?
options: Puerto Rico
Taiwan
Lebanon
Japan
Brazil
questions.explain: It found the same trend in Puerto Rico, Canada, Italy, Germany, France, Taiwan, Lebanon and New Zealand.

questions.section: A Cost of Modernity: Rising Rates of Depression
questions.q: How do the age of first depression and the generation relate, according to the international data Goleman cites?
questions.a: Each successive generation since the start of the century has had a higher lifetime risk of major depression, and for each generation the first episode tends to occur at an earlier age. Childhood depression, once virtually unknown, is emerging as a fixture of the modern scene.

questions.section: A Cost of Modernity: Rising Rates of Depression
questions.q: Summarize the three explanations offered by experts for why depression is rising among the young.
questions.a: Goodwin pointed to the erosion of the nuclear family, with more divorce, less parental time and more mobility. Kupfer cited growing parental indifference after industrialization, which creates a vulnerability. Seligman cited individualism and the waning of religion and community supports that buffer setbacks.

questions.section: A Cost of Modernity: Rising Rates of Depression
questions.q: Put these generations in the order of rising lifetime risk of major depression, from lowest to highest.
items: Born before 1905
Born between 1905 and 1914
Born between 1945 and 1954
Born after 1955
questions.explain: Risk climbs with each generation, and those born after 1955 are at three times or more the risk of their grandparents.

questions.section: The Course of Depression in the Young
questions.q: What assumption does the finding that even mild childhood depression foretells later severe episodes challenge?
options: That depression is more common in adults than in children
That children grow out of depression, so it does not matter in the long run
That depression in the young is always caused by divorce
That depression can only be treated with medication
questions.explain: Goleman argues depression should be prevented, not just treated, in children.

questions.section: The Course of Depression in the Young
questions.q: In Kovacs's study, what share of children whose depression was severe enough for referral had a later severe episode?
options: One quarter
One half
Three quarters
Nearly all
questions.explain: Kovacs followed children diagnosed as early as eight until some were twenty-four.

questions.section: The Course of Depression in the Young
questions.q: How did the duration of mild depression in Kovacs's study compare with that of major depression?
options: Mild lasted about the same time as major
Mild was shorter, averaging about eleven months
Mild was longer and more incapacitating
Mild was less incapacitating but lasted far longer, about four years on average, versus about eleven months for major
questions.explain: A minor depression can also intensify into a major one, called a double depression.

questions.section: The Course of Depression in the Young
questions.q: Why do depressed children end up missing out on learning social skills from play?
options: Their sadness leads them to avoid initiating contact or to look away, which others take as a rebuff, so they are rejected or neglected
Their parents keep them out of school during episodes
Other children bully them out of the playground
They prefer to play only with older children
questions.explain: That gap leaves them social and emotional laggards with much catching up to do after the depression lifts.

questions.section: The Course of Depression in the Young
questions.q: A ten-year-old has been mildly depressed for a year. Her friends stopped inviting her to play after she repeatedly turned away when they approached. What does Kovacs's work suggest about this?
options: Her classmates are the cause of her depression
Her withdrawal is being read as rejection, costing her peer learning she will later have to make up
The depression will end once she gets older
She will do as well as her classmates in school
questions.explain: Depressed children's social signals are misread as rebuffs and lead to neglect.

questions.section: The Course of Depression in the Young
questions.q: A child with minor depression who develops a major depression on top of it has what Kovacs called ____ depression.
questions.explain: Those with double depression are much more prone to recurring episodes.

questions.section: The Course of Depression in the Young
questions.q: The Pittsburgh psychologist who followed children diagnosed with depression from age eight to as old as twenty-four is Maria ____.
questions.explain: Kovacs found that grades dropped the longer a child had been depressed.

questions.section: The Course of Depression in the Young
questions.q: True or false: Kovacs found that the longer a child had been depressed, the more grades dropped and the more likely the child was to be held back in school.
questions.explain: Depression interferes with memory and concentration and leaves a child without energy for challenging lessons.

questions.section: The Course of Depression in the Young
questions.q: Put these steps in the order Goleman gives for how childhood depression damages social learning.
items: Sadness leads the child to avoid or look away from others
Other children take this as a rebuff
The depressed child is rejected or neglected on the playground
The child misses the rough-and-tumble where social skills are learned
The child is left a social and emotional laggard
questions.explain: The social signal of a depressed child is misread, which then costs experience.

questions.section: The Course of Depression in the Young
questions.q: Sort each of these facts into major depression or mild depression in Kovacs's findings.

items.t: Episodes last about eleven months on average
One in six lasted as long as eighteen months
Less incapacitating
Lasts an average of about four years
Can begin as early as age five
Can be preceded by a minor depression that intensifies

questions.explain: Major episodes were shorter, with a minority lasting eighteen months, while mild depression was milder but chronic.

questions.section: The Course of Depression in the Young
questions.q: Why does Goleman say childhood depression should be prevented and not only treated?
questions.a: Even mild episodes can augur more severe ones later, and Kovacs found three quarters of severely depressed children had another severe episode. Beyond suffering, depression costs children social learning with peers and school performance, and these losses compound the depression.

questions.section: The Course of Depression in the Young
questions.q: How does depression damage a child's schoolwork, and why does this compound the depression?
questions.a: Depression interferes with memory and concentration and removes the energy to master challenging lessons, so grades fall in step with the length of the episode and children may be held back. Flunking school and sitting at home alone add to the original depression, as Kovacs observes.

questions.section: The Course of Depression in the Young
questions.q: Match each Kovacs finding with the measure it describes.
pairs: Average length of major depression episodes
Share of referred children with a later severe episode
Time spent depressed in adolescence and early adulthood
questions.explain: These are the figures Kovacs reported for the course of depression.

questions.q: What new finding about pessimistic thinking creates a window of opportunity for inoculating children against depression?
options: Pessimism is caused only by depression itself
Pessimistic children never become depressed
Children most prone to melancholy tend toward pessimism before they become depressed
Pessimism appears only after adolescence
questions.explain: It had long been known that depressed people think pessimistically; what is new is that it comes first.

questions.q: In the study of fifth and sixth graders after report cards, which children felt more depressed after a worse grade than expected?
options: Those who explained it by something they could change
Those who got the best grades overall
Those who did not care about grades
Those who saw it as a personal flaw such as being stupid
questions.explain: Children who said they would work harder were less depressed.

questions.q: What distinguished rejected third to fifth graders who became depressed from those who did not?
options: How they explained the rejection: blaming a flaw in themselves versus believing they could change things
How many friends their older siblings had
Whether their parents were divorced
How well they performed on achievement tests
questions.explain: Optimists who thought they could do something were not especially depressed despite continuing rejection.

questions.q: In the five-year study starting in third grade, what was the strongest predictor of depression among the younger children?
options: A high IQ combined with a shy temperament
A pessimistic outlook coupled with a major blow such as parents divorcing or a death in the family
Poor grades combined with being unpopular
Aggressive behavior combined with weak parents
questions.explain: The blow left the child upset and parents less able to give a buffer.

questions.q: After a depression lifts, Goleman says a child can be left with an emotional ____, a set of fixed convictions that make later depression more likely.
questions.explain: The experience of depression reinforces pessimistic ways of thinking.

questions.q: Over the third to fifth grades, children increasingly ascribe good and bad events to their own ____, as in 'I don't have many friends because I'm no fun.'
questions.explain: That shift lets pessimistic children fall prey to depressed moods after setbacks.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says the recent discovery is that children most prone to melancholy think pessimistically before they become depressed.
questions.explain: That depressed people think pessimistically was long known; the new point is that it comes first.

questions.q: Which of these convictions does Goleman say depression can solidify in a child's mind?
options: He cannot do well in school
He is unlikable
He can do nothing to escape his own brooding moods
His parents do not love him
His teachers are unfair to him
questions.explain: These fixed ideas form an emotional scar that leaves the child vulnerable to another depression.

questions.q: Match each study of pessimism with what it found.
pairs: Fifth and sixth graders after report cards
Blaming a personal flaw brought more depression than blaming something changeable
Optimists who thought they could change things were not especially depressed
Pessimists became depressed in response to school hassles and extra stress at home
Pessimism plus a major blow best predicted depression in younger children
questions.explain: All four lines of evidence point to pessimistic interpretation as a vulnerability.

questions.q: Sort each of these explanations of a bad result into the pessimistic or hopeful style.

items.t: I got a bad grade because I'm stupid
I have no friends because I'm no fun
There is nothing I can do about it
If I work harder on math I will get a better grade
I can do something to change things for the better
I will study harder after doing poorly on this exam

questions.explain: Seeing the cause as a fixed flaw feeds helplessness, while seeing it as changeable protects against it.

questions.q: Put in order the sequence the five-year study describes as children grow through elementary school.
items: A pessimistic outlook plus a major blow predicts depression in younger children
Children increasingly ascribe events to their own traits across third to fifth grades
Pessimistic children fall into depressed moods after setbacks
Depression reinforces the pessimism and leaves an emotional scar
questions.explain: The shift to trait explanations sets up depression in reaction to setbacks, which then entrenches the pessimism.

questions.q: Why does it matter that pessimistic thinking comes before depression in vulnerable children?
questions.a: Because it suggests a window of opportunity for inoculating children against depression before it strikes. If a way of explaining defeat predisposes them, then teaching more productive ways of interpreting setbacks could lower their risk.

questions.q: Describe the shift Goleman reports in how children explain good and bad events as they move through elementary school.
questions.a: Across third to fifth grades children increasingly ascribe the events of their lives to their own traits, as in 'I'm getting good grades because I'm smart' or 'I don't have many friends because I'm no fun.' Those who attribute setbacks to a dire flaw in themselves begin to fall prey to depressed moods in reaction to setbacks.

questions.q: In the Oregon high school study, roughly what share of students had a low-level depression?
options: About one in twenty
About one in two
About one in four
About one in ten
questions.explain: It was not severe enough to be beyond ordinary unhappiness, but some students may have been in the early stage of depression.

questions.q: After the eight-week after-school program, how did the recovery of mildly depressed students compare with that of a similar group not in the program?
options: 14 percent versus 8 percent
About the same in both groups
29 percent versus 44 percent
55 percent had recovered versus about a quarter of those not in the program
questions.explain: A year later 14 percent of the program group had fallen into major depression, compared with about a quarter of the comparison group.

questions.q: In Seligman's twelve-week class for ten-to-thirteen-year-olds, how many of those in the course versus the comparison group scored moderate-to-severe on a depression test a year later?
options: 8 percent versus 29 percent
29 percent versus 8 percent
20 percent versus 44 percent
14 percent versus 25 percent
questions.explain: After two years about 20 percent of the course group showed signs of at least mild depression, versus 44 percent of the comparison group.

questions.q: Why does Seligman say disputing depressing thoughts becomes a habit?
options: Because teachers reward the children with prizes
Because it vanquishes the gathering gloom, it is an instant reinforcer
Because it makes them forget their problems
Because it is required by their parents
questions.explain: Children learn that moods do not descend uncontrollably but can be changed by what they think.

questions.q: A parent wants to protect an eleven-year-old who is quarreling with her and showing signs of low mood. Which approach does the chapter's evidence support?
options: Waiting, since children grow out of it
Starting tricyclic antidepressants, which work for children as for adults
A class that teaches handling disagreements, thinking before acting and challenging pessimistic beliefs
Having the child avoid peers until her mood lifts
questions.explain: Programs of this type cut depression rates roughly in half, even two years later; the footnote notes medication is not a clear alternative for children.

questions.q: Kovacs called the new prevention programs a psychological ____, since you have to act before the kids get sick in the first place.
questions.explain: Prevention before illness, like vaccination, is the logic of the programs.

questions.q: Seligman said disputing depressing thoughts is an instant ____ that becomes a habit.
questions.explain: The relief from gloom rewards the habit of challenging pessimistic thoughts.

questions.q: True or false: The footnote says tricyclic antidepressants have proved better than placebo in controlled studies with children.
questions.explain: They are often successful with adults but have failed to prove better than an inactive placebo in children.

questions.q: Which of these were taught in the Oregon after-school class for mildly depressed students?
options: Challenging thinking patterns associated with depression
Becoming better at making friends
Getting along better with parents
Taking medication regularly
Ranking their friends by popularity
questions.explain: The class also encouraged more social activities they found pleasant.

questions.q: Match each program group with the outcome reported.
pairs: Oregon students in the program, eight weeks later
Oregon students in the program, a year later
Seligman class a year after ending
Seligman comparison group a year later
questions.explain: Both programs roughly halved depression rates relative to comparison groups.

questions.q: Put these stages in order for the Oregon program's results, from earliest to latest.
items: Mildly depressed students attend an eight-week class
Students learn to challenge pessimistic thoughts and improve friendships
55 percent recover versus about a quarter of the comparison group
A year later 14 percent versus a quarter have major depression
questions.explain: The program ran eight sessions, and the benefits held a year on.

questions.q: Sort each skill into whether it targets thinking or relationships in the prevention classes.

items.t: Challenge pessimistic beliefs
Dispute depressing thoughts
Resolve to study harder instead of thinking I'm not smart enough
Make friends more readily
Get along better with parents
Handle disagreements

questions.explain: The programs combined cognitive skills with social skills.

questions.q: What evidence shows that teaching children to challenge pessimistic thinking lowers their depression risk?
questions.a: In Oregon, an eight-week class helped 55 percent of mildly depressed students recover, versus about a quarter of the comparison group, and a year later 14 percent versus a quarter had major depression. Seligman's twelve-week class for ten-to-thirteen-year-olds cut depression rates by half, which still held two years later.

questions.q: Why does Seligman think the lesson is especially useful at the cusp of adolescence?
questions.a: It is a crucial window of risk for depression, and children who learned the skills then handle the routine teenage agonies of rejection better. The lesson also seems to persist and grow stronger over the years, which suggests the children are using it in daily life.

questions.q: What did Hilda Bruch propose as one underlying cause of eating disorders in women who starved themselves?
options: Intrusive mothers who enmesh daughters in a web of guilt
A fear of adult sexuality at puberty
An inability to label and respond appropriately to bodily urges such as hunger
Unattainably high standards of beauty alone
questions.explain: Bruch published her seminal article in 1969 and pointed to a deficit in recognizing bodily signals.

questions.q: Why did Goleman prefer the Minneapolis study to earlier hypotheses about eating disorders?
options: It used only girls who were already in treatment
It relied on mothers' memories of their daughters
It compared girls with eating disorders to boys
It followed a large group of girls over several years to see who developed the problem, instead of extrapolating from therapy
questions.explain: Prospective studies allow a clean comparison and can separate real causes from conditions found equally in people without the problem.

questions.q: What did Gloria Leon find to be the strongest single predictor that girls would develop an eating disorder within two years?
options: Poor awareness of their feelings and body signals
Overly controlling parents
Low self-esteem
Early onset of puberty
questions.explain: These girls could not tell bored, angry, depressed and hungry apart, and learned to soothe themselves by eating.

questions.q: True or false: The Minneapolis study found that overly controlling parents did not play a prime role in causing eating disorders.
questions.explain: Parents can become intensely controlling in response to a daughter's eating disorder, so hindsight theories mislead.

questions.q: True or false: The Minneapolis study found that an obsession with being overweight was in itself sufficient to explain which girls developed eating disorders.
questions.explain: Many girls were preoccupied with weight; what mattered was the combination with unsoothed distress and poor emotional awareness.

questions.q: The pioneer who published a seminal article on eating disorders in 1969 was Hilda ____.
questions.explain: Bruch also warned that theories based on hindsight were unlikely to be accurate.

questions.q: The University of Minnesota psychologist who studied young girls and eating disorders is Gloria ____.
questions.explain: Leon said that if you address emotional deficits, therapy works better.

questions.q: Which of these were judged irrelevant as popular explanations of eating disorders in the Minneapolis study?
options: Fear of sexuality
Early onset of puberty
Low self-esteem
Poor awareness of feelings
Intense negative feelings the girl cannot soothe
questions.explain: The key factors were emotional deficits combined with body dissatisfaction.

questions.q: Which of these combine, according to the Minneapolis study, to lead to anorexia or bulimia?
options: Intense negative reactions the girls could not soothe
Poor awareness of exactly what they were feeling
High dissatisfaction with their bodies
Overly controlling mothers
An early start of puberty
questions.explain: When the two emotional tendencies were coupled with body dissatisfaction, the outcome was an eating disorder.

questions.q: Put these links in order in the causal chain revealed by the prospective study.
items: Growing up in a society preoccupied with thinness
Girls become self-conscious about weight well before adolescence
Poor awareness of feelings and trouble soothing distress
Eating to feel better becomes an entrenched habit
Pressure to stay thin leads to bingeing, vomiting, laxatives or not eating
questions.explain: The cultural pressure meets an emotional deficit and produces the disorder.

questions.q: Match each behavior with how Leon links it to emotional confusion.
pairs: Learning to feel better by eating
Undoing weight gain to stay thin
A way to feel some control over overwhelming feelings
Not knowing whether one is angry, anxious or depressed
questions.explain: Each shows an emotional struggle expressed through eating.

questions.q: Sort each factor into whether the Minneapolis study found it a key cause or judged it irrelevant.

items.t: Failure to tell distressing feelings apart
Failure to control distressing feelings
Dissatisfaction with the body
Overly controlling parents
Fear of sexuality
Low self-esteem

questions.explain: Emotional deficits plus body dissatisfaction drove the outcome; the popular explanations did not.

questions.q: Why did Goleman consider the Minneapolis prospective study more trustworthy than hypotheses based on observations in therapy?
questions.a: Theories from therapy are extrapolations made in hindsight, whereas a study that follows large groups over several years can show who actually develops the problem. It can identify the cluster of conditions that lead to it and exclude those that are as common in people without it, and it showed that controlling parents did not play a prime role.

questions.q: How does emotional confusion lead a girl toward an eating disorder, in Leon's account?
questions.a: Girls with poor awareness of their feelings experience a diffuse emotional storm and learn to soothe themselves by eating, which becomes an entrenched habit. Combined with pressure to be thin, they turn to vomiting, laxatives or exercise after bingeing, or to not eating as a way to feel in control, and weak social skills mean they cannot soothe the relationship or themselves.

questions.q: What is most telling about Ben's reaction when his friend Jason tries to repair their quarrel?
options: He immediately forgives Jason and rejoins the game
He fails to respond to Jason's efforts, extending his plight when it might have ended
He asks a teacher to settle the dispute
He talks it out with a group of girls
questions.explain: Such inability to seize key cues is typical of unpopular children.

questions.q: How does the dropout rate of children rejected by peers compare with that of children who have friends?
options: About the same
Slightly higher
Between two and eight times greater
About half
questions.explain: One study found about 25 percent of unpopular elementary-school children dropped out before finishing high school, versus a general rate of 8 percent.

questions.q: What did grade schoolers with few friends do worse than popular children when matching emotions to faces?
options: They refused to take part
They matched emotions faster
They made no mismatches
They made far more mismatches
questions.explain: Unpopular children are off in the emotional signals they send and read.

questions.q: What did Goleman say is a better predictor of mental-health problems at age eighteen than teachers' and nurses' ratings, school performance, IQ or psychological tests?
options: How popular a child was in third grade
Number of siblings
Parents' income
Height at age eight
questions.explain: Rejected children report great anxiety, worry, depression and loneliness.

questions.q: Unpopular children asked what to do when two children want the same toy came up with self-defeating answers such as '____ him.'
questions.explain: Their social incompetence becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy.

questions.q: The psychoanalyst who said we learn to negotiate intimate relations in our first close friendships with same-sex chums is Harry Stack ____.
questions.explain: Socially rejected children are only half as likely to have a best friend in elementary school.

questions.q: Goleman writes that unpopular children are not seen as fun, and observed that they are much more likely to cheat, sulk, quit when losing, or ____ about winning.
questions.explain: They fail to contain emotional reactions that undermine friendship.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says one friend can make a difference for a rejected child even when all others turn their backs.
questions.explain: Even a friendship that is not very solid helps.

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says children who go through a temporary period of feeling left out face the same risks as those continually rejected.
questions.explain: The outcast status that clings to the continually excluded is what carries the greater risk.

questions.q: Which of these are the two kinds of emotional proclivities that lead children to be social outcasts?
options: Propensity to angry outbursts and perceiving hostility where none is intended
Being timid, anxious and socially shy
Being gifted academically
Being overly confident
Having been abused
questions.explain: Besides these temperaments, children who are off, whose awkwardness makes people uncomfortable, are shunted aside.

questions.q: Which of these did Goleman observe in unpopular children at play?
options: Cheating
Sulking
Quitting when losing
Containing their reaction to losing
Congratulating the winner
questions.explain: Popular children contain their emotional reaction so it does not undermine friendship.

questions.q: Match each task given to unpopular children with how they performed.
pairs: Far more mismatches than popular children
Explaining how to make friends or avoid fights
Self-defeating answers or vague appeals for adult help
More likely to cheat, sulk, quit or brag
questions.explain: These show unpopular children read and send emotional signals poorly.

questions.q: Match each finding with the statistic Goleman cites.
pairs: Dropout rate of rejected children versus those with friends
Unpopular elementary students who dropped out
About 25 percent versus a general 8 percent
Rejected children having a best friend
Best predictor of mental health problems at eighteen
questions.explain: Rejection has measurable costs.

questions.q: Put these events in Ben's lunchtime story in the order they happen.
items: Jason says he will play with Chad instead
Ben cries, then yells that he hates Jason
Jason and Chad try to talk to Ben, who covers his ears
Girls try to make peace and Ben tells them to leave him alone
questions.explain: Ben rebuffs each effort to repair the friendship.

questions.q: Sort each of these into the temperament-related route or the awkward-signals route to being a social outcast.

items.t: Perceiving hostility where none is meant
Being timid and anxious
Being socially shy
Mismatching emotions and faces
Giving unconvincing portrayals of feelings
Offering self-defeating answers about making friends

questions.explain: Over and above temperament, awkward signals make people uncomfortable.

questions.q: Why is dropping out especially a risk for socially rejected children?
questions.a: Their dropout rate is two to eight times that of children with friends, and about 25 percent of unpopular elementary students drop out versus a general rate of 8 percent. Goleman says it is small wonder, imagine spending thirty hours a week in a place where no one likes you.

questions.q: Why does the social incompetence of unpopular children become a self-fulfilling prophecy?
questions.a: They come to feel helpless to do better at making friends, and instead of learning new approaches they keep doing the same unsuccessful things or come up with even more inept responses. They are also not seen as fun or able to make others feel good, so they stay rejected.

questions.q: What do children lose by being excluded from friendships, according to Goleman?
questions.a: In the cauldron of close friendships and play, children refine the social and emotional skills they bring to later relationships, so excluded children are disadvantaged. Rejected children are half as likely to have a best friend in elementary school, and chronically lonely adults face greater risk of disease and early death.

questions.q: How did Asher avoid stigma when coaching the least-liked third and fourth graders?
options: He coached them in secret from classmates
He told them they were acting as consultants to the coach, who wanted to learn what made games more enjoyable
He told them they were chosen for being gifted
He coached them together with the most popular children
questions.explain: The sessions were presented as making playing games more fun.

questions.q: The University of Illinois psychologist who designed friendship coaching sessions for unpopular children is Steven ____.
questions.explain: Asher's sessions were six in number.

questions.q: Coached children played games such as ____ with a classmate and were coached afterward on how well they did.
questions.explain: They practiced social amenities in real play.

questions.q: True or false: A year after Asher's coaching, the coached children were solidly in the middle of classroom popularity.
questions.explain: None were social stars, but none were rejects.

questions.q: Which of these did Asher coach unpopular children to do?
options: Suggest alternatives and compromises instead of fighting over rules
Ask questions of the other child while playing
Say something nice when the other child does well
Let the other child win every game
Avoid talking to the other child
questions.explain: These were behaviors found typical of more popular children.

questions.q: Put the steps of Nowicki's program in order.
items: Children practice expressing feelings like happiness and sadness
They are videotaped doing so
They are coached to improve expressiveness
They try out the skills with a child they want as a friend
questions.explain: The program trains outcasts to read and respond to others' feelings.

questions.q: Match each researcher with the program he designed.
pairs: Friendship coaching for unpopular third and fourth graders
Training social outcasts to read and express feelings
questions.explain: These are programs mentioned in this chapter.

questions.q: What results do such coaching programs achieve, and for whom do they work best?
questions.a: They report a 50 to 60 percent success rate in raising the popularity of rejected children. They work best for third and fourth graders and for socially inept rather than highly aggressive children, but the hopeful sign is that many rejected children can be brought into the circle of friendship with basic emotional coaching.

questions.section: Drinking and Drugs: Addiction as Self- Medication
questions.q: What is the scientific theory Goleman offers for why some people who experiment with drugs or alcohol go on to dependence while most do not?
options: They are the ones who first try substances at the youngest ages
Those who stay with the habit are using the substance as a medication to soothe anxiety, anger or depression
They are the ones with the most friends who use drugs
They are the ones who feel guilty about use
questions.explain: Over 90 percent of students try alcohol but only about 14 percent become alcoholics; the vulnerable find an instant way to soothe long-standing distress.

questions.section: Drinking and Drugs: Addiction as Self- Medication
questions.q: One biological marker for the anxious path to alcoholism is undersecretion of ____, a neurotransmitter that regulates anxiety.
questions.explain: Too little GABA is experienced as a high level of tension, and sons of alcoholics with low levels saw anxiety fall as GABA rose with drinking.

questions.section: Drinking and Drugs: Addiction as Self- Medication
questions.q: The Pittsburgh psychologist who said many recovering abusers report feeling normal for the first time at their first drug is Ralph ____.
questions.explain: For people biologically predisposed, the first drink is immensely reinforcing.

questions.section: Drinking and Drugs: Addiction as Self- Medication
questions.q: Goleman calls the short-term good feeling in exchange for the steady meltdown of one's life the devil's ____ of addiction.
questions.explain: Addiction trades a quick fix for long-term ruin.

questions.section: Drinking and Drugs: Addiction as Self- Medication
questions.q: Which of these does Goleman list as raising the risk of substance abuse among those exposed to drugs?
options: Living where crack is sold on the corner and dealers model success
Easy access
A peer culture that glamorizes drugs
Having too much free time at school
Having parents who are strict
questions.explain: Peer glamorization raises risk in any neighborhood, even the well-off.

questions.section: Drinking and Drugs: Addiction as Self- Medication
questions.q: Which of these describe the second emotional pathway to alcoholism?
options: Restless, cranky and hard to handle in infancy
Fidgets, hyperactivity and trouble in grade school
Impulsive search for risk and excitement when bored
Being highly strung and anxious from childhood
Having low frontal-lobe functioning at age twelve
questions.explain: The first pathway involves childhood anxiety; the second involves agitation, impulsivity and boredom.

questions.section: Drinking and Drugs: Addiction as Self- Medication
questions.q: Marisol is a twenty-year-old who has been chronically unhappy for years and has now started abusing a drug. According to the chapter, which substances is she more likely to be drawn to, and which not?
options: Cocaine, an antidote to feeling depressed
Other stimulants
Alcohol as her main relief
Heroin and opioids as her main relief
Sedatives to calm anxiety
questions.explain: Chronic unhappiness raises the risk for stimulants such as cocaine; alcohol is used more to calm anxiety, and opioids relate to anger.

questions.section: Drinking and Drugs: Addiction as Self- Medication
questions.q: True or false: Goleman says alcohol is a lasting remedy for depression because it lifts mood.
questions.explain: Alcohol's metabolic effects often simply worsen depression after a short lift; people drink more often for anxiety.

questions.section: Drinking and Drugs: Addiction as Self- Medication
questions.q: Put in order the way Goleman describes a person being drawn into addiction as self-medication.
items: Emotional distress that has tormented the person for years
Early experimentation reveals a chemical fix
The substance becomes an instant way to soothe the distress
Dependence develops and life melts down
questions.explain: Distress comes first and the substance becomes the medication.

questions.section: Drinking and Drugs: Addiction as Self- Medication
questions.q: Put these in the order in which Goleman presents the emotional routes into addiction.
items: Anxiety leading to alcohol
Agitation and impulsivity leading to alcohol and many drugs
Depression leading to cocaine
Anger leading to opioids
questions.explain: The chapter gives two pathways to alcoholism and then depression and anger as paths to other drugs.

questions.section: Drinking and Drugs: Addiction as Self- Medication
questions.q: Match each emotional state with the substance people use to relieve it.
pairs: Chronic anger and quickness to rage
An almost random list of drugs besides alcohol
questions.explain: Each emotional pattern seems to make a particular substance appealing.

questions.section: Drinking and Drugs: Addiction as Self- Medication
questions.q: Match each study with what it found.
pairs: Seventh and eighth graders tracked for two years
Higher emotional distress predicted the highest substance abuse
Low GABA and high anxiety, with drinking raising GABA
Most at-risk children reported chronic high anxiety
More than half would have been diagnosed with severe depression before the habit
questions.explain: These findings support self-medication.

questions.section: Drinking and Drugs: Addiction as Self- Medication
questions.q: Sort each trait into the anxious or the impulsive pathway to alcoholism.

items.t: Highly strung in childhood
Often sons of alcoholics who drink to calm nerves
Undersecretion of GABA
Restless, cranky infants
Mainly men, with a tendency toward antisocial personality disorder
Unable to stand monotony

questions.explain: One path seeks calm, the other seeks relief from agitation and boredom.

questions.section: Drinking and Drugs: Addiction as Self- Medication
questions.q: Sort each fact into drinking among students or the first-experiment statistics.

items.t: Drinking to black means bingeing to the point of passing out
Alcohol is involved in 90 percent of reported campus rapes
35 percent of college women said they drank to get drunk
Over 90 percent of students have tried alcohol
About 14 percent become alcoholics
Fewer than 5 percent who tried cocaine became addicted

questions.explain: The first group are patterns of student drinking; the second show most experimenters do not become addicted.

questions.section: Drinking and Drugs: Addiction as Self- Medication
questions.q: Sort these into things the chapter says make addiction likelier or things that make it less likely.

items.t: Chronic anxiety
Quickness to rage
Lifelong emotional distress
Ability to soothe anxiety
Ability to lift depression
Ability to calm rage

questions.explain: Learning to handle feelings removes the impetus to use drugs.

questions.section: Drinking and Drugs: Addiction as Self- Medication
questions.q: Why do so many young people experiment with drinking without becoming addicted while others become dependent almost from the start?
questions.a: Those most vulnerable seem to find in the drug or alcohol an instant way to soothe emotions that have distressed them for years, a chemical fix. Others have no such need, so the experiment stays an experiment.

questions.section: Drinking and Drugs: Addiction as Self- Medication
questions.q: Explain the first emotional pathway to alcoholism and its biological marker.
questions.a: A child who is highly strung and anxious discovers as a teenager that alcohol calms the anxiety, often being a son of an alcoholic. Undersecretion of GABA is a marker: sons of alcoholic fathers had low GABA and high anxiety, and drinking raised their GABA as anxiety fell.

questions.section: Drinking and Drugs: Addiction as Self- Medication
questions.q: Why might poor frontal lobe functioning in anxious sons of alcoholics support a slide into alcoholism?
questions.a: The prefrontal areas that help ease anxiety and control impulsiveness give them less help, and the prefrontal lobes also handle working memory, which holds the consequences of actions in mind. Their deficit lets them ignore the long-term drawbacks of drinking while they enjoy immediate sedation.

questions.section: Drinking and Drugs: Addiction as Self- Medication
questions.q: What does Goleman say about the possibility of handling the feelings that drive self-medication without drink or drugs?
questions.a: He says that although the predisposition may be brain-based, the feelings can be handled without medication, as Alcoholics Anonymous and other recovery programs have shown. Learning to soothe anxiety, lift depression and calm rage removes the impetus to use, and these skills would be better learned early than taught remedially.

questions.section: Drinking and Drugs: Addiction as Self- Medication
questions.q: Describe the second pathway to alcoholism and what the alcohol does for people on it.
questions.a: It begins with high agitation, impulsivity and boredom, showing as a restless, cranky infant, a fidgety, hyperactive grade schooler and sometimes a criminal career, mostly in men. As adults, alcohol soothes their agitation, and their intolerance of monotony and impulsivity make them ready to abuse an almost random list of other drugs.

questions.section: NO More Wars: a Final Common Preventive Pathway
questions.q: Why does Goleman say the series of 'wars' on teen pregnancy, dropping out, drugs and violence is the wrong approach?
options: They fund only programs that target a single age group
They distract from the need to build more prisons
They come too late, after the problem has taken root, like sending an ambulance instead of giving an inoculation
They teach children information they already know
questions.explain: He proposes following the logic of prevention by giving children skills that help avoid any of these fates.

questions.section: NO More Wars: a Final Common Preventive Pathway
questions.q: What did the programs in the W. T. Grant Foundation consortium's five-year project turn out to share?
options: A focus on one problem such as drug use
Heavy reliance on information campaigns
A requirement that parents not take part
A common set of skills that reads like the ingredients of emotional intelligence, whatever the specific problem
questions.explain: The consortium distilled the active ingredients of programs that impartial evaluations showed to be effective.

questions.section: NO More Wars: a Final Common Preventive Pathway
questions.q: Long-term studies of resilient children found a winning ____ that draws people to them, along with self-confidence and optimistic persistence.
questions.explain: Resilient children also recover quickly from upsets and have an easygoing nature.

questions.section: NO More Wars: a Final Common Preventive Pathway
questions.q: In the study of 8,098 Americans, ____ percent suffered at least one psychiatric problem in their lifetime.
questions.explain: The most troubled 14 percent had three or more problems at once.

questions.section: NO More Wars: a Final Common Preventive Pathway
questions.q: The University of Michigan sociologist who led the study of 8,098 Americans and urged early intervention is Ronald ____.
questions.explain: He described a girl with sixth-grade social phobia who starts drinking in junior high.

questions.section: NO More Wars: a Final Common Preventive Pathway
questions.q: Goleman says children given only basic sexual abuse information were actually half as likely to ____ it afterward than children with no program at all.
questions.explain: Those with only basic programs and later victimized were less likely to report.

questions.section: NO More Wars: a Final Common Preventive Pathway
questions.q: Which of these made the more comprehensive sexual abuse prevention programs work?
options: They were given at different levels several times over a child's school career
They enlisted parents to deliver the message
They taught emotional and social skills such as assertiveness
They were a single assembly in the school year
They focused only on good and bad touching
questions.explain: Children whose parents helped did best at resisting threats.

questions.section: NO More Wars: a Final Common Preventive Pathway
questions.q: Which of these are among the interpersonal skills named in the list of active ingredients?
options: Reading social and emotional cues
Listening
Taking others' perspectives
Delaying gratification
Handling stress
questions.explain: Delaying gratification and handling stress are listed among the emotional skills.

questions.section: NO More Wars: a Final Common Preventive Pathway
questions.q: A principal wants a program that will protect her pupils from abuse and bullies. Based on the chapter, which features should she choose?
options: Repeated lessons at several grade levels
Involving parents
Teaching assertiveness and building self-confidence
One-off assembly on good and bad touching
Information only
questions.explain: Information alone was little better than nothing.

questions.section: NO More Wars: a Final Common Preventive Pathway
questions.q: True or false: Goleman says that emotional deficits are the only cause of problems such as dropping out and violence.
questions.explain: He says the causes are complex, and emotional remedies should be paid attention to along with, not to the exclusion of, other answers.

questions.section: NO More Wars: a Final Common Preventive Pathway
questions.q: True or false: Goleman says some widely used prevention programs even seemed to increase the problems they aimed to prevent.
questions.explain: He cites drug abuse and teen sex as examples.

questions.section: NO More Wars: a Final Common Preventive Pathway
questions.q: Put these steps of impulse control in the order Goleman describes.
items: Control the impulse to act
Identify alternative actions
Consider the consequences before acting
Make a better emotional decision
questions.explain: Knowing the difference between feelings and actions underlies better emotional decisions.

questions.section: NO More Wars: a Final Common Preventive Pathway
questions.q: Put the sexual abuse programs findings in order.
items: Basic information programs are tried widely
They prove little better than nothing
Comprehensive programs add emotional and social skills
Children in those programs report abuse three times more often
questions.explain: Adding skills turned out to be the difference.

questions.section: NO More Wars: a Final Common Preventive Pathway
questions.q: Match each source of hardship with its effect on children.
pairs: More fearful, anxious and sad, with more tantrums
Less parental warmth and more harsh punishment
More depression, often single and jobless
questions.explain: Poverty delivers emotional blows; emotional skills support resilience.

questions.section: NO More Wars: a Final Common Preventive Pathway
questions.q: Match each figure with what it describes in the 8,098-person study.
pairs: Had at least one psychiatric problem in their lifetime
Developed three or more problems at once
Share of all current disorders accounted for by that group
Share of the most severe and disabling disorders
questions.explain: The most troubled group is relatively small but accounts for most severe disorders.

questions.section: NO More Wars: a Final Common Preventive Pathway
questions.q: Match each figure about child sexual abuse with what it describes.
pairs: Substantiated cases reported annually in the United States in 1993
Share of girls who are victims of some form of abuse by seventeen
How much more often children in comprehensive programs reported abuse
Average rate of victims for child molesters studied in their forties
questions.explain: These figures show the scale of the problem and the benefit of better programs.

questions.section: NO More Wars: a Final Common Preventive Pathway
questions.q: Sort each skill into emotional or interpersonal.

items.t: Self-awareness
Delaying gratification
Handling stress and anxiety
Reading social cues
Listening
Resisting negative influences

questions.explain: The first three are inner; the last three involve others.

questions.section: NO More Wars: a Final Common Preventive Pathway
questions.q: Sort each of these into a hardship factor or a resilience trait.

items.t: Fragmented or abusive family
Impoverished, drug-ridden neighborhood
Harsh punishments from parents under poverty's strain
Optimistic persistence in the face of failure
Ability to recover quickly from upsets
Easygoing nature

questions.explain: Resilient children share key emotional skills.

questions.section: NO More Wars: a Final Common Preventive Pathway
questions.q: Sort each program feature into more effective or less effective.

items.t: Only information about good and bad touching
Given once
Children less likely to report later
Repeated at different levels over several years
Parents enlisted
Teaches assertiveness and self-confidence

questions.explain: Comprehensive programs worked better.

questions.section: NO More Wars: a Final Common Preventive Pathway
questions.q: Why does Goleman argue that emotional competence may matter over and above family and economic forces?
questions.a: It may be decisive in whether a child is undone by hardships or finds a core of resilience. Children resilient despite poverty or abuse tend to share emotional skills such as sociability, self-confidence, optimistic persistence, quick recovery and an easygoing nature.

questions.section: NO More Wars: a Final Common Preventive Pathway
questions.q: Why were basic sexual abuse programs worse than nothing in one respect, and what worked better?
questions.a: Children who had only basic information and later were victimized were half as likely to report it than children with no program. Better programs added emotional and social skills, repeated over school years with parents, so children were three times more likely to report.

questions.section: NO More Wars: a Final Common Preventive Pathway
questions.q: Explain what a child needs beyond information about good and bad touching in order to resist abuse.
questions.a: Self-awareness to sense a situation feels wrong before touching begins, self-confidence and assertiveness to act on that feeling even against reassurance, and a repertoire of ways to disrupt it, from running away to threatening to tell. They also need to know their boundaries and have a network of support.

questions.section: NO More Wars: a Final Common Preventive Pathway
questions.q: What does the study of 8,098 Americans suggest about prevention?
questions.a: 48 percent had a psychiatric problem and a group of 14 percent with three or more accounted for 60 percent of current disorders and 90 percent of the most severe. Not every disorder can be prevented, but some and perhaps many can, so intervening early could head off a downward spiral.

questions.section: NO More Wars: a Final Common Preventive Pathway
questions.q: How does Goleman answer concerns that focusing on emotional deficits ignores other risk factors?
questions.a: He does not deny other risks such as chaotic families or crime-ridden neighborhoods, and says causes are complex. But emotional deficits add a great deal of risk, so emotional remedies should be pursued along with other answers, not instead of them.

questions.q: What does the title 'The Cost of Emotional Illiteracy' signal about this chapter's job in the book?
options: It explains the brain circuitry that makes emotional skills possible
It shows the price paid, in violence, depression, eating disorders, dropping out and addiction, when emotional skills are not learned
It describes how a school curriculum in emotions is taught
It argues that emotional skills are innate and cannot be taught
questions.explain: The brain is the subject of Part One and the classes come in the next chapter; this one documents the hazards of deficits.

questions.q: This chapter opens Part ____ of the book, titled Emotional Literacy.
questions.explain: Part Five explores the hazards awaiting those who fail to master the emotional realm and then visits schools teaching emotional skills.

questions.q: The chapter that follows this one, which visits innovative classes, is titled Schooling the ____.
questions.explain: The closing question of Chapter 15 is what an education in the emotions would look like.

questions.q: True or false: This chapter concludes that emotional remedies should be pursued along with other answers to the problems of the young, not to their exclusion.
questions.explain: Goleman says no single intervention can do the whole job.

questions.q: Which of these earlier chapters does this chapter explicitly point back to?
options: The Social Arts, on socially rejected children misreading signals
Intimate Enemies, on rising divorce rates
Temperament Is Not Destiny, on temperament changing for the better
Mind and Medicine, on health
Anatomy of an Emotional Hijacking, on the amygdala
questions.explain: Each is cited in passing: divorce in Chapter 9, rejected children in Chapter 8, temperament in Chapter 14.

questions.q: Which of these does the Prologue's road-map say Part Five will cover?
options: How deficiencies in emotional intelligence raise risks from depression and violence to eating disorders and drug abuse
How pioneering schools teach children emotional and social skills
How the brain's emotional architecture works
How the workplace rewards emotional intelligence
How emotions affect physical health
questions.explain: Brain, workplace and health belong to other Parts.

questions.q: Which of these does this chapter do for the book's overall argument?
options: Gives evidence that emotional deficits add a great deal to children's risk
Sets up the question of what an emotional education would look like
Bases its case on a range of problems whose choice is almost arbitrary
Proves that IQ cannot be changed
Introduces the idea of the emotional hijacking
questions.explain: The chapter prepares the ground for Chapter 16.

questions.q: Put these sections of the chapter in the order they appear.
items: Taming Aggression
Preventing Depression
Eating Disorders
Only the Lonely: Dropouts
Drinking and Drugs
questions.explain: The chapter moves from aggression through depression, eating disorders and dropouts to addiction, and ends by drawing out a common preventive pathway.

questions.q: Put these chapters in the order they appear in the book.
items: Temperament Is Not Destiny
The Cost of Emotional Illiteracy
Schooling the Emotions
questions.explain: Chapter 14 ends Part Four and Chapters 15 and 16 make up Part Five.

questions.q: Put these in the order the chapter closes its argument.
items: Wars on single problems come too late
Resilient children share emotional skills
Programs that give only information fail
The active ingredients reflect emotional intelligence
What would an education in the emotions look like?
questions.explain: The closing sections move from criticism of crisis programs to what works, ending with a question for the next chapter.

questions.q: Match each Part of the book with its title.
questions.explain: This chapter opens Part Five.

questions.q: Match each chapter with its subject.
pairs: Skills for reading and managing other people's emotions
The hazards of failing to master the emotional realm
questions.explain: These give the sequence of ideas leading into and out of the chapter.

questions.q: Why is this chapter placed after Chapter 14, Temperament Is Not Destiny?
questions.a: Chapter 14 showed that the emotional lessons children learn shape brain circuitry and that temperament can change for the better, so childhood is a window of opportunity. Chapter 15 then shows what is at stake when that window is missed, and the costs of emotional illiteracy argue for deliberate teaching.

questions.q: How does this chapter link to the Prologue's road-map of the book?
questions.a: The Prologue says Part Five explores how deficiencies in emotional intelligence raise a spectrum of risks, from depression or violence to eating disorders and drug abuse, and then documents schools teaching emotional skills. This chapter delivers the first half; Chapter 16 delivers the second.

questions.q: What role does Chapter 15's long list of problems play in Goleman's overall argument?
questions.a: It supplies evidence that emotional deficits underlie many problems of the young, so emotional competence is a shared point of prevention. He says the choice of problems is nearly arbitrary, since cases could be made for teen pregnancy or suicide too, and that leads to the question of what emotional education would look like.

questions.q: How does the chapter's argument about prevention differ from the idea of waging 'wars' on social problems?
questions.a: Wars come too late, after the problem has taken root, like sending an ambulance. The chapter argues for inoculation, teaching children skills for facing life, which equips them to avoid many fates at once, as the earlier sections on aggression, depression, eating disorders, dropouts and addiction suggest.

questions.q: How do Chapters 8 and 9 connect to this chapter?
questions.a: Chapter 8 showed that socially rejected children are poor at reading emotional and social signals, which this chapter uses to explain unpopular children becoming dropouts. Chapter 9 supplied the divorce rates that this chapter cites as a bleak long-term prospect for today's children.

questions.q: In the Self Science roll call at the Nueva Learning Center, what do students say instead of the usual “Here”?
questions.explain: Each child answers the roll with a number from one (low spirits) to ten (high energy), which puts feelings on the table at the start of class.
options: A number that shows how they feel, from low spirits to high energy
A number that shows how well they prepared for the day’s lesson
A word naming the subject they most want to study that day
A number that shows how many friends they expect to play with

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says emotional-literacy classes are meant mainly as a remedial program for children identified as troubled.
questions.explain: He says the goal is a set of skills and understandings essential for every child, not something taught only to those who are faltering.

questions.q: Karen Stone McCown says being emotionally literate is as important for learning as instruction in math and ____.
questions.explain: McCown pairs emotional literacy with the basic academic subjects.

questions.q: Goleman says the emotional-literacy movement turns the term affective education inside out: instead of using affect to educate, it educates ____ itself.
questions.explain: Affective education of the 1960s used feeling as a means of teaching; emotional literacy makes feeling the thing taught.

questions.q: Which of these are names Goleman says are given to classes like Self Science?
questions.explain: Goleman lists social development, life skills and social and emotional learning, and notes some use Gardner’s term personal intelligences; remedial counseling is exactly what he says these are not.
options: Remedial counseling
Moral instruction
Social development
Life skills
Social and emotional learning

questions.q: True or false: The W. T. Grant Consortium study found prevention programs were far more effective when they taught a core of emotional and social competences.
questions.explain: Impulse control, anger management and creative social problem solving were the core skills, which led to a new generation of interventions.

questions.q: Goleman says emotional-literacy classes can look uneventful at first glance. Why does he say they nevertheless work?
questions.explain: Like good childrearing, the lessons are small but delivered over a sustained period, so repeated experience becomes neural habit.
options: A single dramatic lesson can permanently change how a child reacts
The classes replace the need for any home upbringing
Children enjoy them so much that they ask for more homework
Small lessons repeated regularly over years strengthen brain pathways that become habits in times of stress

questions.q: How does the emotional-literacy approach treat feelings differently from the way most schools do?
questions.a: It makes emotions and social life themselves topics of study. Most schools treat them as irrelevant intrusions and, when feelings erupt, send the child for an occasional disciplinary trip to the counselor or principal.

questions.q: A school sends every child who erupts in anger straight to the principal’s office and carries on with the lesson. In Goleman’s terms, what is it failing to do?
questions.explain: Goleman contrasts relegating eruptions to disciplinary trips with making emotions themselves the topic.
options: Punish the behavior severely enough to deter it
Treat the emotions and social life that caused the eruption as a subject to be taught
Separate academic work from teaching about feelings
Screen out children who are unsuited to the class

questions.q: Match each person or movement named in the chapter’s opening to what Goleman connects it with.
pairs: Developer of the Self Science Curriculum and director of Nueva
Source of the idea of multiple intelligences, behind the term personal intelligences
Study showing prevention works best when it teaches emotional and social competences
1960s movement that used experience of feeling to teach concepts
questions.explain: Each is introduced in the opening pages as part of the background to emotional-literacy courses.

questions.q: Sort each description by the approach it fits.

items.t: Uses an immediate experience of feeling to teach concepts
Treats feeling as a means of learning psychological lessons
Educates affect itself
Makes emotions and relationships the actual subject

questions.explain: Affective education used affect to educate; emotional literacy educates affect.

questions.q: When Rahman’s group is stuck, he lightens the mood by holding two puzzle pieces in front of his eyes like a ____.
questions.explain: His partners giggle, and this proves a pivotal moment in the day’s lesson.

questions.q: Put these moments from the struggling group’s puzzle session in order.
items: Rahman holds two pieces over his eyes and his partners giggle
The teacher invites finished groups to give one specific hint
Dagan suggests moving two jutting pieces
The pieces fall into place and the class applauds
questions.explain: The joke eases tension, the hint follows, and the group then solves all the puzzles.

questions.q: True or false: In Cooperation Squares, the second group began with each member working on a separate puzzle but later worked together as a unit.
questions.explain: They started with solitary parallel efforts that got nowhere, then slowly began to assemble the first square collectively.

questions.q: What really lay behind Rahman’s angry argument with Tucker about whether offering a piece counts as gesturing?
questions.explain: The dispute about gesturing was cover for Rahman’s hurt over the word disruptive, which he kept glancing at on the sheet.
options: Tucker had written Rahman’s name under “Who is disruptive?” on the evaluation sheet
Rahman believed his group had been given harder puzzles
Tucker had broken the no-gesturing rule himself
Rahman had been excluded from a hint-giving round

questions.q: True or false: Varga tells Tucker and Rahman that they handled the group exercise poorly and failed to cooperate.
questions.explain: She says explicitly that it is not a criticism and that they cooperated very well.

questions.q: Varga sees the heated exchange as a critical ____, a spontaneous exchange of heated feeling in which lessons can be taught most profitably.
questions.explain: Such electric moments make lessons last in students’ memories.

questions.q: How does Varga use the quarrel between Rahman and Tucker as a lesson?
questions.a: She notices the raised voices, guesses that Rahman is hurt by the negative word disruptive, and coaches Tucker to explain his intent and to hear and accept Rahman’s feelings. She also praises Rahman for being assertive without attacking, and checks at the end that both feel better.

questions.q: Which of these did Varga do while coaching the two boys?
questions.explain: She named the likely feeling, praised assertiveness and offered a positive reading of the behavior; she did not remove either boy or order the sheet changed.
options: Sent Rahman out of the room to calm down
Guessed that Rahman felt hurt by the word disruptive
Reframed disruptive as possibly lightening a frustrating moment
Praised Rahman for being assertive rather than attacking
Ordered Tucker to rewrite the evaluation sheet

questions.q: Two children argue loudly over whether a move broke a game rule, but one keeps glancing at a score sheet where he has been labeled badly. Following Varga’s reading of the Tucker and Rahman scene, what is most likely going on?
questions.explain: Varga reads the heat as about the offending word, and she addresses the feeling before the rule.
options: The children simply disagree about the rule and need it clarified
The child with the label is trying to distract from his own error
The rule dispute is a cover for hurt over the label, so the feeling needs to be heard
The louder child is trying to take the lead in the game

questions.q: True or false: By the end of the exchange, Rahman says he feels okay and his voice is softer because he feels heard and understood.
questions.explain: Being heard is what cools him down, and the boys then leave together.

questions.section: Postmortem: A Fight That Did Not Break Out
questions.q: According to Varga, what typically escalates a disagreement into conflict?
questions.explain: Her list is about poor communication, which is what the Self Science conflict lessons target.
options: Disagreeing openly in front of other students
Having too little supervision from adults
Competing for grades in front of the class
Not communicating, making assumptions, jumping to conclusions and sending a hard message
