questions.section: Postmortem: A Fight That Did Not Break Out
questions.q: True or false: Students in Self Science are taught that the goal is to avoid conflict completely.
questions.explain: The point is to resolve disagreement and resentment before it spirals into an out-and-out fight.

questions.section: Postmortem: A Fight That Did Not Break Out
questions.q: Assertiveness, as distinct from aggression or passivity, is taught at Nueva from ____ grade on.
questions.explain: Assertiveness means expressing feelings forthrightly without spiraling into aggression.

questions.section: Postmortem: A Fight That Did Not Break Out
questions.q: Why does Goleman say mastery in the emotional domain is especially difficult?
questions.explain: Calm is when learning is easy, but emotional skills are needed, and so must be practiced, in moments of distress.
options: Feelings cannot be described in words
The skills must be learned when people are upset and least able to take in new habits
Children resist any instruction about feelings
Emotional skills are inborn and cannot be taught

questions.section: Postmortem: A Fight That Did Not Break Out
questions.q: Sort each behavior by whether Tucker and Rahman showed it or avoided it.

items.t: Facing each other with eye contact
Stating their views without blaming
Lowering their voices after coaching
Contemptuous name-calling
Stalking out of the room
Coming to blows

questions.explain: Both boys asserted their views without blaming, name-calling or yelling, and neither cut the other off or fought.

questions.section: Postmortem: A Fight That Did Not Break Out
questions.q: Why does Varga say coaching in the middle of an upset helps, and what does she say the learner has to do?
questions.a: Anyone, adult or fifth grader, needs help being a self-observer when upset. With a pounding heart and jittery hands, you must listen clearly and hold your self-control to avoid screaming, blaming or clamming up in defensiveness, and a coach helps with that.

questions.q: Match each setting to the troubles Goleman links with it.
pairs: Teasing, feeling left out and fears
Hurt over dates, immature friends and pressure to smoke
Lunch, the bus, a friend’s house
Where children’s pressing troubles usually get aired, if at all
questions.explain: Goleman notes concerns change with grade, and that these gripping topics are normally aired only on the periphery of school.

questions.q: True or false: The Self Science lesson plan is fixed, so teachers cannot make use of an unplanned conflict between students.
questions.explain: The plan is flexible precisely so moments like the Rahman and Tucker conflict can be capitalized on.

questions.q: The explicit goal of Self Science is illuminating the child’s sense of self and relationships with ____.
questions.explain: Student concerns give living examples for applying the skills.

questions.q: A class has a lesson plan, but two students suddenly begin quarrelling. Which approach matches the Self Science model?
questions.explain: In Self Science the issues students bring up are the material to which skills are applied.
options: Stop the quarrel and return strictly to the scheduled lesson
Wait until the end of the term to discuss quarrels
Ask the class to ignore it to avoid embarrassing anyone
Treat the quarrel as a living example for applying conflict-resolution skills

questions.q: Why does Goleman see value in letting children bring their own troubles into Self Science?
questions.a: These topics are of gripping import to a child, yet usually get aired only at lunch or on the bus, if at all. Often children obsess about them alone at night with no one to mull them over with; in class they can become topics of the day.

questions.q: What does Karen Stone McCown say kids learn about anger in Self Science?
questions.explain: She adds that children also learn they always have choices about how to respond to an emotion.
options: That it is almost always a secondary reaction, so look for what is underneath, such as hurt or jealousy
That it should be suppressed until the child is alone
That it is a sign of a weak character
That it is a reaction that cannot be changed

questions.q: The Self Science curriculum had been in use for close to ____ years when Goleman wrote.
questions.explain: It stands as a model for teaching emotional intelligence.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman list as part of the self-awareness taught in Self Science?
questions.explain: Self-awareness includes naming feelings, linking thoughts, feelings and reactions, and realistic self-assessment.
options: Recognizing feelings and building a vocabulary for them
Learning to suppress feelings that disturb the class
Seeing yourself in a positive but realistic light
Memorizing the muscle movements of each facial expression
Seeing the links between thoughts, feelings and reactions

questions.q: Match each emotional-intelligence area to a topic Self Science teaches under it.
pairs: Realizing what is behind a feeling, such as the hurt that triggers anger
Taking others’ perspectives and respecting differences in feeling
Being assertive rather than angry or passive
questions.explain: These match the ingredients of emotional intelligence Goleman describes.

questions.q: True or false: Students in Self Science receive letter grades like those in other subjects.
questions.explain: There are no grades; life itself is the final exam, though eighth graders do take an oral Socratic examination.

questions.q: What two lessons about emotional responses does Karen Stone McCown say Self Science children learn?
questions.a: They learn that anger is almost always a secondary reaction, so it pays to look at what lies under it, such as hurt or jealousy. They also learn they always have choices about how to respond to an emotion, and the more ways they know, the richer their lives can be.

questions.q: Sort each Self Science topic into the group it belongs to.

items.t: Recognizing and naming feelings
Handling anxiety, anger and sadness
Following through on commitments
Seeing links between thoughts, feelings and reactions
Being a good listener
Negotiating compromise
Taking another person’s perspective

questions.explain: The first group is about managing oneself; the second is about dealing with others.

questions.q: A child says she is furious that a friend left her off a party list. Following McCown’s lesson on anger, what would a teacher encourage her to ask?
questions.explain: Anger is usually secondary, so the teacher helps the child find the hurt or jealousy beneath it.
options: How to make the friend feel as bad as she does
Why she should never feel angry
Whether the party was worth attending
Whether she is hurt or jealous underneath the anger

questions.q: Goleman says that Aristotle, so concerned with emotional ____, might approve of Self Science.
questions.explain: The remark links the chapter back to Aristotle’s challenge in the Prologue.

questions.section: Emotional Literacy in the Inner City
questions.q: In the 1980s a group of Yale psychologists and educators designed the ____ Competence Program for New Haven schools.
questions.explain: It covers virtually the same terrain as Nueva’s Self Science curriculum.

questions.section: Emotional Literacy in the Inner City
questions.q: What does Mary Ellen Collins say happens once a child knows a teacher will listen to emotional problems?
questions.explain: She says she can no longer teach only academic skills given the problems kids face.
options: The child stops attending academic lessons
The teacher becomes responsible for all home problems
The child is referred out of the school
The avenue opens to talk about problems such as AIDS in the family

questions.section: Emotional Literacy in the Inner City
questions.q: Mary Ellen Collins is the school’s ____, an all-purpose ombudsman who helps teachers with the social competence curriculum.
questions.explain: If a teacher is unsure how to teach a lesson, Collins comes to the class to show how.

questions.section: Emotional Literacy in the Inner City
questions.q: True or false: Joyce Andrews’s fifth graders at Troup have the social competence class three times a week.
questions.explain: Andrews, like the other fifth-grade teachers, took a special summer course in how to teach it.

questions.section: Emotional Literacy in the Inner City
questions.q: Which of these are among the six basic emotions on Andrews’s worksheet?
questions.explain: The sheet shows happy, sad, angry, surprised, afraid and disgusted; jealousy and shame are not among them.
options: Ashamed
Afraid
Disgusted
Surprised
Jealous

questions.section: Emotional Literacy in the Inner City
questions.q: The facial-expression worksheet in Andrews’s class comes straight from whose research?
questions.explain: Goleman notes it is taught in most introductory college psychology courses and rarely in grade school.
options: Howard Gardner’s theory of multiple intelligences
Paul Ekman’s research on facial expression
Eric Schaps’s Child Development Project
Linda Lantieri’s conflict-resolution work

questions.section: Emotional Literacy in the Inner City
questions.q: Why does Goleman say a lesson linking names, feelings and faces, though obvious, may still be needed?
questions.explain: He also notes that girls with eating disorders fail to distinguish anger from anxiety from hunger.
options: It makes children better at drawing
It prepares students for college psychology
It may counter lapses such as bullies misreading neutral expressions as hostile
It lets teachers grade feelings objectively

questions.section: Emotional Literacy in the Inner City
questions.q: Why does Goleman say that at Troup the connection to the topics is more direct and raw than at Nueva?
questions.a: Troup students face the problems of the inner city in their own lives. New Haven has the highest proportion of women with AIDS in the United States, some Troup mothers and students have the disease, and some children’s homes are so chaotic they cannot get to school some days.

questions.section: Emotional Literacy in the Inner City
questions.q: Match each person or place to its role in the Troup visit.
pairs: Fifth-grade teacher leading the lesson on naming feelings
Facilitator who helps teachers teach the social competence lessons
Researcher whose work on faces underlies the worksheet
Inner-city New Haven school with enriched science curriculum
questions.explain: Each plays a part in Goleman’s answer to the skeptics.

questions.section: Emotional Literacy in the Inner City
questions.q: A boy often lashes out because he reads a classmate’s blank face as hostile. Which Troup-style lesson would Goleman say addresses this?
questions.explain: Goleman says such a lesson may serve as an antidote to lapses in emotional literacy like misreading neutral expressions.
options: Learning to ignore other children’s faces
Practicing silent puzzle solving
Memorizing the school rules on fighting
Connecting a name with a feeling and the facial expression that matches it

questions.q: What is the Child Development Project, directed by Eric Schaps?
questions.explain: It offers prepackaged materials that fit into existing courses.
options: A new school subject that replaces social studies
An essentially invisible emotional and social course woven into school life, based in Oakland
A private tutoring service for troubled children
A research study run only by psychologists

questions.q: In the Child Development Project, first graders discuss friendship through a story titled Frog and Toad Are ____.
questions.explain: Frog tricks hibernating Toad to get him up early, opening a discussion of feelings.

questions.q: Three first graders push to be first in the lunch line. A teacher has them each guess a number and the winner goes first. What deeper teaching does Goleman see in this?
questions.explain: It offers a fairer message than the authoritarian “Stop that!”
options: That disputes can be negotiated rather than decided by force or an order
That the biggest child should lead
That guessing is a good way to learn numbers
That lines are not important

questions.q: Which of these skills does the Child Development program say misbehavior moments can teach?
questions.explain: The program sees discipline as a chance to teach lacking emotional skills rather than coerce.
options: Impulse control
Explaining their feelings
Memorizing classroom rules
Obeying without question
Resolving conflicts

questions.q: Why does Goleman describe the Child Development Project as an invisible emotional and social competence course?
questions.a: It takes no separate class time. Its materials fit into existing courses such as reading, and its approach to discipline reshapes school life. Children learn about empathy, perspective-taking and caring through stories and everyday moments.

questions.q: What is the “mailbox” at John Muir Elementary School in Seattle?
questions.explain: The class talks over the problems, and the teacher keeps the names out of the discussion.
options: A box for secret grades
A painted box where children post complaints and problems for class discussion
A box where parents leave notes for the teacher
A place to collect lost items

questions.q: Why does the mailbox suit the “emotional timetable” of childhood?
questions.explain: Emotional lessons must be pegged to development and repeated at different ages.
options: It saves time by limiting talk to one topic
It lets the teacher avoid emotional topics
It lets the subject shift with the preoccupations of the hour rather than follow a rigid agenda
It replaces age-specific lessons

questions.q: Head Start graduates, when the program is run well, show fewer drug problems and arrests, better marriages and greater ____ power.
questions.explain: Goleman adds the caveat that Head Start must be well run.

questions.q: The kindergarten year marks a peak ripening of the “social ____,” feelings such as insecurity, humility, jealousy and pride.
questions.explain: These feelings all require comparing oneself with others.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman list among the social emotions that ripen at kindergarten age?
questions.explain: The social emotions all require comparing oneself with others.
options: Humility
Jealousy and envy
Disgust
Sadness at loss
Pride and confidence

questions.q: Hamburg says a child’s sense of self-worth depends substantially on his or her ability to achieve in ____.
questions.explain: A child who fails in school sets in motion self-defeating attitudes.

questions.q: Which of these does Hamburg list as essentials for profiting from school?
questions.explain: Goleman notes these amount to emotional intelligence.
options: Maintaining control over emotions
Winning peer popularity
Having an optimistic outlook
Strong athletic skill
Postponing gratification

questions.q: Which loss does Goleman call one of the greatest blows when students enter middle school?
questions.explain: Virtually all students dip in self-confidence and jump in self-consciousness.
options: Social self-esteem, the confidence they can make and keep friends
Academic honors
Athletic status
Respect from teachers

questions.q: True or false: Hamburg observes that students who had emotional-literacy classes find middle-school pressures less troubling than their peers do.
questions.explain: They have mastered abilities that at least for the short term inoculate them.

questions.q: Match each age or stage to what Goleman says about emotional development.
pairs: Braggadocio, before self-consciousness that breeds humility
Peak ripening of social emotions such as envy and pride
Dip in self-confidence and blow to social self-esteem
Intense feelings but a primitive repertoire
questions.explain: Each stage ties to the biological clock of development.

questions.q: Why must emotional lessons be matched to a child’s developmental stage?
questions.a: Emotions ripen on an innate biological clock tied to cognition and brain maturation, and the preoccupation of the hour changes as children grow. Lessons must be pegged to the child’s development and repeated at different ages in ways that fit changing understanding.

questions.q: A parent scolds a four-year-old for bragging and demands humility. Which idea from the chapter best explains the difficulty?
questions.explain: Adults often expect maturity beyond a child’s years.
options: The child has been spoiled by too much praise
Each emotion has a preprogrammed moment of appearance, and humility typically comes later
Four-year-olds are incapable of any feeling
Parents should ignore all misbehavior

questions.q: In first grade in New Haven, students roll the “feelings ____,” a cube with words such as sad or excited on each side.
questions.explain: They describe a time they had that feeling.

questions.q: Put the six steps of the New Haven stoplight poster in order.
items: Stop, calm down, and think before you act
Say the problem and how you feel
Set a positive goal
Think of lots of solutions
Think ahead to the consequences
Go ahead and try the best plan
questions.explain: Red light is step one, yellow covers steps two to five, and green is the final step of acting.

questions.q: Match each grade level to the lesson Goleman describes for it.
pairs: Empathy, impulse control and anger management, with the stoplight
Temptations and pressures for sex, drugs or drinking
Taking multiple perspectives in ambiguous social situations
questions.explain: The New Haven program matches lessons to the point of development.

questions.q: A ninth grader is furious because he saw his girlfriend talking with another boy. According to the New Haven teacher, what would he be encouraged to do?
questions.explain: By ninth grade the lessons stress taking multiple perspectives.
options: Confront her immediately to show his feelings
Consider what might be going on from their point of view before confronting
Ignore his feelings completely
Ask friends to settle it for him

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says the Troup fifth graders’ lesson on reading emotions from faces is essentially about empathizing.
questions.explain: Reading facial expressions is a basic step toward empathy.

questions.q: Explain what the stoplight method is for and when it is used.
questions.a: It is a six-step poster used when a child is about to strike out in anger, withdraw in a huff or burst into tears at teasing. Red means stop, calm down and think; yellow means state the problem and feeling, set a goal, think of solutions and consequences; green means try the best plan.

questions.q: The founder of the Resolving Conflict Creatively Program is Linda ____.
questions.explain: She directs the national center for the approach in Manhattan.

questions.q: What is one key to the success of the conflict-resolution program?
questions.explain: Tempers are more likely to explode in those places, so some students are trained as mediators.
options: Keeping it only in the classroom
Using it only with at-risk students
Extending it beyond the classroom to the playground and cafeteria
Having adults handle every dispute

questions.q: Put the steps of a schoolyard mediation in the order the chapter describes.
items: Sit down and have each person listen without interruption or insults
Have each party calm down and state a position
Have each party paraphrase what was said
Together think of solutions both sides can live with
Often record the settlement in a signed agreement
questions.explain: Mediators follow this sequence, taking care to seem impartial.

questions.q: True or false: Schoolyard mediators must phrase their statements so that both parties feel the mediator is impartial.
questions.explain: This is part of their training.

questions.q: What does Lantieri point to with as much pride as drops in fights and name-calling?
questions.explain: Her view is that violence prevention cannot be separated from the full spectrum of emotional competence.
options: An increase in caring among the kids
Higher test scores
Larger enrollment
More parent volunteers

questions.q: Why does Lantieri say the program touches on feelings beyond anger?
questions.explain: Skills to head off violence cannot be separated from emotional competence.
options: Anger is not a real emotion
Knowing what you feel and how to handle impulse or grief matters as much for violence prevention
Parents ask for it
Teachers dislike discussing anger

questions.q: Put the path most boys on a trajectory toward crime take in the order described.
items: Impulsiveness and quickness to anger in earliest school years
Becoming social rejects by the end of grade school
Bonding with a circle of similar others in middle school
Beginning crime sprees
Police records and readiness for violence by early adulthood
questions.explain: Dozens of studies showed this path, which led to PATHS.

questions.q: PATHS stands for Parents and Teachers Helping ____.
questions.explain: The curriculum was developed by a consortium including Mark Greenberg.

questions.q: True or false: PATHS is taught only to the subgroup of children identified as at risk for crime.
questions.explain: It is given to all in a class, avoiding stigmatizing a more troubled subgroup.

questions.q: Which skill is most important for aggression-prone children in the PATHS emotional-awareness lessons?
questions.explain: This is the lesson most important for those prone to aggression.
options: Hiding their own anger
Memorizing facial muscles
Recognizing when someone is actually hostile rather than attributing hostility oneself
Avoiding others

questions.q: Sort these feelings by when PATHS introduces them.

items.t: Happiness
Anger
Jealousy
Pride
Guilt

questions.explain: The fifty lessons begin with basic emotions and later cover more complicated feelings.

questions.q: A boy shoved in a crowded hallway assumes the other boy meant to attack him and hits back, though it was an accident. Which PATHS lesson targets this?
questions.explain: The error is attributing hostility that is not there.
options: Recognizing when someone is actually hostile rather than attributing hostility oneself
Taking turns in the lunch line
Naming six basic emotions
Brainstorming with a mediator

questions.q: Why did the psychologists who tried to help boys on a path to crime end up designing an emotional-literacy program?
questions.a: Studies showed the path starting in impulsiveness and quick anger and then social rejection. Their interventions converged on teaching impulse control, recognizing feelings, anger management and friendship skills, the core of emotional literacy, to the whole class.

questions.section: Rethinking Schools: Teaching by Being, Communities That Care
questions.q: Why does Goleman say the quality of the teacher matters so much for emotional literacy?
questions.explain: Whenever she responds to one student, twenty or thirty others learn a lesson.
options: Teachers grade emotional skills
Teachers are the only adults children trust
Teachers need advanced degrees
How a teacher handles her class is itself a model, a lesson in emotional competence

questions.section: Rethinking Schools: Teaching by Being, Communities That Care
questions.q: Goleman says that whenever a teacher responds to one student, twenty or thirty others learn a ____.
questions.explain: Teaching by being is as important as teaching by curriculum.

questions.section: Rethinking Schools: Teaching by Being, Communities That Care
questions.q: True or false: Goleman says the standard education of teachers prepares them well for talking about feelings.
questions.explain: There is little or nothing in standard teacher education for this, so programs give several weeks of special training.

questions.section: Rethinking Schools: Teaching by Being, Communities That Care
questions.q: Why does Goleman say whether there is a separate emotional-literacy class may matter less than how the lessons are taught?
questions.a: There is perhaps no subject where teacher quality matters so much, since how a teacher handles the class models emotional competence or its absence. The lessons are taught as much by being as by curriculum.

questions.section: Rethinking Schools: Teaching by Being, Communities That Care
questions.q: A teacher publicly sneers at a student who cries after being teased. According to Goleman, what are the other students learning?
questions.explain: A teacher’s way of handling a class is a de facto lesson.
options: Nothing, because only the lesson plan teaches
A lesson in emotional competence, or the lack of it, from the teacher’s example
That the student deserved it
That sneering is a conflict-resolution method

questions.q: In the New Haven schools, what does Tim Shriver say happens when kids get into a beef in the cafeteria?
questions.explain: Coaches use the technique on the playing field too.
options: They are suspended immediately
The lunch aide decides who is right
A parent is called in
They are sent to a peer mediator who uses the perspective-taking technique learned in class

questions.q: How do New Haven schools help students whose home life is shaky?
questions.explain: Caring community members get engaged with foundering students.
options: Students are moved to boarding schools
Responsible adults volunteer as mentors and regular companions
Teachers adopt them
They are placed in separate classes

questions.q: The optimal design of emotional-literacy programs is to begin early, be age-appropriate, run throughout the ____ years, and intertwine school, home and community.
questions.explain: Parallel reinforcement makes lessons tested in real life.

questions.q: Which of these does Goleman list as hurdles to getting such programs into schools?
questions.explain: He names parental, teacher, child and quality concerns.
options: Children may resist intrusion on their privacy
The programs cost more than textbooks
No research on the topic exists
Parents may feel the topic is too personal for schools
Slick marketers may peddle ineptly designed programs

questions.q: A child learns perspective-taking at school, but at home parents respond to every dispute with “Stop that!” Which idea from the chapter applies?
questions.explain: Parallel lines of reinforcement help lessons stay beyond school.
options: Home life has no effect on school lessons
Parents should not know what is taught
Lessons work best when school and home give consistent messages
Schools should keep lessons secret

questions.q: Why does Goleman say emotional-literacy lessons should be coordinated across school, home and community?
questions.a: Consistent messages about emotional competence in every part of children’s lives help lessons be tested, practiced and sharpened in the actual challenges of life instead of staying behind at school.

questions.section: Does Emotional Literacy Make a Difference
questions.q: In the SOCS problem-solving method, the letters stand for Situation, Options, Consequence and ____.
questions.explain: The method is a grown-up version of the stoplight.

questions.section: Does Emotional Literacy Make a Difference
questions.q: What did Lamont whisper to Tim Shriver in the hospital?
questions.explain: It shows the lessons had stuck but too late.
options: That when he got out he would use the SOCS method
That he forgave the shooter
That school had been useless
That he wanted to return to football

questions.section: Does Emotional Literacy Make a Difference
questions.q: True or false: Goleman says it is certain Lamont’s life would have turned out differently had he had social-development classes throughout school.
questions.explain: The signs point to a possible yes, though no one can say for sure.

questions.section: Does Emotional Literacy Make a Difference
questions.q: In the seventh-grade story, how did the twelve-year-old avoid a fight?
questions.explain: She had previously been expelled elsewhere for fighting.
options: She reported to the principal
She asked the other girl why she had said that stuff before reacting
She ignored the rumor
She asked a friend to fight

questions.section: Does Emotional Literacy Make a Difference
questions.q: Goleman says the item demanding special attention is that programs improve academic achievement ____.
questions.explain: The finding recurs again and again.

questions.section: Does Emotional Literacy Make a Difference
questions.q: Which of these appear under Managing Emotions in Goleman’s list of benefits?
questions.explain: Achievement scores fall under harnessing emotions productively and listening under empathy.
options: Better frustration tolerance and anger management
Fewer suspensions and expulsions
Improved scores on achievement tests
Better at listening to others
Less loneliness and social anxiety

questions.section: Does Emotional Literacy Make a Difference
questions.q: Match each benefit category to a listed benefit.
pairs: Recognizing the difference between feelings and actions
More democratic in dealing with others
questions.explain: Goleman’s list groups the benefits by these headings.

questions.section: Does Emotional Literacy Make a Difference
questions.q: Sort these benefits by category.

items.t: Fewer put-downs, fights and disruptions
Less loneliness and social anxiety
Better at handling stress
More sought out by peers
Better at negotiating disagreements
More sharing and cooperation

questions.explain: The first group is about handling one’s own emotions and the second about dealing with others.

questions.section: Does Emotional Literacy Make a Difference
questions.q: What did the Troup sixth grader’s note to her teacher reveal?
questions.explain: It shows students trust teachers who listen.
options: She wanted to switch classes
She had been bullied
Her best friend was pregnant, had no one to talk to, and planned suicide, but she trusted the teacher to care
She had failed a test

questions.section: Does Emotional Literacy Make a Difference
questions.q: What does the evidence suggest about emotional-literacy classes, according to Goleman?
questions.a: They do not change anyone overnight, but improve the tone of a school and the outlook and emotional competence of students, with better behavior and higher achievement scores. They seem to help children fulfil their roles as friends, students, and future workers and parents.

questions.section: Does Emotional Literacy Make a Difference
questions.q: A school board proposes cutting emotional-literacy classes as a frill during a back-to-basics push. What argument from Goleman best answers this?
questions.explain: He says they help reverse educational decline.
options: The classes are required by law
They are cheaper than academics
They are what students enjoy
The classes improve achievement and strengthen schools’ ability to teach, so they are worth the investment

questions.section: Character, Morality, and the Arts of Democracy
questions.q: What old-fashioned word does Goleman give for the body of skills emotional intelligence represents?
questions.explain: He quotes Etzioni on character.
options: Character
Virtue
Charisma
Etiquette

questions.section: Character, Morality, and the Arts of Democracy
questions.q: Etzioni describes character as the psychological ____ that moral conduct requires.
questions.explain: Character is the strength needed for moral conduct.

questions.section: Character, Morality, and the Arts of Democracy
questions.q: What did John Dewey see about moral education?
questions.explain: This is the mode of emotional literacy.
options: It should avoid real events
It is most potent when taught in the course of real events, not as abstract lessons
It belongs only at home
It is only for the gifted

questions.section: Character, Morality, and the Arts of Democracy
questions.q: The ability to defer gratification and control urges was in a former day called ____.
questions.explain: It is a basic emotional skill.

questions.section: Character, Morality, and the Arts of Democracy
questions.q: True or false: Goleman says lecturing children about values is enough to develop character.
questions.explain: They need to practice them as they build emotional and social skills.

questions.section: Character, Morality, and the Arts of Democracy
questions.q: How does Goleman connect emotional intelligence with character and democracy?
questions.a: Self-discipline and motivation form the bedrock of character, while setting aside self-focus opens the way to empathy, listening and perspective-taking. These enable mutual respect and public discourse, the arts of democracy, so emotional literacy goes hand in hand with education for character and citizenship.

questions.q: Justice Department figures showed a ____ percent jump from 1988 to 1992 in juveniles charged with violent crimes.
questions.explain: Aggravated assault alone was up 80 percent.

questions.q: Why does Goleman say teenagers are so poor at avoiding disputes?
questions.explain: Emotional lessons are left to chance.
options: They are born aggressive
Their parents are indifferent
They lack intelligence
Society has not made sure every child is taught anger management or conflict resolution

questions.q: True or false: Goleman says emotional-literacy courses are already widespread across American schools.
questions.explain: They are as yet rare, with best models in a handful of private schools and few hundred public ones.

questions.q: What risk does Goleman say we run by leaving children’s emotional lessons to chance?
questions.a: We risk wasting the window of opportunity presented by the slow maturation of the brain to help children cultivate a healthy emotional repertoire. Given the crises and the hope offered by emotional literacy, he asks whether we should teach these skills to every child.

questions.q: The book’s final line asks, if not now, ____?
questions.explain: It closes the call to teach emotional skills to every child.

questions.q: In the book’s structure, which Part do Chapter 15 and Chapter 16 together form?
questions.explain: The Part Five chapters are The Cost of Emotional Illiteracy and Schooling the Emotions.
options: Part Five, Emotional Literacy
Part Four, Windows of Opportunity
Part Three, Emotional Intelligence Applied
Part Two, The Nature of Emotional Intelligence

questions.q: How does Chapter 16 build on the interventions described in Chapter 15?
questions.explain: The next step is to turn research-run programs into preventive education.
options: It shows those interventions failed
It limits them to at-risk children
It generalizes focused skill-building interventions into prevention for entire school populations taught by ordinary teachers
It replaces them with clinical therapy

questions.q: Put these Parts of the book in the order Goleman presents them.
items: The emotional brain and its neurological givens
Emotional intelligence as an aptitude
Emotional intelligence applied to relationships, work and health
Windows of opportunity in childhood
Emotional literacy and the cost of its lack
questions.explain: These follow the Prologue’s road-map: Parts One to Five.

questions.q: What does the title Schooling the Emotions signal about the chapter’s subject?
questions.explain: The chapter shows classes teaching emotional intelligence to every child.
options: That emotions must be kept out of school
That schooling is an emotional ordeal
That only parents can teach feelings
That emotional skills can be taught in schools as part of regular education

questions.q: Why does the chapter visit Troup Middle School after Nueva?
questions.explain: It shows emotional competence can be taught in the inner city.
options: To answer the skeptics who say emotional lessons only work in privileged private schools
To show a school that rejected the program
To compare funding levels
To introduce a different theory

questions.q: Put these sections of Chapter 16 in the order they appear.
items: A Lesson in Cooperation
Emotional Literacy in the Inner City
The Emotional Timetable
Emotional Literacy as Prevention
A Last Word
questions.explain: The chapter moves from a Nueva classroom through New Haven, development and prevention to the closing call.

questions.q: True or false: Chapter 16 closes the book by pointing to rising teenage violence as a reason to teach emotional skills to every child.
questions.explain: The Last Word cites rising murder rates and juvenile violence to argue we cannot leave emotional lessons to chance.

questions.q: Chapter 12 is cited in Chapter 16 for what point?
questions.explain: Goleman uses it to support emphasizing social and emotional skills in preschool programs.
options: That temperament cannot change
That divorce rates are rising
That children’s readiness to learn depends on acquiring basic emotional skills
That emotional hijacking occurs in the amygdala

questions.q: Match each earlier part of the book to what Chapter 16 draws from it.
pairs: Readiness to learn depends on basic emotional skills
The W. T. Grant finding and the path toward crime
Road-map promising visits to innovative classes at journey’s end
questions.explain: Chapter 16 looks back on each of these.

questions.q: Why does the book end with a chapter on schools rather than on individual self-help?
questions.a: Goleman argues that leaving children’s emotional education to chance yields disastrous results, and that the remedy lies in how we prepare the young for life. Schools can reach nearly every child, so the final chapter shows classes that teach the basics of emotional intelligence.

questions.q: How does the idea of a “window of opportunity” connect Chapter 16 to the earlier Part Four?
questions.a: Part Four says childhood and adolescence are critical for setting down emotional habits. Chapter 16 ends by warning that leaving lessons to chance wastes the window opened by the brain’s slow maturation.

questions.q: Why does Chapter 16 begin inside a Self Science classroom before arguing for emotional literacy in general?
questions.explain: The opening scenes of Nueva’s class give a model course in emotional intelligence before the wider case is made.
options: To prove the program is expensive
To show that private schools are better
To introduce the study of the amygdala
To show concretely what teaching emotional intelligence looks like, with feelings treated as a lesson

questions.q: Chapter 16’s account of the Self Science curriculum ends by invoking Aristotle. What link does Goleman draw?
questions.explain: Goleman says Aristotle, so concerned with emotional skillfulness, might well approve of the Self Science examination.
options: It links the ABC’s of Self Science back to Aristotle’s challenge of emotional skillfulness
It argues Aristotle opposed schooling
It shows Aristotle invented Self Science
It rejects emotional skills as unlearnable

questions.q: In the Cooperation Squares game, how did the three groups differ, and what did the struggling group’s joke and the final hint do for them?
questions.a: One group worked efficiently at once, a second began with parallel solitary efforts before working collectively, and the third struggled and grew frustrated. Rahman’s mask joke eased the tension, and Dagan’s hint to move two pieces let him grasp the pattern so all the puzzles were solved.

questions.section: Postmortem: A Fight That Did Not Break Out
questions.q: What signs did Goleman see that Tucker and Rahman used assertiveness and active listening, and why does he find that remarkable?
questions.a: Both expressed their views without blaming, name-calling or yelling, and began to face each other, make eye contact and signal that they were listening. This is remarkable because fifth-grade boys often come to blows over less, and the boys turned a possible battle into practice at conflict resolution.

questions.q: What kinds of relationship skills does Self Science teach, according to Goleman?
questions.a: It teaches being a good listener and question-asker, separating what someone says or does from your own reactions and judgments, and being assertive rather than angry or passive. It also teaches cooperation, conflict resolution and negotiating compromise.

questions.section: Emotional Literacy in the Inner City
questions.q: Why does Goleman think a lesson on naming feelings and matching them to faces matters even though it seems obvious?
questions.a: Connecting a name with a feeling and with the facial expression that matches it may serve as an antidote to common lapses in emotional literacy. Schoolyard bullies often strike out because they misread neutral expressions as hostile, and girls with eating disorders fail to tell anger from anxiety from hunger.

questions.q: How does the Child Development Project turn a discipline moment such as pushing in the lunch line into an emotional lesson?
questions.a: It treats misbehavior as a chance to teach lacking skills such as impulse control and resolving conflicts, rather than coercing. If three first graders push to be first, the teacher might have them guess a number and let the winner go first, teaching that fair, impartial ways exist and that disputes can be negotiated.

questions.q: What does David Hamburg say about the two crucial points of transition in a child’s school years?
questions.a: He sees the move into grade school and the move into junior high or middle school as crucial points. In the first, school becomes a crucible that shapes self-worth, and in the second students dip in self-confidence and suffer in social self-esteem, so building relationship skills and confidence helps most.

questions.q: How do the New Haven lessons change from first grade to ninth grade?
questions.a: In first grade children roll the feelings cube to link feelings to words; by fourth and fifth grade they learn empathy, impulse control and anger management. In sixth grade the lessons turn to pressures for sex, drugs and drinking, and by ninth grade they stress taking multiple perspectives.

questions.q: How do trained schoolyard mediators help settle a dispute?
questions.a: They sit the parties down, get them to listen without interruption or insults, have each calm down and state a position, and have each paraphrase the other. Then all try to find solutions both sides can live with, often recorded in a signed agreement, and the mediators phrase things so they seem impartial.

questions.section: Rethinking Schools: Teaching by Being, Communities That Care
questions.q: What does the New Haven teacher survey show about training and reluctance?
questions.a: When teachers first learned they would teach the new courses, 31 percent said they were reluctant. After a year of teaching them, more than 90 percent were pleased and wanted to teach them again, which suggests once teachers try, most are pleased rather than put off.

questions.q: What hurdles does Goleman expect in getting emotional-literacy programs into schools?
questions.a: Parents may feel the topic is too personal for schools, teachers may resist giving up class time or feel uncomfortable, and children may resist intrusion on their privacy. There is also the danger that slick marketers will sell ineptly designed programs, like ill-conceived courses on drugs or teen pregnancy.

questions.section: Does Emotional Literacy Make a Difference
questions.q: What is the story of Lamont, and what does Goleman take from it?
questions.a: Lamont, a popular student who enjoyed Tim Shriver’s problem-solving club, was shot nine times at twenty-six and whispered that he would use the SOCS method when he got out. He had gone to school before the social-development course existed, so Goleman says the signs point to a possible yes that such lessons might have helped, though no one can say for sure.

questions.section: Does Emotional Literacy Make a Difference
questions.q: What happened with the twelve-year-old girl and the rumor, and what does the principal’s data add?
questions.a: The girl, previously expelled for fighting, heard that another girl wanted to fight her, but asked her why she said it and no fight happened. The principal reported suspensions fell from 106 last year to 26 so far this year as the classes were phased in.

questions.section: Character, Morality, and the Arts of Democracy
questions.q: What do Etzioni, Dewey and Lickona each contribute to Goleman’s case that emotional literacy is education for character?
questions.a: Etzioni calls character the psychological muscle moral conduct requires, and says schools cultivate it through self-discipline and empathy. Dewey held that moral education is most potent in the course of real events, and Lickona says it takes will to keep emotion under the control of reason.

questions.q: Why does Goleman think the trends he cites make emotional literacy urgent?
questions.a: Juvenile violent crime is rising, teenagers have access to guns and automatic weapons, and disputes that once led to fistfights can now lead to shootings. Yet teens are poor at avoiding disputes because society has not taught handling anger, empathy or impulse control.
